descs.en: He blew open a shipping container expecting guns and found a princess. She won’t go home. She keeps coming back.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Lee Jun Hyuk goes to West Basin at midnight to kill the man who signs the papers. He blows the lock on the wrong container, expecting guns, and finds five women who have been in the dark for two days. One of them is standing between the door and the others with her hands open.

He gets them to a hospital and won’t give his name. Evangeline Lin finds him anyway. She’s the Lins’ quiet daughter, the paper twin, kept secret since she was three days old. He’s a big, kind, talkative man who hunts the people who move people, and he has a rule for everything.

She follows every rule but one. She keeps coming back.

Protector hero · He talks, she listens · Touch her and die · Complete in four volumes, plus ten side stories

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Evangeline says almost nothing in Thorns. I wanted to know what she’d say if someone waited long enough. The answer was: not much, and every word of it on purpose. So I gave her the man who talks more than anyone else in the series.

It’s a dark book in places. He has done terrible things for reasons he thinks are good, and the book doesn’t pretend otherwise. But mostly it’s about small things in dangerous rooms: towels folded in thirds, a lamp left on, a man practising a woman’s name in the shower.

He’s rich, by the way. He just never had anyone to spend it on.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers.

A dark romance with a lot of tenderness in it. It includes:

• Human trafficking, including a lorry where eleven women died

• Killings by the hero, on the page

• An infected knife wound and a high fever

• A dying man and morphine

• A photograph of a captive sold online

• An abduction attempt, a head injury and a shooting

• A man found dead in a refrigerated container

• A mother’s death in an aid station, remembered by her child

• Love scenes on the page

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
West Basin — The container terminal where it starts. Row K, the old control tower.
Nam's Noodles — Eleven tables on River Bridge Road in the border town. Phones go in a jar between the chilli oil and the soy sauce.
The karaoke flat — Two rooms over a karaoke bar that closed in 2019. Painted windows, three locks, a camp bed.
The menu — Nam's takeaway menu, taped inside the door, with his rules on the back (and two of hers).
The textile building — Eight storeys by the harbour. He owns it. Sixth floor: five windows of glass you can shoot at all day.
The window box — A steel greenhouse bolted to a twenty-centimetre ledge, behind a hatch cut into bulletproof glass.
The rabbit book — His school exercise book of names, boats and payments. There are ten in the end.
The Grey Lanterns — The border unit that took him in at eight. Old Ko's unit.
The court language — The language of the country she was born in, which is never named. She taught herself.
The heron — The gold crest on the blanket she was carried in: a heron over three peaks.
No. 9 Fig Tree Lane — The house with a real address. Thirty-one windows, and every one of them opens.
The Open Door — The foundation she starts for people who come out of boxes.
Rule seven — Don't come back.

chapters.title: The Container Had a Princess in It
chapters.desc: He went to West Basin to kill the man who signs the papers. On the way, he opens the wrong box.
chapters.epigraph: “If you want to live, stay behind me.”
chapters.content:
West Basin smelled of salt and diesel and rain that hadn’t fallen yet.

Lee Jun Hyuk had been lying on top of a forty-foot container in row K for forty-three minutes, flat on the cold corrugated steel with his jacket buttoned to the chin, and he didn’t mind. Patience was one of the few things his work had ever taught him to like. Men got careless when they were nervous. They checked their watches. They smoked down to the filter. They rang people. They gave themselves away in a hundred small ways while he lay still and watched them do it.

It was eleven forty-seven on Thursday the thirteenth of October. Below him a line of lorries crawled through the east gate under the floodlights, their headlamps sweeping the stacks and lighting up a number on a container door and moving on. Out past the cranes a ship’s horn went once, long and low.

Deputy Port Commissioner Kuang Yaoming was due at midnight.

For eleven months Kuang had been signing the manifests that let certain containers through West Basin without anybody opening them. Jun Hyuk had spent six of those months following the money, three working out whose money it was, and the last two making sure the evidence would outlive the man. Tonight was supposed to be simple. Find him. Take the ledger he kept in his tower office. Leave him there.

His phone buzzed once against his ribs. He looked at it without moving his head.

Nam: His car left the restaurant after midnight last week. Drunk man, drunk driver. He’ll come in the east gate with his lights off and think he’s clever. Come by after. There’s brisket. Don’t get shot, Ox. You owe me for a duck.

He put the phone away and almost smiled.

Then something knocked on the steel underneath him.

Three knocks. A pause. Two.

He went still.

It came again. Three. Two. Not cargo shifting, not the tick of metal cooling in the night air. A fist. On the inside of the box he was lying on.

He looked over the edge. The door at his end was sealed, new padlock, old seal. The manifest in its plastic sleeve on the door said agricultural machinery, 14,000 kg. The lorry that had dropped it that afternoon had been riding high on its springs, like a lorry carrying something much lighter than fourteen tonnes of tractors. He had noted it at four and decided it was guns. Kuang’s people moved guns too.

He slid down the end of the stack into the gap between two rows, landed without a sound, and waited.

A man came round the corner of row K in a grey hooded top, talking low into a phone, with a torch in his other hand. He looked both ways. He went to the box Jun Hyuk had been lying on and shone the torch on the seal and reached for the padlock.

“Looking for something?” said Jun Hyuk pleasantly, behind him.

The man didn’t have time to turn round. Jun Hyuk hit him once, behind the ear, and caught him by the collar before his head reached the concrete, and laid him down between two pallets like a man putting a drunk friend to bed. He went through his pockets. A phone. A ring of keys that didn’t fit the padlock. A knife. Cigarettes. He took the man’s shoelaces out of his own trainers and tied his wrists behind him with them, and then his thumbs together, which was worse.

“You’ll have a headache,” he told him, although he couldn’t hear. “You’ll live. You smoke, you did this to yourself.”

The knocking came again. And after it, something quieter.

A voice. A woman’s. Saying something he couldn’t make out through steel.

His face changed.

✦ ✦ ✦

He had a small shaped charge in the inside pocket of his jacket for exactly the kind of padlock that didn’t want to come off. He pressed it to the shackle, ran back along the row, and touched the wire.

It went with a flat crack, like a door slammed in another building, and the lock fell off in two pieces. He waited ten seconds for the sound to go wherever sounds go in a port at midnight. Nobody shouted. He walked back, put his shoulder to the bar and hauled, and the door came open on a smell that stopped him where he stood: sweat and urine and old fear, hot, a week of it, rolling out into the cold.

His mind refused to understand what he was looking at.

Five women.

They were packed into the far end of the box behind a wall of crates wrapped in plastic, on the bare boards, in what little room the crates left. A few empty water bottles. Somebody had torn a cardboard box into strips and put them under the knees of a girl whose legs were bleeding. One woman was crying without any sound at all. One, young, lay against the wall with her eyes half shut and her lips grey.

And one was standing up.

She had put herself between the door and the others. She was barefoot. Her pale dress, which had once been good, was filthy to the knee, and her dark hair had come down out of what had once been an elegant knot, with a crushed black ribbon still caught in it. There was a bruise at her temple the colour of a plum. Her wrists were raw where something had been tied too tight.

She stood in front of four women in a steel box as if she had the smallest reason to believe she could stop him.

“Don’t come in,” she said.

He didn’t move.

He was big. He knew what he looked like in a doorway: a shape against the floodlights, wide as the door. So he did what he always did with frightened people. He got down. He crouched in the doorway on his heels with both hands open and empty on his knees, where she could see them, and he started to talk.

“Hello. Hello, listen to me. I’m not with them. I’m not with anybody. I came here for something else entirely and I found you. Now I’m getting you out. That’s it. That’s the whole story.”

“That’s what the last one said.”

Her voice was hoarse. There was no confusion in it at all.

“I believe you. He’s asleep on the ground over there with his shoes off. You can look if you like.” He tipped his head at the gap. “How many of you?”

“Five.”

“Anyone hurt badly?”

She hesitated. Then she moved her head, a small movement, at the girl against the wall.

“Her.”

“What’s her name?”

The woman turned. “Nuo.” Gently. “Nuo, can you hear me?”

The girl’s eyes moved. She nodded.

“Nuo!” said Jun Hyuk. “Good name. Nuo, I’m going to get you a bottle of water the size of your head. Two bottles. I’ve got them in the truck. Promise.” He looked back up at the woman standing over them. “I need to get to her. I’m going to check she’s breathing properly, and then I’m going to carry her out. All right?”

“Tell me what you’re going to do. Before you touch her.”

He looked at her for a second. Then, without meaning to, the corner of his mouth went up.

“You’re negotiating with me?”

“I’m asking you not to touch them without saying.”

Five women in a box, one of them half dead, the men who’d put them there somewhere out in the dark, and this one was setting terms. He had spent fifteen years around men who frightened people for a living. He found her a great deal harder to frighten.

“Fair,” he said. “I’m going to come in on my knees. I’m going to put two fingers on her neck. Then I’m going to wrap her up in something warm and pick her up. That’s all.”

The woman looked at him, as if she were reading something written small on his face.

Then she stepped aside.

He went in on his knees, the way he’d said, and put two fingers on the girl’s neck. Fast and thin, but there. Her skin was cold and wet. Shock and thirst and two days of heat in a steel box; and the cut on her shin was red and swollen round the edges, which meant infection.

“She’s alive,” he said. “She needs a hospital tonight. All of you do.”

“All of us?”

“All of you.”

He pulled off the fleece he wore under his jacket and wrapped it round Nuo and lifted her. She weighed nothing. He backed out into the air with her, and turned, and the woman was already behind him, helping the others up off the boards one by one, saying something to each of them, quiet, steady, in a voice like a hand on the back of the neck.

She came last. She came to the door and stopped at the lip of it, and looked out at the port: rows and rows of stacked boxes going away into the dark, the floodlights, the cranes, the distance. He watched her look at it and saw how far away everything was.

She took one step down. Then another. Her legs went.

He caught her with his free arm before she hit the concrete. She flinched from him like a burnt hand. He let go at once.

“Easy.”

“I’m fine.”

He looked at her bare feet, and at the dark marks they’d left on the steel lip of the door.

“Course you are,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He knelt to put Nuo’s weight on his shoulder properly and pulled the radio off his belt.

“Five out of K. One bad. Get me the east road clear and keep everything else in this row shut. Nobody moves a box till I say.” He listened, and clipped it back. Then he looked at the four women standing close together in the gap between the stacks, holding each other’s arms, and the fifth in front of them.

“Who are you?” she said.

“Somebody who’s getting you out.”

“That isn’t a name.”

“No,” he agreed.

Somewhere beyond the next row, a car door shut. Then voices. Two, maybe three, coming this way, not hurrying yet.

He stood up with Nuo across his shoulders and held out his free hand to the woman in the torn dress.

“Now. One rule. It’s easy. Are you listening?”

She looked at him.

“If you want to live, stay behind me,” he said. “And don’t stop moving.”

He expected her to do as she was told. Frightened people mostly did, with him; they followed the voice. He was armed and trained and very much more able to deal with whatever came round that corner than she was.

She looked at his hand. Then she took it.

Her fingers were ice cold. And she didn’t go behind him. She came up beside him, gripping his hand hard, and turned and looked at the others.

“Hold on to each other,” she told them. “Don’t let go.”

Then, without asking him at all, she led the little chain of women out between the stacks of row K, into the dark, and he caught himself walking at her pace.

He looked down at their hands.

He had come to West Basin to kill a man. Instead he’d found a box full of women and one in a ruined dress who apparently had no intention of following instructions from anybody.

“You’d better be careful,” he said.

“Of what?”

“Me.”

She glanced up at him in the floodlight, filthy and barefoot and bruised, and gave him the smallest, most exhausted smile he’d ever seen.

“I’m not afraid of you,” she said.

He looked at her.

“No,” he said. “I noticed.”

chapters.title: Don’t Stop Moving
chapters.desc: She runs through the stacks holding a stranger’s hand while he talks the whole way. He goes up a tower for four minutes, and she counts every second of them.
chapters.epigraph: “If I’m not back in four minutes, you’re in charge. You look like you’re already in charge.”
chapters.content:
The first thing she noticed about him was that he talked too much.

They had met eleven minutes ago in a box that smelled of rust and fear. Now she was running through a shipping yard in the middle of the night with her hand in a stranger’s, five women in a chain behind her, and he hadn’t stopped talking once.

“Left here. Good. Mind the cable, Nuo’s got her eyes shut, that’s fine, I’ve got her. Big step. Good. You’re all doing brilliantly. Better than me. I’ve done this before and I’m wheezing.”

“Done this how many times?” said the woman behind her, the one whose knees were bleeding.

“Ooh. Rude. Don’t ask a man his numbers.” He swung them round a corner between two stacks so high they shut out the sky. “Don’t look at the lights. Look at the ground. The ground’s your friend. The ground has never let anyone down in its life.”

She looked at the ground. A chain lay across the concrete in the dark. She nearly went over it.

“That’s a chain, not a snake,” he said, without turning round. “You can look at it.”

She looked at the back of his head instead.

His hand stayed round hers the whole time, firm enough to keep her up, never tight enough to hurt. He moved through the stacks as if he’d laid them out himself, never once stopping to think which way, the girl called Nuo slung over his shoulder in his fleece like a rolled carpet. Behind them, a long way off, somebody was shouting. Torches swung across the ends of the rows.

“They’ve gone the wrong way,” he said. “Course they have. They went towards the noise. Amateurs.”

She didn’t know what time it was. She’d stopped knowing on Tuesday. On Tuesday morning she had gone ahead of the man who walked three steps behind her, at the flower market under the old viaduct, because the orchid sellers set out their white trays at six and she liked to see them before anyone else had touched them. She had been bending over a tray when two men in good jackets came and stood either side of her, too close, and one of them had smiled and bowed his head a little, as the people in her father’s house sometimes did when nobody else was watching, and said Your Highness.

Then a van door. A hand. A cloth that smelt of something sweet and chemical.

She had thought, at first, that it was a warning. Now, running between steel walls with her feet bleeding, she understood that it had been recognition.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stopped so she walked into his back.

“Quiet.”

An engine had started somewhere close. Close. He looked at the end of the row, and then at a line of refrigerated containers on their stands to the left, humming, their machinery throbbing above a narrow gap at ground level no higher than a man’s knee.

“In there,” he said. “On your stomachs, all the way along to the third post. It’s warm. It smells of fish and hot dust and you’ll hate it. Nobody has looked under there in the history of the world.”

They went in one by one, the women, on their elbows, into the dark under the humming boxes. He laid Nuo down at the mouth of it and the woman from the container crawled in beside her and pulled the fleece back round her shoulders.

He crouched at the gap.

“I’ve got a job to do,” he said. “It takes four minutes.”

“Four minutes is a long time.”

“It’s nothing. You can boil an egg in four minutes.” He looked along the row. “You lot stay here. Flat. Quiet. Behind the blue one at the end there’s a hole in the fence, big enough for a fat man. I know, because I’m the fat man who cut it.” He looked at her. “If I’m not back in four minutes, you’re in charge.”

“Why me?”

“You look like you’re already in charge. You might as well be.”

She didn’t answer. He could see her face in the slatted light under the containers, pale, the bruise at her temple, her eyes fixed on him.

“Four minutes,” he said. “Don’t come looking for me. I mean it.”

He held out his hand to her, palm up.

He didn’t take hers this time. He waited.

She looked at his hand, and understood what he was asking, and put her fingers in it. His thumb moved once across her knuckles. A small, absent movement. Almost nothing.

“I’ll be back,” he said.

“Promise?”

“Yes.”

Then he let go, and was gone, and the dark between the stacks closed over the place where he had been.

✦ ✦ ✦

The tower stood at the head of the yard, a glass box on legs with stairs up the outside and two lights still on at the top.

He went up the service stair at the back on the outside edges of the treads, where the metal didn’t ring. There were two men on the landing outside the door. One was looking at his phone. The other was looking at the yard, where the torches were, and he turned at the very last moment and his hand went to his belt.

Jun Hyuk was already on him. He took the hand and the wrist and the gun at the same time and turned the man into the railing and drove his head once into the steel upright, hard, and the man folded. The second one dropped his phone and opened his mouth to shout, and Jun Hyuk hit him in the throat with the side of his hand, and then, as the man doubled, behind the ear, and he went down across the first one on the landing. Neither of them had made a sound louder than a cough. It had taken less than three seconds.

He stepped over them and opened the door.

Kuang Yaoming was at the long window with a phone at his ear, watching his men’s torches go the wrong way through his yard. He was sixty-one, soft round the middle, with silver at the temples and a good watch. He turned at the sound of the door and his face was entirely blank.

Then he knew him.

“Lee,” he said.

“Commissioner.” Jun Hyuk shut the door behind him.

Kuang’s eyes went to the landing, to the two shapes on it through the glass. Then to Jun Hyuk’s hands. “Do you know who I am?”

“Unfortunately,” said Jun Hyuk. “I’ve read your manifests.”

“Whatever you’re being paid—”

“Nobody’s paying me.”

That frightened Kuang more than anything else could have. Jun Hyuk watched it go into his face. Kuang’s free hand moved, slowly, toward the drawer of the desk beside him.

“There are five women in a box in row K,” said Jun Hyuk conversationally, “who’ve been in it since Tuesday with eight bottles of water between them. Did you know that?”

“I don’t open the boxes.”

“No,” said Jun Hyuk. “You sign them.”

Kuang’s hand jerked the drawer open.

Jun Hyuk had already drawn. He fired once. The sound was enormous inside the glass. Kuang went back against the window and hung there for a second with a look of great surprise, as if someone had told him an unexpected price, and then slid down it, leaving a long red mark on the glass, and sat on the floor with the phone still in his hand and the voice on the other end saying hello? hello?

Jun Hyuk took the phone and ended the call. He went to the drawer: a pistol, which he left, and under it a black ledger, which he took. He went to the safe behind the desk, which Kuang had never once in eleven months remembered to lock when he was in the room, and took the two cloth bags on the top shelf and put them inside his shirt. He looked once at the man on the floor.

He felt nothing at all. He never did, with this kind. He’d lose no sleep tonight over Kuang Yaoming.

He went out over the two men on the landing and down the stairs on the edges of the treads.

✦ ✦ ✦

Under the containers, she had heard the shot.

It came across the yard flat and short, like a book dropped on a table. Nuo jerked beside her. The other women began whispering, high and frightened, and somebody was saying they’ve shot him, they’ve shot him, and somebody else was saying what if he doesn’t come back—

“Hush,” she said. “Hush. He said four minutes.”

She looked at her wrist. Her little watch had stopped some time on Tuesday in the van, its glass cracked, the hands at sixteen minutes past eight.

So she counted.

One. Two. Three. She thought of his face when he’d said yes. Four. Five. Six. He had looked so certain. Seven. Eight. She had known men who made promises with beautiful manners. Men who bowed their heads to her when her father wasn’t looking and talked about loyalty as if it were a family heirloom. Nine. Ten. Not one of them had ever meant it. Eleven. She wanted this one to be different. Twelve. She didn’t even know him. That was the ridiculous part. Thirteen. Fourteen.

At two hundred and forty she stopped telling herself not to.

At two hundred and fifty she crawled out from under the humming boxes, and stood up, and looked toward the tower.

“Evan—” someone hissed behind her. She didn’t turn.

At two hundred and seventy-two he came round the end of the row at a run with blood on his sleeve and a black book in his hand, and saw her standing out in the open, and stopped dead.

“What are you doing?”

“You were gone.”

“I noticed.”

“You said four minutes.”

“I was thirty-two seconds over. I had to stop for a book.” He looked at her, standing in the open between the stacks in her ruined dress, and something went across his face that she didn’t understand. “I told you not to come looking.”

“I didn’t. I stood up.”

Then her eyes went to his sleeve. “You’re bleeding.”

“It isn’t mine.”

She looked at his face, his shoulder, his hands, one after the other, as if checking that all the pieces had come back. He saw her do it. He stood still and let her.

“I’m here,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The truck was an old flatbed with a canvas tilt over the back, parked in the dark past the hole in the fence behind the blue container. There were sacks in the back, and a plastic crate of bottled water, and a folded tarpaulin.

“It’s not a limousine,” he told them, lifting Nuo in over the tailboard. “I’m sorry. The limousine’s at the cleaners. Here. Water. Little sips, Nuo, little sips, or you’ll be sick on my sacks, and I love those sacks.” He tore the plastic off the crate and handed bottles round. “I promised her one the size of her head. I’m a man of my word. Have two.”

The women laughed. She heard them do it, in the back of a truck in the middle of the night, filthy, bleeding, and she didn’t know how he’d done it.

He came round to the passenger side and opened the door. “You’re in the front.”

She looked at the cab. Then at him.

“Where are we going?”

“Harbourside General. Twenty minutes. There’s a doctor on tonight I’d trust with my own leg.”

She didn’t move. He didn’t rush her. He stood back from the door and waited, the way he’d waited with his hand out under the containers, and let her decide. After a while she climbed in.

She was shivering. She hadn’t known it until the door shut and the cab was warm and her whole body started to shake. He saw it before she did. He reached behind the seat and pulled out his jacket, the black one, heavy, smelling of rain and wood.

“Here.”

“I’m fine.”

“You’re shaking.”

“It’s cold.”

“Exactly,” he said, and put it round her.

It was far too big. The shoulders came down past her elbows. He leaned across and took the two sides of it and drew them together under her chin, and did up the buttons, one at a time, without hurrying. The first. The second. His knuckles brushed the edge of her jaw. She held her breath. He looked up, and their eyes were close in the dashboard light, and she saw how tired he was, tired the way people are tired who have stayed awake for years while everybody else slept.

“Better?”

She nodded. He did the last button and sat back.

“Good.”

He drove with one hand on the wheel and checked the mirror every eight seconds. The port fell away behind them, the stacks going small and colourless in the side mirror, and she sat inside his jacket and understood for the first time since Tuesday that she was actually leaving.

Tucked in the frame of the speedometer was a small laminated card, bent at one corner. A menu. NAM’S NOODLES, it said across the top, over a faded photograph of a bowl of noodles with a heap of spring onions on top. Underneath, in small print: 14 River Bridge Road. Open 6 a.m. And a telephone number.

“What’s that?”

He glanced at it. “Lunch.”

“You keep a menu in your car?”

“Best beef noodles on the border. Extra spring onions.” He changed down for the roundabout. “I owe the man for a duck.”

She looked at the card for nearly a minute. Nam’s Noodles. 14 River Bridge Road. Open 6 a.m. She read the number three times, and then she shut her eyes and read it again in the dark behind her eyelids. She didn’t know why. It was the first ordinary thing she’d seen since Tuesday. A noodle shop. A man who liked extra spring onions and owed somebody for a duck.

“You’ve been looking at that menu for a minute,” he said.

“I haven’t.”

“You have.”

She looked out of the window.

The hospital came up at the top of the hill, too bright for three in the morning. He pulled in short of the ambulance bay, under a broken lamp, and kept the engine running. She turned to him before he could get out.

“Who are you?”

He went quiet. It was an ordinary question. He looked at her as if she’d asked him something very much harder.

“Nobody,” he said.

He said it without any self-pity. As if he were giving his occupation.

She looked down at the jacket buttoned under her chin.

“Me too,” she said.

For the first time that night, he didn’t have an answer ready. He looked at her.

“No,” he said at last. “You’re not.”

chapters.title: He Leaves Her at a Hospital
chapters.desc: Harbourside General, three in the morning. He won’t give her his name, and he doesn’t look back. She keeps his jacket anyway.
chapters.epigraph: “I think I do.”
chapters.content:
Harbourside General was too bright for three in the morning.

He got out under the broken lamp and came round and opened her door, and then the tailboard, and lifted Nuo down in his arms, and walked her the forty metres to the ambulance bay himself while the other three women followed him in a tight little knot and the woman in his jacket walked at the back, as she had in the port, looking over her shoulder at the dark.

Under the canopy he put Nuo into the arms of a porter who had come running, and said, “Infected cut on the left shin, two days without enough water, very cold. Get the duty doctor. Tell him the big man sent her,” and the porter looked up at him, and up some more, and ran.

Then he turned to her and took a folded sheet of paper out of his back pocket.

“Give this to whoever comes. Police. Not the hospital people, the police. If there’s a detective called Song, give it to him. He’s the only one I’d—” He stopped. “Just the police.”

She took it. She didn’t open it. “What do I tell them about you?”

“Tell them a man let you out and drove you here. You didn’t see his face. It was dark. And he was very ugly.”

She looked at his face in the light from the doors.

“That bit’s true,” he said. “Go on. Inside. You’ll be warm.”

She didn’t go inside. She stood under the canopy in his jacket with the paper in her hand and looked at him.

“Your name,” she said.

He had expected it. He’d still hoped she wouldn’t ask.

“I told you.”

“You said nobody.”

“That’s the one I use.”

“Your real one.”

The doors hissed open beside them and shut again. A nurse was coming out with a wheelchair. The light over the bay hummed.

She put out her hand and caught his sleeve. Not hard. She wasn’t pulling him back. She was only holding on to a small piece of cloth, as if she needed a moment longer before she let go.

He looked at her hand on his sleeve. Then at her face. Then, for a fraction of a second, without meaning to, at her mouth.

She saw him do it. He saw that she’d seen.

“No,” he said.

“Why?”

“Because you don’t need it.”

She thought about that, quite seriously, standing there barefoot with her wrists raw. “I think I do.”

Something moved in his jaw. He looked as if he might change his mind.

Then he reached down and loosened her fingers from his sleeve, gently, one at a time.

“Get some sleep,” he said.

He didn’t say goodbye. He didn’t look back. He walked to the truck under the broken lamp and got in and drove out of the bay, and she stood under the canopy and watched his tail-lights all the way to the gate, and the nurse with the wheelchair said, “Miss? Miss, please sit down,” and she read the last three characters of his number plate in the light from the gatehouse as the truck turned out onto the hill road, and kept them.

✦ ✦ ✦

He got as far as the end of the hospital road before he stopped.

There was a convenience store on the corner opposite the main entrance, its sign flickering, the only light on the hill apart from the hospital. He parked across the road from it with the engine off and bought a bottle of water he didn’t want and sat in the cab with it.

He told himself he was waiting for confirmation that her family had come. That was reasonable. He’d brought her in. It was reasonable to see somebody take over.

He took a cigarette out of the packet in the door and held it between his fingers and didn’t light it. He’d given them up years ago. On bad nights his hand still went for them.

Through the glass doors of the emergency department he could see the reception desk, a row of plastic chairs, a television high in the corner playing to nobody.

A nurse came out with a clipboard. A taxi came and went. Two men went in. Ten minutes. Then fifteen.

Then he saw her. They had moved her out of a cubicle into a wheelchair by the desk, and she was sitting in it straight, with her hair tied back now and her face washed, and she wasn’t wearing the hospital’s thin blue blanket. She was wearing his jacket, buttoned to the chin, the sleeves pushed up to her wrists, and she was holding the folded paper in both hands in her lap.

He put his forehead on the steering wheel and laughed, once.

“Unbelievable.”

He took out his phone. He could ring the duty doctor and ask whether she’d eaten anything. He could ask somebody to give her a blanket she’d actually use.

He put the phone face down on the passenger seat instead, and watched the doors.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father’s voice reached her before he did.

“Where is she? Where is my daughter?”

Lin Jian came through the doors with his coat buttoned on the wrong buttons and his grey hair standing up and his reading glasses still in his breast pocket, and a nurse trying to stop him, and stopped by himself in the middle of the floor, and saw her.

“Evangeline.”

He crossed the room in four strides and put his arms round her in the wheelchair so hard that she felt his whole body shaking against hers.

“Oh, God. Oh, God, oh, God.”

“Papa.”

He drew back far enough to look at her and his hands went over her face, her hair, her shoulders, her bandaged wrists, as if to be certain all of her was there.

“Did they hurt you? Where were you? Why didn’t you—” His voice broke, and stopped.

She stared at him. She had never in her life seen her father cry. Not at Mama’s funeral, when she was four and he’d stood at the grave in the black suit he still wore to everything that mattered. Not when the business nearly went under, not in the front room on the day in June last year when he’d sat the five of them down and told them, in his flat careful voice, what she was and where she’d come from and what he’d been paid to do with her when she was three days old.

He was crying now. He didn’t try to stop.

“I’m sorry,” he said. “I’m sorry.”

She put her face in his shoulder, in his wrongly buttoned coat, and held on.

Behind him Raiden had come in, in a black windbreaker over a T-shirt, his hair wet as if he’d come straight out of a shower, his round glasses fogged from the cold. He’d been ringing every hospital in the district since midnight, when a man who wouldn’t give his name had telephoned the house and said Harbourside, the emergency doors, before three.

“Princess,” he said, and tried to smile, and couldn’t.

“You scared the hell out of us,” he said instead, and crouched beside the chair. His eyes went to her wrists and something cold came into his face.

“Who did this?”

“I don’t know.”

“Not now,” said Lin Jian without letting go of her. “Not now, son.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Within a quarter of an hour the emergency department was full of Lins.

Elowen came in a long dark coat thrown over her nightdress with her hair down, and went straight to her knees in front of the chair and took both her hands. “Oh, darling. Look at you.” Her voice shook. “Have you eaten? Of course you haven’t.” She turned to the nurses’ station like a general. “Can she eat?”

Eliana came behind her in an enormous hoodie with her glasses crooked, and stood with both hands over her mouth, and when Evangeline looked at her she burst into tears and put her arms round her carefully, as if she might break.

And Zhao Zhendong came last, in a beige suit at four in the morning with the collar open and the rings on his hands and one strand of black hair down over his forehead, and he didn’t go to the chair at all. He went to Raiden.

“Where?”

“West Basin. Row K. A container.”

“Who brought her in?”

“A man. He left.”

“Name?”

Raiden looked at Evangeline. She looked at the folded paper in her lap.

Zhao turned to the man who had come in at his shoulder, big, shaved head, a scar through one eyebrow, as still as furniture. “Bao. I want every van that went in or out of West Basin since Tuesday morning. Port cameras, road cameras, the petrol station on the ring road, everything. Then I want the van from the flower market. Then I want the men in it.” His voice was perfectly pleasant, which was what made Eliana stop crying. “I don’t care how far it goes.”

Bao went.

Zhao looked down at Evangeline at last, at the black jacket buttoned to her chin, and his narrow eyes went narrower.

“Whose is that?”

“The man who found us.”

“He gave you his jacket?”

“Yes.”

“And left.”

“Yes.”

“Did he tell you where?”

“No.”

“Did he give you a number? A name?”

She shook her head.

Raiden stared at her. “You don’t know how to find the man who saved your life?”

She said nothing. She pulled the jacket closer.

“We’ll find him,” said Zhao.

“Why?” It came out of her so fast that everyone looked round. She lowered her eyes. “I mean. Why do you need to?”

“Because he’s a witness,” said Zhao, watching her face. “And because we owe him.” He paused. “And because I’d like to know who in this city walks into West Basin at midnight and walks out again.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The detective came at ten to four.

He was young, not more than twenty-seven, still, in a black coat with rain on the shoulders, with dark hair falling over deep-set eyes and the face of a man who had already read the first report in the car and disliked everything in it. He introduced himself to Lin Jian, and to Zhao, whom he looked at longer, and then he came and pulled a plastic chair round and sat down in front of her so that his head was lower than hers.

“Miss Lin. I’m Detective Song. I’m sorry. I know you’ve had the worst night of your life. I won’t keep you long.”

“Is this necessary now?” said Lin Jian.

“No, sir. But there are some things that are easier while they’re fresh.”

“It’s all right, Papa,” she said.

Song took out a notebook. Where had she been taken? The flower market under the viaduct, Tuesday, a little after six, before the stalls had opened properly. She’d gone ahead of her security to look at the orchids. Two men. A van. A cloth.

“Did they say anything to you?”

She looked at the floor. “Your Highness.”

The emergency department went quiet. Elowen’s hand tightened on hers.

Song’s pen stopped. “They called you that?”

“Yes.”

“Did they know who you were?”

She looked at her father. Lin Jian’s face had gone grey.

“Yes,” she said.

Song wrote. “Can you describe them?”

The hands she could remember. The smell inside the van. A man’s watch, gold, too big for his wrist. A voice. She could remember voices better than faces. “One was tall.”

“Anything else?”

“No.”

“And the man who let you out?”

“He was tall too.”

Song looked at her without writing anything. Then he wrote one word.

She held out the folded paper. “He said to give you this. Only you.”

Song unfolded it. It was a page torn out of a ledger: dates, container numbers, amounts, a column of initials, and at the bottom, in a different hand, in pencil, small and square: K.Y.M. — signed out every box on this page. Tower, West Basin. You’ll find the rest of the book on his desk if I don’t take it, and I’m taking it. Ask about Silver Star Employment.

Underneath that, the women’s names, all five, in the same square pencil, the last one left blank.

Song read it twice. His face didn’t change at all, except at the corner of his mouth.

“Did he say who he was?”

“No.”

“Did you see where he went?”

“It was dark,” she said.

Song folded the page and put it inside his coat and stood up.

“Thank you, Miss Lin. We’ll speak again when you’ve slept.” He nodded to her father, and to Zhao, and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

She wasn’t asleep when they talked outside the cubicle. Elowen had dozed off in the chair beside her with her head on her own arm. Eliana had gone for water. The curtain didn’t close properly.

“They knew who she was,” her father was saying, low. “They used the word. Highness. They knew before they took her.”

“Then somebody told them.” Zhao’s voice.

“Somebody who knew. Somebody who knew her schedule, her security, the market, that she’d go ahead of her man to look at the orchids.” A long breath. “Whoever did this knew exactly whose daughter she was. Not mine. His.”

She lay still under the thin blanket with his jacket on top of it.

Not random. They’d known. They had called her by the title of a man she had never met, in a country she had never seen, and put her in a box and shipped her like something to be sold.

She turned her face into the collar of the jacket. Clean soap, something woody, rain.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four thirty-seven, across the road, Lee Jun Hyuk watched a black sedan and then another pull up under the canopy, and a big man with a shaved head get out of the second and stand by the door looking at the road, and he started his engine.

He knew Zhao Zhendong’s man when he saw him. He knew then whose house she belonged to.

He drove north. Three hours, to a town on the river where the border ran down the middle of the water, and nobody asked anybody where they’d been.

It was only when he got there, at twenty to eight, and reached for his jacket to go into Nam’s, that he remembered.

“Keep it, then,” he said to nobody, and went in without it.

chapters.title: She Does Not Go Home
chapters.desc: Her father sends a car to the hospital, and for the first time in her life she sends it back. Then, before dawn, she asks Zhao Zhendong one question.
chapters.epigraph: “No.”
chapters.content:
The car was waiting under the canopy at twenty past seven: her father’s long black saloon, washed that morning, with two of his men beside it, one holding the back door open and one speaking into his phone. It was the kind of arrangement she’d grown up inside. A car arrived before she needed one. Somebody opened the door. Somebody knew where she was going before she’d said. Somebody walked three steps behind her looking at the people she never had to look at twice.

It had always been normal. Until this morning.

“Miss Evangeline. Your father’s had your room aired. Two men on the door, three on the street. Nobody will come near you.”

She was sitting on the edge of a hospital bed in a white blouse and loose trousers that Elowen had brought, with clean dressings on her wrists and a smaller one at her temple. The black jacket lay folded on the chair beside her.

The house with the high walls, she thought. The gates that opened on their own. The men who knew her timetable. The staff who would smile when she came in and not notice if she’d been crying. The house in which somebody had known that on Tuesday mornings she walked ahead to the orchid trays.

“No,” she said.

The man at the door looked at the nurse. “I’m sorry, miss?”

“I don’t want to go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father came twenty minutes later in a clean shirt, still looking as if he hadn’t slept, with his reading glasses in his breast pocket and his phone in his hand, and his face softened the moment he saw her.

“Sweetheart. How’s your head?”

“Better.”

“Then let’s get you home. You can rest there.” He reached for the jacket on the chair. “Give that to the driver, he’ll put it in the car—”

Her hand closed on it. “No.”

He stopped.

“I’m keeping it.”

“All right. Keep it.” He didn’t ask. He held out his hand instead. “Come on. The car’s here.”

She looked at his hand. Then past him at the glass doors and the black car outside them, and she remembered the van. The smell inside it. The hands. The man who’d smiled and bowed his head.

“I’m not coming home, Papa.”

His face changed. “Why?”

She couldn’t explain it. Because the house was meant to be the safe place, and someone had known where she would be. Because every room she knew now had a door in it that somebody else might be watching.

“I just don’t.”

“The doctor’s cleared you. Your room’s ready. Elowen’s arranged everything, there’ll be your own men, and—”

“Papa.” She looked at him. “No.”

It was a small word. Not loud, not angry. But Lin Jian stood in the middle of the room and looked at her as if she’d hit him. In twenty-four years she had never once said it to him like that.

He sat down slowly on the bed beside her.

“All right,” he said. “Tell me what you want.”

“I don’t know.”

“Do you want to stay here?”

“No.”

“Then where?”

“I don’t know.”

He nodded, slowly, rubbing his palms together the way he did when the numbers wouldn’t come out. “Then we don’t decide this morning.” He looked at her. “I’m not angry with you. Is that what you think? Sweetheart. I’m only glad you’re here.”

He took her hand, careful of the bandage, and bent his head over it and pressed it against his forehead. She felt something warm land on her knuckles. Her father was crying again. He had taught her that some things were better handled; that you didn’t need to raise your voice to be heard; that nobody could give you dignity or take it away. And he was sitting on a hospital bed holding her hand to his forehead, crying as if he’d run out of ways to stay in one piece.

“I should have known,” he said. “Someone was watching you, and I didn’t see.”

“You couldn’t have.”

“I should have.” He lifted his head. “There’s something you have to know. The detective told me in the car park at five.” He took a breath. “Do you remember Feng?”

She did. Feng had worked for her father for years, in the black jacket, always near a door. He’d been in prison since the June before last. Song Wei Long had put him there.

“Somebody went to see him in prison this summer,” said her father. “Paid him. And he told them what I told the five of you in the front room last year. He’d known it for twenty-four years. He drove the car the night I brought you home. Who your mother was. Who your father was. Where I put you, and why. Everything.” His jaw tightened. “And the man who bought it from him sold you.”

She stared at him.

“Sold me.”

“To the people with the box. As what you are. Not as a girl from a good family. As a king’s daughter. With a price to match.” His voice had gone cold, and quiet. “I’m going to find every one of them. Every man who bought it, every man who arranged it, every man who knew and said nothing.”

She looked down at her bandaged wrists.

“He brought me a cake once,” she said. “Feng. When I had a fever. Strawberry, because he knew I liked it.”

Her father had no answer to that. That was the worst part.

“I don’t want to be sold again,” she said. “I don’t want anybody deciding where I go. I don’t want somebody knowing where I am before I do.”

He put his arms round her.

“Then you won’t go home,” he said. And this time there was no hesitation in it at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the afternoon it was arranged. She would stay with Elowen and Zhao, in the house on the hill, behind the gates and the dogs and Zhao’s men, a long way from her father’s routines. Her father wanted to stay with her too. She asked him not to. Not because she didn’t want him; because she couldn’t watch him blame himself every time she shut her eyes.

When it was settled he sat by her one more time.

“Can I hug you?” he said.

She hadn’t known that question could hurt so much. She moved into his arms. He held her carefully, away from the wrists.

“I love you,” he said into her hair.

“I love you too, Papa.”

At the lift he turned round. She lifted her hand. He smiled at her, a small cracked smile, and the doors closed on it.

Elowen drove her up the hill herself in the shop van, with a bucket of eucalyptus rattling in the back and Zhao following in the black car three metres behind.

“If he rear-ends us,” said Elowen, glaring at the mirror, “I’m divorcing him.”

Evangeline looked at her.

“Don’t laugh. I mean it. I’ll pull over and divorce him on the hard shoulder.” She reached across and squeezed her hand without taking her eyes off the road. “Stay as long as you like. Forever, if you want. Zhendong won’t mind. He’ll pretend to mind. He’s never minded anything I wanted.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The room Elowen had made ready was on the first floor over the garden: a reading lamp, clean sheets, a table by the window, a jar of white anemones, and nothing that belonged to anyone else.

“I brought your things,” Elowen said. “Raiden fetched them. Your brush, your charger, some clothes.” She looked at the jacket over Evangeline’s arm. “Is that the one?”

“Yes.”

“Shall I have it cleaned?”

“No.” Too quickly. “Not yet.”

“All right,” said Elowen. “Not yet.”

At nine that night Zhao knocked twice and came in with two cups of tea and sat in the chair by the window, his long legs crossed, the rings catching the lamp.

“Elowen says you’ve had three spoons of rice since Tuesday.”

“Four.”

He let that go. He talked about the dogs, and the garden, and the doctor who’d come in the morning. He didn’t ask about the box. Then his eyes went to the jacket over the back of her chair.

“Did he tell you his name?”

“No.”

“What he does?”

“No.”

He turned his cup. “There’s a man on the border,” he said. “Up at the river, where it runs between two countries and nobody owns the water. Nobody knows his name. Some people say he was a soldier. Some say he’s a hired man who got tired of being hired. Big. Talks a great deal, they say, which is unusual in that line of work.” He drank. “He’s killed four men in five years that I know of. A customs officer. A man who ran boats on the river. A man who ran lorries on the river road. All of them men who moved people. And last night, a deputy port commissioner, in his own tower at West Basin, with one shot.”

She didn’t move.

“They weren’t good men, the ones he’s killed. I did business with two of them, once, a long time ago, before I knew what else they carried.” Zhao looked at her steadily. “He’d kill me one day too, I think, if he thought he had reason. He doesn’t like men like me.”

“Why are you telling me?”

“Because you asked me four questions without asking any.” He stood up. “Stay away from that world, Evangeline. Men like that don’t have ordinary lives. Whatever good they do, they live where violence is the language. And people who get close to them don’t get to choose when they leave.” At the door he stopped. “Don’t mistake somebody dangerous for somebody safe because he was kind to you once.”

“I won’t,” she said.

He looked at her a moment longer, as if he didn’t believe her either, and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

Song came on the Monday with a recorder and a notebook and took her through it from the beginning, slowly, at the kitchen table, with Elowen beside her. The flower market. The van. The two days in the dark. Nuo. The water running out. The men’s voices through the steel. The name she’d heard through the wall, Kuang, and the word tower.

“And the man who opened the container?”

“Tall,” she said.

“How tall?”

“Taller than most people.”

“Age?”

“Older than me.”

“Hair? Eyes? Anything you’d know him by?”

She thought of the small cut at his eyebrow. The way he’d crouched in the doorway with his hands on his knees. His thumb across her knuckles.

“It was dark,” she said.

Song looked at her. Then he closed his notebook.

“We’ll need to talk to him,” he said. “Eventually.”

“Will you find him?”

“I expect,” said Song, “he’ll find me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The nights were the worst. She woke at two or three with the certainty that she’d heard a steel door close. Some nights her hands shook too much to hold the glass of water by the bed. Elowen never asked why. She just woke, from across the landing, and put the lamp on and came and sat with her until the room was a room again.

On the fourth day she ate breakfast without being told. On the fifth she walked round the garden with the dogs. On the sixth she watched a film with Eliana that neither of them liked, and they laughed at it, and for two hours nobody said the word container.

She slept every night with the black jacket over the blanket.

On the seventh day she washed it herself, in the basin in her bathroom, with Elowen’s mild soap. Before she put it in the water she went through the pockets. A diesel receipt, crumpled soft, from a petrol station on the river road, the eighth of October, a time at the top: 06:12. And a boiled sweet in a twist of paper, lemon.

She put the receipt in the drawer of her bedside table. She ate the sweet.

On the eighth day Raiden brought her a new phone. “Only Papa and Elowen and Zhao and I have the number. You can use it normally. Within reason. No going out alone.”

“All right.”

He didn’t believe her. She could tell. On his way out she asked him, as if it had just come into her head, how long the bus took to the river.

He stopped with his hand on the door. “Which river?”

“The border one.”

“Three hours. Why?”

“No reason.”

“Evangeline. Don’t.”

“I haven’t thought of anything.”

“That,” said Raiden, “is what worries me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At eighteen minutes past five on Monday morning, the tenth day, she sat on the edge of her bed fully dressed in a pale blue jumper and dark trousers and flat shoes, with her hair tied back in a black ribbon and a canvas bag at her feet with the jacket folded inside it, and a bottle of water, and her phone, and money.

Zhao’s men changed shift at half past five. Elowen slept till seven.

She knew it wasn’t clever. She knew Raiden would be furious and Zhao would be worse. But for ten days she’d been told to rest and stay inside and wait for the police and let other people decide what happened next, and she found she couldn’t do it for one more day. She didn’t want to be anybody’s princess. Not this morning. She wanted to be a person who could get on a bus without explaining herself to anyone. And, if she was honest, she wanted to know whether the noodles were as good as he’d said.

She didn’t expect to find him. She only wanted to try.

At five thirty-one the guard on the pedestrian gate turned to say something to the man relieving him, and she went through it, and down the hill, and nobody called her name.

At the bottom, a woman was putting buckets of white chrysanthemums out in front of a flower stall. Evangeline stopped. Her chest went tight. She stood there and looked at the flowers until it passed.

She didn’t want to be afraid of flowers.

The six o’clock bus north was nearly empty. The driver didn’t know her father. He didn’t know where she’d been eleven days ago. He didn’t know that the woman who sat by the window halfway down had been in a steel box at West Basin. He gave her a ticket.

“Where to?”

“River Bridge Road.”

“End of the line, then,” he said.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Kept Showing Up
chapters.desc: Three days at a corner table in a noodle shop by the river bridge, two bowls every time. On the fourth day he comes in out of the rain and sits down at the cold one.
chapters.epigraph: “She orders two bowls. Every time. One for her and one that goes cold. I’ve stopped charging her for the cold one.”
chapters.content:
Nam’s Noodles was a narrow shop at the town end of River Bridge Road, with eleven tables, a jar for phones between the chilli oil and the soy sauce, a steamed-up window, a radio on the shelf over the counter and a pot of broth on the back burner that hadn’t, as far as anybody knew, been allowed to go cold since 1991. The bridge ran away past the window into a white mist, and somewhere in the middle of the mist the river stopped being one country and became another.

Nam was seventy, bald, with forearms like a stevedore’s and a dish towel over one shoulder, and on Monday the twenty-fourth of October at ten past nine a young woman he had never seen before came in out of the cold with a canvas bag and sat at the table in the window and asked, politely, for the beef noodles.

“Extra spring onions?” said Nam.

She looked up at him with something like alarm. “Yes. How did you know?”

“Everybody who knows to ask for the beef asks for extra spring onions.” He wrote it down. “Anything else?”

“Another one. The same.”

“Somebody coming?”

She looked at the door. “Maybe.”

He brought two bowls. She ate one slowly, looking at the door each time the bell over it rang: a lorry driver, an old man for a coffee, a woman with a sleeping child on her back. The second bowl sat across the table from her until the broth went still and grew a skin. At twenty past two she asked him to pack it, and paid for both, and thanked him, and walked to the bus stand with it in a paper bag, and got on the half-past-two bus south.

On Tuesday she came in at four minutes past nine and ordered two bowls.

On Wednesday at nine sharp, two bowls.

By then the whole of River Bridge Road knew about the girl in the window. The man from the hardware shop came in to look at her. The two old women from the pharmacy came in together for a tea neither of them wanted. Nam told them all to mind their own business, and then minded it for them.

“Lots of big men eat here,” he said to her on Wednesday, putting down the second bowl.

She looked at him.

“Lots,” said Nam. “Fishermen. Lorry men. Soldiers off the other bank when they think nobody’s counting. If you’re waiting for a big man, I’ve got a good selection.” He wiped the table that didn’t need wiping. “There’s one who owes me for a duck. If you see him.”

Her face went still and careful. “What does he look like?”

“Big,” said Nam. “Talks.”

She lowered her eyes to the bowl. But he’d seen it, and he went back behind the counter and stood with his hands flat on it, and thought about telephones.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday it poured. Not rain. Weather. It came down the river in grey sheets and turned River Bridge Road into a brown stream and set every gutter in town roaring, and the bus from the south came in forty minutes late with its wipers going like a heartbeat.

She came in at ten to ten, soaked to the knee, with her hair coming down out of its ribbon, and sat in the window and ordered two bowls.

At twenty to eleven the door banged open on its bell so hard the bell came off.

“Nam.”

The big man stood in the doorway with the rain coming in round him, water running off his hair and down his face and soaking his shirt black at the shoulders, and his expression so thoroughly furious that the old man at the corner table got up and left without finishing his coffee.

“Coffee,” said the big man. “Black. And then you and I—”

He stopped.

He’d seen the table in the window.

She sat still with her chopsticks in her hand. He looked at her. At the two bowls, one empty, one cold. At her again.

He turned slowly to Nam.

“How long?”

“How long what?” said Nam, polishing a glass.

“Don’t.”

“She orders two bowls,” said Nam, without looking up. “Every time. One for her and one that goes cold. I’ve stopped charging her for the cold one.”

“How long, Nam?”

“Four days,” said Nam. “Three hours each way on the bus. A heron that’s decided to stand in your river till you give it a fish.” He put the glass down. “I rang you on Tuesday. You didn’t pick up.”

“I was across the water. On Tuesday.” The big man looked at the girl again. Then he crossed the shop in four strides with water running off him and stood over her table.

“Good morning,” she said.

“Get up.”

Her face fell. “What?”

“Get up. No. Don’t. Sit there.” He pulled out the chair opposite her, the one with the cold bowl in front of it, and sat in it so hard the legs shrieked on the tiles. He leaned across the table and lowered his voice and it came out anyway like a man shouting in a cupboard.

“Do you have any idea what this is? Any idea at all? You don’t know what this place is. You don’t know who I am. I’m not a nice man. You think I’m nice because I gave you a bottle of water. I was at West Basin for a reason, and you know what the reason was, you heard it. Didn’t you? You heard it. And you got on a bus anyway, on your own, three hours, to a town where people go missing for a living.” He put both hands flat on the table. “And you have been sitting in a window, for four days, where anybody on that bridge can see you, with your face, with that face, while a man who sells girls like you to men across that river eats his lunch two doors down at the dumpling place on Tuesdays and Fridays—”

“I didn’t know that,” she said.

“No! Of course you didn’t!”

She looked at him, quite steadily.

“I thought you might come,” she said.

He stared at her. Water dripped off the end of his nose onto the table.

“That’s not a reason.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

She had spent three hours on a bus every morning for four days rehearsing explanations, and they had all been ridiculous, so she gave him the true one.

“Because you said you liked the noodles,” she said.

The shop was quiet. The rain hammered on the window.

He looked at the cold bowl in front of him. Then at her.

“You came three hours on a bus,” he said slowly, “four days running, and ordered two breakfasts, and sat in a window, because I mentioned a noodle shop.”

She thought about it honestly. “Yes.”

He rubbed both hands down his wet face. “Unbelievable.”

“Are you angry?”

“What do you think?”

“A little?”

“A little.” He laughed once, without any humour in it at all.

Then he picked up the chopsticks on his side of the table, and pulled the cold bowl towards him, and began to eat it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nam brought him coffee, and a hot bowl to replace the cold one, and took the cold one away, and he ate both. He didn’t seem pleased to be there. His wet shirt stuck to his shoulders. There was a crease between his eyebrows like a cut. But he was eating, and she found she was smiling at her bowl and couldn’t stop.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re smiling.”

“Am I not allowed?”

“Not while you’re being shouted at.”

She lowered her face so he wouldn’t see. Then she reached into the canvas bag beside her chair and took out his jacket.

It was clean. It had been washed by hand and dried flat and folded into a perfect square, and all the buttons were done up.

He looked at it.

“You came three hours on a bus to give me back a jacket,” he said.

“Four days,” said Nam, from the counter.

“Nam.”

“Yes.”

He took it. He ran his thumb along the sleeve. He’d worn that jacket through rain and dust and worse places than either of them would ever say out loud, and she’d washed it as if it were made of something that could break.

“Thank you,” he said.

“You’re welcome.”

“Now we’re even. You’ve given back the jacket. I’ve—” He made a small movement with one hand. “We’re done.”

She looked at him. Then at the jacket. Then at him again.

“That isn’t how it works,” she said.

“No?”

“No. You still owe me breakfast. And your name.”

He looked at her across the table.

“You first,” he said. “Your real one. Not nobody.”

She was quiet. Then she said it.

“Evangeline.”

He sat back. He said it under his breath to himself, the whole of it, all four syllables, as if feeling the shape of something heavy in his hand.

“That’s not a name,” he said at last. “That’s a sentence.”

“Lin,” she said. “Evangeline Lin.”

He’d guessed the Lin at the hospital, when Zhao Zhendong’s man got out of the second car. He hadn’t known the rest. Evangeline. He thought she was the only person he’d ever met who looked exactly as long as her name.

“And yours?” she said.

“Eat your noodles.”

“That isn’t fair.”

“Nothing’s fair,” he said. “Eat.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He stopped eating with the chopsticks halfway to his mouth.

“Don’t turn round.”

She didn’t.

“Two men in a silver car across the road, outside the pharmacy. They’ve been watching this window since I sat down. Engine running so the windscreen doesn’t steam. Know them?”

She lifted her eyes to the window and looked at the reflection in it, not through it. A silver saloon. A man in the passenger seat with his collar up. She knew the shape of his head.

“My father’s,” she said. “Uncle Mok. He drove me to school for twelve years.”

“How long has he been following you?”

“I don’t know.”

“You don’t know?”

“They’re usually further back.”

“Usually.” He put the chopsticks down gently, which was worse than if he’d thrown them. “So your father’s men followed you here. Which means anybody who follows your father’s men followed you here. Which means the man from the dumpling place has had four days to look at you.” He stood up. “Through the kitchen. Don’t look at the window.”

“Where?”

“Somewhere that isn’t here.”

“Will you tell me where?”

“Eventually.”

He held out his hand. This time he didn’t have to wait at all.

Nam was at the kitchen door as they went through, between the steaming pots and the back step and the rain.

“Ox,” he said.

“Busy.”

Nam looked at the girl, and at the two hands, and his eyebrows went up into the place where his hair used to be.

“Ah,” he said.

“Don’t.”

“Usual table tomorrow?”

“Absolutely not.”

“Goodbye, Nam,” said Evangeline over her shoulder.

“Mind how you go, little heron,” said Nam.

✦ ✦ ✦

The karaoke bar was three streets back from the river, up a stair at the side of a building whose ground floor had been a bank and was now nothing. The sign over the street door said GOLDEN NIGHTINGALE — PRIVATE ROOMS — LATE, with half the bulbs gone. He let them in at a side door with a key and took her up a staircase that smelled of dust and old smoke, past a corridor of dark rooms with dead screens in them, closed since 2019, to a door at the far end that had three locks.

Inside was one room, and a smaller one through a sliding door: a sofa, a narrow counter with a kettle, a table, a camp bed, and two windows painted over from the inside, grey, so that no light went out. It was bare and scrupulously tidy. A folded blanket. Bottles of water. A first-aid box. Nothing on the walls.

“This is your house?”

“Not exactly.”

“Whose, then?”

“Mine when I need it.” He took his watch off and put it on the table, face down. “Sit.”

She sat on the sofa. He filled a glass at the tap and gave it to her and leaned on the counter with his arms folded and watched her drink it.

“Why?” he said. “Really.”

“Because you left. At the hospital. You didn’t say where. I didn’t know where else to look.” She held the glass in both hands. “And then you didn’t come on Monday. Or Tuesday. Or Wednesday.”

“I was across the river.”

“I know that now.”

“You don’t know anything,” he said, and then, more, “I’m listening.”

“That’s all,” she said. “I wanted to see you.”

He didn’t say anything.

“You’re not going to look for me any more,” he said finally. “I’m going to put you on the morning bus and you’re going to go home to your sister’s, and you’re not going to come back.”

She looked at him over the glass, and didn’t say anything at all, and he knew perfectly well what that meant.

He gave her the room with the camp bed and a clean shirt of his to sleep in, and sent Nam a message to send two bowls of broth up the back stair with the boy, and texted nobody, and sat on the sofa in the dark with a thin line of the river’s lights showing where the paint on the window had chipped and the jacket she’d washed folded beside him.

At midnight he went to the sliding door.

She was lying on her side on the camp bed in his shirt with the blanket pulled up, her hair loose on the pillow, one hand lying palm up on the blanket beside her face. The dressings on her wrists were new. Under them the skin was still purple.

He crouched beside the bed.

He looked at her open hand. He remembered the first time she’d taken his: not because he’d offered it, because she’d chosen to. His own hand moved. It hovered over hers, a few centimetres away. He could have touched her. She’d probably not have woken.

He took his hand back. He had no business making himself comfortable in her life. Not with the life he had.

He stood up and turned to go.

“You can,” she said in the dark.

He stopped. She hadn’t moved. Her eyes were open. They had been open, he realised, the whole time.

He stood in the doorway. Then he pulled the blanket up over her open hand and tucked it in, and said, “Sleep,” in a voice he didn’t recognise, and went back to the sofa, and didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning he put her on the seven o’clock bus south at the stand by the bridge, with her bag and a paper cup of Nam’s broth, and stood on the kerb with one hand in his pocket while it pulled away. She looked at him through the steamed window. He lifted two fingers. Not quite a wave.

Then he went back for the truck, and followed the bus.

Three hours. Far enough back that she wouldn’t see. He watched her get off at the bottom of the hill road. He watched her walk up it. He watched Zhao’s man open the gate for her with a face like thunder.

He told himself it was the last time.

On Sunday she was back at Nam’s at nine with a flask of soup she’d made in Elowen’s kitchen, and Nam took a small brass key on a blue plastic tag out of the till and put it beside her cup.

“Back door,” he said. “For if it’s raining and I’m late opening. Lock it after you.”

“Why are you giving me this?”

“Because you’ll come anyway,” said Nam. “And I’d rather you came in the back than sat in the window.”

She came every Sunday after that. And every Sunday, three hours behind her bus home, a big man in a flatbed truck followed it down the river road, all the way to the bottom of the hill, and watched her walk up to the gate, and turned round.

He never once told her. It had become a habit before he noticed it was one.

chapters.title: He Does Not Own Towels
chapters.desc: He dries himself with yesterday’s T-shirt, so she brings him three white towels. On a Sunday she catches him folding them wrong, and he asks if he can kiss her.
chapters.epigraph: “You own something, you have to go back for it. Old Ko said that. Old Ko owned one spoon.”
chapters.content:
The flower market under the old viaduct opened at six, and on Tuesday the eighth of November, at ten to six, Evangeline Lin was standing at the end of it with her hands in her coat pockets, not going in.

It was where they’d taken her. The orchid man’s trays were where they’d always been, white and green under the striplights, and the smell was the same, wet earth and cut stems and the diesel from the vans backing in. She had come every Tuesday and Saturday since she was sixteen. She hadn’t been back in four weeks.

She told herself to walk. Her feet didn’t.

“Tuesdays and Saturdays,” said a voice beside her, low. “On your own. Before it’s light.”

She didn’t jump. Afterwards she was proud of that.

He was leaning on a pillar of the viaduct in his black jacket with a paper cup in his hand, as if he’d been there all night, which, from his face, he might have been.

“How do you know?”

“Nam told me. Don’t be cross with Nam. Nam tells me everything, it’s his only hobby.” He looked down the market at the trays. “This is where.”

“Yes.”

“You don’t have to go in.”

“I want to.”

“Then not on your own.” He pushed himself off the pillar. “I’ll be here. Tuesdays and Saturdays. I’ll stand by the orchids and look at vans. You won’t even know I’m here.”

“You’re three hours away.”

“There’s a road,” he said. “It goes both directions.”

She walked into the market. He walked three steps behind her, on the side where the vans were. She bent over the white trays the way she always had. He stood at her shoulder and looked at every van that came in, and every man who got out of one, and every man who looked at her for more than a second, and one man, a florist’s driver with a cigarette, he looked at for so long that the man put his cigarette out and got back in his van and left.

She didn’t buy anything that morning. Her hands were shaking too much. But she went in, and walked to the end, and walked out, and he walked her to the bus stop at the bottom of the hill road and stood there until she was on it.

On Saturday she bought a single stem. On the Tuesday after, two. He was by the pillar every time before she got there, with his paper cup, and never once said good morning first.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Saturday in November she stood in front of the orchid man’s trays.

There was a whole tray of them that morning, twenty-four pots of a small pure white moth orchid that she’d never seen him bring before, each flower like a folded letter. She looked at them for so long that the orchid man came out from behind his trestle and asked if she was all right, and she said yes, and chose one, and paid, and turned round with it in her hands.

He was holding the tray.

The whole tray. Twenty-four pots in a black plastic flat, propped against his chest. The orchid man was counting notes.

“I only wanted one,” she said.

“You didn’t say you wanted one. You didn’t say anything. You looked at them.” He shifted the tray. “You looked at that tray for about a year. I was watching.”

“Bodyguards don’t buy the tray.”

“I’m not a bodyguard,” he said. “Go on. Your arms’ll fall off.”

He carried it up the hill road from the bus stop to the gate of the house on the hill, all twenty-four pots, eleven minutes uphill, without putting it down once, while she walked beside him with her one orchid and Zhao’s man watched them come from the gatehouse with an expression of profound disbelief. At the gate he put the tray into the man’s arms without a word, and nodded to her, and walked back down the hill.

Elowen put them on every windowsill in the house. Evangeline kept hers by her bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sundays she went north.

She let herself into Nam’s by the back door with the brass key at nine, and ate with Nam in the kitchen if the big man hadn’t come down, and if he had, they ate at the window table and then went up the side stair of the Golden Nightingale to the room with three locks. He never asked her to. He never told her not to. She came anyway, and the room began, slowly, to change.

A proper kettle. Two mugs that matched. A cushion for the sofa. A second blanket. A jar of honey from the hill village. A small pot plant on the painted windowsill that she said needed light and he said needed a better owner. A tin of tea. A tin of biscuits. He never once asked for any of it. Some Sundays he’d come back and find something new on the counter and complain, and move it somewhere else, and complain about that. He never threw anything away.

On the third Sunday he came out of the little shower room behind the sliding door with his hair wet and a damp grey T-shirt in his hand, drying the back of his neck with it, and she looked at it.

“What’s that?”

“A T-shirt.”

“Why are you drying yourself with a T-shirt?”

“It’s clean. It was clean. Yesterday.” He looked at it. “It’s cloth. It dries things. That’s what cloth’s for. Partly.”

“Where are your towels?”

“I don’t own towels.”

She stared at him.

“Don’t,” he said.

“I’m not saying anything.”

“Your face is.” He threw the T-shirt over the back of a chair. “It’s a rule. You don’t own things. You own something, you have to go back for it. Old Ko said that.” He went to put the kettle on. “You leave a room with nothing in it, you never have to go back. You can walk out in the middle of the night and you’ve lost nothing.”

“Who’s Old Ko?”

He was quiet with his back to her.

“A sergeant,” he said. “In a unit on the border. The Grey Lanterns. On the other side of the river, back when it was a war and not a river. My parents got killed in the shelling when I was eight and there wasn’t anybody, so he took me in. He wasn’t a good man, exactly. Nobody in that unit was good. But he was good to me.” He turned round with two mugs. “He taught me to read. He taught me to talk. I didn’t, for a year. Not a word. So every night he made me tell him three things. Three things I’d seen that day. Three things I’d learned. And one thing I was glad of.”

“Every night?”

“Every night. Especially when I didn’t want to.” He put her mug in front of her. “Once I told him I was glad the dog next door had stopped barking. He said that wasn’t gladness, it was relief, and made me find another.”

She laughed, and he looked pleased with himself, and sat down at the other end of the sofa.

“And then I didn’t stop talking,” he said. “Ever. He said he’d created a monster.” He drank. “Old Ko owned one spoon. Kept it in his top pocket. When he died they buried it with him, because it was everything he had in the world. A spoon.” He looked at the room, at the cushion and the honey and the plant on the sill. “So. That was Old Ko. And I don’t own towels.”

She didn’t say anything. But on the fourth Sunday she came up the side stair of the Golden Nightingale with a large paper bag and put it on the sofa.

“What’s that?”

“Nothing.”

“That’s a big nothing.”

She opened it. Three thick white bath towels. Three white hand towels. A bottle of mild washing liquid. A packet of wooden pegs.

He looked at them.

“You bought towels,” he said.

“Yes.”

“Because I dried myself with a T-shirt.”

“Yes.”

“Do you think I’m incapable of buying towels?”

She looked at the T-shirt on the back of the chair, where he’d thrown it seven days before. “Apparently.”

He laughed. Not because it was especially funny. Because he had no idea at all how to argue with her.

“Why three?”

“One to use, one spare, and one for when the other two are drying.”

He picked one up. It was thick and soft and white, much nicer than anything he would have bought, and he ran his thumb over it once and his face did something she couldn’t read.

“How much?”

“It doesn’t matter.”

“Evangeline.”

“Jun Hyuk,” she said.

It was the first time she’d said his name. He’d told her it the week before, at Nam’s, between one spoonful of broth and the next, as if it were nothing, because she’d asked him for the sixth time and he’d run out of ways not to answer. Lee Jun Hyuk. She’d said nothing then. She said it now, as if she’d been keeping it somewhere safe, and he forgot what he’d been arguing about.

He put his hand back in his pocket without the wallet.

“You’re not buying anything else,” he said.

“All right,” she said.

They both knew she was lying.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday the fourth of December he came out of the shower with damp hair and one of the white towels round his neck, and she looked up from her book on the sofa.

“Did you use the towel?”

“What else would I use?”

“Nothing,” she said, and smiled at the book.

He hung it over the back of a chair. Folded. Badly. Badly, in a lump, like a dropped coat.

She put the book down.

“That isn’t how you fold it.”

“It’s a towel.”

“I know.”

“Then what’s the problem?”

She got up and came over. “Come here.”

“Why?”

“I’ll show you.”

He looked at the towel. Then at her. Something moved at the corner of his mouth. “All right.”

She spread the towel out on the counter. “In half. Long ways. Then again.” She folded it. “Then in thirds. Like that. So it sits on the shelf with the edges inside.”

He did it. His hands were large and the towel looked small between them.

“Like that?”

She looked. “No.”

“What’s wrong with it?”

“The edges aren’t straight.”

They were almost perfectly straight.

“Nobody’ll notice.”

“I’ll notice.”

“Course you will,” he said.

She put her hands over his on the towel. “Here.” She moved his left hand a little to the side and squared the corner with her own. “There. See? Now it’s straight.”

He wasn’t looking at the towel. He was looking at her. Her brows drawn together, concentrating. A strand of hair loose against her cheek. Her fingers still lying over his on a folded towel as if teaching him to fold it were the most important thing either of them would do all year.

“You’re not looking,” she said.

“I am.”

“You’re looking at me.”

“You told me to come here.”

She took her hands away. “You’re not taking it seriously.”

“I’m trying.”

“No, you’re not.” She took the towel and folded it herself, and put it on the shelf over the sink with the others, edges in.

“Evangeline,” he said.

She turned.

He had stopped talking. She noticed that before anything else. The big kind voice that never stopped, that had talked five women out of a box and through a port in the dark, had gone quiet, and he was standing by the counter looking at her as if he’d run out of words altogether.

“What?”

He reached out and pushed the loose strand of hair back off her cheek. His hand stayed there, his thumb by her ear.

“I’ve been thinking about something,” he said. “For about five weeks.”

“What?”

He looked at her mouth. Then back at her eyes.

“Can I kiss you?”

She went still.

He didn’t come closer. He didn’t assume anything. His hand stayed where it was, light against her face, and he waited, the way he’d waited under the containers with his hand held out for hers.

“Why are you asking?” she said.

“Because I want to.”

“Only that?”

“Mostly that.”
