She looked at him. Then, slowly, she turned her face and leaned her cheek into his palm.

It was such a small movement. It was enough.

“All right,” he said, so quietly she barely heard it, and bent his head.

The first kiss was gentle. Almost careful. His mouth touched hers and stopped there, and stayed, giving her time to change her mind.

She didn’t. Her hands came up and took hold of the front of his shirt.

He kissed her again, longer this time, his other hand coming to her waist, drawing her in without hurrying her. She closed her eyes. She’d imagined this a great deal more often than she would ever have admitted: across Nam’s window table, at the bus stand by the bridge, under the viaduct among the orchid trays. She had never once imagined it beside a shelf of folded towels.

It was exactly right.

When he drew back his forehead rested against hers. Neither of them said anything.

“All right?” he said at last.

She nodded. She was overwhelmingly shy, and looked down, and he laughed under his breath.

“You’re blushing.”

“Don’t look.”

“How am I meant to do that?”

She tried to step back. He let her. But before she’d gone half a step she caught the front of his shirt again in her fist, and pulled.

He came.

And she kissed him. This time she didn’t wait for him to decide anything. She came up on her toes with his shirt in both hands and put her mouth on his with a certainty that surprised them both. He went still for half a second. Then his hand spread on her back and he kissed her back, deeper, warmer, not careful at all, until she had to let go of his shirt and hold on to his shoulders instead.

When they came apart she was breathing fast.

“That was unexpected,” he said. His voice wasn’t quite steady.

“Why?”

“You’re usually so polite.”

She hit him on the chest. He caught her hand.

“Don’t tease me.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He bent and kissed her forehead. Then her cheek.

“That doesn’t count,” she said.

His eyebrows went up. “No?”

“No.”

“What counts, then?”

She looked at him. Then she pulled his shirt a third time, and he laughed against her mouth, the big helpless laugh she’d first heard over a bag of towels, and kissed her again, and the towels sat on the shelf over the sink with all their edges in.

chapters.title: Rules of a Safe House
chapters.desc: He comes home at three with another man’s blood on his cuff and finds the lamp still on. So he writes her seven rules on the back of a noodle menu, and she keeps six.
chapters.epigraph: “7. Don’t come back.”
chapters.content:
The lamp was still on.

Lee Jun Hyuk saw it before anything else when he let himself in at eight minutes past three on the Monday morning, and he stood in the doorway with his key in the third lock and looked at it as if it had done something to him. It was her lamp. She’d carried it up the side stair three Sundays ago, a small brass thing with a paper shade, because the room was too dark to read in, and he’d said that was the point of the room.

Two mugs on the counter, one with a skin of cold tea. Her book face down on the sofa arm. Evangeline asleep at the other end with her head against the cushion and her phone in her hand, still in the pale cardigan she’d had on at ten, when he put his jacket on and said, Don’t wait up.

His right cuff was stiff. The blood on it had dried in places and was still tacky in others, and it wasn’t his.

The lock clicked behind him and she woke at once. Her eyes went over his face, his hands, his sleeve, and she stood up too fast.

“Jun Hyuk.”

“Why are you awake?”

“I was waiting.”

“I told you not to.”

“I know.”

She came towards him. “What happened? Your sleeve—”

“Don’t.”

It came out hard enough that she stopped where she was. He hadn’t meant it to. His shoulder ached and the night was still on him, metal and cold air and a drain somewhere, and here were the lamp and the two mugs and her.

“You can’t sit up till three waiting for me,” he said. “Somebody follows me back, they see a light in a window that’s been dark for three years. Somebody comes up that stair while you’re asleep with your shoes off.”

“I locked them.”

“That isn’t the point.”

“I know how to—”

“No,” he said. “You don’t.”

He saw it land. He saw her try not to let it show, the small stillness, her shoulders drawing in as if the room had got colder, and he wanted the words back and was too tired to find better ones.

“Go to Nam’s,” he said. “First bus is at six.”

She looked at him. “All right.”

At the door, her hand on the first lock, she stopped. “Are you hurt?”

“No.”

She looked at his sleeve once more, and went.

He watched from the landing window where the paint had chipped until the light came on over Nam’s back door. Then he sat down on the sofa beside her book, and didn’t turn the lamp off.

✦ ✦ ✦

The man’s name was Geng Lisheng, and his business cards said recruiter.

Silver Star Employment had a clean office in a market town an hour down the river road: plastic chairs, a water cooler, a poster of a smiling girl in a hotel uniform. OVERSEAS OPPORTUNITIES. ACCOMMODATION PROVIDED. Kuang’s ledger page had named the company in pencil, and Detective Song had spent seven weeks finding nothing wrong with it. Jun Hyuk had spent four days.

Geng was working late, tie off, instant noodles going cold by his keyboard. He smiled the smile he used on mothers, saw the size of the man who’d closed the door behind him, and stopped.

“We’re closed.”

“I’m not applying.” Jun Hyuk sat down across the desk. “West Basin. Five women in a box in row K. You found them and took their papers and told their families about the hotel. I want to know where the ones before went.”

Geng tried money, which was quick. He tried names, which took longer, because Jun Hyuk kept asking until they stopped being lies. Then he leaned back and said there were serious people above him who’d be unhappy if anything happened.

“I’m going to make them unhappy too,” said Jun Hyuk. “Where were they taken?”

Geng’s right hand went to the second drawer.

Jun Hyuk was round the desk before it opened. He slammed the drawer on the wrist, and Geng came up out of the chair with the letter knife off the blotter and drove it at his face, and Jun Hyuk took it off him and put it through the side of his throat and held him against the filing cabinet until it was done. Geng’s heel drummed twice on the bottom drawer. The noodles went over. The room smelled of broth and blood.

There was no speech, and nothing he’d have called satisfaction. A man who’d written girls down as entries in a ledger had come to the end of his own page.

The drawer held a pistol. Behind a false panel under the desk there was a bundle of identity cards in a rubber band. Fourteen. Some of them were children, near enough that it wouldn’t have mattered in that office. The ninth was Nuo’s. She looked about twelve in it, with her fringe cut badly. He held it for a while before he put it back in its place.

He photographed everything and sealed the originals in one of Silver Star’s own envelopes, and from the car he rang Song Wei Long, who answered on the fourth ring sounding as if he’d been dropped down a well.

“Do you know what time it is?”

“Fourteen girls’ cards. Silver Star Employment. One’s Nuo. The man who ran it is dead.”

A silence. “You killed him.”

Jun Hyuk looked at his cuff. “Yes.”

“Send me everything. Don’t touch anything else.”

“Too late,” said Jun Hyuk, and rang off. The cards would go to Song by post in the morning, by a route that put them in the evidence room before anybody upstairs knew they existed. He drove the hour home and found the lamp on.

✦ ✦ ✦

At one that afternoon Nam put a bowl down in front of him harder than he needed to.

“She went home on the six o’clock,” Nam said. “No breakfast. With a face.”

“Then stop asking.”

There was a stack of takeaway menus by the till. Jun Hyuk turned one over and took out a pen, and Nam leaned on the counter.

“A love letter,” said Nam. “I’ve been praying seventy years for this day.”

Jun Hyuk wrote.

1. Lock the door behind you. Every time.

2. Never open it unless you know who’s outside.

3. If someone follows you, don’t come here. Go somewhere with people and call me.

4. Don’t tell anyone the address. Not your father. Not your sister.

5. If I tell you to leave, you leave. No arguing.

6. If anything feels wrong, call me. Don’t go and look.

He looked at the space at the bottom. Then he wrote the last one.

7. Don’t come back.

He put it in the drawer under the kettle, where she kept the tea, and told himself that if she kept the first six the seventh would never matter.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came back on Sunday at four minutes past ten, knocked two and one the way he’d taught her, locked all three locks behind her and tried the handle before she said good morning.

“Are you still angry?”

“No.”

“Then why do you look like that?”

He looked at the wall. She put a covered bowl on the counter, Nam’s extra, and moved round the room putting it right, the mugs washed, the cushion turned, the towel on the chair refolded into thirds. Then she opened the drawer for the tea.

He watched her read it. Her mouth was still soft at the fourth rule. By the seventh it wasn’t.

“Those are the rules,” he said.

“I can see that.”

Her thumb rested on Don’t come back. She folded the menu along its crease and laid it on the counter.

“All right,” she said. “Thank you for writing them.”

He’d had his answers ready for an argument. She filled the kettle instead, and drank her tea, and at two she took her bag and locked the door behind her and tried the handle, and followed every rule he’d written.

Including the seventh.

✦ ✦ ✦

He wasn’t at the pillar on Tuesday. He was across the road by a florist’s van, talking to a man who owed him something about Silver Star, and if anybody had asked he’d have said he was there for the man. He saw her come under the viaduct at ten to six with a basket over her arm and stop at a bucket of white lilies, and he said “Later” in the middle of the man’s sentence and crossed the road.

“You’re here,” she said.

“Work.”

“At the flower market?”

“People do business here.” He looked at the van backing in, and at two men by the café, and at the lilies. “Those drop pollen. You’ll get it on your coat.”

She held a bunch up anyway. “Do you like them?”

“Yes.”

“I thought so.”

He walked her to the bus stop on the side nearest the traffic, without taking her hand or saying a word about the menu, and stood on the kerb until she’d sat down. On Saturday he was across the road again, and the Tuesday after that he was by the café pretending to read his phone. When a man with a crate cut between them in the narrowest aisle, his hand went to the small of her back and stayed a second longer than it needed to.

“Watch where you’re going,” he said.

“Yes, sir,” said Evangeline, and laughed at his face.

She bought too much and tried to carry it all, and he took the heavy bag off her, and the third time she stopped reaching for it back. Walking up the hill road with her flowers in his fist, he found he liked having something of hers to carry, and didn’t look at that too closely.

She didn’t come north on Sunday. Or the Sunday after.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Thursday she was on the stair at a quarter to seven with a carrier bag and the face of somebody who’d come three hours on a bus to say I told you so and would be too polite to say it.

“Nam says you haven’t eaten since Sunday.”

“Nam’s a liar.”

She was looking at his hand on the doorframe. Two knuckles split and swollen, a cut across the first he’d cleaned badly. She came in, locked the locks, took down the first-aid box and pointed at the chair.

“Does it hurt?”

“No.”

She looked at him.

“A little,” he said.

She cleaned it with the brown bottle that stung and taped a dressing over it without a word. He waited for the questions he’d have asked, who and where and whose blood had been on his sleeve. None came. When she’d finished she held his hand in both of hers, bent her head, and put her mouth to his split knuckles. Once. Then she looked up.

He’d gone completely still.

“You don’t have to do that,” he said.

“I know.”

She was smiling a little, the way she did when she’d won something without trying. He put his good hand on her waist and drew her down.

“You’re making it very hard to be sensible.”

“How?”

He kissed her instead of explaining, slowly, her hands still holding his on the table between them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The menu stayed in the drawer. She took it out with the tea every time she came, and kept the first six, and put it back. The seventh she left alone, except that once he saw her lay a fingertip on Don’t come back and hold it there, and fold the menu up again. He said nothing.

On Friday morning he was checking the locks while she put white chrysanthemums in a jar, and he said, without thinking, “Princess, pass me the—”

Her hand stopped on the stem.

For one second she looked exactly as she had in the box in row K, still, deciding what kind of danger had come into the room. Your Highness, the men at the flower market had said.

“Don’t,” she said, low. “Please don’t call me that.”

“All right.” He came over slowly, hands loose where she could see them. “You’re not there. You’re in my terrible room. You’re Evangeline.” He touched her cheek with the backs of his fingers. “Just Evangeline.”

She nodded, and he kissed her forehead and held her by the chrysanthemums, and didn’t ask her to explain anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

The argument, when it came, had nothing to do with a rule.

He came back at eight minutes to midnight from meeting Song in a lay-by on the river road, short-tempered, and found her at the table with dinner kept warm under a plate. He told her she should have gone home. She said she’d wanted to see him. He said wanting something didn’t make it safe, and she asked him to stop deciding what she understood, and then he said the thing he’d regret.

“You can’t keep making this your home.”

“Why not?”

“Because it isn’t. It’s a safe house.”

“Is that all I am?” She didn’t raise her voice. “Somebody you keep in your safe house?”

“No.”

“Then why do you keep telling me to leave?” She took the menu out of the drawer and didn’t need to read it. “I keep six. I can’t keep the seventh.”

“Why?”

“Because I don’t want to stop coming back.” She put it down. “Tell me it’s dangerous. Tell me when you need me gone. Don’t write it down like I’m something you can rub out.”

She picked up her bag and turned to the door, and he caught her wrist. Not hard.

“Don’t go.”

She looked at his hand, and he let go at once, because he’d seen men hold women’s wrists before.

“I didn’t mean it like that.”

“Then how did you mean it?”

For once in his life he had nothing ready. He crossed the space between them and kissed her, not carefully, one hand at her waist and the other flat on the steel door beside her head, and she caught his shirt in both fists and held on. When he lifted his head she was breathing as if she’d run up the stair.

“I’m sorry,” he said, his forehead on hers. “I don’t know how to make this safe for you.”

“Then don’t make me disappear.”

He kissed her again, and this time she came up on her toes into it. When he drew back his thumb moved along her cheekbone.

“Keep the six,” he said.

“And the seventh?”

“Don’t ask me to write another one.”

She laughed against his collar.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went home on the Saturday morning, the last day of the year, for New Year’s Eve at the Walled City. A woman had set up a fried-chicken stall on the corner by the bus stand, and hot batter smelled across the pavement in the cold.

“Text me when you’re home,” he said. “Not the back way behind the market. If anyone—”

“I know.”

She reached for his hand. The bus turned onto the bridge in the distance and he bent and kissed her in front of everybody. It was getting to be an ordinary thing. It still made her face go warm.

“You’re getting used to this,” she said.

“Not yet.”

The chicken woman had been watching over her wok with enormous interest. “If you’re going to keep kissing her, young man, marry her. The registry’s open Saturdays.”

Evangeline put both hands over her face. “Auntie.”

“I’m only telling you.”

Even the tips of her ears had gone pink. “Good to know,” said Jun Hyuk.

“Don’t.”

The bus pulled in. She turned at the top step and waved, and it went over the bridge. The chicken woman turned a piece in the oil.

“She’s a good girl,” she said. “Don’t waste her time.”

His phone went before he’d reached the end of the road.

Evangeline: The chicken lady is very nosy.

Jun Hyuk: She’s right about the registry.

Three dots. Gone. Back.

Evangeline: Jun Hyuk.

Jun Hyuk: What?

Evangeline: Don’t tease me.

He stood on the corner with that for a while.

Jun Hyuk: I’m not teasing.

The menu was still in the drawer. He’d written the last line because he’d thought the safest thing he could do for her was keep her away from him. But he’d come up the stair three nights that week and found the lamp on, the towels in thirds, the chrysanthemums in their jar, and a woman who knew exactly which door she meant to keep walking through. He was beginning to suspect the seventh rule had been for his own sake all along, and he wasn’t sure any more that he wanted to keep it.

chapters.title: She Watches the Exits
chapters.desc: Feet on the stair, and a back window he thought nobody knew about. She got there first. Then, in Nam’s back room, she tells him what she was raised to be.
chapters.epigraph: “Every house has a place where the sound carries. I’d found them all by the time I was seven.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Evangeline heard was a foot on the stair.

Not a neighbour coming home late, or a boy from the bar downstairs that hadn’t been a bar since 2019. These were careful. One step, a pause, another. She opened her eyes in the dark. The lamp was off because he’d switched it off himself before he went out at midnight, and she’d kept every rule after it: three locks, the curtain, the phone charged on the cushion by her head. She’d been reading on the sofa when she fell asleep. It was seventeen minutes past two on Sunday morning, the second week of January, and there were three men on the stair, perhaps four.

They stopped on the landing below. One murmured. Another answered. The stair creaked again.

She didn’t ring him. Not yet. She put her shoes on and picked up her bag, and she didn’t go anywhere near the front door. She went through the sliding door into the little room with the camp bed and pulled the wooden cabinet away from the wall.

Behind it, under a fold of old curtain, was a third window. It was painted grey like the other two, and it opened onto an iron service landing hardly wider than her shoulders, and a flight of steep steps going down into the alley behind the building. He’d never shown it to her. He’d never said it was there. She’d found it on her second visit, the Sunday after the rain, while he was in the kitchen arguing with somebody on the phone and she was looking for somewhere to put a plant. There’d been a draught under the curtain and a straight line in the wall where there shouldn’t have been one. She’d opened it, and looked, and shut it again, and moved the cabinet back exactly as it had been, and never mentioned it.

Three blows on the front door.

“Open up,” said a man. And then, after a moment, “Police.”

She looked at her phone, and at the window, and sent one message.

Evangeline: Someone is at the door. Using the back window.

The frame was cold under her palms. Her shoe scraped the sill and she caught it before it rang on the iron. Behind her, through two rooms, the front door shook, and she was on the service landing with the steps going down under her into the dark when she heard the first lock give.

✦ ✦ ✦

Jun Hyuk was two streets away, beside his truck, talking to one of the men who did things for him.

He read the message once. Then again.

“Go,” he said.

“What?”

“Get out of here.” He was already running. He rang her and it rang out, and he rang again and it rang out, and he stopped ringing and ran.

In the room over the Golden Nightingale two men came in first, one with a torch and one with a gun held down along his thigh. The torch went over a dark lamp, an empty sofa, a book open on the cushion, a kettle that was cold.

“She’s here.”

They went through it fast, the shower room, the kitchen corner, the cupboard. The first man came back into the middle of the room and stood there, and the curtain over the sliding door moved, slightly, in air that shouldn’t have been there.

He went through. The cabinet was pulled out. The grey window stood open on the night.

“Back!”

By the time the second man got to the iron landing there was nobody on the steps.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was at the bottom of the alley with one hand on the wall when he answered.

“Where are you?”

“Behind the building.”

“Hurt?”

“No.”

“Alone?”

“Yes.”

“Keep walking. Don’t stop. Go to Nam’s. Not the main road, take the street behind the pharmacy, you know the one, with the bins, I know it smells, that’s why nobody uses it, keep going—”

A car door slammed somewhere behind her. She looked back. A figure had come round the far end of the alley.

She ran.

“Evangeline?”

“I’m running.”

“Good. Keep going. Keep going.”

She could hear him breathing, and it wasn’t on the phone. She came round the corner by the pharmacy bins and went straight into him, and he caught her by both shoulders.

Neither of them could say anything at all. His eyes went over her face, her arms, her coat.

“Are you hurt?”

She shook her head.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

He pulled her in against him so hard her feet left the ground. He put his face down into her hair with one hand spread across her back, and she felt his breath at her temple, and felt the thing she would remember afterwards longer than the stair or the window: he was shaking. Only a little. But she had her arms round his neck, and she felt it.

“You’re all right,” he said, which didn’t sound as if it was meant for her.

“I’m all right.”

He held her away from him to look. “How did you know about the window?”

“I found it.”

“When?”

“My second visit. You were on the phone.”

He stared at her. Then he let out a breath that was nearly a laugh.

“Of course you did,” he said, and lifted her again, and kissed her.

It was hard and sudden, his hands tight at her waist and his mouth on hers with everything he’d been holding since he read the message, and she held on to his shoulders and kissed him back the same way, in an alley that smelled of the pharmacy’s bins, with her feet off the ground.

“Don’t ever do that to me again,” he said against her forehead.

“I didn’t have much time.”

“I know. I know you didn’t.” He set her down and took her hand. “Come on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nam opened his back door in his slippers at six minutes past three, took one look at Jun Hyuk’s face, and stood aside.

“Inside.”

The shop was dark, the chairs up on the tables, the cats asleep in a heap on the warm tiles by the stockpot. Nam put them in his own little room at the back, a table and two chairs and an old sofa and a window onto the yard, and brought them water.

“Police don’t knock in this town at two in the morning,” Nam said. “Police ring me first and ask if they can.”

“They weren’t police,” said Jun Hyuk.

He stayed long enough to see her sitting down with a glass of water in both hands. Then he said, “Forty minutes,” to Nam, and went out of the back door again before either of them could argue.

He was gone fifty. When he came back his hands were empty and there was nothing in his face at all, and he said to Nam, “They left the door off. I’ll put a new one in on Monday. A real one,” and Nam looked at him and went to make tea without asking where he’d been.

Jun Hyuk shut the door of the little room and pulled out the chair across from her.

“How long have you known about the window?”

“Since my second visit.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“You never mentioned it.”

“Because I didn’t want you using it.”

She tilted her head. “Why?”

“Because it’s a way out. You’re not meant to be looking for ways out.”

She looked at the window onto Nam’s yard. Out in the dark under the one security light, the grey cat was walking along the top of the wall.

“I always look for exits,” she said.

He waited.

“When I was little, I learned to notice doors.” She turned the glass round in her hands. “Every house has a place where the sound carries. I’d found them all by the time I was seven.”

“Why?”

“Because I wasn’t supposed to be anywhere for long.” She was quiet, and he didn’t help her, and she seemed to be grateful for that. “I was raised to be a secret. My father always had people round him. Men he did business with, men who drove for him. Everyone knew his family.” She looked at the table. “Nobody was meant to know about me. I’m not in any photographs. If somebody came to the house without telephoning first, I was taken into another room. I learned not to make a noise. Not to ask who it was. Not to stand by windows.”

“How old were you?”

“Always.”

He didn’t say anything to that. He found he couldn’t.

“My father was paid to make me disappear,” she said.

The room went still.

“I was two days old. The family of the man I was born to paid him to take me away and make sure I was never found. He’s told us all of it now, my brother and sisters and me. They said gone, he says. They didn’t say anything more than that, and they paid him enough that he understood they didn’t mind which.” Her voice didn’t change. “The man I was born to is a king. I’ve never seen him. I don’t know his name. I found his crest once, in our attic, when I was fifteen, on the blanket they’d sent me away in.”

Jun Hyuk sat across from her and said nothing at all, and she noticed that, because she knew by now what it meant when he went quiet.

“He kept the money,” she said. “And he kept me. He says it was because I cried. He also says it was because a king’s daughter alive might be worth something one day. He told us both reasons. I think both are true.”

“And then he hid you.”

“He was frightened. He thought if anyone knew about me, they’d come back.” She looked at her hands. “I believe him. But sometimes I wonder what it would be like if somebody wanted me without needing to put me in the next room.”

He reached across the table and put his hand over hers.

“And then the box,” he said.

“That was different.”

“How?”

“Nobody was pretending it was for my own good.”

He lowered his head. She thought he was going to say something angry, and instead he lifted her hand and pressed his mouth to the backs of her fingers and held it there.

“I’m sorry.”

“You didn’t do it.”

“No.” He looked up. “But I know what it is to spend your whole life ready to leave. I’ve been ready since I was eight. I don’t own towels.” The corner of his mouth went, not quite a smile. “I don’t want you to have to do that here.”

She touched his cheek. He turned his face into her palm.

“Then don’t make me,” she said.

“I’ll try.”

She leaned across the table and kissed him, small and quiet, over two glasses of water in an old man’s back room. He held her hand a long time after.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the morning of Lunar New Year she came in at Nam’s front door at a quarter past eight with a big insulated box and a red cloth bag, off the first bus, with her cheeks pink from the cold.

Jun Hyuk was already there. He’d been up since five carrying sacks of flour in from Nam’s van and checking the back door three times, and he looked up from the counter.

“What’s all that?”

“New Year.”

“Food?”

“Dumplings.”

“How many?”

“Enough.”

“She made them herself,” Nam said, coming out of the kitchen. “With her sister. Yesterday, at the Walled City.”

Nam lifted the lid and the steam came up out of the box. Rows of them, pleated and neat, cabbage and mushroom, and in one corner one that had come out wrong, lopsided and pinched shut at the end like a fist.

Nam picked it out. “This one was made by a cat.”

Evangeline laughed. “I know.”

“Which did you make?” said Jun Hyuk.

She pointed at it.

“Then I’ll have that one.”

“Course you will,” said Nam.

At the word cats two of them came out from under the tables, the grey one and the orange one, and wound round her ankles. She crouched down. “Happy New Year,” she told the grey one, which was shy and didn’t like being picked up, and she scratched the orange one behind its ears, where it liked it, and moved her bag out of its reach, because it stole. She knew all that about them. She’d learned the whole of this place, the back door and the old table and the kettle that shrieked and the cats, and him.

They ate at the window table. She put a bowl in front of him and said “Eat,” and he said, “You’re giving me orders now?”

“Yes.”

“Good,” said Nam. “Somebody should.”

He ate the crooked one first. She watched him.

“Good,” he said.

“Really?”

“Really.”

“He’s lying,” said Nam. “He loves them.”

Jun Hyuk looked at him. “Do you want to eat or not?”

Nam immediately took another dumpling.

After a while she took a small red paper packet out of her bag and put it beside his bowl. Inside was an ordinary coin wrapped in red paper, with a note folded round it in her careful handwriting.

For good fortune. For safe journeys. For coming home.

He read it twice.

“I wanted you to have something lucky,” she said.

“Why?”

“Because you always go somewhere dangerous.” She put her hand over his. “And because I want you to come home.”

He didn’t say anything. Nam had stopped eating.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took the coin back from him a little later, and went out into the yard, and he found her crouched by the pots along the back wall pressing it into the soil at the foot of a small green plant.

“You’re planting it?”

“Not really. I’m putting it here.”

“You could have kept it.”

She brushed the earth off her fingers. “Good fortune should have somewhere to live.”

He crouched down beside her and looked at the little pot, and at her, and understood that she wasn’t making the place pretty. She was giving it something to grow into.

“Come here,” he said, and kissed her with his hand on her cheek and earth on her fingers.

“You’re getting better at that,” she said, when he let her go.

“Am I?”

“Much better.”

He kissed her again to make sure.

When they went back in Nam was putting down a tray of tea and the cats had taken the empty chairs.

“You’re making a mess of my restaurant,” said Nam.

“We’re eating,” said Jun Hyuk.

“You’re kissing. In my yard. Even the cats have better manners.” The orange one jumped up onto the table, and Nam sighed. “Not you.”

Evangeline laughed. Jun Hyuk reached for her hand under the table, and then he leaned over and kissed her right there, across the window table, in front of Nam and two cats and what was left of the dumplings.

Nam put the teapot down slowly.

“I’ve fed you for years,” he said. “I’ve given you a bed. I’ve listened to your moods. And this is what I get?”

“What do you want?”

“An apology.”

“No.”

Nam stared at him, and then burst out laughing, and so did she, with her face hidden in Jun Hyuk’s shoulder. His hand stayed round hers. He didn’t look at the door. He didn’t count the people in the room or work out how fast he could get them all out through the kitchen. He sat at Nam’s table and ate dumplings on New Year’s morning, and the city outside was waking up, and in a pot in the yard there was a coin under the soil, because a woman who’d spent her childhood learning where to hide had decided to plant something instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when Nam was in the kitchen, she found him by the back door looking out at the yard, and gave him a red envelope.

“Another one?”

Inside was a slip of paper. One wish for the new year.

“What did you wish for?” he asked.

“I can’t tell you. Then it won’t come true.” She tilted her head. “What did you wish for?”

“I haven’t made one.”

“Why not?”

He took her hand and lifted her fingers to his mouth. “Because I’ve already got it.” And then, so quietly she almost didn’t hear, “I want to keep coming home.”

She couldn’t say anything. She stepped in and rested her forehead against his chest, and he put his arms round her and held her there in the open doorway, with the cats going in and out round their feet and Nam shouting for someone to bring in the empty bowls, and didn’t ask her to go anywhere.

chapters.title: The Night He Had a Fever
chapters.desc: A knife wound sewn up in a village, six days of lying about it, and a fever of forty degrees. For once he can’t talk, so she does.
chapters.epigraph: “When people are scared, you keep talking, so they hear a voice that isn’t scared, and they follow the voice.”
chapters.content:
The first lie was that it didn’t hurt. The second was that it was nothing. The third was that he’d already seen to it. Lee Jun Hyuk had been telling all three, in that order, since he was about eleven, and he was good at them.

On the first Saturday in February he found the men who had come up the stair in January. Three of them, in a cold store behind the eastern warehouses, playing cards on a pallet. Two of them didn’t get up again. The third had a knife in his boot, and he got it into Jun Hyuk under the right ribs before Jun Hyuk broke his arm and then his neck, and for a second, standing in the cold store with the cards all over the floor, Jun Hyuk thought it was only a cut.

Then he looked down.

He drove himself to a clinic in a village forty minutes outside town, paid cash, didn’t give his name, and lay on his side while a tired doctor put in eleven stitches and told him what to watch for. He nodded at everything. He was out of the door before she’d finished writing.

He changed the dressing himself. He kept working. And for six days he told Evangeline nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

She noticed the first thing on Sunday, at Nam’s, the day of the lantern festival. He was holding his tea in his left hand. He didn’t usually care which hand he used. And when she reached across the table to take his empty bowl he moved, slightly, away from her.

“You’re sitting strangely.”

“Am I?”

“Yes.”

“Maybe you’re looking too closely.”

She let it go, for the moment, and went home on the evening bus with a lantern from Nam for Eliana.

On Monday evening her father came up to her room at the house on the hill. Lin Jian rarely came to Elowen’s without telephoning first. He had learned to knock, and not to ask too many questions, and slowly, with enormous effort, to let her decide things. He found her at the table by the window sorting a first-aid box: gauze, tape, bandages, a brown bottle of antiseptic nearly empty.

“What’s that?”

“Replacing a few things.”

He looked at the bottle and said nothing about it. He touched her hair when he left and told her to eat properly.

On Tuesday morning there was a new bottle of antiseptic in the box. It was the old-fashioned kind with the green label, the one their mother had kept in the bathroom cabinet at the Walled City, the one her father had gone on buying for years after there was nobody left in the house who needed it. Evangeline stood with it in her hand for a minute. Then she put it carefully in the box.

He wasn’t at the flower market that morning. Not by the pillar, not across the road, not leaning on a parked van pretending to read his phone.

Evangeline: Are you busy today?

Twenty minutes later:

Jun Hyuk: Yes.

Evangeline: Have you eaten?

Jun Hyuk: Yes.

Evangeline: What did you eat?

Nothing came back. She looked at the screen, and at the bucket of white stock in front of her, and on Wednesday she took the bus north.

✦ ✦ ✦

He kissed her when she came in at Nam’s. It was brief, and afterwards he didn’t put his arm round her, and when he turned to speak to Nam she saw that he was holding his right arm close against his side.

“Jun Hyuk. Are you hurt?”

“No.”

It came too quickly. He bent and kissed her forehead.

“Don’t worry,” he said, which was the wrong thing, because now she was worried.

On Thursday she brought dinner up to the room. He ate a little of it and pushed the bowl away, and she saw the sweat at his hairline.

“Your forehead’s hot.”

“It’s the room.”

She reached up. He caught her wrist before her hand touched his face, not roughly, but firmly, and held it, and then let it go.

“Go back to Nam’s,” he said. “Go to sleep.”

“Let me see your side.”

“No.”

It was quiet, and it was final. She didn’t argue. She looked at him, and he knew she’d seen, and she went.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven seventeen he sent her a message.

Jun Hyuk: Sleeping. Don’t come over.

She answered Good night. Rest well and didn’t believe a word of it. At a quarter to two she started ringing him from Nam’s spare room. At two forty-three she was standing at the new steel door with the keys he’d given her in January, letting herself in.

The room was hot and close. The curtain was drawn. A glass of water stood on the table, full.

“Jun Hyuk?”

She found him on the camp bed through the sliding door, in his shirt and trousers, with the blanket half on the floor. His face was flushed dark and his hair was soaked. When she put her hand on his forehead she took it off again as if she’d touched the stove.

The thermometer in the first-aid box took three tries, because her hands were shaking. 40.0, it said.

“Jun Hyuk.”

His eyes came half open. They knew her. Then they slid away.

“Ko,” he said. “Old Ko. Don’t—don’t put it there.”

She bent close. “What?”

His hand went out across the blanket towards nothing. “The box. Have to keep the box. Don’t let him—”

“There’s no box.” She took his hand. It was burning. “You’re here.”

He shook his head, and his eyes closed, and he went on breathing far too fast. She looked at the thermometer once more and rang her sister.

Elara answered on the fifth ring, thick with sleep. “Evangeline?”

“I need you.”

Elara was awake. “What’s happened?”

“Jun Hyuk. He’s burning. Forty. He’s not making sense.” She looked down. There was a dark patch on his shirt over the right side that she hadn’t seen in the bad light, and her stomach turned over. “I think he’s hurt.”

“Ring an ambulance now. A fever like that and he’s confused, with a wound, that’s an emergency. Do it now, I’ll hold.”

She rang. She gave the address in a voice she didn’t recognise and said fever and confused and infected cut. Then she was back on the line with Elara.

“Can you see it?”

She lifted the edge of his shirt. The dressing underneath was wet. There was a smell she didn’t know, and then did. The skin round it was swollen tight and angry red, out past the edges of the tape, and a line of black stitches ran under the gauze.

“Don’t pull at it,” said Elara. “Ask him when.”

“Jun Hyuk. When did you get hurt?”

His eyes opened and looked at her without any recognition at all. “Saturday.”

It was Friday.

“Did you get stitches?”

A faint nod. “Eleven.”

Six days, she thought. He’d been walking about with it for six days and kissing her forehead and telling her not to worry.

When the ambulance came he fought them without knowing he was doing it. His body went rigid and his hand closed on the edge of the camp bed. “Don’t,” he said. “Don’t take—”

“I’m staying,” said Evangeline, close to his face.

His eyes found her. He saw her.

“Evangeline,” he said. “Stay.”

“I’m here.”

His fingers found hers before the doors closed. They were hot. She held them all the way across the bridge.

✦ ✦ ✦

The county hospital was too bright. She sat in a plastic chair outside the treatment room with his shirt in a paper bag on her knees while they took blood and cleaned the wound and put a line into his arm. The infection was deep. The fever had come from it. He’d been lucky, a doctor told her, to come in when he did, and looked at her as if she might be the reason.

Elara got there just after six, in a coat over the clothes she’d slept in, after three hours of empty motorway. She kept her hands in her coat pockets the whole time and sat down beside her.

“How is he?”

“They’re treating him.” Evangeline looked at the bag. “He told me eleven stitches. Saturday. Six days, Elara.”

“Six days.” Elara breathed out through her nose. “He’s in the right place now.”

Evangeline nodded. She didn’t feel any better.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Saturday morning he was awake, more or less. The fever was down a little. There was a drip in the back of his hand and a frame over his side to keep the sheet off it.

He looked at her, and at the drip. “Hospital?”

“Yes.”

He shut his eyes. “Unnecessary.”

“Unnecessary?”

He opened one eye, saw her face, and decided not to go on.

“Do you know what day it is?”

“Saturday.”

“Good.”

“You’re angry.”

“Very.”

“All right,” he said, and closed his eyes, and then opened them. “Evangeline. Sorry.”

It was the first time he’d said it. It made her feel worse. She leaned over and put her mouth to his forehead, and he was still too warm.

✦ ✦ ✦

They let him out on Monday on the condition that someone kept an eye on him. Evangeline said that would be her, in a voice that made the young doctor write it down. She also said he’d stay in Nam’s back room and not in his own, and he didn’t like that at all.

Nam had made the room up with clean sheets, a kettle, a bowl of tangerines. She lined up his tablets and his instructions on the table in the order he had to take them.

He sat on the bed and looked at it all. “You’ve taken over.”

“Yes.”

“Do I need permission to drink water?”

She handed him a glass. “Yes.”

He drank it. She was nearly smiling.

“You’re enjoying this,” he said.

“A little.”

On Tuesday Elara came up again to go through the clinic’s papers with them, and he lay on Nam’s bed looking deeply insulted by the whole idea of medicine.

“They want to see it again tomorrow,” said Elara.

“I’ve got things to do.”

“You’ve got an infection,” said Evangeline.

“Wonderful. Two of you.”

“Three,” said Evangeline, “if Nam joins in.”

“Already have,” said Nam, from the kitchen.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the clinic on Wednesday the doctor looked at the wound and said the stitches had to come out, all of them. Sewn shut, it had kept the infection in. Now it would be cleaned and packed and left open to heal from the bottom up, and dressed every day.

“I can do it myself,” said Jun Hyuk.

The doctor looked at him. “No.”

He looked at Evangeline. She raised her eyebrows. He looked away.

He was tense from the first one, his jaw set, his free hand gripping the edge of the couch so hard the paper tore. She stood on his other side and took that hand.

“One,” she said, when the first stitch came out.

He glanced up. “You’re counting?”

“So you know how many are left.” She watched the doctor’s hands, not his face. “Two.”

Then she kept talking. She’d never talked so much in her life. She told him about the flower market and the new stall that sold nothing but ferns. She told him the grey cat had stolen a piece of chicken off Nam’s counter while Nam was looking straight at it. She told him the smallest orchid on his painted windowsill had put out a new bud while he was in the hospital, so somebody would have to tell it he’d been unwell.

“You’re talking too much,” he muttered, at the seventh.

“You talk to frightened people.”

He looked at her. “Old Ko’s rule. When people are scared, you keep talking, so they hear a voice that isn’t scared, and they follow the voice.”

“I know. I heard you do it. In the box.” She squeezed his hand. “Eight.”

At the eleventh she looked at the doctor. “That’s all?”

“That’s all.”

“Eleven,” she told him.

He looked at her. “Thank you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The fever broke at twenty-six minutes past two on Thursday morning.

She knew because she’d been checking so often she knew every change in his breathing, and it had changed. She put her palm on his forehead in the dark. Cooler. She found the thermometer and read it under the light from the kitchen, and checked it again, and again.

Normal.

She sat down on the edge of Nam’s bed and her shoulders began to shake. She’d held herself together for six days. Through the ambulance and the plastic chair and the doctors, through every time he’d tried to stand up when he should have stayed down. Now, with his skin cool under her hand, she couldn’t hold any of it.

She got up so as not to wake him, and went through to the shop.

Nam was at the corner table with a cup of tea in the dark. He looked up. “Evangeline?”

She tried to speak and couldn’t.

He was on his feet. “Has it gone up?”

She shook her head. “Down.” Her hands went over her face. “It’s down.”

“Oh,” said Nam, and his shoulders came down a long way. “Good.”

And she began to cry, not quietly and not politely, with her hands over her face and her breath catching hard in her throat, and Nam didn’t ask her to stop. He opened his arms, and she walked into them, and he held her the way an old man holds somebody who’s been brave for much too long.

“I thought—” she said into his shoulder.

“I know.”

“He wouldn’t tell me.”

“I know.”

“Six days.”

“That stubborn idiot,” said Nam, and she laughed, and cried harder.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she went back in, he was awake. His eyes followed her across the room.

“Have you been crying?”

“No.”

He looked at her swollen eyes. He lifted his hand, and she came to the bed, and he drew her down until her face was close to his and kissed one eyelid, and then the other, slow and tired, and then the corner of her eye where a tear had dried.

“Don’t cry.”

“You don’t get to tell me that.”

“All right.”

She put her hand on his cheek. “Lee Jun Hyuk.”

He looked at her. She’d never once said all of it. She said it slowly now, as if she wanted him to hear every part.

“That’s me,” he said.

“Don’t make me say it to an empty room.”

He went still. Then he brought her hand to his mouth. “I won’t.”

She kissed him, gently, and it had six days in it.

“Did I say anything strange?” he asked, afterwards.

“Old Ko. And a box.”

He shut his eyes. “God.”

“What box?”

He was quiet a moment. “Ko Baek-san kept a box under his bed for me. Things he thought I should have when I was grown. A few letters. A photograph of my mother. My father’s watch, stopped. He said I wasn’t allowed to open it till I was old enough to understand what was in it.”

“Did you open it?”

“Yes.”

“What was in it?”

He looked at the ceiling. “Mostly things I didn’t know I’d lost.”

“Where is it?”

“Somewhere safe.”

“Good,” she said, and sat down on the floor by the bed with her head against the mattress, and he found her hand and didn’t let go of it even when he fell asleep.

Nam found them like that at seven, and put a cup of tea on the table, and pulled the blanket over her legs, and left the door open a crack.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke at half past ten to the smell of tea. She was on the chair beside him with a book.

“How do you feel?”

He thought about it. “Bad.”

“Honest.”

“It still hurts.”

“I know.”

“Next time you get hurt,” she said, “you tell me. At once. And you don’t let somebody sew you up in a village and pretend it didn’t happen.”

He sighed.

“Say it properly.”

He looked at her, with the faintest smile.

“If I get hurt,” said Lee Jun Hyuk, “I’ll tell you.”

“Good.”

He drew her down onto the bed and she lay carefully beside him on his good side, and after a while he said she was bossy, and she said somebody had to be, and he laughed, a tired sound, a living one. Out in the shop Nam was putting the chairs down. The cats were waiting by the back door for breakfast. The kettle was coming up to the boil. And for the first time in a week, Lee Jun Hyuk was warm only because somebody was holding his hand.

chapters.title: Four Syllables
chapters.desc: Three weeks of healing, a spoon for a birthday that isn’t one, and a man practising four syllables in the shower.
chapters.epigraph: “That’s not a name. That’s a sentence.”
chapters.content:
“You’re pulling at it.”

“I’m breathing.”

“You’re breathing with your whole body.”

He looked down at her. She looked back, entirely unimpressed, with a roll of tape between her teeth.

It was the first of March, raining on and off, and the wound under his ribs had closed in some places and stayed stubbornly open in others, a narrow pink trench under the dressing that she cleaned and packed every evening exactly as the clinic had shown her. He’d come back to the room over the Golden Nightingale from Nam’s after a week. He’d taken every tablet. Two days ago he had also tried to carry a crate of bottled water up the side stair, and she hadn’t spoken to him for nearly an hour afterwards. It had been a terrible hour. She’d sat beside him with her lips pressed together, looking as if she were deciding whether a person could be put on a high shelf until he learned to behave.

He’d said sorry. She’d told him that saying sorry and understanding were two different things. He’d been quiet ever since.

That was the strange part. He was a man who talked to everybody about everything, to frightened women and cats and the man at the petrol station, and since the fever he’d hardly said a word that wasn’t necessary. She’d been sleeping in the room more than at her sister’s. The first night she’d sat up in the chair. The second she’d folded a blanket on the floor, and when he found her there in the morning he’d said there was no reason to sleep on the floor, and she’d said there was no reason for him to pretend he was comfortable either. The next day a second camp bed had come up the stair in its box. She’d put it together herself. He’d watched her fight one of the metal joints for several minutes and finally got up to help, and she’d told him to sit down, and he’d sat down.

It was becoming a habit. He didn’t like what it said about him.

“Hold still.”

“I am.”

“You’re watching me.”

“I can do both.”

“Then watch the wall.”

He turned his head and watched the wall. She smiled. He caught it at the edge of his eye.

“There.”

“What?”

“You smiled.”

“I didn’t.”

He turned back and she was smiling properly now, and it did something inconvenient to his chest. The fever had left something behind that he didn’t have a word for: waking and finding her there, her voice breaking when she thought he couldn’t hear, her hand holding his when his was too weak to hold back. He’d spent most of his life being the one who stayed awake. He’d never once thought about what it would feel like to be the one somebody waited up for.

She pressed the last of the tape down. “Done.”

He caught her wrist before she could gather up the gauze, and drew her in until she stood between his knees, and leaned forward and rested his forehead against her stomach. She had one hand up to argue. It stopped in his hair.

“You’ve been very quiet,” she said.

“Have I?”

“Are you still unwell?”

“No.”

“Then what is it?”

He lifted his head. He looked at her eyes and her mouth and her eyes again, and she could see him looking for a word, and not finding one.

“Nothing,” he said.

She didn’t believe him, and didn’t make him say it. She bent and kissed his forehead instead. He shut his eyes, and found it harder to bear than the dressing.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Thursday she caught him watching her from under his eyelids while she read.

“You’re awake.”

“No.”

“Your eyes are open.”

“Involuntary.”

She put the book down. “Do you want something?”

He considered it. “Yes. You.”

She stared at him. “I’m sitting right here.”

“Then come closer.”

She sighed and went, meaning only to sit on the edge of the camp bed, and he got an arm round her waist and pulled her into his lap.

“Jun Hyuk. Your side—”

“Is fine. You’ve told me to sit down all day.”

“Because you keep getting up.”

He kissed her before she could finish. It wasn’t hurried. His hand was warm on her back and his mouth moved on hers with the slow certainty she’d missed all through the days he could hardly bear to be touched, and she’d been frightened for him for so long that she’d almost forgotten how easily he could make her forget about it.

“Still nagging?” he said, when he let her go.

“Yes.”

He smiled. She kissed him again, and this time it was him who forgot to say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

His birthday wasn’t his birthday.

The date on his papers was the eleventh of March. It had been put there by a clerk when he was nine and somebody needed one for a form, and he’d never thought of it as anything but an administrative convenience. Old Ko had known the real one. Old Ko’s idea of a celebration had been an extra egg in the rice and a warning not to get arrogant about it. Once, when Jun Hyuk was sixteen, he’d been given a pair of socks. They’d been too big. He’d worn them anyway.

When Evangeline asked him in January when his birthday was, he’d given her the date on his papers. She’d written it down. He’d forgotten all about it. She hadn’t.

On the Saturday she came up the stair with a paper bag and an expression he didn’t trust.

“What’s that?”

“Something ordinary.”

She took out a small round cake with white icing and four strawberries on top, and one candle, and put a narrow box beside it.

“Happy birthday.”

He looked at the cake, and at her. “It’s not my birthday.”

“It is on your papers.”

“Those are wrong.”

“I know. Nam told me.” She lit the candle. “I have one of those too.”

He’d forgotten that. Seventh of April for the people who’d sent her away; ninth for the clinic that was a dry-cleaner’s now. He sat and looked at the little flame, and she didn’t ask him to wish or to blow it out. She sat down beside him.

“Nam also says you got an extra egg,” she said. “And socks once. Too big.”

“I’m going to have a word with Nam.”

“Did you wear them?”

“Yes.”

“Then he knew you would.”

Something old moved behind his eyes. He looked at the box. “What’s that?”

She pushed it towards him. Inside was a silver spoon. Old, heavy, the handle worn smooth where fingers had held it, the silver gone dark in the grooves of a pattern along the stem. It wasn’t Old Ko’s. Old Ko’s was in the ground with him, in his top pocket, where it had lived his whole life. But it was the same shape, the same weight, the same kind of spoon nobody made any more, and Jun Hyuk turned it over in his hand and couldn’t say anything.

“An antique shop by the old market,” she said. “I described it. She said this one was from the same years.”

“You remembered.”

“You told me. When you didn’t own towels.”

The last time he’d held a spoon like that, Old Ko had been telling a sixteen-year-old he ate too slowly. Jun Hyuk could have said that. He said, “Thank you,” and kissed her knuckles, and put the spoon back in its box. He didn’t put it away. He left it on the table beside his cup.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nam came up that afternoon with a pot of braised beef and a newspaper under his arm, looked at the cake and the box, and said, “Ah. So you remembered.”

“Get out,” said Jun Hyuk.

Nam ate a piece of cake without asking. Then he unfolded the paper, and put his finger on a short item on page six, and the room changed.

“Something came over the river,” he said. “East crossing, last week. A man of mine at the freight yard saw it. Three vehicles, no markings, after midnight, down the old customs road. They moved people.”

“Who?”

“Somebody they call the Ferryman. He heard one of the drivers say it.”

Evangeline’s hand tightened on her cup. Jun Hyuk saw it without looking at her.

“Tell your man to forget it,” he said. “No questions. No following.”

“He knows.”

“April,” said Jun Hyuk. “I’ll go over in April.”

“You’ll need more than yourself.”

“I know.”

Nam looked at him. Then he looked at Evangeline, who’d gone still, and put both hands flat on the table.

“Before you go chasing men across rivers,” he said, “you should marry her.”

Her cup stopped halfway to her mouth.

“Why are we talking about marriage?”

“Because you keep bringing her here, and she keeps looking after you, and you keep looking at her like the rest of the world is a nuisance. And because you’re going over that river in April. Do it before.”

“The registry’s open on Saturdays,” said Jun Hyuk flatly. “I know. A woman selling chicken told me.”

“I rang them,” said Nam, “to check.”

“You rang the registry?”

“I have a telephone. Somebody in this room should be thinking ahead.” He stood and tucked the newspaper back under his arm, and stopped by Evangeline’s chair. “Eat your cake, child. He won’t finish it unless you make him.”

The door shut behind him. Neither of them said anything for a while.

“Would you?” she said.

“Would I what?”

“Go to the registry.”

She was trying to sound as if it didn’t matter. He could see it in the way she held her shoulders. He wanted to give her the answer that would make her stop worrying, and he’d never in his life made a promise just because it was a comforting thing to say.

“Yes,” he said.

“Before April?”

“If you want that.” He reached across the table and took her hand. “Not because Nam says so before I go. Because I want to come back to you, and I don’t want you sitting here wondering what you are to me while I’m gone. I want you to be my wife, Evangeline.”

He said it plainly. As if he’d been carrying it about for weeks and had finally found somewhere to put it down.

She looked almost frightened by how much she wanted to say yes. Then she smiled. “Then ask properly.”

“Will you marry me?”

She leaned across the table and kissed him before she’d found any words, and kept her forehead against his.

“Yes.”

He shut his eyes. “Good.”

“That’s all?”

“No,” he said, and kissed her again. It wasn’t nearly all.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening he was in the shower behind the sliding door with a waterproof dressing taped over his side, and she was drying the cups, and she heard him say something.

She stopped. At first she thought he was talking to himself the way he talked to the kettle. Then she heard it properly, low under the water.

“E-van-ge-line.”

A pause.

“Evangeline.”

Another pause. Slower. “Evan. Ge. Line.”

She stood with a cup in her hand and didn’t move. He came out ten minutes later with a towel round his neck and found her looking at him.

“What?”

“You were practising.”

He didn’t deny it. He sat down on the end of the camp bed. “I told you in October. That’s not a name. That’s a sentence.” He looked at the towel in his hands. “I can say it to Nam. I can say it to Song. To you, when it’s something that matters, it gets stuck.”

“Why?”

“Because it matters.”

She put the cup down and came and took his face in both her hands, her thumbs by the corners of his mouth, and he held still.

“Say it,” she said.

“Evangeline.”

All four syllables, perfectly, no catch anywhere in it. She bent and kissed him, slowly, her hair falling round both their faces, and when she lifted her head he said it again, and then once more against her mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

She liked the lamp on. He’d never asked her why. That night he turned it to face the wall so the light lay soft across the room instead of on the bed.

“Better?”

“Yes.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

She looked at the narrow camp bed and then at his side. “Your ribs.”

“Are better.”

“That’s not the same as fine.”

“No,” he said. “But I’ll be careful.”

She considered him. Then she reached for the hem of his shirt and drew it up, and he lifted his arms and let her take it off over his head, and she folded it, because she was who she was, and put it on the chair.

“Tell me if anything hurts,” he said, low.

“I will.”

“And if you want me to stop—”

“I’ll tell you.” She put her palm flat on his chest, above the dressing. “I’m not frightened of you. And I’m not doing this because you’re going away in April.” She swallowed. “I want to be here.”

He took her hand and kissed the inside of it. “I want you here.”

He undid the buttons of her cardigan one at a time, watching her face rather than his fingers, and she stood still and let him, though her breath had gone uneven by the third. Underneath it she wore a thin white slip. He pushed the straps off her shoulders and it went down to her waist and he looked at her in the lamplight as if he’d been told he couldn’t, and then bent his head and put his mouth to her collarbone, and the hollow of her throat, and lower. She made a small surprised sound and caught the back of his neck.

She was the one who got him onto the bed. She pushed him down onto his back by the shoulders, carefully, and when he tried to turn towards her she shook her head.

“You’re not allowed to move,” she said. “You’ll pull it.”

“I’m allowed to move a little.”

“A little.”

He laughed under his breath and let her. She knelt over him, the slip gone now, and his hands came up and spread on her waist and held her as if she were something he’d been given and might be asked to give back. He touched her everywhere he could reach. His palm slid down over her stomach, slow, and between her thighs, and she pressed her forehead to his and breathed against his mouth while his fingers moved, gentle and then not so gentle, until she was trembling and holding his wrist there with her own hand.

“Evangeline,” he said, and it didn’t catch at all.

She reached down between them and guided him, and sank onto him by degrees, slowly, her lips parted, her eyes on his, and he went completely still under her with his hands tight on her hips and his head back against the thin pillow, because it was the most anyone had ever given him and he didn’t know where to put it. Then she moved. The camp bed creaked. Neither of them cared. She found the rhythm herself, careful of his side at first and then less careful, and he rose to meet her as much as she’d allow, and murmured an apology when he moved too fast, and she kissed it off his mouth. Her fingers went over the faint lines at the corners of his eyes as if she were learning a face she’d known for months. When it came for her it came all at once, and she cried out and folded down onto his chest with her face in his neck, and he held her through it and followed her with her name in his mouth, all four syllables, broken into pieces.

Afterwards she lay along his good side with her cheek over his heart, and the lamp was still on.

“Comfortable?”

She nodded. “Jun Hyuk. Are you happy?”

The question caught him somewhere he’d forgotten to guard. He thought of the box at West Basin, and two bowls at Nam’s window table, and a silver spoon by his cup.

“Yes,” he said. And then, into her hair, “Very.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Much later, when she was asleep, he eased his arm out from under her. She stirred and her fingers went looking for him and found the edge of the blanket.

“I’m here,” he whispered, and she settled.

There was a reel of black thread in the drawer by the bed, from Nam’s mending basket. He took a length of it and held it a moment. Her left hand lay open on the blanket between them in the light from the wall. He lifted it carefully and wound the thread once round her ring finger, loose enough not to mark, and pinched it at the place where it met, and eased it off. He did it again to be sure. He tied a small knot at the place.

It looked absurd in his hand. He looked at it.

There were things he couldn’t give her: a life without danger, or a promise he’d always be back before dark.

He could give her his name. A place beside him that wouldn’t disappear every time he went out of the door.

He folded the thread and put it in the pocket of his trousers on the chair, and lay down again, and she came back against him in her sleep.

“Jun Hyuk,” she murmured.

She was still asleep. He kissed her forehead.

“I’m here.”

chapters.title: A Silver Ring With Coordinates Inside
chapters.desc: On her real birthday he puts a plain silver ring by her teacup. On Saturday a clerk by the bridge stamps the form, and at four in the morning she finds out why he was in a hurry.
chapters.epigraph: “If I don’t come back, this ring has the coordinates to a life where no one can find you. If I do come back, you’re mine.”
chapters.content:
Nam had bought a hat.

It was an ugly hat, a brown felt thing with a brim, and Jun Hyuk had told him so twice, once when Nam came in wearing it and once when he took it off and put it on the table beside the tea.

“You look like you’re about to rob a bank.”

“And you look like a man who hasn’t slept properly in a month,” said Nam, and picked up the newspaper, and that was the end of it.

It was Friday evening, the seventh of April, and Evangeline had come up on the five o’clock bus from her birthday. Her real one. Her father had kept it with her every year since she was small, the two of them alone, never at the table with the others, because the ninth was the date on her papers and the seventh belonged to the people who’d sent her away. They’d had lunch in his office at the Walled City, and he’d given her a new phone in a pale green case, the first thing he’d ever chosen for her himself instead of sending somebody out for it, and told her she should have something reliable when she was away from home.

She’d thanked him and kissed his cheek and promised to keep it charged. Then she’d brought it three hours north and put it on Nam’s counter beside her old one.

“Your father gave you a phone?” said Jun Hyuk.

“For my birthday.”

He looked at the green case, and then at her, and said, “Good,” and she smiled at him for not saying anything else about her father’s present. When she came back from fetching her bag, the new phone had gone.

“Where did you put it?”

“In Nam’s jar.”

The jar stood between the chilli oil and the soy sauce, where the customers put their phones when Nam told them to. A green phone lay in the bottom now among two spare keys and a brass button that had come off Jun Hyuk’s coat years ago.

“I don’t need two phones,” said Evangeline.

“In a jar?”

“It’s a very safe jar.”

“Excellent security,” said Nam, from behind the newspaper.

She slipped her fingers through Jun Hyuk’s. “I’ll use it when I need it.” He looked at their hands and let it go. She had a way of deciding where things belonged, and once she’d decided, there was no moving her. The phone was in the jar. That was where it would stay.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d been carrying the ring for eleven days.

It was plain silver, a little wider than the ones in the jeweller’s window. No stone, no pattern. For the inscription Jun Hyuk had written a string of numbers on the back of the order form.

“Coordinates? On a wedding ring?”

“Yes.”

The man had wisely stopped asking.

They weren’t anywhere she knew. They belonged to a small house across the river, past the old customs road, that the Ferryman’s people had once used to keep people in before moving them inland. Nobody had used it since the autumn. It had a back door, a working telephone, a water tank, and a lane that went down to a village outside the crossing where nobody asked questions. There’d be a woman there from now on, paid by him, who knew to expect someone and wouldn’t ask why. The numbers were cut inside the band, small enough that you’d only see them if you tilted it to the light.

He hadn’t told her. That night, back in the room with the rain starting again, he put it down beside her teacup.

She’d been reading the same paragraph for five minutes. She looked at the ring, and at him.

“I want to marry you,” he said.

“I know.”

“Tomorrow.”

Her fingers closed round the silver. “Tomorrow?”

“If you still want to.”

She searched his face. There was a tightness round his mouth that hadn’t been there in March. He was calm, and she could see what the calm was costing him.

“Are you in a hurry?”

“Yes.” He reached across the table and covered her hand. “Not to rush you. Because I want to be your husband.”

There was more under it. She could feel it the way she could feel him holding pain behind his teeth. She didn’t want this to turn into an interrogation. She wanted to marry him, and that was the truth she had.

“Yes,” she said.

“Yes?”

“Yes, Jun Hyuk.”

He bent his head over her hand and kissed it. “May I?”

He put it on her finger. It fitted. He sat looking at it, his thumb going over the band and then over her knuckles, and she turned her hand so the silver caught the lamp.

“It’s beautiful.”

“It’s plain.”

“I like plain.” She reached into the pocket of her cardigan. “Now it’s your turn.”

She held out a short length of black thread with a knot in it, and he recognised it at once.

“You kept that?”

“I found it. In your trouser pocket.” She was smiling a little. “You’re not very good at hiding things.”

She took his left hand and wound the thread round his ring finger, careful not to pull it tight, and tied it off, and tucked the loose ends under.

“Black thread,” he said.

“Silver’s for me. Thread’s for you.” She smoothed the knot with her thumb. “Because you measure things when you think I’m not looking. And because I want you to have something that reminds you to come back.”

His face changed. He closed his fingers round hers. “It’s perfect.”

She climbed into his lap before he could say anything else, and he caught her round the waist.

“I’m going to kiss my future husband,” she told him.

“Then I won’t stop you.”

She kissed him with both hands on his face, the new ring cold against his cheek.

✦ ✦ ✦

The River Bridge registry opened at nine on Saturdays. Jun Hyuk was outside it at twenty past eight in a dark shirt and his good jacket, shaved, with a line between his eyebrows that suggested he’d spent the night working out every way the morning could go wrong. Nam came at twenty-five past, in the hat. Evangeline came down River Bridge Road at twenty to nine with Auntie Fen from the chicken stall by the bus stand, who’d been asked on Friday night to be the second witness, had said “Finally,” and had shut the stall for the morning.

Auntie Fen had a small bunch of white freesias from the market tied with ribbon, the paper spotted with oil. She pushed them into Evangeline’s hands on the step.

“You should have flowers,” she said. “Even if it’s for twenty minutes.”

Evangeline took Jun Hyuk’s hand. The black thread was still there under his cuff.

“I thought you might take it off,” she said, “to look respectable.”

“I don’t need to look respectable.”

“That’s true,” said Nam.

The clerk’s room had two desks, a filing cabinet, a framed notice about registration, and a window over the river with the morning light lying on the water. The clerk checked their papers. “Both here of your own free will?”

“Yes,” said Evangeline, and he said it at the same time.

“Good. I have to ask. Any previous marriages?”

“No.”

“No.”

She started on the form. Jun Hyuk stood beside Evangeline with the backs of their hands touching.

“You’re nervous,” she said under her breath.

“No.”

“Your hand’s cold.”

“It’s raining.”

The sky in the window was perfectly clear. “Maybe a little,” he said.

The clerk turned the form round. Evangeline signed, slowly, every letter. He signed underneath. Lee Jun Hyuk. The clerk reached for her stamp and lined the paper up, and in the second while she did it Jun Hyuk turned and put his hand on Evangeline’s cheek.

“Wife,” he said, low.

Her breath went. The stamp came down, a flat official thump, and the clerk said that was that, and he kissed her.

Nothing polite about it for a registry office: he’d been waiting for the sound of that stamp since March. She laughed against his mouth with one hand fisted in the front of his jacket, and he pulled her closer, and something gave under her fingers with a small definite rip.

They broke apart. The seam of his jacket had split at the shoulder.

Nam started laughing. “Married less than a minute and you’ve ruined his clothes.”

“I tore your good jacket,” said Evangeline, horrified.

The clerk, who had seen most things in that room but not this, handed over the certificate. Evangeline took it in both hands and looked at the stamp, and at her name, and at his, and her eyes filled.

“Hey,” he said.

“I’m married.”

“Yes.”

“To you.”

“That’s right,” he said, and kissed her forehead.

Outside on the step Nam took three photographs with his phone. In the first Evangeline was looking at Jun Hyuk. In the second he was looking at her. In the third they were both laughing, and the torn seam was showing, and Auntie Fen was in the corner of the frame with her eyes shut. Nam kept them all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The room looked the same that evening, and wasn’t. Auntie Fen’s freesias were in a jar on the table and the certificate was on the shelf beside the silver spoon, and he’d called her his wife three times since they came in, the last time with his chin on her shoulder at the sink.

“Mrs. Lee,” he said now, turning her hand so the ring caught the lamp.

“Don’t say it like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re surprised.”

“I’m not surprised.” He kissed the ring. “Wife.”

He was healed enough by then that she didn’t have to tell him not to move, and he didn’t let her. He took her cardigan off and then her dress, slowly, and laid her down on the narrow camp bed and knelt between her knees and looked at her in the lamplight for so long that she put her arm over her eyes, and he took it away and kissed the inside of her wrist.

“Let me look,” he said. “I married you this morning. I’m allowed to look.”

He kissed her mouth and her throat and her breasts, unhurried, as if there were no river and no April, and went lower, and held her hips still with his hands when she arched, and put his mouth on her until she was saying his name in a voice she didn’t know she had and gripping the frame of the bed. When he came up over her she pulled him down by the shoulders. He went into her slowly, watching her face, and stopped there with his forehead against hers and his eyes shut as if he had to be sure.

“Wife,” he said again, against her mouth, and began to move.

This time he wasn’t careful. Deep and steady and then not steady at all, the bed complaining under them, her heels at the backs of his thighs, his hand under her head so it wouldn’t knock the frame. She came apart round him with a sound she’d have been embarrassed by on any other night, and he held her through it, and a moment later his whole body locked and he said her name into her hair, all of it, and held on.

Afterwards she lay on his chest with her ring hand spread over his heart. “Wife,” he whispered once more, into the dark.

“I’m here.”

He shut his eyes. For a while he let himself believe the world outside could wait.

✦ ✦ ✦

He got up at seventeen minutes past two.

He eased his arm from under her head and waited till she settled, and dressed in the dark in the clothes he’d put ready. His boots were by the door. His bag was packed. The knife was where he’d left it. On the table he put a folded paper beside the certificate: a copy of the numbers inside her ring. Under it, a note. He’d written it twice before this one.

If anything happens, go to the numbers inside the ring. Someone will be waiting.

Don’t cross the river alone. Call Song.

He hadn’t written goodbye. He couldn’t.

He’d married her first so she’d have something that stayed if he didn’t. He’d told himself he kept quiet to protect her. He knew it was only part of it. If she looked at him and asked him not to go, he’d stay.

He bent and kissed her forehead. “I’m sorry,” he said, and stood up.

At three minutes past four, with his hand on the first lock, he heard her say his name.

She was sitting up in the lamplight with the blanket at her waist. She looked at his boots, and the bag, and the jacket he’d changed into. Then at the table.

“Go back to sleep,” he said.

“Where are you going?”

“Work.”

“At four in the morning?”

She got up and picked up the folded paper before he could reach it, and read it, and read it again, and he watched her understand.

“What’s there?”

“A house. Over the river. If anything happens, you go there. Someone’s waiting.”

“You made this for me.” Her voice had gone quiet. “Before the wedding. You knew you were going.” She looked at the ring on her own hand. “You put the way out inside my wedding ring.”

“If I don’t come back, this ring has the coordinates to a life where no one can find you,” he said. “If I do come back, you’re mine.”

“You married me to bury yourself.”

“That isn’t what I did.”

“Then what did you do?”

“I married you because I wanted to.”

“Then why are you leaving like this?”

He looked away. She stepped closer.

“Look at me.”

He looked. “The Ferryman,” he said. “The man Nam told me about. He owned the route your box came down. Kuang signed for it. Kuang wasn’t the one who ran it.”

She went still. The metal walls came back, and the dark, and a man in a broken doorway with a torch saying Stay behind me.

“And you’re going to find him.”

“Yes.”

“Alone?”

“No. People I trust.”

“And you didn’t tell me.”

“I didn’t want you lying awake all night.”

“Do you think I’d have slept?” She held up her hand with the ring on it. “I said yes to marrying you. Not to being left behind with a map.” She didn’t raise her voice. She didn’t need to. “I know what you are. I knew before I loved you. But you don’t get to decide that my whole part in this marriage is to survive you.”

He shut his eyes.

“Come back to me,” she said.

“I’ll try.”

“No. Don’t give me that answer.”

He opened his eyes and leaned his forehead down against hers. “I will come back.”

“Again.”

“I will come back.”

She took hold of his collar, and before he could do anything about it she pulled him down and kissed him, hard, angry and frightened and in love all at once, and when he drew back for breath she followed him with her fingers still twisted in his collar.

“You stupid ox,” she said.

He stared at her. Then, out of nowhere, he laughed. “Ox?”

“Nam’s right about you.”

“That’s what you call your husband?”

“When he’s being one.” She touched his face. “Don’t make me sorry I married you.”

The laugh went out of him. “I won’t.”

She let go of his collar. “Go and do what you have to do. And come back.”

At the door he turned round. She was standing under the lamp with her hand over the ring.

“Wife,” he said.

“Come home,” said Evangeline.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sunday was the ninth, the date on her papers and her brother’s real birthday, and Ah Sim had made two cakes, the way she did every year. Elowen and Zhao couldn’t come. Zhao still couldn’t sit in a car for that long, and Elowen wouldn’t leave him.

Raiden noticed the ring before the soup. He was sitting next to her, as he always did on the ninth, and her left hand was on the cloth, and he looked at it and then at her. He didn’t ask why nobody had told him. He touched something at his own collar, a habit he had, and asked one thing.

“Is he kind to you?”

She thought of a man practising four syllables in the shower, and of a door closing at four in the morning.

“Yes,” she said. “He is.”

“Good,” said Raiden, and went back to his soup, and didn’t ask where he was.

Her father saw it when he put the fish down. His hand stopped. He looked at her face and then at the band.

“You married?”

“Yesterday.”

He sat down slowly and took her hand and held it with the ring between his fingers and looked at it. He didn’t ask who. He didn’t ask why the man who’d married his daughter wasn’t at his table. He didn’t ask anything at all. After a while he let her hand go and passed her the fish, and lunch went on, and under her sleeve the silver ring sat on her finger with the numbers hidden inside it where nobody at the table could see.

She knew where they led now. She knew why he’d chosen them. And she knew something he hadn’t understood when he went out of the door. A safe house could keep her alive, and a name could make her his wife, and neither of them was the man who’d promised to come home.

chapters.title: The Target Is a Judge
chapters.desc: He comes back over the river after thirteen days with honey and no Ferryman. In June he climbs seven flights to a judge who has left his door unlocked since March.
chapters.epigraph: “I wondered when you’d come. I’ve been leaving the door unlocked since March.”
chapters.content:
Thirteen days.

She hadn’t meant to count.
