On the first morning she’d made a mark on the calendar by Nam’s kitchen door, and on the second she’d crossed it through, and by the fourth she’d stopped looking at the calendar and started listening for feet at the back step instead. By the seventh, Nam had begun leaving the kettle warm for her. By the tenth he’d stopped pretending not to watch her. She went down to the city on the Tuesdays and Saturdays for the market because she’d told her sister she would, and came back up on the next bus, and slept in the room over the Golden Nightingale with the lamp on and the three locks done.

On the thirteenth morning, a Saturday, she was at the corner table with her tea gone cold in both hands when the bell over Nam’s door rang.

He was thinner. His hair had grown. His clothes were dusty to the knee and there was a cut across his lower lip, half healed, and the shadows under his eyes had gone dark as bruises. But he was standing in the doorway, breathing, with a canvas bag in one hand.

“Hello,” he said.

Her chair went over. She didn’t hear it. She crossed the shop and he barely got the bag down before she reached him and put her arms round his waist, carefully, in case of whatever he wasn’t saying, and her face against his chest. He shut his eyes. His hand came up to the back of her head.

“Thirteen days,” she said into his shirt.

“I know.”

“You said you’d come back.”

“I did. I have.”

She held him away to look, the way she’d looked at him with a fever, his face, his throat, his hands, as if she could find everything he was hiding by looking long enough. Then at his mouth.

“It’s small,” he said, before she could ask.

She touched the cut with her thumb, and he flinched, slightly, and her face changed.

“Sit down.”

Nam was behind the counter looking unbearably pleased with himself. “Welcome home. Did you bring anything?”

Jun Hyuk lifted the bag. “Honey.”

Nam looked inside it. “You crossed the river for honey?”

“No.”

“Good. I was worried you’d gone soft.”

Evangeline laughed. It came out broken, and she put her face against his shoulder again, and he said, “Come on. Let me sit down before you start crying.”

“I’m not crying.”

“Course not.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The honey was in a small jar with a handwritten label stuck on crooked, dark amber, nearly gold where the window light came through it. He put it in front of her.

“You liked Nam’s, last winter.”

She’d said so once, eating toast in the room over the bar, that it tasted of something that wasn’t sugar, of a hillside. She hadn’t thought he was listening.

“Did you go to the village?”

“On the way back. It wasn’t far.”

She looked at the dirt on his cuffs. “You’re lying.”

“Probably.”

She cleaned his lip with the brown bottle and he let her. His eyes went to the calendar by the kitchen door, and the row of crossed-through days, and back to her.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“Don’t move.”

He didn’t. When she’d put the box away she sat down across from him, and for a while they only looked at each other. Then she reached across the table.

“Husband,” she said.

He went completely still.

She hadn’t called him that before. She seemed to realise it only after it was out, and her face went pink, and her fingers curled on the tabletop.

“Say it again,” he said.

He wasn’t smiling. His face had gone strangely open, as if she’d put her hand somewhere inside him without warning and he didn’t know what to do with what she’d found there.

“My husband.”

He looked down at their hands. Then he lifted hers and kissed it, and his mouth found the ring.

“Again.”

“Husband.”

He bent his head over her hand. For the first time since she’d known him, Lee Jun Hyuk was so happy he hadn’t a single word for it.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she took the black thread off him.

It had gone filthy. The knot was still there, but the thread had faded and frayed and gone dark where it rubbed, after thirteen days over the river and whatever had cut his lip.

“You should have let me change it before you went.”

“It was still on.”

“That’s not the same as all right.”

She unwound it and tied a new length round his finger, a little tighter, and tucked the knot under. Then she folded the old one small and put it in an envelope and wrote the date on the front.

“You’re keeping it?”

“Every one.”

“It’s dirty thread.”

She looked at him and he stopped. She put the envelope in the drawer under the kettle with the menu. He held his hand out, and she put hers in it, and he turned it over and pressed his mouth to the middle of her palm.

The menu had grown. A week after the wedding she’d written underneath his seven, in her small careful hand:

8. If you’re going to be late, say so. If I’ve been worried, I’ll say so.

He’d read it and said nothing. A few days later another line had appeared under hers, in his.

9. When I’m home, I sleep lying down.

“That’s a rule?” she’d asked.

“Apparently.”

“You made a rule for yourself.”

“Somebody had to.”

Three days after he came back she found him asleep sitting up on the camp bed, boots on, one arm across his chest and his head fallen sideways. She took his boots off. He stirred.

“Lie down.”

“I’m resting.”

She went to the drawer and took out the menu and a pen. He opened one eye. She drew a line through his rule nine, and wrote underneath it:

9. When you’re home, let me look after you too.

He read it twice.

“Now lie down,” said Evangeline, and he did, and caught her wrist before she could get up, and said “Stay,” and was asleep in minutes. She sat with him a long while. He’d spent thirteen days awake. He’d come home with honey and a split lip and tried to behave as if nothing had happened.

“You don’t have to be awake all the time,” she said. He didn’t hear her. That was all right.

✦ ✦ ✦

May was almost ordinary. He went back to work and told her when he’d be late. She went to the market. Nam complained about the price of spring onions. The orchids on the painted sill flowered again. Over the river, the Ferryman had vanished: the route had gone quiet, the vehicles were changing, the men who drove them had new names. Jun Hyuk didn’t talk about it much. He told her what he could without frightening her with the parts that would.

He’d found enough to know the man had friends who’d never been anywhere near a container. People whose names went on official letters. People who could make a complaint disappear with a telephone call.

One of them was a judge.

Judge Chau Wing-hang had heard the Ferryman’s case in February. The man had been arrested, the evidence had been good, and Judge Chau had let him walk out of the courtroom. Not because the case was weak. Because somebody had paid him to find it weak.

The first confirmation came in May. That night Jun Hyuk sat at the table after dinner reading the same page for an hour, and when she put tea down by his hand he thanked her, and when she asked if it was the Ferryman he folded the page.

“It’s connected. I’ll tell you when I know enough.”

He kissed her ring and put the page away.

✦ ✦ ✦

The judge lived alone on the seventh floor of an old narrow building where the lift had been broken since winter. Jun Hyuk spent three weeks learning his days. The cleaner came twice a week and said he’d stopped having visitors in March. His medicines came on Thursdays. A light stayed on all night in the front room. And his front door was never locked.

On the evening of Tuesday the twentieth of June, Jun Hyuk climbed seven flights in no hurry at all, and stood outside it, and pushed it open.

“Judge Chau.”

The flat smelled of medicine and old paper and a meal left on a plate. A television was murmuring the news to nobody. The judge sat in an armchair by the window with a blanket over his knees, an old man, thinner than his photographs, his hair nearly white, and he looked up at the big man in his doorway without any surprise at all.

“I wondered when you’d come,” he said. “I’ve been leaving the door unlocked since March.”

“Why?”

“Because I knew somebody would, in the end.” The old man looked at Jun Hyuk’s hands. “Are you going to kill me?”

Jun Hyuk didn’t answer.

“Perhaps you should. It would be simpler.”

“Why did you let him go?”

Chau shut his eyes, as if that was the question he’d been sitting up for every night. When he opened them he looked older.

“Because I was paid.”

No excuse. No denial.

“How much?”

“Enough to make a coward of me.”

“I want the names.”

“I have them.” He reached towards the table at his elbow, and Jun Hyuk was across the room before his hand got there, and the old man stopped and smiled slightly. “A folder. Still careful, I see.”

It was thick. Handwritten pages, copies of letters, bank transfers, signed statements, some old and some written in the last month in a hand that shook. A deputy director. Two men from the transport authority. A clerk who’d changed a record. A senior officer who’d told a witness to go home. And, on every page, the judge’s own signature.

“Forty-one pages,” said Chau. “I signed every one. The names are in the order they paid me.”

“Why keep it?”

“Because I thought I could undo it. Then I was afraid of prison. Then I was afraid of the people I’d helped.” He looked round his flat. “Then I found I was more afraid of dying with it. I’m dying, you see. The doctors have told me what to expect. I find I’m mostly tired.”

“So you leave the door open,” said Jun Hyuk, “and wait for somebody to come and do it for you.”

The judge didn’t deny it. “I heard about West Basin. The women in the box. That one of them was a young woman from a family that matters. That a man opened the door.” He looked up. “I’ve thought about that door ever since.”

“Do you know how many people went down that road because you signed?”

“No.”

“Then don’t tell me you’re sorry.”

“I won’t.”

He asked for water. Jun Hyuk brought it, and the old man drank with both hands round the glass.

“There’s one more thing,” he said. “The trucks. Years ago, before I was ever on a bench, I was a magistrate on the border commission. The first transfer at the east crossing. I had a telephone call, and I signed an order: let them through, no inspection, no questions. Four that night. More after.” His voice went thin. “I was in the car at the barrier, waiting for my driver. It was raining. The papers got wet in my hand. I remember the soldier at the barrier, a very big young man, who read my stamp in the rain and waved them on.” He looked at the window. “I remember thinking they were only trucks. I didn’t ask what was in them.”

Jun Hyuk didn’t move.

The room narrowed to a point. He could see it too clearly, because he’d been there: rain coming sideways off the river, a stamp gone soft on wet paper, a big young man in a uniform with water running off his cap, his hand coming up, a truck moving forward.

“When,” he said. His voice sounded perfectly ordinary. “What year.”

“Twenty fifteen. The autumn.”

Jun Hyuk looked down at the folder for some time. Then he closed it.

“I’m taking this. Detective Song gets it tonight. You’ll make a statement to him.”

The judge looked surprised. “You’re not going to kill me?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because I won’t do your last cowardly act for you.” At the door he stopped. “You left this open so somebody else would decide what happened to you. You don’t get to choose that any more.”

He went down the seven flights. He left the door open behind him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Judge Chau died at twenty to seven the next morning in the armchair by the window, with the television on and a full glass of water on the table, of the thing his doctors had told him to expect. By the time the doctor rang the building manager and the manager rang the police and somebody rang Song, Jun Hyuk had already sent him everything. Forty-one signed pages, through the secure channel, and a second copy by a different road.

Chau’s confession. Keep the originals. Start with pages six and seventeen.

Song rang within minutes. “Did he give you these?”

“Yes.”

“Did you kill him?”

“No. He was alive when I left.”

A long breath. “There’s enough here to open half a building.”

“Then open it. Don’t let the pages go missing.”

He rang off. He stood in the room over the Golden Nightingale. The folder was gone off the table and the words were still there. A very big young man, who read my stamp in the rain and waved them on. In the drawer under the kettle, rule nine was in her handwriting. He didn’t take it out.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t talk much after that.

On the first day he made her tea and left breakfast by the bed and said he had work, and didn’t kiss her when he went.

On the third he came home after dark and ate her soup without looking up, and said Song had the papers, and nodded when she asked if that was good, and lay on his back in the dark looking at the ceiling. She turned the lamp off. He didn’t reach for her.

On the sixth Nam found him in the little room behind the kitchen with a pistol in pieces on a cloth, cleaning it with the attention he gave everything he could still control. “You look terrible,” Nam said. “Have you eaten? Today?” No answer. Nam put noodles down in front of him and said “Eat,” and stayed, and didn’t ask.

On the ninth she was at the drawer, looking at the envelopes. There were four now, each with a date. She touched the newest and closed the drawer, and turned round, and he was in the doorway.

She went to him. He gave her his hand. She touched the knot of the thread.

“Do you want to tell me?”

She thought he’d say no. Instead he bowed his head. “Chau said he remembered the trucks. At the crossing, years ago. He signed them through.” His voice was low. “He remembered the rain. The papers getting wet. Waiting for his driver. He remembered all that.”

“And the people?”

“He didn’t ask what was in them.”

She put her arms round him. He stood rigid, as if he’d forgotten how. Then his arms came round her.

“You brought it back,” she said into his chest. “Forty-one pages. You didn’t let him take them with him.”

His arms tightened.

“And you didn’t kill him.” She looked up. “I’m proud of you.”

It was small, what happened in his face. Hardly anything. She saw it. He bent and kissed her forehead and then put his face down into her neck and let her hold him there, in the doorway.

The silence didn’t end all at once. That night when she made tea he asked if she wanted honey, and took the jar from the shelf. It was nearly empty. He scraped the last of it into her cup with the silver spoon.

“You kept it,” she said.

“Of course I did.”

He brought her the tea, and sat down on the camp bed beside her, and stretched out his legs, and lay down. She put her head on his shoulder. His hand found hers under the blanket, the ring against his fingers, the thread against her palm. Somewhere in the city men were being named and searched for. Forty-one pages were in Song’s hands. A judge was dead. The Ferryman was still missing. And Jun Hyuk held his wife’s hand and slept, lying down, and let her look after him.

chapters.title: She Asks Nothing
chapters.desc: In the dark her husband tells her about a barrier in the rain and waits for her to leave. Then the typhoon takes the power, and she lights the three candles from the drawer.
chapters.epigraph: “You opened mine.”
chapters.content:
The first thing he said was that he had waved the truck through.

It was the night of the ninth day, the end of June, and the rain had started on the roof. She was lying on her side on the camp bed with her hand on his chest, and he’d been awake. She knew because his breathing had never settled. Every so often his fingers moved on the sheet as if he were counting something he couldn’t see. She didn’t ask what. After nine days she’d learned that sometimes he needed the room quiet before he could find his way back into it.

“Twenty fifteen,” he said.

Her thumb stopped.

“The east crossing. It was raining. My unit had been given the barrier that month, with authority to pass certain vehicles without inspection. The papers came through the car window. A signature and a stamp. I checked both.” His jaw moved. “Then I waved it on.”

The rain came harder.

“Chau was in the car. He was the signature. He remembered a big young soldier reading his stamp in the rain.” He was looking at the ceiling. “That was me.”

Under her palm his heart was going much too fast.

“I didn’t know what was in it. Eleven women. They were dead when it got where it was going.” He said it plainly, with nothing in front of it to soften the number. “I didn’t open it. I didn’t ask the driver to open it. I had the authority to stop it, and I let it go.”

She moved closer, and he flinched, not away from her, but the way a man flinches when he expects a blow.

“How did you find out?”

“Later. We stopped another one, and a man talked, and gave us the route and the dates. By then they’d been gone a month.” His fingers closed on the sheet. “I kept thinking there should have been something. A noise. Somebody shouting. Something that would have made me turn round. I was close enough to see the driver’s face, Evangeline. I could have asked him to open the back.”

She didn’t tell him he couldn’t have known. She didn’t tell him it wasn’t his fault. He wasn’t asking for an absolution she had no right to give. She took her hand off his chest and put it on his cheek, and at last he looked at her.

“There’s more,” he said. “Six men. Not in a fight, not because they had a gun on me. I went and found them because of what they’d done, and killed them. Four before I ever met you. Kuang. The man in December.” His eyes went to her hand. “Some of them should have stood trial. Some would have bought their way out of one, and I didn’t give them the chance. I’ve told myself it was necessary because the courts are slow and the women they sold would never see anything done. Sometimes that was true. Sometimes I just wanted them dead.” He breathed. “I need you to know what I am. I don’t want you waking up one morning married to somebody you don’t recognise.”

She was quiet. He took it for the start of an answer.

“I can arrange somewhere for you. Your father would—”

“Don’t.”

He stopped.

“Don’t arrange anything for me while I’m lying next to you.”

“I should have told you before we married.”

“Yes,” she said.

He looked at her, startled. She didn’t pretend he’d done everything right. Some of what he’d said frightened her. Some of it she’d need time with, and some of it she might never agree with. None of it changed the man lying beside her. The man who’d buttoned his jacket under her chin in a truck at three in the morning. Who’d learned to sleep lying down because she’d written it on a menu. Who’d eaten her crooked dumpling first. Who’d come back over the river with honey, and walked a judge’s confession out into the light instead of giving him the death he’d sat up waiting for.

She leaned in and kissed the corner of his mouth.

“You opened mine,” she whispered. “At the right time.”

His eyes closed. “That doesn’t make it the same.”

“No. It doesn’t.” She held his face. “I don’t think you’re innocent, Jun Hyuk. I think you’ve done terrible things, and saved people, and failed people, and you carry all of it. And I think you’re frightened that if I see the whole of it I’ll go.” She put her forehead against his. “You don’t have to be someone else to be loved by me.”

His face changed. A tightening round the eyes, a breath that shook. Then he turned his head and pressed his mouth into her palm and stayed there.

“I thought you’d leave,” he said.

“I know.”

He drew her in, carefully at first, as if he still wasn’t sure he was allowed. She tucked herself under his chin and listened to his heart going too fast, and stayed until it slowed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The typhoon came on the Saturday.

By the afternoon the river had gone the colour of old steel and the wind was throwing the rain flat against the painted windows. Nam sent a message telling them to stay in.

Jun Hyuk: Understood.

Nam: And don’t come over pretending you need noodles.

He put the phone down without answering, and Evangeline, watching from the counter, smiled.

He’d checked the locks twice. He’d moved the table away from the windows and brought the emergency box through, and put a torch beside her cup where she’d be able to find it. She looked at the torch and then at him.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

He took her tea out of her hand and drank some. “Too hot.”

“You didn’t wait.”

Something heavy hit the side of the building. The lights went twice, and then went out altogether. The fridge stopped. The fan stopped. The rain became enormous.

“Don’t move,” he said, finding the torch.

“I wasn’t going to.” She was already at the drawer. “I know where the candles are.”

There were three. She’d brought them up the stair in November, the first month, along with the kettle and the honey, and they’d never once been lit. She struck a match and held it to the first wick, and the second, and the third, and the room went gold. The storm was still there, leaning on every wall, but the room had got smaller and warmer round them, and the white orchids on the sill were pale shapes in the light.

He was watching her.

“You’re doing it again,” she said.

“Doing what?”

“Looking at me as if you’ve forgotten what you were going to say.”

“I usually know what I’m going to say.”

“Not to me.”

“No,” he said. “Come here.”

She went. His hand settled at the back of her neck and stayed there a moment with his thumb under her ear. Then he kissed her, not cautiously, not with the careful restraint he’d worn since he came back over the river, but as if the nine days had run out of places to hide.

“I’ve wanted to do that all day,” he said, with his forehead on hers.

“You could have.”

“I know.” He looked at her mouth. “Not asking this time.”

“Good,” said Evangeline.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, with the worst of the wind moving inland, she sat on the edge of the camp bed and watched him take his shirt off.

She knew his scars. Some of them she could have found in the dark. The pale line at his shoulder. The small round one under his ribs. The new pink one from February, closed now. Tonight she wanted to count them.

“Come here.”

He came and stood between her knees, and she put her hands at his waist and leaned in and kissed the scar under his collarbone, and he went still.

“How many?”

“Too many.”

“That isn’t a number.”

“Forty-four.”

She looked up. “You counted?”

“Once. Years ago.”

She began again, slowly, touching each one with the tip of one finger. He let her. Some were hardly there. Some were raised and rough. She went from his shoulder across his chest, down his ribs, round to his back when he turned for her, under the candle, counting under her breath. At forty-four she laid her palm flat on his side.

“Forty-four.”

“Yes.”

“I wish you didn’t have them.” She looked up at him. “I’m glad you’re here.”

He bent and kissed her forehead. She took hold of the waistband of his trousers and pulled him down, and he laughed under his breath and caught himself on one hand beside her.

“Impatient.”

“You’ve been home for nine days.”

“I’ve been home.”

“Not properly.”

He undressed her by candlelight, which took a long time because he kept stopping. Her blouse. The clasp at her back, which defeated him, and she laughed at him and undid it herself. He put his mouth to the curve of her breast, and lower, and took his time, and she lay back on the thin mattress with her fingers in his short hair and her breath going ragged. When she drew him up and over her, he paused with his weight on his arms and looked down at her, the question still in him out of habit, and she answered it by wrapping her legs round him and pulling him in.

He sank into her slowly and she held his face and watched him do it. He moved as if he’d been imagining the distance between them for nine days and meant to close every inch of it. She found the places on his back between the scars with her hands and held on. When her breath changed he slowed, and each time she pulled him back, until she was arching off the mattress with his name breaking in her throat and his hand flat under her back, holding her up to him. He followed her with his face in her hair, shaking, and said her name, and she kissed it off his mouth.

The candles shivered in a draught. She lay with her cheek on his shoulder and her fingers resting on the old marks, and the storm went on without them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The camp bed broke at seventeen minutes past one.

It wasn’t dramatic. There was no collapse. There was a sharp, miserable crack from somewhere underneath them, and then a slow and unmistakable tilt of one whole side of the frame.

He froze. She blinked. He looked down at the bed. She looked at him.

“Don’t,” he said.

Her mouth began to shake.

“Evangeline. Don’t laugh.”

That did it. A laugh came out of her, small, and then it wasn’t small at all, it was helpless, and she turned her face into his shoulder and it only made her laugh harder, and the bed creaked again under them.

He stared at the ceiling. “Very sturdy,” he said flatly.

She laughed until her eyes ran. It wasn’t a polite smile or a soft sound made to put somebody at ease. It shook all the way through her, and she hadn’t heard herself laugh like that in years, and he watched her as if he were trying to learn the exact shape of it by heart. Then his own mouth went, and he put his forehead down on hers and laughed too.

“I like that sound,” he said, and kissed the corner of her wet eye.

“Even when it’s because your bed’s broken?”

“Especially then.”

“Perhaps it’s jealous.”

“Of what?”

“Us.”

“You’re blaming the bed?”

“I’m being generous.”

He laughed into her hair. They lay still on the side of the frame that was still standing, trying not to upset it, and after a while he said “I love you.”

Her laughter went.

He wasn’t smiling. He looked almost startled, as if it had come out before he’d decided whether he was ready.

She put her hand on his face. “Say it again.”

“I love you.”

She kissed him, once. “I love you too.”

He shut his eyes. She’d never seen anybody look so relieved.

“I should have said it sooner,” he said.

“You’ve been saying it.”

“Not with those words.”

“No.”

“Then I’ll say it properly. I love you, Evangeline. I’ll say it again tomorrow.”

“I’ll expect you to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning the river was swollen and the streets were full of branches, and the camp bed stood at an angle in the corner like a drunk. He crouched over it with the concentration of a man examining a structural failure, and pressed one hand on the frame, and it gave a small defeated creak.

“Can it be fixed?”

“No.”

“We could buy a proper bed,” she said. “With a mattress. And a headboard.”

“You’re making a list.”

“I am.”

He looked at the broken frame, and at the second camp bed folded against the wall. “Or.”

He dragged the second one out and set it up beside the first, and when one of the joints wouldn’t seat he went to the emergency box for the coil of rope and tied the two frames together, leg to leg, with the calm efficiency of a man who’d spent years making temporary things hold. Then he sat back on his heels.

“Is that safe?”

“Yes. I tied it.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the one you’re getting.”

She sat down on the join. It shifted, and settled, and held.

“That looks a great deal like a married bed,” she said.

He looked at her. “It is a married bed.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nam came up the stair at two with shopping and a bag of fresh noodles, and stopped dead in the doorway.

“What’s that?”

“A bed.”

“Two camp beds.”

“Yes.”

“Tied together. With rope.” Nam turned to Evangeline. “And you agreed to this.”

“I thought it was clever.”

“He’s tied two beds together and told you it’s clever.” Nam bent to look at the knot. “A lorry knot. You don’t call a lorry knot a marriage. That’s ugly.”

“It’s secure.”

“Ugly and secure. Like you.” He straightened up. “Buy a proper one.”

“When the river goes down and you stop asking.”

Nam snorted, and then he looked at Evangeline and his face softened. “Comfortable?”

She looked at the bed, and then at her husband, who’d gone to the counter to put the shopping away and had his back to them.

“Very.”

Nam watched Jun Hyuk for a while, putting the tea in its place and checking the bread, with an ease in his shoulders that hadn’t been there in a week, as if he’d stopped expecting somebody to call him away.

“He looks better,” Nam said, low.

“Yes.”

“Good.” He didn’t ask what had been said in the dark. He folded the empty shopping bag neatly and stopped at the door. “Next time the bed breaks, come over. I’ve got a perfectly good floor.”

“She isn’t sleeping on your floor,” said Jun Hyuk from the counter.

“Then buy a bed!”

Evangeline laughed again. Jun Hyuk turned round with a packet of noodles in his hand and looked at her, and she looked back at him, and neither of them said anything.

That evening he lay beside her on the joined beds. The rope held. The mattresses dipped where they met, so their shoulders touched without either of them moving to make it happen. She put her hand over his heart, and he put his over it.

“I love you,” he said, as he’d promised.

“I love you too.”

Outside the river went up and down under a grey sky. Inside, the three candles were back in their drawer half burnt, and two bad camp beds held a married couple who’d worked out, finally, how to stay.

chapters.title: Her Sister Visits, Carrying Groceries
chapters.desc: Elowen comes up the border road with four bags of shopping and five of their mother’s lemons, and finally asks about the ring. Down on the bridge, her husband waits in a car.
chapters.epigraph: “I married a man who says one word. You found one who says all of them.”
chapters.content:
Elowen came up the side stair of the Golden Nightingale on the eighth of July with four bags of shopping, five lemons, and the expression of a woman who’d been inconvenienced by the entire journey and meant to make it everybody else’s problem.

Evangeline heard her before she saw her.

“Honestly. If I’d known what the road was like I’d have come on a horse.”

She had a bag on each wrist and another in the crook of her arm and a paper sack tucked under her chin, and her hair was coming out of its clip. She stopped in the doorway and looked at the room. Then she put everything down on the floor, took her sister’s face in both hands, and looked at that instead, the cheeks and the forehead and the faint shadows under the eyes, as if she were checking that every part of her had arrived.

“You look well,” said Elowen.

“I am.”

“Eating?”

“Yes.”

“Sleeping?”

“Mostly.”

“Mostly?”

“He snores sometimes.”

“Where is he?”

“On the bridge.” Evangeline looked at the window, where the paint had chipped and you could see a slice of the river. “He saw Zhendong’s car come over. He went down to say hello.”

Elowen’s eyebrows went up. “Zhendong’s waiting in the car because he says it isn’t his business. Your man’s gone to make it his business.” She picked the bags up again. “Show me your kitchen.”

He’d given Elowen the address himself, on the telephone, after Evangeline asked him to. That was how she knew he meant it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The room had changed since Elowen had last pictured it, which was from a description Evangeline had given her in February in about a dozen words. It was still bare walls and practical furniture. But there was a kettle by the window and two mugs that matched, a brass lamp, folded blankets, white orchids on the painted sill, a photograph of the river, a jar of freesias gone papery and kept anyway. And in the inner room, through the sliding door, two camp beds tied together leg to leg with a length of rope.

Elowen stopped. She looked at it for some time.

“Don’t,” said Evangeline.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face has.”

They unpacked at the counter. Rice, eggs, ginger, dried mushrooms, cooking oil, tea, a packet of biscuits, a small jar of honey.

“I didn’t ask you to bring anything,” said Evangeline.

“I know. That’s why I brought it.”

The lemons were wrapped separately in an old tea towel so they wouldn’t bruise. Five of them, uneven and fragrant, still green round the stalks. Evangeline picked one up and rolled it between her palms and the smell came up bright and sharp, and she was small, in a garden at the Walled City, and their mother was standing under the tree with a basket, and Elowen was complaining that the branches were too high.

“Mama’s tree,” she said.

“I picked them myself. It’s growing into the wall. Zhendong says he’ll cut it back.”

“He won’t.”

“No. He won’t.” They smiled at each other over the lemons. “Mama always said they were sweeter if you picked them after rain.”

“It rained on Thursday.”

“I know,” said Elowen. “I waited.”

She put the lemons in a bowl and sat down at the table, and Evangeline sat across from her, and Elowen looked at her sister’s left hand. She’d seen it at the door. She’d said nothing while she checked her face, nothing while they unpacked. She hadn’t forgotten.

“Can I see?”

Evangeline turned the ring round and round on her finger. Then she held her hand out across the table.

Elowen took it. Plain silver. No stone. You’d miss it unless you knew to look.

“How long?”

“Since April.”

“April?”

“The eighth.”

“And you didn’t tell me.”

“I wanted to.” Evangeline looked at the window, at the slice of river. “I was afraid.”

“Of me?”

“Of everything changing.”

“Has it?”

She thought about it. A broken bed and three candles. A coin in a pot in Nam’s yard. His shirts hanging next to hers. The way he took her hand without looking when they walked anywhere.

“Yes,” she said. “Not the way I was afraid of.”

And then, directly, to her sister’s face: “I’m married.”

Elowen didn’t move. She looked as if she’d heard something in another language and was waiting for it to mean something. Then her eyes filled.

“Oh, Evangeline.”

She came round the table and held her, one hand going over the back of her head the way it had when they were small and Evangeline woke up from the dreams she never talked about.

“I’d have come,” Elowen said. “If you’d told me. I’d have brought groceries.”

Evangeline laughed into her shoulder. “You did.”

“Who else knows?”

“Nam. Auntie Fen, who sells chicken by the bus stand. She signed as a witness. Baba and Raiden saw the ring.”

“A woman who sells chicken knew before I did.”

“She told him to marry me. In December.” She held on. “Don’t tell anyone else. Not even Zhendong. Not yet.”

Elowen went quiet against her. She had never in her marriage kept a single thing from her husband.

“All right,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car was parked at the far end of the bridge under a camphor tree, a dark saloon with the engine off. The driver’s window came down as Jun Hyuk reached it.

Zhao Zhendong looked at him. Jun Hyuk looked back. They’d never met, and each of them knew more about the other than he’d have liked.

“So you’re the one,” said Zhao.

“I suppose I am.”

“Elowen said her sister had somebody up here. She didn’t say who.”

“No,” said Jun Hyuk. “She wouldn’t.”

Zhao didn’t waste words. He had the face of a man who’d spent years making decisions under pressure and keeping people safe without telling them what from, and Jun Hyuk knew that kind of silence well enough not to fill it straight away.

“She came to me,” Zhao said, “the week after the box. She wouldn’t go home. She kept asking about a man whose name she didn’t know. She remembered your jacket. And the menu on your dashboard.”

“She’s got a good memory.”

“I told her to stay away from you.”

“I heard.”

“She didn’t listen.”

“No,” said Jun Hyuk, looking up the hill at the side of the Golden Nightingale. “She doesn’t. I wanted to thank you.”

“For what?”

“For telling her the truth about me and letting her decide.”

Zhao’s mouth moved. It might have been a smile. It might not.

“You kill men who move people,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I move rifles.”

“I know. Velde.”

Zhao’s face changed, only slightly, and Jun Hyuk saw it.

“In April,” said Jun Hyuk. “I was over the river thirteen days, after the Ferryman. His route goes up past the old customs road to a crossing nobody watches. Your refusal went out in March on the lawyers’ letterhead. The brokers went looking for another carrier. They found the Ferryman’s trucks.” He kept his voice level. “They didn’t cross.”

“You stopped them.”

“Some of the men behind them, I found. The rifles didn’t get to the highlands.”

Zhao looked out along the river.

“How many died?”

“Fewer than would have, if they’d got there.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“It wasn’t mine to tell. And you don’t know me.”

“You’re not very good at explaining yourself.”

“I’ve been told.” Jun Hyuk glanced up the hill again. “I’m better at talking.”

“Elowen said that too.” Zhao’s face eased, a little. “She seems happy. Evangeline.”

“She is.”

“Are you?”

He hadn’t expected the question. The answer came more slowly. “Yes.”

“Then keep her that way,” said Zhao, and the window started to go up.

“Zhao.”

It stopped halfway.

“Thank you for not making her choose between you and me.”

Zhao looked at him through the gap. Then the window closed. The car stayed under the camphor tree, and Jun Hyuk walked back up the hill.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came up the stair talking.

“There’s a camphor tree at the end of that bridge older than Nam, and your husband’s parked under it with the engine off so he can’t run the fan, Elowen, he’ll be boiled. I said so. He didn’t answer. Is that normal? Did you get up here all right? That stair’s got a loose board on the turn, the fourth from the top, I keep meaning to fix it. You brought lemons. You brought a lot of rice.” He’d stopped in the doorway. Both sisters were looking at him. “What?”

Elowen looked at Evangeline. “He’s always like this?”

“With people he likes.”

“I married a man who says one word,” said Elowen. “You found one who says all of them.”

Then she stood up and came across the room and pointed one finger at his chest.

“Elowen,” said Evangeline.

“No. Let me finish.” Elowen held his eyes. “If you hurt her, I will find you. I don’t care how far you go or how many people are frightened of you. I will find you.”

“I understand.”

“And if she cries because of you, I’ll make you regret it.”

“Understood.”

She looked almost disappointed by how calmly he took it.

“He isn’t frightened of you,” said Evangeline.

“He’s sensible enough to pretend.” Elowen kept the finger where it was. “Do you love her?”

There was no gap at all. “Yes.”

“Are you kind to her?”

“Whenever I can be.”

“That wasn’t the question.”

“I know.” He looked at Evangeline, and back. “I try. When I don’t manage it, I try to put it right.”

Elowen looked at him a while longer, searching for something under the answer. Then she let her hand drop, and folded her arms.

“Well. Brother-in-law.”

He blinked. Nobody in her family had called him that.

“Don’t look so surprised. You’ve been married to my sister for three months.” She glanced through the sliding door. “What happened to the other bed?”

“It broke,” said Evangeline.

“How?”

He went to put the rice away. “It was old.”

“Of course,” said Elowen. “Buy a proper one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t tell Zhao.

He asked in the car, on the long road south, whether Evangeline had seemed well. Elowen said yes. He asked if there was anything he should know. She said no. He asked why she’d taken so much shopping, and she said her sister hadn’t been eating properly, which was true. All of it was true except the most important thing. She didn’t tell him her sister had a husband, or that she’d met him, or that she’d looked at a plain silver ring on Evangeline’s hand and seen a kind of happiness she’d once thought her sister would never be allowed.

She didn’t think he’d be cruel. She knew he’d worry. He’d want to know the man’s history, his enemies, his work, and he’d stand between Evangeline and every danger he could think of, because that was the only way he knew how to love anyone. And Evangeline had spent long enough behind other people.

“Did you enjoy seeing her?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Then why are you smiling?”

“Because she’s happy.”

He looked at her sideways. “That’s a good reason.”

She turned to the window. It was the first thing she’d ever kept from him. She understood, now, why her sister had.

✦ ✦ ✦

The lemons took most of the evening.

“Salt first,” Evangeline said. “Then you pack them tight, so they’re covered.”

He stood at the counter with her and did as he was told, badly. She’d washed and dried each one and cut a cross into the end the way their mother had, not quite through, and he was supposed to open it with his thumbs and pack the salt in and press it down into the jar.

“Not like that.”

“How?”

“Turn it. Now press. Gently.”

He pressed.

“You’re crushing it.”

He let go. She laughed, and he picked up the next one.

“Show me.”

She put her hands over his on the lemon. “Here. You have to leave room for the salt.”

“I see.” He wasn’t looking at the lemon.

“You’re not learning.”

“I am.”

She tried to look stern and her mouth wouldn’t do it, and he bent and kissed her with salt on both their hands. When he drew back she put her palm on his cheek.

“I told her,” she said.

He stared at her. Then he took her by the wrist and pulled her away from the counter, and she laughed as he led her across the room to the steel door, the same door she’d once stood beside deciding whether to leave, and put his hand on her waist and kissed her against it. He didn’t kiss her like someone asking if he was welcome. He kissed her like a husband who’d just found out his wife had said it out loud to somebody who mattered, and found it terrifying and unbearably sweet at once.

“You told her,” he said, when he let her breathe.

“I did.”

“That we’re married.”

“Yes, Jun Hyuk.”

He put his forehead on hers. “You told her.”

“Are you going to keep saying that?”

“Probably. I like hearing it.”

She touched the ring. “Then hear it again. I’m your wife.”

“Yes.”

“And you’re my husband.” She pushed him gently in the chest. “Now let me finish the lemons.”

They sealed the jar just before midnight. She wiped the glass and set it on the shelf beside the tea, and the lemons glowed through it, bright against the salt.

“Three months,” she said.

He stood behind her with his arms loose round her waist. “Three months.”

“When they’re ready, I’ll make dinner.”

“What dinner?”

“Something with lemons.”

“That doesn’t tell me anything.”

“You’ll find out.”

He put his chin on her hair. Outside the river moved in the dark. Five lemons off their mother’s tree had come up the border road in a tea towel and were sitting on a shelf in the room where she’d decided to make a life, and she could wait three months. She’d waited a great deal longer than that for something that felt like home.

“What are you thinking?” he asked.

“That Elowen knows. And she called you brother-in-law.”

“I heard.”

“What did it feel like?”

He was quiet. “Like something I didn’t know I wanted.”

She turned round in his arms. “Then you’ve got it.”

There was no road waiting for him beyond the door that night. No name to follow, no man to find. There was the jar on the shelf and her hand in his, and three months to wait.

chapters.title: She Wants a Window Box
chapters.desc: Strangers are asking about him at the border, so he moves them to a sixth floor with windows nobody can shoot through. They don’t open. She mentions basil once.
chapters.epigraph: “Basil would grow there.”
chapters.content:
The first man asked about him on a Tuesday in August.

He came into Nam’s just before closing, ordered nothing, and stood at the counter long enough for Nam to notice he wasn’t looking at the menu.

“Lee Jun Hyuk,” he said.

Nam went on wiping the counter. “Never heard of him.”

“Big man. Quiet. Spends time by the river.”

“Then ask the river,” said Nam.

Two days later a second man stood outside the bakery by the bridge where Nuo worked now, the job Nam had found her in the spring, and asked her if she’d seen somebody tall with a scar through one eyebrow. She said no, and went inside, and rang Evangeline with her hands shaking. A third man asked nobody anything. He sat on a motorbike at the end of the border road for an afternoon, watching the side stair of the Golden Nightingale, and was gone when one of Nam’s neighbours walked over to ask what he wanted.

By Friday Jun Hyuk had four reports. He didn’t tell her straight away. He watched her water the orchids and listened to her talk about the price of eggs, and let her put too much ginger in the soup, and checked the locks before bed. She noticed anyway. She’d learned the difference between his ordinary quiet and the kind that meant he’d already decided something.

On Saturday morning he put a cup of tea down by her hand. “We’re moving.”

“Where?”

“The city.”

“Why?”

“People have been asking about me.”

“How many?”

“Enough.”

“Because of the Ferryman?”

“Or because of the men who worked for him and want to know where their friends went.” He sat down across from her. “Nam’s all right. Nuo’s all right, I’ve talked to her. Zhao knows. It isn’t them I’m worried about.” He turned her hand over and ran his thumb once across the ring. “I don’t want somebody deciding it’s easier to ask you than to ask me.”

She looked at the window, at the slice of river through the chipped paint. She thought of the bridge, and Nam’s cats asleep in the yard, and the pot by the back wall with a coin under it.

“Today?”

“If you’re ready.”

She was quiet a long moment. Then she nodded. “Let me pack the lemons.”

He blinked. “The lemons?”

“They won’t be ready till October. I’m not leaving them.”

He looked at the jar on the shelf, gone deep gold. “All right,” he said, and started clearing the table, and she watched him.

“Is it somewhere safe?”

He came back round and crouched until their eyes were level. “Yes.”

She believed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The building had a textile company’s name over the door: six floors of offices and storage in an ordinary street in an ordinary part of the city, with a narrow lobby and a man at a security desk, vans in and out of the loading bay, a café on the ground floor. He drove into the garage underneath. A key card took the lift to the sixth floor, and the doors opened on a quiet corridor with one flat at the end of it.

It was bigger than the room over the bar and not grand at all. A long living room with a wide sofa. A dining table. A proper kitchen with a real stove and an oven. Two bedrooms, a bathroom with a bath in it, a little utility room. No photographs, no orchids, nothing of theirs yet.

And the windows were enormous.

She went straight to them. The city lay six floors down, roofs and traffic and towers gone soft in the summer haze. She put her hand on the handle. It didn’t move.

“Jun Hyuk? The window.”

“It doesn’t open.”

“None of them?”

“No. Reinforced glass, armoured frames. The air comes through the vents.”

“Could someone shoot through it?”

“No.”

She laid her palm on the glass. It was so clear she felt she could step through it. She knew it was safer than the border road, safer than a room strangers could stand under and ask for her husband by name. She still looked at it.

He came and stood behind her. “You don’t like it.”

“I like the view. I can’t open it.” She leaned back against him. “Will I get used to it?”

“Maybe.” He put his arms round her. “We’ll make it ours. The orchids. The coin. Your lemons.”

“Already packed?”

“First thing in the van.” He kissed the top of her head. “Come on. There’s something I want to show you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was on the fifth floor, behind a door he unlocked with a key from his own ring. She’d thought it would be the textile company’s storeroom. It was a dozen wooden crates with metal corners, and one of them stood open.

Bundles of notes in paper bands. Small boxes of gold bars. Sealed packets that rattled, which turned out to be stones. Another crate full of ledgers and a jangle of old keys.

She looked at all of it, and then at him. “Why do you have so much money?”

“It’s accumulated.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

His own words. His mouth moved. “Some came from jobs. Some from property. Some from things I bought and didn’t sell.”

“Property?”

He looked at the ceiling. “This building. And the one next door.”

She stared at him. “You own this building.”

“Yes.”

“And the one next door.”

“Yes.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I didn’t think it was important.” She gave him a look, and he corrected himself. “I didn’t think it was relevant.”

“Are they from the people you worked with?”

“Some were paid before I owned the company. Some were payment for work. Some I kept instead of changing them into anything.” He didn’t sound proud of it, or ashamed either. It was a part of his life that had been there before she came, that was all.

“Are we rich?”

He thought about it. “We’re comfortable.”

“That’s a very strange word for this room.”

“I don’t like rich. People think it tells them something about you.”

She looked at the gold more, and then she took his hand. “Does it make you happy?”

He looked down at their fingers. “No.”

“Then I don’t suppose it matters very much.”

“You’re not going to ask for anything?”

She looked at him, genuinely puzzled. “What would I ask for?”

He had no answer. She squeezed his hand and went out, and he stood a while longer by the open crate. He’d expected questions. He’d expected her to work out what the money meant and what kind of man kept it in boxes. He hadn’t expected her to ask whether it made him happy. He shut the lid and followed his wife upstairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

She unpacked the kettle first. Then the jar of lemons. Then the pot from Nam’s yard, which she set on the kitchen counter in the light. When she went to make tea there were already tins in the top cupboard: hers, his, and the ginger Elowen had brought in July.

“You bought tea.”

“I knew you’d want tea.”

She kissed him for that, and he caught her hand before she could turn away and took something out of his pocket. It was the noodle menu. Soft at the folds now, the ink faded, her eight under his seven, his nine crossed out and rewritten in her hand. He flattened it on the counter and uncapped a pen.

10. SHE NEVER PAYS.

“Excuse me?” said Evangeline.

“Rule ten.”

“I can read.”

“Good.”

“I don’t agree.”

“I know.”

“I have my own money.”

“I know.” He put three bank cards down on the counter one after another. “One for the house. One for you. One for if something happens, and you don’t touch that one unless it does.”

She didn’t pick them up. “Is this because you think I can’t look after myself?”

“No.” He leaned on the counter. “You shouldn’t ever have to ask me for money when you want something. You’ve spent your whole life being told what you could have and where you could go. Not here.”

Her face softened. “And what if I want to buy you something?”

He considered this. “Use your own money.”

“So rule ten has an exception.”

“No. That’s different. It’s for me.”

She laughed, and he folded her fingers round the cards. She looked at the menu a moment longer. Then she took the pen out of his hand and wrote underneath, small:

He is allowed to be spoiled too.

“That’s not a rule,” he said.

“It is now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first week in the city was quiet. No neighbours who knew them, no noodle shop at the end of the road, no cats at the back step. There was the lift and the security desk and the city going about its business under the sealed glass.

The first time she used the household card she bought rice, vegetables, milk, eggs and a packet of biscuits. He looked at the bags.

“That’s all?”

“We don’t need more.”

He reached for the receipt. She took it out of his hand.

“Don’t inspect my groceries.”

“I wasn’t inspecting. I was reading.”

She gave him a look, and he smiled, and she went to the kitchen.

Later she was at the stove and she was humming, and he stopped in the doorway.

It was a tune he hadn’t heard since the crossing. A few notes going round and round with a rough little lift at the end. It had belonged to his unit, a work song one of the older men had started when they were hauling equipment through the rain, and the rest had picked up. Nobody had ever written it down.

“Where did you hear that?”

She looked round. “What?”

“That song.”

“I don’t know.”

“Sing it again.”

She did. It was softer in her voice, slower, almost cheerful, and he knew every turn of it.

“I’ve never sung you that,” he said.

“Then I heard it somewhere.”

“Is it sad?” she asked, going back to the soup.

“No. It’s for carrying things.”

“Teach me the words.”

“Maybe later.”

The song belonged to a muddy road and heavy boxes and men who’d been young enough to believe a good rhythm could make anything lighter. He hadn’t thought of it in years. And here was his wife humming it at a stove six floors over the city. He came up behind her while she stirred and put his arms round her waist and his mouth to the side of her neck, and she went still and then leaned back into him, and when he did it again she turned round in his arms with the spoon still in her hand and kissed him properly against the counter until the soup caught.

“You hum it when you’re asleep,” she said, against his mouth. “That’s where. You don’t know you do.”

He didn’t know what to say to that. He kissed her again instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nuo rang on a Wednesday.

“Are you busy?”

“No. What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.” Nuo laughed. “I always ring as if something’s wrong. I’m at work. The morning finished early. I burnt two trays of rolls yesterday and the manager told me to think about nothing except the oven.” A pause. “I like it. I like knowing what I’m doing tomorrow. I like that the bread has to rise and you can’t hurry it.”

“I’m glad.”

“I’m thinking of training to be a nurse. There’s a course that takes people with no experience. It’ll be years.”

“Apply.”

“You make it sound easy.”

“It won’t be easy. Apply.”

Nuo was quiet a moment. “I want to be the one who knows what to do when somebody’s frightened.”

“You’d be very good at that,” said Evangeline.

When she rang off she sat with the phone in her hand, smiling. For the first time since the box she could think of Nuo without seeing the dark inside it. She could see her behind a counter with flour on her sleeves and bread cooling on racks. She wanted to keep that.

“Tell her congratulations,” said Jun Hyuk, from the sink.

✦ ✦ ✦

The kitchen became her favourite room. It had a good stove and deep drawers and enough counter for two people, and a window over the city that didn’t open. She’d tried it twice more. He’d reminded her both times. She’d nodded both times and gone on looking at it as if the glass might change its mind.

One evening, drying the dishes, she said, “Basil would grow there.”

He looked up from the sink. “Where?”

“On a ledge. If there were one.” She nodded at the window.

He looked at the glass. “Would it get enough light?”

“Probably.”

“How much water?”

“Not much. Why?”

“Just wondering.”

She smiled and kissed his cheek and went out. He stood there with his hands in the water, looking at the window.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three in the morning he was standing in front of it with a measuring tape.

The city was dark except for scattered lights in the towers across the road. A motorbike went by far below and faded out. He measured the width of the glass and the depth of the frame and wrote it down in a small notebook, and measured again. Sealed into an armoured frame. No mechanism. No ledge. Nothing you could safely fix to the outside.

He stood back. A narrow planter on the inside might work, with drainage and a tray. Deep enough for roots. He could have one made to fit. He measured the floor.

“Jun Hyuk?”

She was in the hall in her nightdress with her hair loose, blinking at him. She looked at the notebook, and the tape, and the window.

“Are you measuring for a window box?”

He didn’t answer.

“At three in the morning?”

“I couldn’t sleep.”

“Because of basil?”

He put the tape down. “Go back to bed.”

She came closer instead and put her hands flat on his chest. “I only said it once.”

“I heard you.”

She came up on her toes and kissed him. He held her by the waist.

“You don’t have to make everything happen at once,” she said.

“I know.”

“We can wait.” She looked at him. “But you’re going to do it.”

He looked at the glass. “Yes.”

She smiled, and he kissed her again, slower, and took her hand and walked her back to bed, and the notebook stayed on the sill with the tape folded beside it.

✦ ✦ ✦

A week later a drawing came. He put it on the counter by her cup without saying anything.

A narrow wooden planter sized to sit under the kitchen window, with a removable tray and drainage holes and room for several small pots.

“You had it made?”

“Not yet. I measured.”

“At three in the morning.” She ran a fingertip round the outline. “Basil. Mint. Rosemary, perhaps.”

“All right.”

“Flowers?”

“If they’ll grow.”

She held the drawing against her chest and came round the counter and put her arms round him.

“Thank you.”

“It’s only a box.”

“No,” she said. “It’s a little piece of outside.”

He looked at her and touched her cheek. Outside, the city went on without them. The guards downstairs knew who to ring if anybody came asking. And on the sixth floor, under the sealed glass, there was a space measured out for basil, and the window looked a little less like a wall.

chapters.title: He Builds One Anyway
chapters.desc: A steel box six floors up, a hatch in the glass, and a pair of mended earrings. Then her sister’s wedding, which her husband attends from a roof across the street.
chapters.epigraph: “Good mend.”
chapters.content:
The first problem was that the window box couldn’t be fixed to the window. The second was that Evangeline wanted it outside, where the rain could get at it. Jun Hyuk found out both things in the first ten minutes with the contractor.

“The glass is armoured,” the man said, tapping the drawings. “We can’t drill the frame. And we can’t hang anything off the outside without compromising the whole system.”

“What if it’s carried by the wall underneath? The structural wall.”

The contractor thought about it. “That can be done. It’d need to be steel, and it’d need to be bolted into the frame of the building. Six floors up, you don’t want it coming off in a typhoon.”

“Then make it steel.”

He showed the man the measurements he’d taken at three in the morning, and the man looked at them for a while.

“That’s not a window box,” he said. “That’s a small balcony.”

“Fine,” said Jun Hyuk.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the first piece of steel in the living room on a Thursday afternoon, wrapped in cloth and leaning on the wall, with a box of bolts beside it and a new set of drawings. He was in the utility room on the phone with his sleeves rolled up and a smear of black grease across one wrist.

The planter would sit outside the kitchen window in an armoured steel case on a frame sunk into the building, with a removable tray and a channel for the water. And there was a square drawn into the glass above it.

“What’s this?”

“The hatch.” He came out, still holding the phone. “A glazier designed it. A small opening in the window, its own sealed frame, a lock. The rest of the glass stays as it is. They’re testing it before it goes in.”

“Does it open?”

“That’s the idea.”

“So I can reach the plants.”

“So you can reach the plants.”

She looked at the grease on his wrist. “How long have you been doing this?”

“Since the day you said basil.”

“That was weeks ago.”

“I know.”

She put the drawing down and went to him and put her arms round his waist, grease and all, and he looked down at her.

“I only said basil would grow there.”

“I heard you.”

“You didn’t have to build a balcony.”

“It’s not a balcony,” he said, and she laughed into his shirt.

The fitting took two days. She wasn’t allowed near the window while they tested the frame. She stood in the kitchen doorway with tea and biscuits and questions, and he answered all of them. He had the bolts checked twice and the seal tested again and made the glazier work the lock in front of him three times before he’d sign for it. By the second afternoon a dark steel box sat outside the glass with room in it for nine small pots, and above it, set into the window, was a little square with a clean frame and a handle.

She knelt on the counter and turned the handle. The hatch opened inwards. Outside air came into the kitchen.

It smelled of rain and warm concrete. A horn went somewhere six floors down. She shut her eyes and breathed it in.

“Outside,” she said.

He was right behind her. “Outside.”

She said it as if he’d brought her something enormous. She turned round on her knees on the counter with her hair blowing, took his face in her hands, grease on his jaw and all, and kissed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the plant market on the far side of the city she walked slowly and he followed with a basket. She stopped at the basil. He picked up two pots. She looked at the mint. He picked one up. She paused by the rosemary, and by a little pot of thyme.

“You don’t have to buy everything I look at.”

“You looked at it.”

“For three seconds.”

“Three seconds is enough.”

She touched a pot of lemon balm. It went in. A pot of purple flowers. In. When she bent towards a small plant with white starry blossoms, he reached for that too, and she caught his wrist.

“We’ve got nine places.”

“Eight.”

“There’s one in your hand.”

He looked at it. She took it from him.

“We’ll have this one too.”

“That’s ten.”

“Yes,” said Evangeline.

“Your husband’s very generous,” said the woman at the till.

“He is.”

He paid. She took the receipt out of his hand, folded it small, and put it in her bag, and he watched her do it and didn’t ask why.

✦ ✦ ✦

The earrings were an accident.

On the way back she wanted to look in a window on Harbour Road, a narrow shop with dark cabinets and warm lights and a jeweller’s name in gold across the glass. She knew the name. It was Aurelia Chen’s, who’d been at school with Elowen and was married to Chen Si, and whom Evangeline had met twice at her sister’s and said perhaps four words to. Aurelia was behind the counter herself, with a loupe on a ribbon round her neck. She looked up and knew her at once, and was too well brought up to look past her at the man in the doorway.

“Evangeline.”

“I like looking at old things.”

“Then come and look at mine.”

Among the new pieces she kept a tray of old ones she’d bought and mended. A silver brooch. A bracelet with a clasp that had clearly been repaired more than once. Evangeline stopped at a pair of earrings, pale aquamarines set in gold, and the gold round one stone had been mended along a fine bright line that ran through the setting like a second design.

“These are beautiful.”

“They were broken when I found them. The setting was very fragile.”

“You didn’t hide the repair.”

“No. I thought it ought to be seen.” Aurelia took them off the tray and laid them in Evangeline’s palm. “The piece survived. I didn’t want to pretend it hadn’t been broken.”

Evangeline said nothing. Then she nodded. “I like that.”

Jun Hyuk had come up behind her. “Do you like them?”

“Yes.”

“Then have them.”

She looked at the price, and then at him, and he sighed.

“All right. I’ll wait.”

She gave them back. “Another time. Thank you for showing me.”

Outside she slipped her hand into his. “You wanted to buy them.”

“I wanted you to have them. Why didn’t you?”

“I liked them,” she said. “That doesn’t mean I need to own them.”

He thought about that, and nodded, and they walked on. He went back on his own three days later. Aurelia recognised him.

“The aquamarines,” he said.

“I wondered if you would.”

He asked what had happened to the setting, and she told him, and he listened, though he cared nothing for jewellery. He cared that his wife had held them in her palm and looked at a mended line of gold as if it had said something to her. He paid.

“Tell her I hope she enjoys them,” said Aurelia, and didn’t ask him a single other thing.

Evangeline found the box by her teacup. She was in one of his shirts, hair still wet from the bath. She opened it and looked at him.

“You went back.”

“Put them on.”

He fastened them for her, carefully, his big fingers slow at her ears, and stepped back.

“Beautiful.”

She touched one. “The earrings?”

“No,” he said, and she kissed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

By September the steel box was a garden. The basil came up fast. The mint went everywhere with alarming confidence. Rosemary and thyme and lemon balm settled in beside it and the little white flowers opened. She watered them every morning and sometimes opened the hatch only to let the air in, and he learned the sound of the latch, and looked up from whatever he was doing every time he heard it. Not to check on her any more. Because he liked knowing she was standing there.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen and Zhao had been married for three and a half years, and on Saturday the twenty-third of September they had the wedding they’d never had, in her flower shop, with the shutters down and the whole place full of white.

Evangeline went early, on her own, with a small pot held in both hands. She put it on the counter in front of her sister. A young orchid, two green leaves and one new root curling over the edge of the soil.

“Mama’s,” she said. “The one by the kitchen window. Everyone said it had died. I kept watering it. In June there was a shoot.” She looked at Elowen, at the shop, at the arch Raiden had built out of old salt-grey timber. “You’ve got a good life. I wanted it here today.”

She was in a soft blue dress and the aquamarines, and Jun Hyuk wasn’t with her. He’d said he would come separately. Too many people there would know his face, or know somebody who did, and it was her sister’s day; he wasn’t going to stand in the middle of it and make the guests look at the doors. He’d told her where he’d be. When she came out of the shop at noon she didn’t look for him, and she didn’t need to.

At four her brother came in with Jinx. Jinx was carrying the bottom tier of Elara’s cake in a steel box she’d made to keep it level on the bike, and on the step she took a ring out of her pocket and put it on, and Raiden broke the string he wore at his neck and put his on too. He walked into the middle of thirty people holding her hand.

“Everyone,” he said. “This is Jinx. My wife. She built Xiao Pan’s bike. Don’t touch her tools.”

The shop went silent.

“Since when?” said Eliana.

“Two years next Saturday.”

Evangeline stood by the coolers and looked at him. She thought of the ninth of April, the soup, his hand going to his collar, and Is he kind to you? and nothing else, no other question at all. Raiden found her eyes across the room. She touched her own ring with her thumb. He saw, and the corner of his mouth went, and that was all either of them said about it.

Later Jinx came and stood beside her by the door. Evangeline had already seen the man across the road, in a grey jacket, standing at the bus stop and letting two buses go. Bao had moved him on twice. Jinx had seen him too. The two of them watched the street together without a word.

The ceremony was at six. Their father walked Elowen up between the chairs and put her hand in Zhao’s, and then came and sat in the front row beside Evangeline and held her hand instead, and didn’t let go of it till it was over. There was no celebrant; there was no paper to sign, they’d signed it years ago. Chen Si stood by Zhao. Aurelia stood by Elowen. Zhao kissed his wife under the arch with both hands on her face, slowly, in front of everybody, and the shop cheered.

Song Wei Long had come in a dark suit. He didn’t sit. He stood at the window most of the evening, and every so often he looked up at the roof of the building across the street, where nothing could possibly be, and then at Evangeline, and said nothing at all.

Nam had sent a basket of food up from the border with a note in his heavy capitals: EAT PROPERLY. WEDDINGS ARE EXPENSIVE ENOUGH WITHOUT PEOPLE FAINTING. She laughed out loud when she read it, and Elowen made her read it twice.

Aurelia found her by the cake, which was lemon, four tiers, covered in sugar camellias so thin you could see the light through them. She glanced at the earrings.

“They’re wearing well.”

“Good mend,” said Evangeline.

Aurelia’s face changed, as if she’d understood exactly what was meant, and a little more besides. “Thank you.”

At nineteen minutes to ten Eliana’s lights came on all at once along every beam and shelf, warm and small, threaded through the leaves, and the whole shop gasped. When the man at the bus stop came back for the third time, Evangeline saw him and so did Jinx, and then, between one bus and the next, he wasn’t there any more.

✦ ✦ ✦

She left before eleven with a slice of cake in a box. The stairs up the building across the street were narrow and went on. At the top the door was heavy, and the wind caught her skirt when she pushed it open.

He was sitting on the wide ledge of the parapet in the dark. He turned at the sound and stood, and looked at her, her face, the dress, the earrings, the box in her hand.

“You came,” he said.

“I did. Song saw you.”

“He didn’t say anything.”

“He looked at this roof all evening. And then at me.”

“That’s Song saying something.” He nodded at the box. “What’s that?”

“Your share.”

“You brought me cake. Up all those stairs.”

“Yes.”

He took the box out of her hands and put it on the parapet and pulled her down into his lap on the ledge. She gave a small surprised laugh.

“You’re cold,” he said, and rubbed her bare arm.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

She leaned into him. Across the street the shop glowed through its windows and music came up from the courtyard.

“The man at the bus stop,” she said.

“I went down the back stairs.”

“And?”

“He won’t come back.” He didn’t say anything else, and she didn’t ask, and she felt him wait to see if she would.

She touched his face. “Elowen was happy.”

“I saw.”

“Zhendong couldn’t stop looking at her.”

“Neither could you.” He opened the box. One slice of lemon cake with a sugar camellia on the top. He took a bite and she watched him.

“Well?”

“Good.”

“You’re meant to say it’s delicious.”

“It is.” He fed her the next bite. They shared it between them on the roof, over the street where her sister had got married, and when it was gone he set the box down and put both arms round her.

“Raiden’s married,” she said.

“I saw that too. You didn’t look surprised.”

“I wasn’t. Not by then.”

He kissed her temple. “Did you have a good day?”

“Yes. Did you?”

He looked down at the lights, and then at her. “Yes.”

“You weren’t lonely?”

She knew it mattered. He’d spent years making himself useful instead of making himself present, standing outside rooms and watching doors and keeping his distance from anything he wanted too much. Tonight he’d watched her sister marry from a roof. He hadn’t been allowed to stand beside his wife in the courtyard. But she’d come to him. She’d brought him cake. She was in his lap with her earrings catching the city.

He kissed her forehead. “Not any more.”

Below them the last guests began to come out into the lane. In the morning the flowers would come down and the chairs would be stacked and the petals swept, and Elowen and Zhao would wake up married all over again. Across the street, on a roof that had kept him apart from all of it, Lee Jun Hyuk sat with his wife in his arms. For once he wasn’t watching the door. He was watching her.

chapters.title: The Traffickers Remember Her
chapters.desc: October is basil and a ridiculous pale blue coat. Then Eliana finds a photograph of Evangeline taken inside the box, and it is for sale.
chapters.epigraph: “Price on request. Serious buyers only. Palace interest welcome.”
chapters.content:
The basil had finally learned to behave.

All through September it had grown too fast, throwing out long silly stems towards the light, and she’d pinched it back and moved the pots round and explained to her husband several mornings running that plants needed patience. He’d listened to this with the face of a man receiving orders from headquarters. Then the weather turned, and one morning in October she opened the hatch and found three tiny new leaves coming up in the smallest pot, and called him before she’d got her slippers on.

“Jun Hyuk. Come here.”

He came from the bedroom with his shirt half buttoned, fast, because she didn’t call him like that. She was kneeling on the counter pointing.

“Look.”

He looked. “Those?”

“Yes.”

“They’re small.”

“They’re supposed to be small.”

He crouched beside her and studied them as if they might be hiding something. “Good,” he said.

“Good?”

“Very good.”

She laughed, and he looked at her instead of the plant, and kept the sound.

He’d started doing that without meaning to. Counting her laughs. Not in any notebook. But he knew the short one she gave when he said something dry, and the breathless one when something really surprised her, and the low soft one when he kissed her somewhere she hadn’t expected. He knew she laughed most in the kitchen. He knew that if he made her laugh twice before breakfast she’d come and kiss him before she left the room. He’d spent most of his life counting things: rounds, exits, footsteps, names, days. He preferred this work.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rice cooker arrived on a Monday. It was a great deal bigger than the old one and had more buttons than she could imagine a use for.

“What does this one do?”

He glanced over from the table. “Rice.”

“And this one?”

“Rice.”

She stared at him. He went back to his tablet. She laughed.

Two days later a set of kitchen knives came. The week after that, a clay teapot, dark reddish-brown, round and plain, with a lid that sat true and a spout that didn’t drip. She held it in both hands.

“Where did you find it?”

“A shop.”

“That’s very helpful.”

He came and turned it in her hands. “The man said it was made by hand.”

She ran her thumb over the faint marks in the clay. “You don’t have to buy me something every time you notice I like it.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“Yes,” he said, and she kissed his cheek, and he went on looking at her as if she’d said something else entirely.

The coat was worse.

It came in the middle of the month in a long garment bag. He unzipped it in front of the sofa while she was reading, and inside was a coat the palest blue there is, the colour of a winter sky just before the sun comes up, with a wide collar and a narrow waist, and when she put it on the sleeves came exactly to her wrists. She went to the long mirror in the hall. Pale blue had always been hers, since her mother first dressed her in it. She turned, watching it move.

“How much was it?”

He didn’t answer. She turned round.

“Jun Hyuk.”

He told her. She looked at him, and at the coat, and took it off.

“That’s ridiculous.”

“It’s very good quality.”

“It’s a coat. I have coats.”

“Not this one.” He frowned as she folded it over her arm. “Why are you taking it off?”

“Because you’re being unreasonable.”

She could see him trying to follow where the argument was going. He’d never learned to think of a price as something that needed protecting. It meant nothing to him at all.

“Please,” he said. He wasn’t smiling. “I wanted to buy it for you.”

She looked at him. Then she put it back on and buttoned it, and walked up to him and took his face in her hands and kissed him, long enough that his hands came to her waist and the price went clean out of the conversation.

“Thank you,” she said. “I love it. But next time—”

He kissed her before she could finish.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday the seventeenth of October, Eliana found the photograph.

She’d been looking for something else. For weeks she’d been helping Song Wei Long, who’d grown up in the Wang house next door and still brought her his laptop to mend, sort through what had survived of the old network after the forty-one pages went to his desk. Seized phones. Copies of copies. Fake job advertisements, forged papers, warehouse addresses, old messages between men who’d once been sure none of it would ever be taken apart. It was tedious work, and Eliana was good at tedious work. She noticed when the same username came back with one letter changed. She noticed when two timestamps were a minute too close.

She was about to close a page when she saw the listing.

The picture was small. At first it was only a girl in a dark room. Then she made it bigger. The flash had blown out half of it. There was black behind, and a strip of ribbed metal, and other shapes at the edges, people, barely there. The girl in the middle was looking straight into the camera. Her face was white. Her hair had fallen across one cheek. She was in a light-coloured dress.

Eliana stopped breathing.

She knew that face. She’d grown up with it across the breakfast table. She knew the crease that came between those eyebrows when Evangeline was frightened and trying not to be, and she’d seen it once before, in a hospital corridor at three in the morning.

ROYAL BLOOD, DOCUMENTED. CURRENTLY UNPROTECTED.

And underneath, smaller:

Price on request. Serious buyers only. Palace interest welcome.

It was the box. The metal wall behind her sister’s shoulder could be nothing else. Somebody had stood in the dark with a camera while she was in there, and kept it.

Eliana’s hands went cold. She took copies of everything: the listing, the seller’s page, the time it went up, the account, every scrap of data hanging off the image. She didn’t send any of it to Evangeline. She rang Elowen.

“Are you alone?”

“Yes. Why?”

“It’s about Evangeline. Not on the phone.”

“What’s happened?”

“There’s a photograph. From the box. Somebody’s selling it.”

She sent it. A few seconds later Elowen rang back, and her voice had gone thin and hard.

“Does she know?”

“No.”

“Don’t tell her yet. And don’t tell Zhendong.”

“El. He’s your husband.”

“He’ll take it out of her hands. He’ll go after whoever did this and bring the whole family down on top of it, and she’s only just—” Elowen stopped. “Let us find out what it is first.”

Eliana looked at the screen. “All right. But promise me something. Don’t let this be another thing everybody keeps from her.”

“I won’t,” said Elowen.

✦ ✦ ✦

The account was called Hwang. Nothing clever: a common name on an account that was four weeks old. But the pictures on it had gone up in an order, and they weren’t all of women: old transport papers, warehouse insides, number plates, men outside buildings. Whoever it was was offering buyers whatever was left of the network that could still be sold.

Eliana didn’t click on any private links or send any messages or pretend to be a buyer. She traced what she could from the outside and sent it to Song. It came down to a payment address, an old phone number, and a place: a mahjong club in the eastern district, on Kiln Street, above a car wash. The registration was in the name of a man who turned up in the Ferryman’s papers.

Song answered at once. “Don’t contact the seller.”

“I haven’t.”

“Don’t go there.”

“I wasn’t going to.” She looked at the girl in the photograph. “Detective Song. It says palace interest welcome.”

He was quiet a moment. “Then it isn’t a sale. It’s a message.”

“To whom?”

“Anybody who still thinks she’s worth something to them.”

“She’s married,” said Eliana. “I think. I haven’t been told. She doesn’t live with any of us, she stopped using Baba’s drivers, and when anyone asks her anything she answers like somebody who’s got somewhere to go home to.”

“Does her husband know about this?”

“No.”

“Then nobody tells her till I’ve talked to him,” said Song. “And Eliana. Whoever put this up wants attention. That doesn’t mean he’s careless.”
