When he’d gone she sat looking at her sister’s face. She thought of the word the men at the flower market had used. Highness. For the first time she wondered whether this picture had been taken for the same reason. Not because they knew who she was. Because they wanted somebody else to know.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen came to the flat that evening. She didn’t bring shopping. She brought her phone.

They sat at the dining table and she put it down between them, and Evangeline looked at it without understanding, and then saw the metal wall and the flash and the dark, and her own face in the middle of it.

She didn’t move.

She’d spent a year making the box smaller in her head. Making the girl in it a different person from the woman with basil in her window. And there the girl was, not a memory at all, a picture, proof that somebody had watched and thought to keep it. She remembered the box. She didn’t remember the camera.

“Who took it?” she said.

“We don’t know.”

“Who would buy it?”

“Somebody who thinks they can use your name.”

Her fingers moved towards the screen, and stopped. She turned the phone face down on the table.

“I’m sorry,” said Elowen.

“Don’t.” She was quiet a moment. “Does Baba know?”

“No. Nor Zhendong.”

“Jun Hyuk has to know.”

“Yes.”

Elowen took her hand across the table. “Eliana asked me if you were married. She’s guessed. I told her she wasn’t allowed to ask you.”

Evangeline almost smiled. “That sounds like you.”

“Are you going to tell her?”

She looked at the hall, where his shoes stood beside hers. “Not yet.”

“Then I’ll keep quiet.” Elowen squeezed her fingers. “But you can, whenever you like.”

“I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came in at twenty to nine. She hadn’t turned the television on. The basil was watered and the dishes were away and her phone was on the counter with the picture open on it, because Elowen had sent it on before she left.

He saw her face as he came through the door. “What happened?”

She turned the phone round.

He looked at it for one second without moving. Then his eyes went to the words under it. He read them once, and again, and his face emptied. Not of anger. Of everything. He made the picture bigger. The flash. The metal. The angle.

“Where?”

“Online. Eliana found it today. An account called Hwang. She traced it to a mahjong club on Kiln Street. Song has it all.”

“Has anyone contacted you? Your father? Zhao?”

“No.”

He put the phone down carefully, and she knew that care. She’d seen it the night he went up the tower after Kuang. She’d seen it when he came home from the eastern warehouses. She’d seen it when a judge told him about the rain.

“Jun Hyuk. Don’t go alone.”

“I need to talk to somebody.”

“Who?”

“Mr. Hwang. I know the name.”

He picked his phone up, and she caught his wrist, and he stopped.

“Look at me.”

He did.

“That picture is something that happened to me,” she said. “I’m here now. Don’t let them take you away from me by making you angry.”

His face moved. He lowered the phone, and took her hand, and brought it to his mouth just above the ring.

“I won’t let them use you again.”

“Then let Song do his work.”

“I’ll speak to Song first.”

“Promise.”

“Yes.”

At twelve minutes past nine Song rang. “Where are you?”

“Home.”

“Good. Stay there. The name’s probably Hwang Seok-jin. I haven’t confirmed it.”

“I know who he is.”

“Then you know you don’t walk up to him without preparing. The listing’s bait. We don’t know who’s looked at it or who’s answered. If you go up those stairs you’ll tell him exactly how much attention he’s got.”

“He’s advertising her. He’s telling people she’s got nobody.”

“Jun Hyuk.”

He said nothing.

“We take the whole chain,” said Song. “Buyer, seller, and whoever held the camera. Not tonight.”

“Not tonight,” said Jun Hyuk. “Tomorrow.”

“Not without me.”

He didn’t answer that, and Song rang off.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the bedroom door he stopped and turned. “I should have found it.”

“You couldn’t have known.”

“I should have.” His hand came to her cheek. “I don’t want anyone looking at you like that ever again.”

She leaned into his palm. “Then look at me. Not the picture. Me.”

He looked. After a moment he bent and kissed her and she reached up and held the back of his neck until she felt him let go of some of it.

“I’m here,” she whispered.

“I know.”

Later, when she was asleep, he got up and went to the kitchen and stood by the window box in the dark. Nine pots, all of them alive. The mint was getting into the rosemary.

His phone lit up.

Song: Do not contact Hwang. We are arranging a meeting.

He read it and put the phone face down on the counter. Somewhere out in the city, under all those lights, a man called Hwang had a picture of his wife in a box and had decided the world should know she could still be bought. His face stayed perfectly calm. He went back to bed and drew her in against him, and she stirred.

“Jun Hyuk?”

“I’m here.”

Her hand found his chest, and he covered it, and in the dark, while she slept, he made himself wait for the morning.

chapters.title: He Goes Hunting
chapters.desc: A mahjong club above a car wash on Kiln Street, a man called Hwang, and four days. She keeps every rule he ever wrote, and doesn’t sleep.
chapters.epigraph: “If I’m not back by Sunday, go to your sister. Don’t wait up.” “I won’t.”
chapters.content:
On Thursday night he kissed her goodbye in the kitchen.

It began as an ordinary kiss, his hand at the back of her neck. Then he drew back far enough to look at her, and kissed her again, longer, and her fingers closed in the front of his shirt.

“You’re going early.”

“Before it’s light.”

“Where?”

“Kiln Street.”

“Mr. Hwang.”

“Yes.”

He didn’t offer anything else. She didn’t ask him to promise nothing would happen. He couldn’t promise that, and she wasn’t going to make him lie. She straightened his collar instead.

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“Properly?”

“Properly.”

He ran his thumb along her cheekbone. “If I’m not back by Sunday, go to your sister. Don’t wait up.”

Her hands stopped on his collar.

“Don’t stay here. Don’t go looking. Don’t ring anybody asking where I am. Go to Elowen’s and let Song know you’re there.”

“I won’t,” she said. They both knew she was lying.

He looked at her as if deciding whether she meant it. Then he kissed her forehead. “Lock the door behind me.”

“Jun Hyuk. You wrote those rules for me. I know them.”

He covered her hands with his. “I know you do.”

At the door he turned round. She nodded. He nodded back. She heard the lift doors close, and then she went to the hatch and opened it and let the night in, and touched the three new leaves in the smallest pot, and stood there a long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

Kiln Street wasn’t the kind of street you’d notice unless you had a reason.

The car wash took up the ground floor of a narrow building between a shuttered furniture warehouse and a shop that sold electrical fittings. Its sign had lost two letters. The pavement in front of it was always wet. Above it, with no sign at all, was the mahjong club, up a stair beside the car wash half hidden behind a stack of plastic crates.

He got there at four thirty-six on Friday morning and didn’t go up. He went into the noodle shop across the road, which belonged to an old woman who fed lorry drivers and night men and took no interest in anyone’s business, and asked for tea, and sat at the window.

He stayed. At seven the car-wash men came in. At nine two men came down the stair, one with a plastic bag, one smoking at his phone. At one the old woman asked if he was waiting for somebody.

“Yes.”

“Long time?”

“Maybe.”

“Your tea’s cold.”

He drank it anyway. Waiting was work. People got careless when they thought nothing was happening. They used the same doors. They bought from the same shops. They stopped looking at the faces round them.

At seventeen minutes past eight that evening Hwang came round the corner. He was shorter than Jun Hyuk had expected, a thickset man of about fifty with a trimmed moustache and a gold watch that flashed whenever he moved his hand, in a dark coat too heavy for the weather, carrying a paper bag from the wonton place two streets down. He stopped to say something to a car-wash man that made the man laugh, and laughed himself, and went up.

Jun Hyuk waited another hour. Then he paid and crossed the road.

Hwang came down again at six minutes past ten and walked to the wonton place with his phone in one hand and ordered at the counter under the awning.

“Hwang Seok-jin?”

Hwang turned, and his smile went. He looked at the size of the man in front of him and something in his face recognised the kind.

“I don’t know you.”

“You know my wife.”

His eyes moved. Jun Hyuk saw the moment he understood, and didn’t give him time to say anything. He took Hwang by the arm above the elbow and walked him round the side of the shop into the passage between the buildings, and when Hwang dragged against him he tightened his grip until Hwang stopped dragging. He took the keys out of the man’s coat pocket and let them in at the club’s back door.

Upstairs two men were clearing tiles off the tables. They looked up.

“Leave,” said Jun Hyuk.

One of them opened his mouth. Jun Hyuk looked at him again. They left.

The back room had a metal table, two chairs, a sink, and a window with the blind down. Jun Hyuk sat Hwang in one chair and took the other and turned the key in the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

Hwang talked for twenty minutes and said nothing. He didn’t know any Evangeline. He didn’t know any photograph. He was a businessman. Jun Hyuk sat with his hands flat on the table and didn’t raise his voice, and asked the same questions again, in the same order.

“Who did you offer it to?”

“You’ve misunderstood the listing. It was old material. Historical documents.”

“Her face.”

“Part of a collection.”

“My wife.”

Hwang’s eyes went to the door.

“Feng,” said Jun Hyuk.

It was small, what happened in Hwang’s face. A tightening round the eyes. A beat before he answered. It was enough.

“Feng sold her from his cell,” said Jun Hyuk. “Her name, her family, her Tuesdays at the market. Who did he sell it to after?”

Hwang looked at the table. “There’s a clerk at his lawyer’s who carries letters out. Feng had a story to sell and a picture to go with it. He said the family might pay to have it back.”

“Which family?”

“The palace. He said there’d be interest.” Hwang licked his lips. “There’s a list. On the computer upstairs. Names that answered.”

“Show me.”

The computer was in a locked office at the far end of the club. There were copies of the picture in several folders, and old papers, and a list of people who’d asked about material from the network, some names real, some not, a few companies behind other companies. Jun Hyuk didn’t touch the keys. He rang Song.

“The office at the back of the club on Kiln Street. The machine’s on. You’ll want it before anyone else does.”

“Where’s Hwang?”

“With me.”

There was a silence on the line that went on for some time.

“Jun Hyuk.”

“He knows things I need. I’ll give him to you on Sunday.”

“Midnight Sunday,” said Song at last. “I’ll have a car at the back door. Alive.”

On the way back down the corridor Hwang said, “I didn’t know she was yours.”

Jun Hyuk stopped. “You knew she was somebody’s daughter. You knew she was a woman in a box.”

Hwang didn’t answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday came in pieces. Song’s officers took the computer at dawn and didn’t open the door of the back room, because Song had told them not to. Jun Hyuk gave nobody a statement and ate nothing. He didn’t ring her. At half past eleven at night he looked at his phone for the first time.

Evangeline: I watered the basil. The new leaves are still there.

He wrote Good, and looked at it, and deleted it.

Jun Hyuk: Are you all right?

Evangeline: Yes. Are you?

He looked at the locked door.

Jun Hyuk: Yes.

He knew she’d know. He sent it anyway.

On Sunday morning Song came up himself, and stood in the back room in his coat with a notebook, and Hwang, seeing a policeman, began to talk as if a policeman were a door he could get out through. Two men who’d come asking about the picture: one who collected papers on old political families, one overseas who’d wanted the image at its original size. A copy sent to a private contact. The words palace interest welcome had been his own idea; he’d thought they’d draw attention. And the name of the clerk at Feng’s lawyer’s, which Song wrote down.

“That’s enough for now,” Song said. “We’ll take it from here. Midnight.” He looked at Jun Hyuk. “The overseas number. Don’t ring it.”

Jun Hyuk nodded. He’d already learned it by heart.

At fourteen minutes past two he rang it. A man answered in English.

“You’ve got a photograph of a woman named Evangeline Lee,” said Jun Hyuk, in the same language. “I’m the man asking you to delete it.”

“I don’t know what you’re—”

“You had it from Hwang Seok-jin last week. I know the account. I know the time. Delete it. Every copy. Then confirm, through the same channel.”

“Are you threatening me?”

“No. I’m telling you what happens next. If you don’t, Detective Song gets your name and your company.” He waited. “I’m not police. I know the people who are.”

The man’s breathing changed. “I’ll delete it.”

“Now.”

Ten minutes later a message came through the go-between’s account. File deleted. No further copies retained. He sent it to Song. It didn’t take the picture out of the world. It didn’t take her out of the box. But there was one fewer person looking at her face.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a few minutes to eleven on Sunday night, with the car an hour away, Hwang got brave.

He’d been watching the clock on the wall. He sat back in his chair and straightened his cuffs over the gold watch.

“A lawyer,” he said. “Bail in a week. Feng’s friends will see to it. And you think there’s one copy.” He tapped his own temple. “She’s in here. I was on the quay when they loaded that box. I took that picture myself, with my own phone, by the door. The others cried. She didn’t. She just looked. That’s why it sells.” He smiled under the moustache. “And now she’s married, she’ll fetch more. Married women have families who pay.”

Jun Hyuk didn’t say anything.

Hwang’s hand went under the edge of the sink. He came up with a short blade that had been taped there for years, and came across the table with it.

Jun Hyuk caught the wrist and drove it down into the steel edge of the table until the knife went skittering, and put his forehead into Hwang’s face, and felt the nose go. Hwang went back into the wall with blood all down his mouth, and Jun Hyuk went after him and got his hands round his throat and held him there against the tiles. Hwang’s fingers tore at his wrists. His heels slid on the wet floor. The gold watch beat against the wall, twice, three times. Jun Hyuk didn’t look away from his face until it was over, and then for a while after that.

He let go. Hwang went down the wall and sat at the bottom of it.

Jun Hyuk ran the tap and put his hands under it, and the water ran pink and then clear, and his hands were shaking a little, which they never did. He turned the tap off and sat down in his chair and waited for midnight.

At midnight he opened the back door. Song came up the stair alone and stood in the doorway of the back room and looked at the man at the bottom of the wall.

“I said alive.”

“He took the picture himself. With his own phone. By the door of the box.”

Song didn’t move. He looked at Hwang, and at the knife on the floor, and at Jun Hyuk’s hands.

“Go home,” he said at last. “Go home before I change my mind.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d done everything he’d ever asked of her. She’d locked the door. She hadn’t gone to Kiln Street. She hadn’t rung the club or Nam or Song, or told her father. She hadn’t gone down to the lobby.

She also hadn’t slept.

On Friday she’d cleaned the kitchen. On Saturday she’d washed the sheets, folded every towel in thirds, wiped the table and reorganised the cupboard under the sink. On Sunday she’d cleaned the whole flat again and found there was nothing left to clean. The knives were in their block. The teapot was by the kettle. His shirts were folded. The pale blue coat hung by the door.

She stood in front of it, and took it down, and put it on and buttoned it, and sat on the sofa.

At nineteen minutes to ten Elowen rang.

“Come here tonight.”

“I’m all right.”

“Evangeline. He said if he wasn’t back by Sunday you’d come to me. It’s Sunday.”

“He said if he wasn’t back by Sunday. He didn’t say I had to leave the first minute after.”

Elowen was silent. Then: “You sound exactly like him.”

“That’s unfortunate.” Her voice cracked on it. “I can’t come yet.”

“Why not?”

“Because he might come home.”

Elowen was quiet a long time. “Keep your phone on. Ring me the second you hear.”

“I promise.”

Monday came without her noticing. At a quarter to one she made tea and at a quarter past she poured it away. She checked the lock. She went to the hatch and touched the soil. At half past two she sat on the floor by the door. She understood now why he hated waiting. It left the mind far too much room.

At seven minutes to three she heard the lift. It stopped on their floor. One set of feet, slow.

The lock turned at two minutes past.

He saw her in the hall in the pale blue coat, barefoot, her hair loose, her face white with tiredness, and neither of them moved.

“You didn’t sleep,” he said.

“I was waiting.”

He looked down at his hands. There was blood under his nails. Not much. Enough. She saw it. Her face changed, but she didn’t step back, and he noticed that too.

“I’ll wash,” he said.

“Did you find him?”

“Yes.”

“The picture?”

“Song has the files. The one overseas has been deleted.”

“And Mr. Hwang?”

He looked at her and didn’t answer, and she waited.

“He’s dead,” said Jun Hyuk.

There was nothing in it. No triumph. A fact, put down on the floor between them. She’d known what her husband was. Hearing it said plainly was different.

“Are you hurt?”

“No.” And then, before she could come any closer: “You should go to Elowen.”

“It was Sunday when you weren’t here. It’s Monday now.”

“That’s not funny.”

“I’m not joking.” She came one step nearer. “Why are you asking me to go?”

He said nothing.

She understood then. It wasn’t that he thought the blood would frighten her. He wanted it to. He wanted to give her a reason to walk out before she saw the rest of him.

“Look at me,” she said. “I saw the picture. I know why you went. I didn’t ask you to bring him back alive.” She held his eyes. “And I didn’t ask you to disappear afterwards.”

His throat moved.

He washed his hands at the kitchen sink, not well enough, while she heated broth and rice and put out a dish of the lemons, the first time she’d opened the jar. He sat on the edge of the bed and ate half the bowl because she watched him until he did. Then he looked at her sleeve.

“You’re going to crease it.”

She stared at him, and then, out of nowhere, she laughed, small and worn out and real, and something in his face let go.

“You spent a ridiculous amount of money on this coat,” she said.

“I remember.”

“And I kissed you to stop you telling me the price.”

“That worked.”

She kissed him again. He didn’t answer at first, as if he’d forgotten what to do with tenderness after four days. Then he turned his face into her hand and his arm came round her and he held on.

“I thought you’d be gone,” he said, into her hair.

“Why would I be gone?”

He didn’t answer. He’d come home with blood under his nails expecting an empty flat, the coat off its hook, the teapot put away, the basil left for nobody to water.

She touched the ring. “I’m your wife. And you’re mine.”

He pulled her in against him so hard she lost her breath, and put his face into her neck, and his breath on her skin wasn’t steady at all.

At thirteen minutes to four she hung the coat back by the door.

“Leave it there,” he said. “I like seeing it.”

In bed he lay facing her with one arm under her pillow.

“Feng’s still selling from his cell,” he said. “There’s a clerk who carries his letters. Song’s going after him.”

“Then we’ll find out.”

“We?”

She touched the crease between his brows. “You don’t get to make me part of your life only when it’s easy.”

“No,” he said. “I suppose I don’t.”

She was asleep in a minute. He stayed awake a little longer, watching her breathe. At some point her fingers slipped under his hand and held it. He turned his palm over and laced their fingers together and shut his eyes, and for the first time in four days he let himself come home.

chapters.title: She Washes His Hands
chapters.desc: Warm water, a nail brush and ten fingers, one at a time. She doesn’t ask whose it was. When he wakes, he tells her about one reply, and the crest on it.
chapters.epigraph: “Why don’t you ask?” “Because you’d tell me.”
chapters.content:
The first thing she noticed was that he hadn’t let go of her hand.

He was asleep on his side facing her, his fingers loose through hers, breathing deep and heavy. The light through the curtain had started to change. Six floors down a van reversed with three short beeps and a shutter went up somewhere with a clatter. Monday. He’d come home at two minutes past three.

There was a crease between his eyebrows even asleep. His hair had fallen across his forehead. He looked younger like that, though not young enough to make her forget what the last four days had cost.

She moved her hand. His fingers tightened without his waking. She waited until they loosened again, and slid out of the bed.

His jacket was over the chair. His shirt was in a heap by the bathroom door, and his shoes were in the hall, one fallen on its side. There was a dark mark at the cuff of the shirt. She didn’t look at it. She put it in the laundry basket, went into the bathroom, ran warm water into the basin, and set the little nail brush beside the soap. Then she stood and looked at it, and went back to the bedroom.

“Jun Hyuk.”

He came awake slowly. For a few seconds he looked at her without knowing the room. Then he found her face.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing. Come with me.”

He sat on the closed lid of the toilet in his shorts and she knelt on the bathmat in front of him with the basin and a clean towel. He looked at the arrangement and then at her.

“Evangeline.”

“Give me your hands.”

“They’re clean. I washed them.”

“Not all of it.”

He looked down. It was still there, faint, under the nails, in the creases at the edges. The kitchen sink at three in the morning hadn’t reached it.

She held her hand out, and he gave her his left.

She started with the little finger. She dipped the brush and worked it under the nail, gently, and rinsed it, and dried it, and moved to the next. One at a time. Ring finger, with the black thread. Middle finger. First finger. Thumb. Then she held out her hand again, and he turned the other one over to make it easier for her, and she began again.

She didn’t ask whose it was. She didn’t ask what had been said in the back room, or how long it had taken, or what he’d done after the man stopped talking. She washed his hands. The bathroom was quiet except for the tap and the small sound of the brush.

When she’d finished she rinsed them both and dried them properly. She knew his hands. The scar at the base of his thumb. The pale mark across one knuckle. The callus along the side of the first finger. She’d kissed them in the room over the bar. She’d held them when they were burning. She’d watched them mend the cupboard hinge and tie two camp beds together and lift her onto the counter when she was being deliberately difficult. They were the same hands.

She put the towel down. He was looking at her.

“Why don’t you ask?” he said.

“Ask what?”

“Whose it was.”

She looked at his hands, and then at him.

“Because you’d tell me.”

He didn’t move.

“You wouldn’t lie to me about that,” she said.

“No.”

“So I don’t need to ask.” She turned one of his hands over in hers. “I let you go. On Thursday. I knew where you were going and why, and I could have asked you not to, and I didn’t. I didn’t want you staying because I was frightened. And I didn’t want you coming home and pretending nothing had happened because you thought I couldn’t bear to hear it.” She rubbed her thumb across his clean knuckles. “I wanted you to come home.”

“That’s all?”

“That’s a great deal.”

He reached for her. His hand went to the back of her neck and he drew her up off the floor, and kissed her, hard, so sudden she had to catch the edge of the sink behind her. His other hand found her waist and pulled her against him. It was a kiss with four days in it and something he’d been holding back since he came through the door, and she made a small sound into his mouth and put her fingers into his hair and held on.

When he lifted his head his hands were on her face. Clean.

“Good,” she whispered.

“Good?”

“Your hands.”

He looked at her a second longer and kissed her again, slower.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went out into the hall and took the pale blue coat off its hook and put it on, and buttoned it. He watched her from the bathroom door and didn’t understand. Then she came back and turned the shower on, and when it ran warm she stepped into it, coat and all.

“Evangeline?”

The blue went dark across her shoulders. She held both arms out.

“Come here.”

He looked at her face. She’d sat up four nights in that coat, by the door, waiting for the lift. He understood, then, what she was doing. He stepped in under the water.

He stood there with it running over his hair and down his shoulders, his eyes on the tiles, breathing. She put her hands on his chest. Then she put her arms round him and laid her cheek against him.

“You’re home,” she said.

She felt it before she heard it. A breath that caught. A small broken sound. Then his arms came round her all at once, and he bent his head into her shoulder, and he began to cry.

There was no noise to it at first. No words. Only the first shuddering breath, and the next, and the tremor going through a man who’d held everything in for so long that he didn’t know how to let any of it out gently. His fingers dug into her back through the wet wool. His face turned into her neck.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“Don’t.”

“I thought I’d come back and—”

He couldn’t finish it. She held him tighter.

“I know. I’m here.”

He shook his head once, as if he couldn’t make himself believe it.

“I’m here, Jun Hyuk.”

She didn’t ask him to stop, and she didn’t tell him everything was all right. She held him under the warm water with the coat going heavy round her until his breathing began to come back to him. When at last he lifted his head his eyes were red.

He looked at the coat. “You’re ruining it.”

She laughed, with her own face wet. “It washes.”

“It’s expensive.”

“So are you,” said Evangeline, and kissed his cheek, and then the other one, and a smile came onto his face as if it had got lost on the way and only just found him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He slept for twelve hours.

She knew because she looked at the clock when he finally shut his eyes, and it said eighteen minutes past ten in the morning. She’d changed the sheets while he was in the shower and found him a clean shirt and put him to bed, and he’d said once that he wasn’t tired, and she’d looked at him, and he’d lain down. He was asleep in minutes.

He didn’t wake when the shopping came. He didn’t wake when she opened the hatch and watered the basil. At noon she put a hand on his forehead. Cool. At two she left a glass of water by the bed. At four she stood in the doorway and watched him.

He looked different. The line had gone from his forehead. His mouth had softened. One hand lay by the pillow, palm open. She thought of the first nights in the room over the Golden Nightingale, when he’d slept on the sofa with one arm over his eyes and his boots near enough to reach without standing up. He’d never really slept, then. Some part of him had always been awake by the door. He’d told her once that he hadn’t slept a night through since he was eight, before the shelling. She sat down on the edge of the bed and touched his hair and he didn’t stir.

At eighteen minutes past ten that night he opened his eyes. She was beside him with a book.

“Hello,” she said.

“What time is it?”

“Ten eighteen.”

“In the morning?”

“No.”

He looked at the window. The city was dark. “How long?”

“Twelve hours.”

He stared at her, and rubbed his face. “I did, didn’t I.”

“Without waking once.”

“Did you stay?”

“Where would I go?”

He reached for her hand and pulled her down to him and kissed her. Once. Then again, longer. When she drew away he looked offended.

“Where are you going?”

“To make you something to eat.”

“Later.”

“Five minutes.”

“Ten.”

“Seven.”

He kissed her once more. “Agreed.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Seven minutes later he followed her into the kitchen. She’d hung the coat up to dry at last and rolled her sleeves to the elbow and was standing at the stove over a pot of soup. He came up behind her and put his arms round her waist.

“You’re meant to be resting.”

“I’ve rested. Twelve hours.”

He put his mouth to the side of her neck. She smiled.

“Don’t distract me.”

He did it again.

“Jun Hyuk. The soup.”

He turned her round by the waist and kissed her against the stove, unhurried, warm with plain happiness at finding her there when he woke, his hands at her waist and hers coming up to his face. Behind her the pot began to rattle.

“Oh—”

She spun round. It had boiled over, and a thin brown stream was running down the side of the pot onto the burner. He reached for the cloth.

“Don’t,” she said. “You did that.”

“I kissed you.”

“Exactly.”

He wiped the stove. She took the pot off the heat. He looked at her sideways.

“You’re blaming me?”

“Completely.”

“Sorry.”

“You’re not.”

“No,” he said, and she laughed.

The soup was still good once she’d added some water and more ginger. He ate two bowls at the table and she watched him over her cup.

“Better?”

“You’re going to feed me till I can’t move.”

“That’s one of my plans.”

They talked about ordinary things. The basil. The new teapot. The mint, which had got into the rosemary and would have to be spoken to. Nam had sent a message asking if they were both still alive, and she said they’d take him a jar of the lemons on Sunday. Then he put his spoon down.

“There was a reply,” he said. “To the listing.”

She looked up.

“Most of them were buyers. People who collect papers, people who want something to sell on. One came in through a different channel. It didn’t ask for the picture. It asked whether the woman in it had been identified. By name. Family. Whether she was still alive.” He kept his voice even. “There was a crest on it. A grey heron standing in water. Mountains behind.”

Her fingers went still round the cup.

She could almost smell the attic at the Walled City: dust and heat and the box of Christmas lights pushed back under the eaves, and the cloth bundle behind it, old silk, pale, and in one corner a bird in grey thread standing in water with mountains behind it. She’d been fifteen. She’d gone up looking for a box of Mama’s things for a school project. She’d put it back exactly where it was and come down and cried in the bathroom, and Raiden had found her there, and thought she’d failed maths.

“I know it,” she said.

He waited.

“It’s on the blanket in our attic. The one they sent me away in.” She put the cup down. “It’s theirs. The family I was born to.”

“You’re sure.”

“I’ve looked at it a hundred times. I go up and look at it sometimes. That’s all.” She looked at the ring on her own finger. “I’d seen it once before that. On an envelope in the locked drawer of my father’s desk. He doesn’t know I saw.”

Jun Hyuk didn’t say anything for a while. He reached across the table and took her hand.

“Then they know there’s a woman in a picture who might be you,” he said. “And they want to know if she’s alive.”

“Should we ask Baba?”

“Not until we know what we’re asking him.”

She thought about it, and nodded. He rubbed his thumb over her knuckles, back and forth.

“I’ll give Song the crest. He’ll trace the channel.”

“And then?”

“And then we’ll see who’s at the other end of it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In bed she lay with her head on his chest. He’d showered again and eaten properly and looked, at last, as if the twelve hours had got all the way into him.

“Did you find the reply because you were looking,” she said, “or because they came looking?”

“Both.”

“Do you think they know me?”

“I think they know there’s a you.” He was quiet. “And they’ve known where to send a question.”

She lay still and thought about that, and about a silk blanket under the eaves, and an envelope in a locked drawer. Not enough, but something.

“Sleep,” he said.

“You too.”

“I will.”

She was asleep a few minutes later. He wasn’t. He lay looking at the small silver ring on the hand spread over his heart. He’d spent four days trying to take one picture out of the world. He’d found the man who sold it, and the people who’d wanted it, and one more who’d answered with a heron in water that his wife had been carrying around in her since she was fifteen. He didn’t know what it meant. He didn’t know what her father had kept in that drawer all these years, or why. But the picture hadn’t been the end of anything. It had been somebody knocking on a door. And somewhere over a border, someone was waiting to see whether it would open.

She murmured something he couldn’t make out and tucked herself further under his arm. He held her. For tonight, that was enough.

chapters.title: He Meets His Father-in-Law (Badly)
chapters.desc: A tracker in a birthday phone, a word on a scrap of paper in a locked drawer, and a knife held very still at her father’s throat. She is in the doorway when he says it.
chapters.epigraph: “Him.”
chapters.content:
The silver car had been across the street three mornings running.

He’d noticed it on Tuesday, parked under a plane tree that was dropping its leaves, a clean dark-silver saloon with tinted glass and nothing written on it. On Wednesday it was there when he came back from the market. On Thursday, the sixteenth of November, he stood at the kitchen window with his coffee and looked at it through the branches, and it was the same make and the same colour as a car he’d once watched through Nam’s steamed-up window, outside the pharmacy, with its engine running so the windscreen wouldn’t fog.

“Jun Hyuk? Is this pot too small?”

Behind him Evangeline was trying to persuade the basil it needed more room.

“Maybe.”

“You’re not looking.”

“I’m looking.”

“You’re looking at the window.” She came and stood beside him. “What is it?”

“There’s a car.”

She found it through the leaves. “Do you know it?”

“I think I’ve seen it before.”

She knew his silences by now. Some meant he was thinking. Some meant he was tired. This one meant he was trying not to frighten her.

“Don’t go down on your own today,” he said.

“I’ve got a delivery. It’s soil.”

“I’ll get it.”

“You’re going to stand over the delivery man because of a bag of soil?”

“If he makes me wait.”

She laughed. His mouth went up at the corner, and then he turned back to the window, and the silver car stayed where it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

The birthday phone was in the second drawer of her bedside table.

She’d taken it out of Nam’s jar when they moved, because it was from her father and the first thing he’d ever chosen for her himself. She used it for photographs, mostly. The basil. The steel box under the hatch. The crooked dumpling from New Year, still in its gallery.

He was looking for a charger that afternoon when the drawer hummed. The screen lit. No message, no call. It went dark. A few seconds later it did it again.

He took it into the spare room where he kept the things he used for checking his own phones, and in less than twenty minutes he knew. There was a small part inside it that hadn’t come from the factory. Something added afterwards, that talked to somebody else, every few minutes, about where the phone was.

He looked through the door. She was in the kitchen washing the clay teapot, and singing a bit under her breath. He waited until she’d put it down.

“Your birthday phone,” he said, when she came in and saw it on the table in front of him. “Somebody’s put a tracker in it.”

She sat down across from him and touched the edge of it.

“How long?”

“I don’t know.”

“Since Baba gave it to me?”

“Possibly.”

“Did I ever leave it anywhere?” She answered herself. “Elowen’s. Baba’s. My bag at the market.” She looked up. “Is that why the car’s there?”

“Possibly.”

“Could it be Baba?”

He didn’t answer straight away, and that was an answer.

“I’ll go and talk to him,” he said, and stood up.

“Jun Hyuk—”

“I’ll talk to him.”

He wasn’t angry yet. That was what frightened her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d never met Lin Jian. He’d seen him once, across the road from Harbourside General at three in the morning, and stayed away since.

He went in at the main gate of the Walled City house on Thursday evening without being announced. Raiden was in the corridor with a roll of drawings.

“Jun Hyuk. Is she with you?”

“No.”

Raiden looked at his face. “What’s happened?”

“I need to talk to your father.”

Raiden hesitated. “He’s in his office.” And then, as Jun Hyuk went past him, Raiden got his phone out.

The office was at the east end of the house, behind two dark doors, with a window over the canal where the barges went by. Lin Jian was at his desk with his reading glasses on and a file in front of him, in a black suit, with grey hair cut much too short. He looked up at the man in his doorway and took the glasses off and put them in his breast pocket.

“So,” he said. “The husband.”

Jun Hyuk shut the doors behind him. “Did you put a tracker in her phone?”

Lin Jian’s face didn’t move. “I gave her that phone. For her birthday.”

“I know. That isn’t what I asked.”

“It was meant to keep her safe.”

“From what?”

Lin Jian said nothing. Jun Hyuk looked at the desk. There was a drawer on the right with a small brass lock.

“Open it.”

“This is my house.”

“Open the drawer.”

“You don’t give orders in my house.”

Jun Hyuk didn’t answer. He stood and waited, and after a while Lin Jian took a key out of his waistcoat pocket and unlocked it.

Papers. A black notebook. An envelope from a law firm abroad, its letterhead in two languages, and in the corner of it, small, pressed into the paper, a grey heron standing in water with mountains behind. And underneath, a scrap of paper with one word on it.

Value?

Jun Hyuk picked it up.

“Put that down,” said Lin Jian.

He opened the envelope instead. It was several years old. It asked, in careful language, after an unnamed female person, and her records, and her family, and whether certain papers could be confirmed. One line had been underlined in pencil. Please advise whether the subject retains any independent legal or hereditary interest.

He read it twice. Then he looked at the scrap again. Value?

“Who was asking?” he said.

“Those matters are complicated.”

“Not to me. Did you put the tracker in her phone?”

Lin Jian looked away. That was enough.

Jun Hyuk was across the desk before the old man had finished turning his head. He took him by the shirt front and walked him back into the bookshelves hard enough to bring a book down, and the knife was in his other hand and then flat against Lin Jian’s throat, under the jaw. Not cutting, not moving. Only there.

The most frightening man the Walled City had ever had went perfectly still.

“Listen to me,” said Jun Hyuk. “She isn’t your asset any more. She’s my wife. You don’t put anything in her things. You don’t follow her. You don’t park men under her window. You don’t decide who gets to know where she sleeps.”

Lin Jian’s breathing stayed even. “You’re making a serious mistake.”

“Try me.”

“She is my daughter.”

“Then act like it. If I find one more tracker, one more car, one more man watching her, I’ll take apart every arrangement you ever made round her. Every name. Every account. Every man you think is keeping your secrets for you. You won’t know which one’s gone until you go to use him.”

The door opened behind him.

“Jun Hyuk.”

He didn’t look round. She was in the doorway with Raiden behind her, out of breath. Her eyes went to her father’s face, to the knife, to her husband, and for one second she didn’t move at all.

“Put it down,” she said.

“Evangeline—”

“Please.”

She came across the room, not fast, not frightened, and put her hand on his wrist. The muscles under her fingers were like wire.

“Look at me.”

He looked.

“Put it down.”

It took a long time. Then he lowered the knife and stepped back, and she took it out of his hand and laid it on the desk. Lin Jian straightened his collar. There was a thin red line under his jaw where the flat of the blade had pressed.

“Why?” said Evangeline.

Her father looked at her. “I wanted to know you were safe.”

“You could have rung me.”

“I didn’t want to disturb you.”

“You could have asked where I was.”

“I knew what you’d say.”

“Then perhaps you should have listened to it.” She looked at the desk, the letter, the scrap of paper. “Did you know somebody was asking about me?”

He didn’t answer.

“Baba.”

“Yes.”

“Who?”

“A firm abroad. The client had no name.”

“And that?”

He looked at the scrap. “Their question. About your position.”

“My value.”

“It wasn’t—”

“That’s what it says.” She was calm. “What did you tell them?”

“That the matter was closed.”

She stared at him. He heard it as she did, too late.

“You’ve spent my whole life deciding which parts of me other people were allowed to see,” she said. “You hid me in the next room. You kept papers about me I didn’t know existed. And when I finally went away, you put something in my phone.” Her voice shook once and steadied. “I was afraid in that box. I was afraid in the hospital. I was afraid when I found out somebody had sold my name. I was never afraid of being yours, Baba. I was afraid I’d never be allowed to belong to myself.”

Lin Jian’s face had begun to come apart.

Jun Hyuk stood by the desk and didn’t move. Every part of him wanted to step between them. He didn’t. This wasn’t his to take over. He’d come in to make the old man understand she wasn’t a thing to be tracked or hidden or priced, and she was making him understand something else. She’d never needed anyone to claim her. She needed her father to ask.

“If you want to know where I am,” she said, “ask. If you want to know if I’m safe, ask.”

Her father opened his mouth and shut it again. He hesitated, and it wasn’t the hesitation of a man working out his answer. It was a man frightened of hearing one.

“Are you happy?” said Lin Jian.

She turned her head and looked at Jun Hyuk.

“Him,” she said. She looked back at her father. “With him. I’m happy with him.”

Jun Hyuk looked down at the carpet, only for a second. She saw it.

Lin Jian picked up the scrap of paper. “I should have burnt this years ago.” He took a small brass lighter off the desk and held the corner in the flame until Value? curled and went black, and dropped it in the ashtray, and watched until there was nothing left. Then he put the envelope with the heron on it into her hands.

“That’s yours. All of it. The firm, the dates, what they asked. They wanted to know whether your mother’s family had left any claim on your name.” He looked at her. “I never answered them. I kept it because I didn’t know what else to do, and because I was afraid if I burnt it I’d lose the only record of what they wanted from you.”

“You can ask me things now,” said Evangeline.

“I know.”

He looked at Jun Hyuk then, the two of them across the desk.

“I’m sorry,” said Lin Jian.

Jun Hyuk didn’t say anything. Evangeline took his hand, and he let her, and that was as far as it went that night.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden walked them out to the car. At the gate she stopped.

“Did you know?”

“I knew Baba was worried. I knew he’d asked somebody to keep an eye on your phone.” He looked at the gravel. “Not what it was.”

“Thank you for ringing me.”

“I should have told you before.”

“Yes,” she said. “Don’t do it again.”

“I won’t.”

In the car she waited until they were on the canal road.

“You were going to kill my father.”

“No.”

She looked at him.

“I wasn’t going to kill him,” he said.

“That isn’t the same as no.” She was quiet a mile. “You were very frightening.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Not because you frightened him. Because you frightened yourself.”

His hands tightened on the wheel. She reached across and put her fingers round his wrist, and he took one hand off the wheel and held hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday he took the part out of the phone and sealed it in an evidence bag for Song, who wasn’t pleased about the office, and said so, and was listened to. She read the lawyer’s letter twice at the dining table and didn’t understand all of it and understood enough. Then she put it in a folder and locked it in the drawer of their own desk. Not hidden, not thrown away. Kept.

“Do you want me to read it with you?”

“Not yet.”

She shut the drawer and walked into his arms.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday she wanted orchids, not because they needed any but because the market under the viaduct smelled of wet leaves and cut stems, and the men there knew her, and she wanted an ordinary morning. He carried the basket with his other hand at the small of her back.

The orchid man looked up from his trays. “You’re back.”

“I am.”

“Your husband buys everything.”

“Not everything,” said Jun Hyuk.

“Last time three pots, because she looked at them.”

“They were nice,” said Evangeline.

“They were ugly,” said the orchid man, and she laughed out loud.

He brought out a tray of small white ones. She bent over them, touching the edge of a petal, one stem with a curve in it, one with a green bud still shut, and Jun Hyuk watched her and said, “Marry me again.”

She turned round.

“In front of them,” he said. “Properly. A garden. Your sister. Your father, if you want him. Nam. Eliana, and Raiden and Jinx. Six people, or however many you decide. A table where nobody has to sit facing the door. No secrets, and nobody leaving before the photographs.”

“We’re already married.”

“I know.”

“Since April. In a registry, with Nam and a woman who sells fried chicken.”

“I remember.”

“Then why again?”

“Because I want you to have a day we didn’t have to steal.” He touched the ring. “I want to stand next to you while everybody knows you’re my wife.”

Her eyes filled. “You don’t have to ask me twice.”

“Is that yes?”

“Yes.”

He bent and kissed her in the middle of the flower market, not hidden and not careful, his hand on her cheek, while people went round them with their buckets. When he drew back the orchid man was taking a small white orchid in a clay pot off his trestle.

“This one’s free,” he said, and pushed Jun Hyuk’s wallet away. “For the second wedding. And buy her flowers more often. Not only when she looks at them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she found him in the bedroom taking his watch off.

“What?” he said.

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me.”

“Am I not allowed?”

She came and stood in front of him and undid the top button of his shirt, and then the next.

“Evangeline. What are you doing?”

“Marrying you again.”

“That’s not till later.”

“I know.” She slid the shirt off his shoulders. “I said yes. I want you to know I haven’t changed my mind.” Her fingers went over an old scar on his chest. “I chose you when you had nothing to give me except a way out of a box. I chose you with blood on your hands. I chose you with a fever, and when you couldn’t sleep, and when you thought I’d go.” Her mouth moved. “I chose you when you bought me a ridiculous coat.”

“It wasn’t ridiculous.”

“You’re my husband. Say it.”

“I’m your husband.”

She kissed him. This time she didn’t let him lead. She kissed his jaw and the corner of his mouth and the small scar under his collarbone, and undid his belt herself, and pushed him back by the chest until he sat on the end of the bed, and pulled her dress off over her head and let it fall. He looked at her as if he’d been told he wasn’t allowed to. She climbed into his lap with her knees either side of him, and when he started to say something she put her mouth on his.

“You don’t have to make me feel better,” he said against it.

“I’m not doing this because of your hands. Or Baba. I’m doing it because I want you.”

He made a sound low in his throat and let her. She took him in her hand and guided him and came down onto him slowly, her forehead against his, watching his face while she did it, and his hands spread on her back and held her as if she might be taken away. She set the pace. She rode him slow and then not slow, his mouth at her breast and then at her throat, her name coming out of him in pieces. When she came she held his head against her and shook, and he turned her down onto the bed without coming out of her and followed with his face in her neck, and held on.

The lamp stayed on. Later she lay tracing the line of his shoulder.

“Do you think Baba will come?”

“I don’t know.”

“Will you be polite?”

“I can be polite.”

“You held a knife to his throat.”

“That was before the invitation.”

She laughed, and he kissed her forehead, and she fell asleep against him.

At sixteen minutes past two he woke. Her hand was over his heart. On the bedside table the little white orchid had opened. He thought of a garden, and a table, and a day when nobody would have to watch a door. In April he’d married her because he was afraid he might not come back. This time he’d marry her because he meant to stay. He turned his hand over and held hers, and shut his eyes.

chapters.title: A Letter From a Palace
chapters.desc: He brings her father a kumquat tree for New Year. In March a letter comes from a palace, in a language she taught herself in a library.
chapters.epigraph: “I am sorry, my daughter.”
chapters.content:
He came through the gate of the Walled City house on New Year’s Eve carrying a kumquat tree.

It came up nearly to his shoulder, in a wide glazed pot with a red ribbon round the trunk, small gold fruit hanging all through the dark leaves and two red envelopes tucked under the bow. Evangeline stood on the front step with a cup of tea and watched him bring it up the path.

“What’s that?”

“A tree.”

“I can see that.”

“Then we’re doing well.” He shifted the pot against his hip. “Your father invited us. For New Year’s Eve. So I brought something.”

“Did you choose it?”

“Nam helped.” That explained the ribbon. “The woman at the nursery says it means money coming in.”

“And you believed her?”

“She had an honest face.”

She laughed, and he looked pleased with himself, and bent and kissed her forehead over the top of the leaves.

“Happy New Year, wife.”

Lin Jian met them in the courtyard. He looked at the tree first and then at the man carrying it. It was the ninth of February, three months since the knife in his office, and they had seen each other twice since, both times for under a minute.

“A kumquat tree,” said Lin Jian.

“Yes.”

“Thank you.”

There was a pause.

“Baba,” said Evangeline. “Where would you like it?”

“By the entrance. It’ll get the light.”

Jun Hyuk carried it over without asking for help. Lin Jian followed. The two of them stood over the pot and considered the space as if they were placing something a great deal more consequential.

“Here?”

“A little to the left.”

He moved it.

“More.”

He moved it again.

“That’s good.”

They looked at each other. Then, for no reason anybody could see, they both nodded, once, and Evangeline had to put her hand over her mouth. She had never once imagined seeing her father and her husband agree about a tree.

✦ ✦ ✦

By evening the house was full. Elowen brought dumplings. Zhao brought a bottle of something her father had been keeping for an occasion. Raiden and Jinx came in arguing about whose fault the parking was, and Jinx went straight over to the kumquat and declared it handsome. Eliana took one look at Jun Hyuk and said, “So you’re the one I wasn’t told about,” and he said, “I’m the one,” and she narrowed her eyes at him for most of dinner.

Zhao had been told at Christmas, by Evangeline, at her sister’s kitchen table. He’d listened and said, “I know.” Since the bridge, he’d said. She’d come down that hill looking at the car the way Elowen looked at him.

Aurelia came with a box of pastries from Harbour Road and gave Evangeline a small wrapped parcel: two silver hairpins shaped like leaves. “For the window box,” she said. Then she looked across the room at Jun Hyuk, who was standing with Raiden with a glass in his hand.

“He talks a great deal,” Aurelia said.

“Does he?”

“To everyone. He asked your father about the tree, and Raiden about his drawings, and Zhao about the road closures on the bridge, and me whether the pastries were made this morning.” She sipped her wine. “But when you came into the room, he stopped.”

Evangeline looked over. As if he felt it, he turned his head, and their eyes met, and the corner of his mouth went.

“There,” said Aurelia. “He does that. As if the rest of us had been turned down.”

“I think he always has,” said Evangeline.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner went on long past the point anybody had planned. The dishes kept coming. Elowen talked about the garden ceremony they hadn’t fixed a date for, and said there should be white orchids along the path, not too many.

“She likes white orchids,” said Jun Hyuk.

Evangeline turned. “I know.”

“I was telling them.”

“Then more,” said Elowen.

“No,” said Evangeline. “Not too many.”

“She doesn’t like too many,” said Jun Hyuk, and Aurelia laughed out loud.

“He’s learned,” she said.

He talked to her father about the building. He asked Zhao about the bridge. He laughed once, at a story Raiden told about a security guard who’d tackled a man delivering a sofa, a real laugh with his head back, and Evangeline looked at him across the table and his hand found her knee under the cloth and stayed there. He still noticed every door. She could see him doing it. But he was here, at her father’s table, and nobody was asking him to leave.

After dinner she went up to find the box of red envelopes Elowen had left in the sitting room, and he caught her on the second landing.

“You’re avoiding me.”

“I’m looking for the envelopes.”

“They’re downstairs. Elowen put them by the tea.”

“Then why didn’t you say?”

“You looked busy.”

The landing was narrow, with a tall window onto the courtyard and the kumquat a dark shape by the gate. Voices came up the stairwell, softened.

“Aurelia says you talk to everybody but me,” she said.

“I’m talking to you now.”

“That isn’t what she meant.”

He tucked a strand of her hair back. “I don’t have to talk to you all the time. I can look at you.”

“You do that too much.”

“I’ve been told.”

He kissed her against the wall, gently at first, her fingers curling into his shirt. Then she came up on her toes and caught his lower lip between hers, and he made a low sound and pressed her back against the panelling with his hand spread at her waist, and kissed her properly, slow and deep, until somebody downstairs called, “Have you found the envelopes?”

She put her face in his chest to keep from laughing.

“Your sister has terrible timing.”

“She’s looking for us.”

“She can wait.” He kissed her once more, and let her go.

Elowen looked at Evangeline’s face when they came down, and then at his, and said, “Found them?” in a voice that meant she knew perfectly well where they’d been.

Jun Hyuk took a red envelope off the table and handed it to her. “Happy New Year.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The letter came on Thursday the fourteenth of March, to the Walled City, in a sealed diplomatic case carried by a man in a dark coat who showed his papers at the gate and asked to see Lin Jian alone. Lin Jian rang his daughter. She and Jun Hyuk drove over within the hour.

It was lying on the table in the front room when they came in. A long envelope the colour of old ivory, closed with dark blue wax, and pressed into the wax, a grey heron standing in water with mountains behind it.

Her hand stopped on the doorframe. She was fifteen again under the eaves, with the box of Christmas lights pushed aside.

“It came for you,” said her father. “From the Royal Household. I haven’t opened it.” He looked at her. “I thought you should decide whether to.”

“Thank you.”

She broke the seal. There were two letters inside. The first was in their own language, formal and careful, addressed to Mrs. Evangeline Lee. The second was in another script altogether, and she knew the first line of it before she’d read it.

Jun Hyuk saw her breath go. “What is it?”

She didn’t answer.

She’d found the grammar on a high shelf in her father’s library when she was fifteen, the same year as the blanket. An old book for students of the court language of a country she had never been to, with royal proclamations and letters printed in the back for practice. She’d taken it upstairs and begun copying the characters into an exercise book, one page a night, and never told anyone, and never really known why she needed so badly to be able to read it.

She sat down at the table and read the original. Not the translation.

It was hard going. The grammar was old and the phrasing older. But she understood enough. The late King had died in his own country with his household round him. The letter was written under the authority of his son, the new King. Then a paragraph about the late King’s will.

She read it twice. Then she read it out, slowly, putting it into their language as she went.

“By the authority of the late King’s testament, the woman named Evangeline Lee is acknowledged as his daughter, born of his blood, and recognised as his lawful child.” She swallowed. “His Majesty further records that the failure to acknowledge her in his lifetime was his own failing, and that he regrets the years in which she was denied the truth.”

Nobody moved.

There was more. A statement of inheritance. Her birth record. A request that she be told before any representative of the new King came near her. And at the very bottom, under the official hand, one line in a different, unsteady writing.

I should have said it to your face.

And under that:

I am sorry, my daughter.

She put the letter down on the table and looked at it.

“He knew,” she said.

“Yes,” said her father.

“He knew I was alive. And he never came.”

Lin Jian was pale. “His people paid me so that he’d never have to.” He sat down across from her. “I never met him. I met the man he sent, once, in a car.”

Jun Hyuk pulled out the chair beside her and sat down and put his hand on the table near hers, not on it.

Raiden had come in from the corridor at the sound of voices, and stood reading over her shoulder. She’d read it a second time and stopped on the date.

“The seventh of April,” Raiden said. “In writing.”

“Yes.”

“So it’s official.” He looked at her, and something eased slightly in his face. “You’re older.”

She let out a breath that was almost a laugh. “By two days.”

“Still older.”

“Don’t encourage her,” said Jun Hyuk. “She’s difficult enough.”

She turned and looked at him, offended, and Raiden laughed, the first laugh in the room, and she smiled with her eyes still wet.

The first letter said the new King meant to send an envoy. He would bring the testament, the birth records, and an invitation for her to decide whether she wished to be received by the Royal Household. There was no order to travel. No threat of ceremony. Only a request for a meeting, the date not yet fixed.

“They want me to go there,” she said.

“They’ve asked to meet you,” said her father. “That isn’t the same thing.”

“Will they accept it if I don’t want to go?”

“I don’t know.”

“They will,” said Jun Hyuk. “They’ve asked. You can answer.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She brought the letter home in a folder in her bag. She hadn’t left it with her father or the man in the dark coat. It was hers.

He made tea and put a cup by her hand and sat across the dining table from her while she looked at it again.

“Do you think he wanted me?”

He took a moment. “I don’t know what he wanted.”

“He wrote that he was sorry. But he didn’t come. He didn’t send for me. He didn’t even tell me.”

He reached across and touched her hand. “I know what you deserved. You deserved to hear it from him while he was alive. To his face. You deserved to know where you came from without teaching yourself a dead court’s grammar under a blanket for eleven years to find out.” His voice dropped. “I’m sorry nobody said it to you.”

Her mouth shook. He came round the table and crouched by her chair so his eyes were level with hers.

“I’m sorry you had to find it in a letter.”

She touched his cheek. “You always know what to say.”

“Not with you.”

“You said enough.”

He kissed her palm and put his forehead to hers.

“I don’t know if I want to meet them.”

“You don’t have to decide tonight.”

“What if they expect me to go?”

“Then they’ll have to learn how to ask.” He held her eyes. “If you go, I’m going. If you don’t, we stay here.”

She was quiet for a while, her forehead against his.

“Do you think I’m a princess?”

She seemed almost embarrassed to have asked. He took it seriously.

“Do you want to be?”

“Not particularly.”

“Then no.” He brushed her hair behind her ear. “You’re Evangeline.”

“Just Evangeline?”

“My wife.”

She laughed, and he kissed her.

Later she sat by the sealed window with the court letter open in her lap and the city lights in the glass, and read the handwritten line once more and traced its last character with her finger. She thought about the girl in the library copying letters she couldn’t pronounce, and the girl in the attic with the heron in grey thread under her fingers. She wished she could tell that girl something. Not that she’d be a king’s daughter in writing one day. Only that she wouldn’t spend her whole life waiting to be chosen. That somebody would open a box at a port at midnight and stand between her and the door. That somebody would give her a window box, a ridiculous coat, a place at the table. That somebody would ask to marry her twice.

She folded the letter and put it beside her ring on the sill.

He came up behind her and rested his chin on her shoulder. “Finished?”

“For tonight.”

She turned her head and kissed his cheek. “Come to bed.”

He took her hand. The letter stayed on the sill with the heron facing the ceiling. For eleven years she’d taught herself the language of a country that had never once called her home, and tonight it had finally said something to her. But when he reached for her in the dark, she knew exactly where she belonged.

chapters.title: The Envoy at the Door
chapters.desc: A polite man in grey gloves, two guards on the step, and an offer with a husband already chosen. She asks him one question he won’t answer.
chapters.epigraph: “And who protects me from the people offering protection?”
chapters.content:
The envoy came at seventeen minutes past eleven on Saturday the sixth of April.

Evangeline knew because she’d been watching the clock. Not anxiously. She’d told herself so. She’d made the tea, set out the cups, moved the jar of white freesias three times and put it back where it had started, and watched the clock.

They’d chosen her mother’s front room at the Walled City because it was the room in the house that belonged least to her father. The low cabinet, the curtains Mama had sewn, the pale mark on the floorboards where a chair had stood for twenty years. Evangeline remembered sitting under the table in this room, small, listening to adults talk over her head. Today she was in a chair.

Her father stood at the window. Elowen and Zhao were on the sofa. Raiden had taken the place nearest the door. Jun Hyuk stood behind her chair with one hand on its back, and he’d said almost nothing for twenty minutes, and that more than anything made her aware of him.

Raiden opened the door to a knock.

The envoy was a polite man in his late fifties with silver at his temples, a charcoal suit, immaculate shoes, and grey gloves although the morning was mild. Two guards stood on the step behind him, one older and still, one young with a broad face and a nick of a scar by his eyebrow. The envoy inclined his head.

“Mr. Lin. Thank you for receiving me. My name is Ahn. His Majesty sends his regards, and his regret for so unusual an introduction.”

“Please sit.”

Envoy Ahn’s eyes went round the room: the family, the tea, the letter on the table. They rested on Evangeline. Then they moved to the man behind her chair and stopped the way a man stops on a stair he hadn’t known was there.

“Mrs. Lee. The court has been eager to make your acquaintance.”

“Then it has taken its time,” said Evangeline.

Elowen looked at her lap to hide her face.

Ahn opened a leather document case. The late King’s acknowledgement, he explained, had been accepted by the royal legal council. Her name had been entered in the private register of the royal family.

“Private,” said Evangeline. “Not public.”

“Not at present. There are matters of succession and protocol. And sensitivities surrounding your mother’s identity, your upbringing, the circumstances of your birth. The court wishes to avoid distress.”

“Whose?”

He folded his gloved hands and didn’t answer that.

“What does the court want from me?”

“Nothing that would inconvenience you.” Jun Hyuk’s hand shifted on the chair. “His Majesty offers you a place at court. A residence, an allowance, a rank befitting the late King’s daughter.”

“Which residence?”

“A private estate in the capital.”

“Would I be allowed to leave it?”

“Naturally there would be security arrangements.”

“Would I be allowed to leave it?”

“Your safety would be our priority.”

She nodded slowly. It was an answer, only not to her question.

“There is one more matter.” He took out a second folder and laid a document on the table. “Given your long absence and the uncertainty of your position, it would be wise to establish an alliance with a family loyal to His Majesty. The son of Minister Yeom. A diplomat, well educated, of excellent family. They would be honoured to welcome you.”

The room went still.

“Welcome me,” said Evangeline. “As his wife.”

“If both parties were to agree.”

Zhao leaned forward. “She is married.”

“I’m aware. But the court has received no official notice of the marriage, and a marriage contracted outside the kingdom may require review before it can enter the royal register.”

Evangeline felt Jun Hyuk’s hand leave her chair. He didn’t step forward. He only stood a little straighter.

“Your husband, I understand, has a complicated occupation,” said Ahn. “The court would prefer you were protected from the uncertainties of such a life.”

“My husband protects me.”

“In his own way, I’m sure.”

“In every way that matters.”

Ahn looked down at his papers. “Then perhaps we should speak of your uncle. His Highness, the late King’s younger brother. He has taken a considerable interest in your recognition.”

“Does he know where I live?”

“His Highness has been told you are safe.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

“Your whereabouts are not a matter I’m authorised to discuss.”

“Then don’t,” said Jun Hyuk.

Ahn turned his head. “Mr. Lee, I believe this conversation is for Mrs. Lee and her family.”

“Then talk to her.”

Ahn turned back. “His Highness believes your return would restore an important branch of the family to its place. He has offered to oversee your introduction at court personally.”

“Why?”

“You are his niece.”

“Is that all?” She held his eyes. “Does he want me at court because I’m family, or because I give him a claim?”

He didn’t answer. It was the first honest thing he’d done all morning.

Her father moved from the window. “That’s enough. You’ve come into my wife’s house and put a marriage on my daughter’s table without asking whether she wants one. Take it back.”

“Mr. Lin, His Majesty’s instructions—”

“Take it back.”

Ahn closed the second folder. The court was divided, he said, more. The new King had inherited a fragile government and an uncle with friends among the old guard. Some called her recognition a correction of the late King’s will. Others called it a danger. “His Highness has supporters. Some of them are not patient. His Majesty wishes to settle this peacefully.”

“By arranging my marriage.”

“By securing your position. With the protection the household can offer.”

Evangeline looked past him at the two guards on the step.

“And who protects me from the people offering protection?”

His face moved for the first time.

The young guard had stepped in to murmur something to him, and couldn’t keep his voice down quite enough. “Sir. We should go. His Highness’s men are already waiting by the south road.”

“Teo.”

The young man shut his mouth. But it was in the room now.

“His Highness’s men,” said Evangeline.

Ahn took off one glove, a finger at a time. “An unfortunate choice of words. They’re part of the wider security arrangement.”

“Whose?” She looked at the young guard. “Teo. Why are they waiting?”

He looked at the floor, and then, miserably, at her. “To bring you to the residence. If the meeting went well.”

“And if it didn’t?”

He didn’t answer.

“How were they going to bring me?”

“By the back door, ma’am.”

Elowen was on her feet. Zhao put a hand on her arm.

Jun Hyuk came round Evangeline’s chair. Worse than the face he wore when he was angry: the one that came before he’d decided what to do with it.

“How many?”

“Mr. Lee, I must insist—”

“How many?”

The older guard answered. “Four by the south road. Two by the river.”

“Armed?”

A pause. “Yes.”

Jun Hyuk walked to the door and stood in front of the older guard, close, and when he spoke his voice was perfectly level.

“Listen carefully. His Highness’s river men can wait wherever they like. If any one of them comes through any door of this house for my wife, they come through me. I don’t need a gun to do it and I won’t be in a hurry. Tell them that, in their own language, so there’s no misunderstanding later.”

The man looked at him, and saw something there, and nodded. “I understand.”

“Good.”

“Jun Hyuk,” said Evangeline.

He turned at once, and the line of his mouth went when he looked at her. She held out her hand and he came and took it.

“Don’t make a scene,” she said, under her breath.

“I haven’t.”

She glanced at the envoy.

“Yet,” he added, and in spite of everything a breath came out of her that was almost a laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ahn asked to speak to her alone. She said no. He asked to speak to her father alone. Her father said no. In the end, with the marriage put back in its folder and the river men left unanswered, he gathered his papers, and put one more sheet on the table.

“Your mother’s name,” he said.

The room went quiet again.

“You know it,” said Evangeline.

“Yes.”

“Then tell me.”

“His Majesty asks that it be told to you in person. He believes you should hear it from him.” He looked at the paper. It had no name on it. Only an invitation to the capital, with an escort and rooms arranged. “He wishes to tell you himself.”

She thought of the unsteady line at the bottom of the court letter. I should have said it to your face. The father had been sorry for never speaking to her. Now the son wanted her to cross a border to hear her own mother’s name.

“One question. If I come to the capital, will I be allowed to leave again?”

He didn’t answer. She waited. The seconds went.

“His Majesty would never wish you to feel a prisoner,” he said at last.

“That isn’t an answer.”

“I can’t make promises for an entire court.”

“Then I have mine.”

He bowed, and went, and left the invitation on the table. Teo was last. At the threshold he looked back at her, and his face held an apology he hadn’t been given permission to make, and she gave him a small nod, and the door shut.

“By the back door,” said Elowen.

“He’s gone,” said Zhao.

“That doesn’t make it better.”

“No.”

Her father picked up the invitation and put it down again. “I should have known they’d send somebody like that. I should have—”

“You didn’t arrange this.”

“I brought you into this house.”

“And you kept me in it.” She went and took his hand. “Please don’t make every bad thing that happens to me into something you did wrong.”

He lifted her hand and pressed his mouth to her knuckles, and said he was sorry, and she said she knew.

Zhao was looking at Jun Hyuk. “The men by the river. Will you find out who they are?”

Jun Hyuk looked at Evangeline. “If she wants me to.”

“I want to know who’s waiting for me.”

“Then I’ll find out.”

Raiden already had his phone out. “Not yet,” said Jun Hyuk. “I want to know if they’re still there before anyone goes near them.” And Evangeline watched his attention split into several places at once, and touched his wrist.

“Come upstairs with me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her old bedroom was smaller than she remembered, or she’d grown. The bed was new. The desk under the window wasn’t; there were still faint grooves in it where she’d pressed too hard with a pencil copying characters out of a book. The grammar was on the bottom shelf, its spine split, the pages yellow at the edges.

“I used to think,” she said, “that if I learned enough of it, I’d understand why I was hidden.”

“Did you?”

“No.” She touched the spine. “I learned the words. I learned to read the old letters. And today a man came into my mother’s house and offered me a husband.”

“He’s not getting one.”

“I know.” She turned round. “I wasn’t frightened of that. I was angry. And when he said my uncle wanted to take me to the capital, I thought I’d spent all these years getting away from people who wanted to decide where I belonged, only to find there were more of them waiting.”

He took her hand. “You don’t belong to them.”

“I know that too.” She looked at him. “I want to know my mother’s name. I want to know why the old King never came, and why my uncle thinks I’m useful. But I don’t want to be something they pass round a table.”

“You won’t be.”

“How can you be sure?”

“Because you decide.”

“Would you come with me? To the capital. If I go.”

“Yes.”

“Even if my uncle’s waiting?”

“Especially then.”

He wasn’t promising nothing would happen. He’d never made that kind of promise. He was promising to be standing next to her when it did. She came up on her toes and kissed him, and he took it gently, his hand spread on her back, and when she drew away he looked at her mouth.

“Again.”

“You’re very demanding.”

“Only with my wife.”

She kissed him again, and this time he drew her in by the back of the neck and it deepened, slow and unhurried, until the envoy and the folder and the men by the river had gone somewhere far outside the shut door.

“You’re thinking too much,” he said, against her forehead.

“I’ve got a lot to think about. You could help.”

“How?”

She looked at the bed. He followed her eyes, and something came into his face, and without another word he slid an arm under her knees and lifted her.

“Jun Hyuk. You could have asked.”

“You were looking at the bed.”

“That isn’t permission.”

He stopped dead, at once, with her in his arms.

She laughed and pushed his hair off his forehead. “I was going to say yes.”

He looked at her a moment more. “May I?”

“Yes.”

He sat down on the edge of the bed with her in his lap and she settled with her knees either side of him and her forehead on his. His hand went slowly up and down her back.

“I used to sit here,” she said, “and imagine what my mother sounded like.”

“What did you imagine?”

“Somebody who laughed easily. I don’t know why. I wanted her to.”

“She might have.”

“She might have been stern.”

“She might have been both.” He brushed his thumb under her ear. “Whatever her name is, you don’t have to earn the right to know it.”

She shut her eyes. He leaned back against the headboard and took her with him, and she tucked her face into his neck and listened to his heart. Downstairs the house went on: voices, a phone, Raiden in the hall talking low, Elowen asking their father whether he’d eaten. The world hadn’t stopped because she was frightened. But for a while, in the room where she’d taught herself the language of a family that had never once written to her, she was a wife in her husband’s arms and a daughter in her mother’s house and a woman who could choose where to go next.

“Stay as long as you like,” he said into her hair.

“With you?”

“Always.”

“That’s a very big promise. You don’t make those.”

“I know,” he said, and she lifted her face and kissed him, and downstairs the royal invitation lay on the table, and for the first time since the letter came she wasn’t thinking about it at all.

chapters.title: She Says No to a Country
chapters.desc: On her real birthday she says no to a country in its own language. Then her husband has an afternoon, eleven telephone calls, and a viola.
chapters.epigraph: “You are my home.”
chapters.content:
At dawn on her birthday she practised refusing a country.

She sat cross-legged on the bed in her old room at the Walled City with an exercise book open on her knees and her hair over one shoulder, and the first light came in a pale strip between the curtains. He was awake beside her. He’d been awake for some time, lying on his side with his arm under the pillow, watching her as if the exercise book were a mildly irritating object that had come between them.

She read the sentence again and crossed it out.

“What was wrong with that one?”

“The verb’s too formal.”

“You’re refusing a king. Formal seems right.”

“It isn’t the formality. It sounds as if I’m asking permission.”

He considered this. “Then don’t ask.”

“I need to get it right.”

“You know what you want to say. Say it badly.”

“That’s your advice?”

“It’s always worked for me.” He reached under the blanket and found her ankle. “Come here.”

“I’m practising.”

“You can practise here.”

He tugged. The book slid off her knees between them as she came, and she knelt facing him with her hands on his shoulders.

“Again,” he said.

She took a breath and said it in the old court language, slowly. He didn’t understand a word. He listened as if he did. When she stopped his hand had found her waist.

“Is that all?”

“There’s one more paragraph.”

“You look different when you speak it,” he said. “As if you’re standing somewhere nobody can get to.”

That quieted her. She looked at the book.

“I used to imagine saying it in a room full of people who knew exactly what I was.”

“And now?”

“Now I’m going to say it to a man who thinks he can arrange my life.”

“Good.”

He bent his head and kissed her knee, so unexpectedly that she looked down at him.

“What was that for?”

“Birthday.”

Her face changed. “You’re the first.”

“It isn’t my fault everyone else is asleep.” He kissed the other knee. “Seventh of April. I know which one.”

She laughed and took his face in both hands. “You’re supposed to kiss me properly.”

“Then come down here.”

She did. Their foreheads touched first, and then his mouth met hers, slow and warm, while the exercise book lay forgotten on the blanket, and she kissed him until the sentence she’d been rehearsing wasn’t the first thing in her head any more.

“Happy birthday, Evangeline,” he said. “Twenty?”

“Don’t.”

“Twenty-one?”

“Jun Hyuk.”

“Twenty-six, and older than your brother,” he said, and she pushed his shoulder, and he caught her hand and kissed the palm, and for a few minutes they stayed like that, knee to knee, while the morning came into the room. Then she reached for the book, and he sighed at the ceiling.

“Your country’s very demanding.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Envoy Ahn came back at ten, alone. The two guards stayed outside the gate, and she noticed neither of them stood anywhere near the back of the house. Perhaps Teo had said something. Perhaps the older guard had passed the message on.
