Her father sat by the window, Elowen beside him. Zhao and Raiden stood by the cabinet. Jun Hyuk stood behind her chair, close enough that she could feel the warmth of him at her back, not touching her. She’d asked him not to. This was hers.

“Have you considered His Majesty’s invitation?”

“Yes. I’ve prepared my answer.”

“Please.”

She stood up and spoke in the court language. The first words came slowly. The second sentence came more easily. By the end, the language she’d taught herself from a book with a split spine had become something solid under her feet. Afterwards, so that her family would know what she’d said, she gave it again in their own.

“Your Majesty, I accept the late King’s declaration and that my name may stand in the family register. I do not seek a title, a residence, an allowance, or any place in the succession. I will not enter a marriage arranged to serve someone else’s influence. I will not come under the protection of a household that cannot promise me I may leave it. If my recognition makes a claim that could be used against the crown, I will renounce it. I will not be a weapon in a quarrel between my father’s relations. I will not be brought to the capital by the front door, or the back door, or any other door, without my consent.” She paused. “I’m grateful the late King acknowledged me. I’m grateful the present King offers to receive me. But I have a life, a family, and a home. I don’t ask the crown to approve of them. I ask it to respect them.”

The room was silent.

“You speak it very well,” said Ahn. “Where did you learn?”

“In a library. By myself.”

“That is a hard language to learn without a teacher.”

“It was a hard language to find a teacher for.”

Something moved in his face. He looked at her father, and back at her.

“Your mother spoke it like a native,” he said. “She was a musician. She played the viola in the royal household orchestra. She wasn’t of the family. She came from a family of musicians and was invited to the court for several seasons.”

Evangeline looked at her father.

Lin Jian shook his head slowly. “I never knew her. The man who came to me never said a word about her.”

“The late King often went to rehearsals,” said Ahn. “He remembered her playing long after she’d left the household.”

“Why did she leave?”

“I can’t speak to that.”

“Do you know her name?”

“I do. His Majesty wishes to tell you himself.”

“Then His Majesty,” said Evangeline, “can wait until I’m ready.”

He inclined his head. “I’ll convey your answer, and your offer to renounce. Such a renunciation can’t be accepted by me. It would go to the council.”

“Tell them I’ll sign whatever is needed.”

He gathered his papers. At the door he looked back at her. “Your mother would have been proud of your command of the language.”

She didn’t answer. She was afraid her voice would go.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father knelt down beside her chair when the door had shut and took her hand, and didn’t ask her what she was thinking.

“A viola,” she said.

“Yes.”

She’d never seen one, except in pictures. She tried to imagine a young woman with a dark wooden instrument under her chin, drawing a bow across it in a room full of music, a woman whose hands had known something besides the careful work of keeping a child hidden. She found she wanted to hear it more than she’d wanted almost anything. Not a recording. The instrument her mother had held.

Jun Hyuk was watching her face. Then he took out his phone and said, “Excuse me,” and went into the hall.

He made eleven calls. The first was to a man who ran private events. The second was to somebody at the botanical gardens. The third was to a cellist he’d once helped with a lost passport and an unhelpful customs officer, who knew a woman who knew a viola teacher. By the sixth he’d taken his jacket off and rolled his sleeves up. The ninth was to Nam.

“No,” said Nam at once.

“I haven’t asked anything.”

“You’re ringing me on a Sunday. You’ve already asked.”

He explained. There was a pause.

“Music,” said Nam. “For your wife’s birthday.”

“Yes.”

“You’re getting very expensive to know.” A sigh. “What do you need?”

By two in the afternoon he had the Glass Pavilion at the botanical gardens for the evening, and the paths round it closed, and a viola player called Mrs. Yoon Mi-ok, who had played in the royal household orchestra thirty years before and now taught children in a room above a piano shop on the far side of the river.

He didn’t tell Evangeline any of it. He came back into the front room and kissed her forehead and asked whether she’d eaten.

“You’re hiding something.”

“Yes. Your birthday.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the only one you’re getting. Your father’s been watching you not eat for twenty minutes.”

Her father looked away. She sighed and picked up her fork.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past six he told her to put on a dress.

“Why?”

“We’re going out.”

“Where?”

“Somewhere.”

“That isn’t a destination.”

“It’s enough of one.” He was in a dark suit with the collar open and one strand of hair already falling over his forehead, and he looked much too handsome to be trusted. “The pale one.”

She wore the pale blue, and the aquamarines with their mended gold, and at the door he reached up and moved one earring that didn’t need moving, and then touched her face.

“Beautiful.”

“You say that every time.”

“You keep being it.”

The Glass Pavilion was lit with candles. She stopped in the doorway. The tall glass walls held the last of the evening sky, so the room seemed to hang among the trees. White orchids stood along the stone paths in clusters, not too many, and the low tables had white flowers on them, and there were no banners and nothing royal anywhere. Just flowers and light, and at the far end, a woman in her sixties with silver hair pinned at the nape of her neck, and a viola resting against her chair.

“Mrs. Lee? I’m Yoon Mi-ok. Your husband asked me to play for you.”

Evangeline went to her. “Did you know my mother? She played viola at court.”

Mrs. Yoon looked at her more carefully, at her eyes, and her own face changed. “Ah,” she said. “Yes. Not well. But I remember her.”

“Was she good?”

“Very. She had a lovely sense of phrasing. She never hurried the end of a note.” Mrs. Yoon lifted the viola. “And she used to stay behind after rehearsals to help the youngest players, when nobody else could be bothered. I was one of them.”

She set it under her chin, and drew the bow, and the room filled.

The sound surprised Evangeline: lower than a violin, warmer, softer at the edges, something human in it that seemed to move through the air instead of only filling it. She stood perfectly still. She imagined her mother in a room at the palace with this same weight under her chin, her hair pinned up perhaps, perhaps a man standing in a doorway listening. Perhaps she’d smiled when she reached the end of a phrase.

Her eyes filled. Jun Hyuk stood beside her and didn’t touch her until her fingers came looking for his, and then he held them.

Mrs. Yoon played a second piece with a melody that rose gently and settled into a long low line. When the last note had gone, nobody said anything for a while.

“Thank you,” said Evangeline.

“Happy birthday, dear.”

They ate under the glass roof, a small white cake with blue flowers and a plate of fruit, and Mrs. Yoon stayed for tea and told her the little she remembered of the orchestra. After she’d gone Evangeline sat beside him looking at the candles.

“Nam says you made eleven calls.”

“Some were short.”

She laughed, and leaned over and kissed him, warm and grateful.

“You’re looking at me as if you’ve got something to say,” she said.

“This morning, in the middle of all that grammar, you said something that wasn’t in your exercise book. You said it to me. Not to the King.”

She went pink. “You noticed.”

“I noticed the sound.”

“It’s from old court poetry. I found it in the back of the grammar when I was sixteen and learned it because I liked the shape of it.” She looked at her hands. “It means You are my home.”

He looked at her, and his face did the thing it always did when she said something that got to him before he could get ready for it. He took her hand and tried the words.

His pronunciation was terrible. Not slightly wrong. Terrible.

She stared at him. He tried again, and somehow made it worse, and she burst out laughing.

“Stop. You’re ruining it.”

“I’m learning.”

“You’re not learning, you’re attacking it.”

He said it a third time with the stress on nearly every wrong syllable, and she laughed until she had to put her hand over her mouth. Then she leaned close and said it slowly for him. He repeated it. Better. She corrected one sound. He tried again, and it came out almost right.

“Better,” she said. “Not perfect.”

“I’ll practise.” He kissed the inside of her wrist. “I’ve got time.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was late when they let themselves into the flat. Her family had left a small box on the table and a note from Elowen promising to ring in the morning. She put the box on the dresser and turned round and he was watching her.

“What?”

“Nothing. I keep looking at you.”

She went to him. He drew her in, and they stood in the dim bedroom still dressed, still carrying the evening, and then she kissed him and he answered slowly with his palm moving up her back, and then not slowly.

He undid her dress with the same care he gave everything he thought precious, and it went down round her feet, and she undid his shirt and pushed it off his shoulders and put her mouth on his chest. He laid her down on the bed and knelt over her and kissed her throat and her breasts, unhurried, until she arched up into him.

“You don’t have to be so careful,” she said.

“I know.”

“Then why are you?”

“Because I love you,” he said, and her face went soft, and she pulled him down.

He went into her slowly, watching her, and held there, and she wrapped her legs round him and took him deeper. They moved together without any hurry at all, and he murmured into her neck, and she held his face and made him look at her while it built, and when she came she said his name and then the court words, the ones from the back of the book, and he felt them break against his mouth and followed her over with his face in her hair.

Afterwards she lay with her cheek on his chest and his fingers going slowly through her hair.

“Did you have a good birthday?”

“Yes.”

“Say it again,” she said, and he knew what she meant, and tried the phrase. It still wasn’t right.

“Again.”

He tried once more. She laughed and lifted her head and kissed him. “You’ll get it.”

“I’ll learn.”

Her mother’s instrument had spoken to her that evening. A man in grey gloves had heard her say no in the language of a court that had never once sent for her. The King still had the name she wanted. But she’d refused the country, and offered to give the claim away, and come home to the man who’d spent a whole afternoon making eleven calls so that her birthday could hold something besides the past.

“Happy birthday, Evangeline.”

“You are my home,” she whispered, in the old words.

This time he understood every one of them.

chapters.title: Two Men Share a Table
chapters.desc: Dinner for four at the house on the hill. Two sisters in the kitchen, two men on the terrace, and a payment for a boat in June.
chapters.epigraph: “If June is meant to be the month somebody comes to take me, I’d rather it was the month we made them sorry they tried.”
chapters.content:
The invitation said dinner for four, and Evangeline knew at once it was a trap.

Not because her sister had ever been unkind to her. Because the message was so innocent. Come to dinner on Saturday. I miss you. Zhendong says he wants to cook. Zhao Zhendong didn’t cook. He supervised cooking. He occasionally cut vegetables with the solemn concentration of a man handling ordnance. He had once burnt a pan of rice to the bottom and blamed the hob.

When she told Jun Hyuk, he asked only one thing. “Will he be there?”

“Of course.”

“Then I’ll come.”

That was how she knew the evening would be interesting.

The house on the hill looked its best in the late light on the eleventh of May. Elowen had planted white flowers along the front steps, the windows were open, and the dogs came down the path to look at Jun Hyuk and decided he was acceptable. He took the basket of fruit out of Evangeline’s hands before she reached the steps.

“I can carry it.”

“I know.”

“Then why did you take it?”

“I wanted to.”

“You’re impossible,” she said, and he kissed her cheek.

Elowen came down the steps in an apron with a wooden spoon in her hand and held her at arm’s length.

“Twelve days. That’s nearly two weeks. Are you eating?”

“Yes.”

“Sleeping?”

“Yes.”

Elowen looked over her shoulder. “Is she?”

“More than she was,” said Jun Hyuk.

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the one I’ve got.”

Elowen narrowed her eyes at him and stood aside. “Come in. Zhendong’s pretending to be useful.”

“I can hear you,” said a voice from the kitchen.

“Good!”

On the step Evangeline caught her husband’s sleeve. “Be nice.”

“I’m always nice.” He kissed her knuckles. “To you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen took her sister into the kitchen. That left the two men in the dining room with a pot of tea and a silence that began almost at once.

Zhao stood at the counter slicing a cucumber. Jun Hyuk sat at the table looking at the garden through the open doors. He watched three slices go.

“You’re cutting those too thick.”

“They’re cucumbers.”

“They’re meant to be slices. Those are blocks.”

Zhao put the knife down. “Do you want to do it?”

“No.”

“Then stop watching.”

“Hard not to,” said Jun Hyuk, and Zhao picked up the knife again.

For a while there was only the knife on the board and the sisters’ voices from the kitchen. Then Zhao said, without looking up, “Is she still having the dreams?”

Jun Hyuk’s eyes went to the kitchen door. “Less often.”

“Good.”

“I want to ask you about Velde.”

The knife stopped. Zhao put it down slowly. “Not tonight. My wife’s invited your wife to dinner. I’d like to eat before we make it unpleasant.”

“Then you should have answered me before tonight.”

Zhao turned round. From the kitchen Elowen laughed at something Evangeline had said, and Zhao looked towards the sound, and then back.

“Outside.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The terrace lights had come on along the railing. Past the hill, the city was going gold and grey. Zhao shut the glass door behind them.

“Say it.”

“The rifles that didn’t cross. I know where they didn’t go. I want to know who you’d sold to before.”

Zhao went to the railing. He was quiet.

“The Ferryman,” he said. “Not that shipment. Years before. I sold to the men who kept his routes open on the far bank. They paid well, and on time, and I didn’t ask what was on the boats.”

“Did you know?”

Zhao didn’t turn round.

“I knew he moved people. I told myself his clients were criminals and his business was his. I knew there were people on those boats.” His hand closed on the rail. “Women. Children. I knew enough to stop asking, and I stopped.”

“Her box came off his route.”

“Yes.”

“Your rifles kept his route open.”

“Yes.”

“And his route took my wife.”

Zhao turned then. “I know.”

“No, you don’t. You don’t get to say you know.”

“Then tell me what you want me to say.”

Jun Hyuk came a step closer. “How many people you helped put on those boats.”

“I don’t know.”

“How much you were paid.”

“Enough.”

“Did you spend it?”

“Some.” Zhao held his eyes. “I’m not asking you to forgive me.”

“Good.”

“I’m telling you because you’ve a right to know.”

“You should have told me before. Before you sat at a table with her. Before you watched her stand next to me. Before you told me on that bridge to keep her happy.”

“Yes.” Zhao’s face had lost its composure. He looked older in the evening light, with whatever he’d been carrying finally visible on him. “I’ve thought about it every day since I found out what happened to her. I was ashamed. That isn’t a reason.”

“No. It isn’t.”

Neither of them said anything for some time. Inside, Elowen opened a cupboard.

“There’s something else,” said Zhao, and took a folded paper out of his jacket. “Three days ago one of my people caught a payment request going through a shipping agent the Ferryman’s people use. I traced it through two companies. One of them belongs to her uncle’s household.”

Jun Hyuk unfolded it. Dates, an amount, a reference, a route code. No names. Initials.

“June,” he said.

“One passenger. One boat. They’ve paid the Ferryman’s people to bring somebody across in June.”

“Do they know where she is?”

“They know she refused the envoy. They may know she lives with you.”

Jun Hyuk looked through the glass. Evangeline was in the kitchen with her head tilted towards her sister, smiling at something. He looked back at Zhao.

“How long?”

“Less than a month.”

“Then we use it.”

“You use it,” said Zhao. “I don’t talk to the police, and I don’t lend my men to anybody. That paper is the end of what I can do.”

“I didn’t ask you for more.”

“I know.” Zhao looked through the glass at his wife. “I’m not asking her for anything either.”

“And Zhao. If those men come for her, your history with them won’t save one of them.”

“I wouldn’t expect it to,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the kitchen Elowen was trying to stop her sister cutting the carrots into pieces of every size.

“They’re meant to cook evenly.”

Evangeline held one up. “This one’s perfectly normal.”

“That one’s a quarter the size of the others.”

“Perhaps it wants to be.”

Elowen stared at her, and then laughed, and they worked a while without talking, the window open and the smell of ginger and garlic coming up off the pan. Elowen hummed when she cooked. Their mother had too. Evangeline watched her reach past for something on the shelf with a streak of flour on her wrist, and thought about the river.

“Elowen. If something happens in June—”

Elowen’s spoon stopped. “Don’t start a sentence like that.”

“I don’t want you worrying before there’s a reason.”

“Then don’t start a sentence like that.”

Evangeline put the knife down. She could have kept it to herself. She knew what it would do to her sister. But she remembered how often she’d been left outside the decisions about her own life, and she wasn’t going to do it to anybody else.

“Somebody’s paid for a boat in June. For one person.”

Elowen went completely still. “Your uncle?”

“Possibly.”

“You’re not going anywhere.”

“I don’t mean to. But I don’t want you to stop living your life because of me.”

“Don’t.”

“I mean it.”

“I know what you mean.”

Elowen reached for the spoon again, and Evangeline caught her wrist, and then stepped in and put both arms round her.

There was no reason for it. No explanation. No hospital corridor, nothing that had just gone wrong. She put her arms round her sister and held on.

Elowen froze. In twenty-six years she’d never once been hugged by Evangeline first. Then her arms came round her, one hand on the back of her head.

“Oh, sweetheart.”

“I’m learning,” said Evangeline, into her shoulder.

“Good.” Elowen kissed her hair, and after a while held her away and wiped the corner of her eye with a floury thumb. “Now. If you’ve finished making me cry, those carrots are still terrible.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was quieter than it might have been. Zhao served. Elowen corrected his portions. Evangeline praised the soup, and Jun Hyuk said nothing at all about the carrots.

“You’re very quiet,” said Zhao.

“I’m eating.”

Elowen looked from one to the other. “Have you two had a fight?”

“No,” they said together.

“Then why do you look as if you’ve swallowed a nail?” she asked her husband.

“Work.”

She let it go, but her eyes stayed on him. Under the table Evangeline found Jun Hyuk’s hand, and it closed round hers. He was eating, but not all of him was at the table. Every few minutes his eyes went to the open doors and the dark garden, and then to her, and she knew that look. He was already planning.

Elowen talked about the garden for the wedding, because somebody had to talk about something. A date in December, she said, before the cold. The orchids. Six guests, or seven, or however many it turned out to be when Nam had finished complaining about the drive. Zhao listened to his wife as if every word were worth keeping, and once, when she wasn’t looking, he looked across the table at Evangeline with something in his face she’d never seen there before, and then down at his plate.

✦ ✦ ✦

After the fruit, Jun Hyuk carried the plates through without being asked. Elowen followed him with the soup pot and found him at the sink, sleeves pushed up, running the water too hot.

“Guests don’t wash up in this house.”

“I’m not a guest. I’m her husband.” He put a bowl on the rack. “And I’d like to know where the plates go.”

She told him. He put them away in the right places, one by one, the way a man memorises a room he means to come back to. She leaned on the counter and watched him.

“Is she safe with you?” she said.

He didn’t answer straight away. He dried his hands on the towel by the stove and folded it in three and hung it back where it had been.

“Safer than anywhere else. Not safe. Nobody is.” He looked at her. “But nobody will ever take her anywhere she hasn’t chosen to go. Not while I’m alive. You can hold me to that.”

“I will.”

“I know. That’s why I said it to you and not to him.”

Elowen looked at him, at the careful hands and the way his eyes had gone, even now, to the window and the dark garden beyond it. Then she reached up and straightened his collar, which didn’t need it, as if he were one of her brothers.

“Breakfast,” she said. “Not tea.”

Elowen hugged her sister again on the step. “Ring me tomorrow. A call, not a message. And eat breakfast.” She pointed at Jun Hyuk. “He knows.”

“Understood,” said Jun Hyuk.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao’s gatekeeper had rung them a taxi. In the back, the city lights went across the windows as they came down off the hill.

“You’re thinking,” said Evangeline.

“Yes.”

“About June. And Zhao.” She waited. “Aren’t you going to tell me what he said?”

“Not in a taxi.”

The driver, who’d heard every word, reached over without a word and put the radio on. Something soft and instrumental came out of it, and Jun Hyuk took her hand and told her: the rifles, years ago, the men on the far bank, the boats.

She didn’t react at once. “Did he know I was on one?”

“No.”

“Did he know the Ferryman took women?”

“Yes.”

She looked out at the dark. “Then I understand why you were angry.”

“You’re not?”

“I am. I’m not surprised.” She turned back. “He told you himself. That matters.”

“It doesn’t undo anything.”

“No.” She leaned her head on his shoulder. “And June. One passenger.”

“That’s what the paper says.”

“Do you think it’s me?”

“I don’t know.”

“Do you think my uncle wants me in the capital?”

“I think he wants to control where you are.”

“Is that why he told you?”

“Partly.”

“You don’t like owing Zhao.”

“I don’t have to like him to use what he knows.”

She smiled, and he looked at her, and her eyes were tired.

“Are you frightened?”

“A little.”

He didn’t tell her she needn’t be. He didn’t promise nothing would happen. He moved closer, and she lifted her face and kissed him, a soft press of her mouth on his, and then again with her hand on his jaw, and he turned into it with his hand at her waist, careful of the gap between the seats, until she smiled against him.

The radio went up two notches.

She pulled away laughing. Jun Hyuk looked at the back of the driver’s head.

“Sorry, sir,” said the driver. “The song was getting quiet.”

“Drive.”

“Yes, sir.”

She laughed into his shoulder. Then she lifted her head and took his hand and put it against her cheek.

“Thank you for telling me.”

“I should have told you sooner.”

“Yes. But you told me now.” She kissed the corner of his mouth. “And Jun Hyuk. If June is meant to be the month somebody comes to take me, I’d rather it was the month we made them sorry they tried.”

He looked at her. A slow, dangerous smile came onto his face.

“All right,” he said.

She settled against him. The taxi took them home. And somewhere across the river somebody had paid for a boat with one passenger in mind, and Jun Hyuk held his wife’s hand all the way back.

chapters.title: The Abduction Attempt
chapters.desc: Nam’s seventy-second birthday, which he refuses to have. A plan, a cake, and four men in a noodle shop at two in the afternoon.
chapters.epigraph: “Not again.”
chapters.content:
He told her everything on the Sunday morning.

Not because he’d got comfortable talking about danger. He hadn’t. He still sometimes mistook silence for protection. But the night before, in the car, she’d asked him what exactly they meant to do if they came for her in June, and he’d said he didn’t know, and she’d looked at him and said, Then tell me what you do know.

So at the kitchen table, with the hatch open on the herbs and the morning coming in, he put a folder down between them.

“The payment went through a go-between. The account belongs to one of your uncle’s companies. The Ferryman’s people took it. Enough for a private crossing. June, no day.”

“One passenger. Across the river.”

“That’s the likeliest reading.”

“To him.”

“I think that’s what he wants.”

“And if I refuse?”

“They may try to make refusing impossible.” He held her eyes. “I don’t know how many men. I don’t know if the boat’s the first step or the last. I don’t know if they’ll take you straight or send somebody to get close first. I know they won’t necessarily look like men who’ve come to hurt you.”

“Like the envoy,” she said. “Like guards. Like somebody holding a car door for me.”

“Yes.”

“Have you found the boat?”

“Not yet.”

“Can it be stopped?”

“Yes. Before it gets anywhere near you.”

She studied him. “You’re planning to leave me here and spend June somewhere else.”

He didn’t answer.

“Jun Hyuk.”

“I haven’t decided.”

“You have.” She reached across and touched his wrist. “Don’t make plans that need me not to know about them.”

He looked at her a long time. “I won’t.”

“Promise.”

“Yes.”

She nodded. Then, before he’d finished breathing out: “I want to go up to Nam’s on the fifteenth.”

“No.”

“I haven’t told you why.”

“His birthday. Seventy-two.”

“He hates birthdays. He says seventy-one was already too many and he doesn’t mean to encourage seventy-two. I want to bake him a cake.”

“The border isn’t safe.”

“Neither is the city.”

“That’s different.”

“How?”

He opened his mouth and shut it again. She tilted her head.

“That’s what I thought.”

He rubbed his forehead. “We plan it properly. Don’t look so pleased. I haven’t agreed to anything.”

“You said we’d plan it.”

“Properly. That isn’t the same as you getting your way.”

“You married me.”

“That was my first mistake.”

She gasped. He caught her hand before she could take it back.

“My favourite one,” he said.

She leaned across the table and kissed him, and when she tried to sit back he followed her over the folder.

“That was meant to be a negotiation,” she said against his mouth.

“It was.”

“You haven’t agreed.”

“I’m considering.” She kissed him again, and his hand went to the back of her neck. “You’re bribing me.”

“Is it working?”

“Unfortunately.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first plan was made on the Monday and the second on the Wednesday, and by the end of the week Eliana had put an app on Evangeline’s phone that would show him where she was every second, and Song, because a boat for one passenger was his case now, had put Sergeant Chiu with her, a quiet heavy man who’d driven the border road twice already, and two constables in plain clothes on the bridge.

“Why two more?”

“Because I said so.”

“That isn’t a reason.”

“Because I don’t want you on your own.”

“Sergeant Chiu’s driving me.”

“Then you’ll have three.”

“That seems a great deal for a birthday cake.”

“Good.”

He was at the counter checking his phone, and she could see the strain under how composed he was. She went and took the phone out of his hand.

“Look at me. I’m going to see Nam. I’m going to give him a cake and drink tea and argue with him about how much sugar he puts in everything. I won’t go anywhere without Chiu. I won’t change the road. I won’t leave the shop on my own. If anything feels wrong I’ll ring you.” She tilted her head. “Now you. Stop looking at me as if you’re already at my funeral.”

His face changed. “I hate this,” he said. “I hate that you have to think about roads and men and doors just to go and see somebody who—”

She came up on her toes and put her mouth over the rest of it.

It was a quiet kiss, placed deliberately in the middle of his sentence. His hand came to her waist and drew her in. When she tried to step back he caught her and walked her back against the kitchen table, his forehead lowered to hers.

“I hate that I can’t promise you’ll be safe.”

“Then don’t promise that. Promise you’ll come home.”

“I will.”

She kissed him once more and slipped out under his arm and picked up her phone and went to the door.

“Where are you going?”

“To buy flour. Seventy-two candles would be ridiculous.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was one thing he didn’t know.

In February she’d asked him to teach her to shoot. Not because she wanted his life. Because she’d spent too long being moved about by other people’s decisions, and she’d seen what happened to somebody who had no way to back up her own.

He hadn’t liked it. He’d gone quiet and asked her why, and she’d told him the truth. I don’t want to be helpless if someone comes for me. He’d looked at her. Then he’d taught her, on Sunday mornings in a closed range north of the city, slowly, with more rules than she’d thought one man could hold in his head. A weapon wasn’t courage. A weapon was a responsibility you carried every second it was on you. Fear made people careless. The best day with a gun was the day you didn’t take it out. She learned to stay calm under his voice. She learned the rules so well she stopped needing them said. She wasn’t good. She was better than she’d been.

On the Saturday morning the small pistol was in a holster under her coat, and he hadn’t seen it and hadn’t asked, and she hadn’t told him. Not to deceive him. Because she wanted the day to feel like a birthday. For once, she wanted to be a woman bringing a cake to an old man who hated birthdays.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday the fourteenth of June, in his own shop, Nam announced that he wasn’t turning seventy-two. He was turning seventy-one again.

“That isn’t how birthdays work,” said Evangeline, behind the counter.

“That’s how mine work.”

“Does the government know?”

“The government has no business with my age.”

She laughed. The shop smelled of broth and spring onions, the tables worn smooth in the places where elbows went, and the bell over the door made the same tired sound it always had. She’d missed it more than she’d expected: the river road, the uneven pavement, the window table where she’d once sat with two bowls waiting for a man who said he was nobody.

Nam looked at the box on the counter. “What’s that?”

“Nothing.”

“That’s a cake box.”

“It’s a very ordinary box.”

He pointed his ladle at it. “No candles.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“And not seventy-two.”

“I brought seventy-one.”

He turned round, and saw her grinning, and pointed the ladle at her. “Get out.”

She laughed so hard she had to hold on to the counter. Elara and Nuo, at the bakery across the road, were coming at three tomorrow for a slice. The cake would sit in Nam’s cold room overnight. Chiu, at the corner table with a bowl of noodles, pretended he hadn’t heard any of it.

She’d baked it that morning in the bakery’s oven across the road, because Nam would have known in a second if she’d used his, with Nuo beside her in a floury apron telling her how long. Nuo had passed her first exams in May. She held the cake tin as if it were a patient. “Seventy-one,” she’d said, when Evangeline told her about the candles, and laughed so hard she’d had to sit down on a sack of flour.

That night, in the old room over the Golden Nightingale with the three locks and the painted windows, Jun Hyuk checked the locks twice. She watched him from the joined camp beds they’d never got round to replacing.

“Everything’s locked.”

“I know.”

“You checked.”

“I know.”

She lifted the blanket. “Your wife’s waiting.”

That brought him back. He turned the lamp to the wall and got in beside her and she put her cheek on his chest.

“Tomorrow will be fine,” she said.

“I know.”

“You don’t sound sure.”

“I’m trying.”

“Nam asked if I’d put raisins in it.”

“Did you?”

“Of course not. I’m not cruel.”

He smiled, and she touched his mouth. “See.”

He caught her hand and kissed the fingers. “Sleep.”

She shut her eyes. He held her and listened to her breathe, and when he thought she was asleep, he said into her hair, “Come home tomorrow.”

She heard him, and squeezed his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

He left early, to meet Song across the bridge about the boat, and said he’d be at Nam’s by two. At two o’clock on Saturday the fifteenth of June four men came into Nam’s Noodles.

The first came in at the front. The second followed. The other two came in from the side passage, the way only the cats used.

Evangeline was at the counter cutting a slice for Nam, who’d been pretending for twenty minutes not to care and had already eaten two. The icing was white with a border of small blue flowers, and across the top she’d written Happy Birthday, Nam in letters that had come out uneven. He’d looked at it and then away.

“Too much icing,” he’d said.

“You like icing.”

“I like a sensible amount.”

“Then don’t eat it.”

He’d taken another bite.

The bell rang. Nam looked up. The first man didn’t look at the menu. He looked at Evangeline.

She felt it before she understood it: the way his eyes fixed on her, the way the other three didn’t spread out like customers but moved like men with places to be. She put the knife down.

“Nam,” she said.

The first man smiled. “Mrs. Lee. We’ve been looking for you.”

Nam stood up. “She’s eating.”

“This doesn’t concern you.”

“Then leave my shop.”

The second man came round the end of the counter. She stepped back.

“Come with us,” said the first man. “Your uncle wants to see you.”

“Then he can send a letter.”

“He’s sent enough letters.”

“Apparently not enough for me to agree.”

The second man reached for her arm, and Nam moved first. He took the big pot off the back ring in both hands and threw it, and a wave of hot broth went across the floor and up the men’s legs, and they went back shouting and swearing, and the pot hit the tiles and rolled under a table.

“Run!” Nam shouted.

She turned for the back passage. A man was already in it, from the side, with a length of iron pipe. It came down on the edge of the counter with a crack she felt in her teeth. Nam tried to shove past him, and the man swung, and Nam went down. His shoulder hit the floor and his head hit the leg of a chair, and he lay there.

“Nam!”

A hand closed on her coat. She twisted. It held. She got her phone out and somebody knocked it out of her fingers, and it went skidding under a table and the screen flashed once and went dark.

The man in front of her caught her wrist. She pulled back. He was much stronger. She felt the old thing come up in her chest, the terrible understanding that somebody had decided her body was something he could move from one place to another.

Not again.

It came quite clearly.

Not again.

She drove her shoulder into him and broke his grip for long enough to step away. Four men. The shop was too small, the tables too close together, Nam on the floor. And Jun Hyuk wasn’t there yet.

✦ ✦ ✦

He reached the bridge at twelve minutes past two, talking to one of the constables, when his phone went twice. Eliana’s app: her dot had stopped moving. Then Chiu.

Chiu: Four men in the shop. Going in.

He didn’t remember crossing the road. He didn’t remember putting the phone away. He remembered the sound of something breaking inside Nam’s, and Chiu’s voice in his ear saying I’m at the front, and coming round the back of the shop by the bins, fast, the way he’d come a hundred times with the brass key, and a man stepping out from the yard behind him.

He heard the movement and turned. Too late. Something heavy came down on the back of his head and the world went white. He caught the wall with one hand. A second blow, and his knees went, and the ground came up hard.

For a while there was nothing.

Then pieces. A shoe. A table leg through the open back door. Somebody shouting. He tried to push himself up and his arm wouldn’t hold him and the yard tipped sideways, and through the door, through the steam and the overturned chairs, he heard her.

He got his eyes open.

Inside, one of the men had reached for her again.

She had one second. One second to do what had kept her alive her whole life. Run. Find the door. Find a place with people in it. Ring somebody.

But Nam was on the floor. And her husband was somewhere outside.

The man reached for her.

Evangeline put her hand under her coat and drew the pistol.

chapters.title: She Shoots First
chapters.desc: Three shots in a noodle shop. The first two hit the duck. She is still very bad at it. It is enough.
chapters.epigraph: “Stay behind me.”
chapters.content:
The first shot was terrible.

It went into the glass cabinet behind the counter and burst the little porcelain duck Nam had kept on the middle shelf for twenty years.

The second was worse. It hit the wall above the menu board, and plaster came down in a white rain over the faded photographs of dishes that hadn’t changed price since 1991.

She flinched at both. Her hand shook. And the man in front of her stopped.

For one long second nobody in Nam’s Noodles seemed to remember how to breathe.

She’d never been good at this. He’d told her so, gently, on the range in March: too tense when she was frightened, too inclined to hold her breath, too busy thinking about what would happen afterwards. She’d got better. Not enough. He’d said he hoped she’d never find out how much better.

Now there was porcelain on the floor and a hole in the wall and a man coming at her round the end of the counter with an iron pipe in his hand.

“Stop,” she said.

He looked at the pistol, and then at her, and his mouth twisted. “You’re not going to shoot me.”

She wished he were right.

He took another step. Past him, through the open back door, she could see Jun Hyuk on the ground in the yard by the bins, half turned over, one arm under him, blood dark in his hair. He was trying to move. She could see him trying to get up.

The man with the pipe looked round at the door.

That was when she fired the third time.

It wasn’t graceful. It wasn’t the way he’d taught her. Her hand jumped and the noise filled the little shop to the ceiling, and the man screamed and the pipe went out of his fingers and clanged on the tiles, and he went down against the side of a table clutching his shoulder.

She stood where she was, with the pistol still up and her arms locked. Her ears were ringing. She could smell broth, and hot metal, and something sharp and chemical from the broken cabinet. She’d shot a man. The thought arrived slowly, almost politely. She’d shot a man.

Then, out in the yard, Jun Hyuk moved again, and nothing else mattered.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d got one knee under himself. His hand was flat on the wet concrete and his arm was shaking with the effort of holding him up. He looked through the doorway and saw her coming, and saw what was in her hand, and his face changed.

“Evangeline—”

“No.”

She stepped through the door and stood over him, between him and the shop.

“Stay behind me,” she said.

He went completely still.

The last man had come to the doorway. He was older than the others, in his fifties, in a pale shirt with his hair combed neatly, and he had the face of a man who was offended by mess. He hadn’t hurried at any point. He hadn’t shouted. He’d watched the others do the work, as if he was used to sending people into rooms and waiting for them to bring back what he’d asked for. His eyes settled on her.

“Put it down.”

She didn’t.

“You’re making a mistake. We came for you, not for an old man’s shop.”

“I said no.”

“Your uncle has been very patient.”

“Then he can go on being patient.”

He took a step. She raised the pistol. He stopped, and for the first time something uncertain crossed his face. Not fear. Recognition. He’d seen her mouth begin to shape the language he’d grown up with.

She’d learned it from a book in a library. She’d used it the week before last to tell a man in grey gloves she wouldn’t be married off. Now she used it on a man who’d come to carry her away.

“Stand where you are. Kneel. Put your hands where I can see them.”

Her accent wasn’t good. The meaning was.

He stared at her. Then he said something short back, in the same language. You have no authority here.

“I have authority over my own body,” she said, in theirs.

“Your uncle is His Highness.”

“And I’m not his property.” She went on, more fluently, in the court words. “You will not touch me. You will not take me. You will not carry me over that river.”

He looked at her. Then he smiled, small and unpleasant.

“Your mother should have taught you better.”

She went still. She’d heard that sentence before, in different words: in the envoy’s careful gaps, in the court’s polite letters, in the way everybody spoke about her mother as if she were a locked room.

“Don’t speak about her.”

“She was a foolish woman. She thought she could walk out of the household and take the King’s child with her.” He watched it land. “There are things you don’t know.”

“I know enough.”

“You know what you’ve been allowed to know.”

Behind her there was a sound. “Ev—”

She didn’t turn round. But the man in the pale shirt did look past her, at the man on the ground, and she understood that he’d stopped looking at her at all. He’d decided Jun Hyuk was the weak one. He’d decided he could get to him.

She moved, half a step, so that she was squarely between them.

“Look at me,” she said. “You’re not taking him either.”

His face changed. And then the front door of the shop went back off its hinges.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chiu came through it like weather. The man in the pale shirt hardly had time to turn round. Chiu hit him, once, and he went over the nearest table and the table went over with him and a bowl smashed, and he tried to get up and Chiu was already on him with a knee in his back.

“Don’t move.”

He moved. Chiu put his face into the tiles.

“I said don’t move.”

The two constables came in behind him, and the shop filled with voices, men being put on the floor, somebody shouting for an ambulance, the young one with the shot shoulder sobbing that he hadn’t done anything, the pipe kicked away into a corner. She heard it all from a great distance.

She lowered the pistol. Her fingers had gone numb round it. She put it down on the step carefully, the way he’d taught her, pointing at nothing, and knelt.

The broth had run out of the door and pooled in the yard, and she knelt in it. It soaked through the knees of her dress, warm. She didn’t notice. He was trying to push himself up again.

“Don’t.”

There was a cut by his eyebrow, through the old scar, and another at his hairline, and blood had run down the side of his face into his collar. She reached for him and his hand found her wrist first.

“Are you hurt?”

She stared at him. He was lying in a yard behind a noodle shop with his head opened, and he was asking her if she was hurt.

“Jun Hyuk.”

“Tell me.”

“I’m all right.”

His eyes went over her face. “The men?”

“Chiu’s got them.”

“The one with the pipe?”

“He’s down.”

“Nam?”

“Breathing. He’s talking. They’re coming.”

His eyes closed for a second.

“Look at me,” she said, and he did, and she bent and kissed him. Not deep, not urgent. Only her mouth on his, as if she could keep him where he was by doing it.

When she lifted her head he was looking at her as if he didn’t know what she was.

“You’ve got a hole in your head,” she whispered.

“Where?”

She nearly laughed. “You were unconscious.”

“Only for a bit.”

“That isn’t comforting.”

His eyes went past her into the shop: the cabinet, the tables over, a man face down under Chiu’s knee. Then back to her.

“Did you shoot?”

“Three times.”

He went still. “Three?”

“The first two were terrible.” She swallowed. “One hit Nam’s cabinet. The other went into the wall.”

He looked at her, and then, with the blood running down his face and pain behind his eyes, he smiled.

“Nam’s going to be furious.”

A sound came out of her that was half a laugh and half a sob. “His duck’s dead.”

“Twenty years, that duck.”

“I know.”

“Don’t sleep,” she said, because his eyes had started to go.

“I’m not.”

“Then look at me.”

He looked. She wiped the blood off the edge of his eyebrow with her thumb, careful of the cut.

“You frightened me.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t.” Her voice shook. “I thought they were going to take me. And then I saw you on the ground.”

“You did what you had to.”

“I was very bad at it.”

“You’re alive.”

“So’s the man I shot.”

“Good,” he said. “That’s what matters.”

His eyes went to the step, where the pistol lay on the stone in the wet.

“You put it down properly,” he said.

“Pointing at nothing.”

“Away from you.”

“Away from me.”

“Good,” he said again, as if it were the most important thing that had happened all afternoon, and something in her that had been holding tight let go a little, and she had to put her forehead down against his shoulder, in the broth, in the yard, with men shouting in the shop behind her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ambulances took nearly twenty minutes to come over the bridge. Elara got there first, running across the road from the bakery with Nuo behind her, and took one look and swore once and knelt down in the broth beside Nam and started giving orders. Nam lay on his side with his arm held against his chest, telling her she’d no business in his kitchen.

“You can own it quietly,” said Elara, without looking up.

Evangeline went to him while they waited. She knelt by his head on the tiles, and his eyes were open, and his face had gone the colour of the broth.

“Don’t,” he said.

“Don’t what?”

“Don’t cry on my birthday.”

A laugh broke out of her. “You’re not allowed to make jokes.”

“Seventy-two,” said Nam. “Too old for this.”

“Seventy-one,” she said. “You told me.”

He shut his eyes. “That’s right. Good girl.” And then, without opening them: “Is he all right? The ox.”

“He’s in the yard. He’s talking.”

“Then he’s all right,” said Nam. “He never stops.”

The young one with the shot shoulder was sitting against the wall with a constable’s hand pressed over the wound, and he looked up as she passed, and he looked about twenty. Under all of it, the shouting and the broth and the plaster dust, she found she couldn’t look at him for long, and she couldn’t look away either. The man in the pale shirt lay under Chiu’s knee with his cheek on the wet tiles and his neat hair spoiled, and he watched her the whole time with no expression at all.

They took Nam in the first ambulance. Jun Hyuk went in the second, and before they lifted him he got hold of Evangeline’s hand.

“Come with me.”

“I’m coming.”

“Don’t let them send you somewhere else.”

“I’ll be right next to you.”

He held on until the paramedic had to move him.

Chiu stood by her at the doors. His face was grey, though his voice was quite steady. “Mrs. Lee. I’m sorry.”

“You came.”

“Not soon enough.”

“You came.” She looked back at the shop. “The one in the pale shirt. Who is he?”

“He was giving the others their orders. We’ve got his papers. Not his name yet.”

“Find out.”

“Yes, ma’am.” He hesitated. “And Mrs. Lee. You didn’t fire till he was close. You fired low.”

She looked down at her hands. “I didn’t want to shoot him.”

“That doesn’t make it wrong.”

She climbed in and sat on the narrow seat beside her husband, and the doors shut on the yard.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the bridge the paramedic asked him his name, loudly, the way they ask, and what day it was.

“Lee Jun Hyuk,” he said. “Saturday.” And then, because the man was looking at Evangeline: “She’s my wife. She stays.”

“She can stay,” said the paramedic, and wrote something down, and the siren went on over the river.

His eyes opened again a little later. She was holding his hand.

“Don’t talk,” she said.

His mouth moved anyway, and she bent to it.

“Nam’s,” he managed. “Did he get it.”

The cake. He was trying to ask about the cake.

“Yes,” she whispered. “He ate two slices.”

“Good,” he said, and was quiet a while, looking up at her from the stretcher with the paramedic’s hand on his wrist. Then, low: “Nobody’s ever stood in front of me.”

She went still.

“Not once,” he said. “Not like that.”

She thought of the yard. Him on the ground. The man in the pale shirt deciding he could reach him. She hadn’t thought about what it meant, to stand in front of a man who’d spent his whole life standing in front of everybody else. She’d only known she wanted to. She put his hair back off his forehead with her fingers, away from the blood, and left her hand there, on his warm skin, because she could.

“Get used to it,” she said.

He looked at her. Then he laughed, and it hurt him, she could see it go through his face.

“Don’t laugh.”

“You said a thing.”

“What?”

“A thing I’d say.” His eyes were closing. “You’re turning into me.”

“Somebody has to,” said Evangeline, and held his hand all the way across the river, and he didn’t let go.

chapters.title: After
chapters.desc: Staples, a scan, a detective who knows exactly what her husband is, and a boat that won’t sail. That night she shakes until three, and he holds her the whole time.
chapters.epigraph: “I was choosing. I chose you.”
chapters.content:
The county hospital on the far side of the bridge had four treatment bays, and that Saturday afternoon three of them were full of people from Nam’s Noodles.

Elara took it over. She’d been a doctor for eleven months, which on paper made her the most junior person in the building, and nobody on the ward seemed to have noticed. She went from bay to bay with her sleeves pushed up, and her hands, Evangeline saw, were perfectly steady.

“Nobody touches the yard till the police have photographed it. Somebody find me his scans from the last time. And why does my sister’s husband have broth in his hair?”

“Nam threw it,” said Evangeline.

“Of course he did.”

In the next bay Nam lay with his arm in a splint and a dressing over his temple, telling a nurse that he’d fed half this town and could he please have his own spoon.

“Don’t talk,” said Elara.

“I own a shop.”

“You can own it quietly.”

His wrist was broken. The cut on his head needed cleaning and a few stitches, and they’d keep him overnight for the bang. He looked smaller in the bed than he had ever looked behind his counter, and he caught Evangeline’s sleeve as she passed.

“Did she bring the cake?” he asked Elara.

“What?”

“The cake. Did she bring it.”

Evangeline’s throat went tight. “Yes, Nam.”

“Where is it?”

It was on the floor of his shop, the box crushed down one side, icing smeared across the lid. He must have seen it go. He looked at her face and then away.

“Never mind.”

“I’ll make another.”

“Not too sweet.”

“I know.”

“No raisins.”

“I know.”

“Seventy-two,” said Elara, “and still giving orders.”

“Seventy-one,” said Nam.

✦ ✦ ✦

The boy she’d shot was in the third bay, with a police officer on a chair outside the curtain. He was younger than she’d thought in the shop. Twenty, perhaps. His face was grey and his shoulder was strapped, and when the curtain moved and he saw her, he looked at her and didn’t look away.

“You shot me,” he said.

“Yes.”

“You could have killed me.”

She held his eyes. “Yes.”

“That’s enough,” said Elara, coming round behind her. “Both of you.”

Evangeline went back into the corridor and found her hands had started again. She tucked them under her arms.

✦ ✦ ✦

Jun Hyuk’s head needed closing. The cut ran a long way back through his hair, and it had bled the way scalp wounds bleed, and the doctor decided on staples. He sat on the edge of the bed while they cleaned it and she stood in front of him.

He’d been quiet since the ambulance. Not tired-quiet. Heavier. His eyes kept going to the doors, the officers, the corridor where they’d wheeled the man in the pale shirt. And to her, every few minutes.

“You’re staring,” she said.

“So are you.”

“I’m allowed. You’re injured.”

The first staple went in and his jaw tightened and he didn’t make a sound. She had his hand, and felt the tendons jump in it.

“Don’t watch,” he said.

“I’m not watching. I’m watching you.”

“That’s worse.”

“Then stop being interesting.”

He nearly laughed, and it pulled at his head. “Don’t make me laugh.”

“Then don’t say things.”

They put the staples in one by one. Elara checked the dressing, and stepped back, and said, “That’s that. He’s still going for a scan.”

“No.”

“That wasn’t a question.” Elara looked at her sister. “Not here. Crestview. I want the good machine and somebody I trust reading it.”

He looked at Evangeline. She nodded.

“You’re both enjoying this,” he said.

“Immensely,” said Elara.

✦ ✦ ✦

Song came at twenty-seven minutes past four with two officers and a thin folder. He’d been made inspector in the spring and it hadn’t improved his temper. He stood at the foot of the bed and looked at the dressing.

“Is the duck dead?”

Evangeline stared at him. “Yes.”

“Nam’s going to be impossible.”

“He already is.”

“Good. Means he’s alive.” He looked at her wrist, where a bruise was coming up in the shape of somebody’s fingers, and at the strapping on her palm where the glass had cut it. “Treated?”

“Yes.”

“Lee.”

“Song.”

“You’re getting predictable.”

“You’re getting old.”

“I’m younger than Nam.”

“That isn’t saying much.”

Song opened the folder. “The man in the pale shirt is Pyo Jae-won. He’s carrying a diplomatic passport from the uncle’s household. It won’t help him. He isn’t accredited here, and a passport isn’t immunity. Conspiracy to abduct. Assault. Trafficking, when I’ve finished with him. He isn’t going home tonight.”

“Can his government ask for him back?” said Evangeline.

“They can ask. They can write letters. It doesn’t change what I’ve got.” Song looked at Jun Hyuk. “And I’ve got a great deal.”

Jun Hyuk said nothing.

“Do you want to tell me why your name keeps turning up in the same files as dead men?”

Jun Hyuk’s face went cold. “Not here.”

“Then I’ll tell you. Six men, connected to this network. A tower at West Basin. A recruiter an hour down the river road with a letter knife in his neck. A cold store behind the eastern warehouses. A back room on Kiln Street.” He didn’t raise his voice. “I know what the courts have proved and what they haven’t. I know which bodies came back and which didn’t. And every time I get close to putting somebody in front of a judge, I find another man who was supposed to stand trial lying on a floor.”

“Then do your job.”

“I’m doing my job. Stop giving me reasons to do it round you.” Song looked at Evangeline, and then back. “You’ve given us names and routes and pages we’d never have found. You’ve also killed people. I’m not going to pretend one cancels the other. Your wife isn’t a shield against the law, Lee. Don’t make me come looking for you for the wrong reason.”

Something went between them. Not friendship, not trust. An exact understanding of how much blood was in the space between them.

Then Song turned a page. “The boat.”

Jun Hyuk’s whole attention came round.

“The June crossing. We took it an hour ago, at a landing past the north warehouses. Two crew. Both in a van. It was ready to go.” He looked at Evangeline. “They had a photograph of you. Your name, your family’s papers, and a copy of the royal letter. And instructions. Deliver her without injury, if possible.”

Without injury. As if the difference between a woman and a parcel was whether it arrived damaged.

“Who gave the instructions?”

“I’m tracing it. The money goes to his household. I haven’t got his own hand on it yet.”

“The Ferryman?” said Jun Hyuk.

“Still out.” Song shut the folder. “But we’ve got his boat. And the men who were meant to sail it.” He looked at Evangeline. “You did well today.”

“I shot somebody.”

“You stopped a kidnapping.”

“I could have killed him.”

“You didn’t. That matters. So does you being alive.” He nodded at Jun Hyuk. “Get the scan.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Crestview was quieter than any hospital had a right to be: soft lights, carpet, a receptionist who whispered when there was nobody to whisper to. He disliked it at once.

“You lost consciousness twice,” said Evangeline.

“Once.”

“Twice.”

“The second time doesn’t count. I don’t remember it.”

She looked at him, and he looked away.

They let her go with him as far as the scanner. Then she sat in a room with a small clock and remembered the sound of the pipe, and the second blow, and him going down, and pressed her palms together until it went quiet.

The doctor came out at last. A concussion, and a small fracture of the skull, not displaced, the bone where it should be. No bleeding inside. Rest, watching, a follow-up. They’d keep him tonight.

A fracture. The word was too big for the room.

Elowen was in the corridor by then, and Raiden with Jinx. Elowen put both arms round her and Evangeline held on.

“He asked if Nam’s duck was all right,” she said into her sister’s shoulder, and Elowen made a sound that was half laughing and half something else.

✦ ✦ ✦

They gave him a room with a window and a nurse who asked if he wanted water, pain relief, anything at all, and he said no to each in turn, and Evangeline said, “Please leave it,” and the nurse left it.

“You don’t have to stay up all night,” he said, when the door had shut.

“I know.”

“You should sleep.”

“I know.”

“You’re exhausted.”

“I know.”

She leaned over the bed rail and kissed him. It was brief, careful of his head, and it stopped him dead in the middle of the next objection.

“That was unfair.”

“Yes.”

“You keep doing that.”

“Only when it’s necessary.”

He moved his hand across the sheet until she took it. “You shouldn’t have had to do that. Stand there with a gun. I should have been in front of you.”

“You were on the ground.”

“I know.”

“Jun Hyuk. If you say that one more time I’m going to kiss you till you forget what you were saying.”

A faint smile came. “That sounds dangerous.”

“It is.”

He turned his hand over and kissed her fingers and shut his eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

They let him go on Sunday evening with a sheet of instructions and a follow-up for the Thursday. Chiu drove them back to the city. Nobody talked much. At the building Chiu offered to come up with them, and Jun Hyuk said no, and Evangeline looked at him, and he said, “Thank you, Chiu,” instead.

The flat was exactly as they’d left it on Friday morning. The blue bowl on the counter. The folded towel. The basil in its steel box. Nothing had changed, and that was what made it hard.

She locked the door and checked it. Then the chain. Then the second lock. Then she looked through the spyhole. He stood in the hall and watched her do it and said nothing.

She took her ruined dress off and washed her hands and put on one of his shirts, and helped him lie down, and brought him water and his tablets.

“Is it worse?”

“No.”

“Dizzy?”

“A little.”

“If it gets worse, we go back.”

“I know.”

He held his hand out. “Come here.”

She sat on the edge of the bed. He looked at her face.

“You’re shaking.”

She looked down. Her hands were going. She tried to close them and it didn’t help.

“It’s nothing.”

He didn’t argue. He held out his arms.

And something in her gave way, and she slid down off the edge of the bed and sat on the floor.

“Love?”

She couldn’t answer. Her body had waited until the door was locked and the hospital was behind them and the man she loved was lying safe in their bed, and then it remembered. The pipe. The sound his head made on the concrete. His eyes shutting. The third shot. The moment in the shop when she understood that if she did nothing at all, someone was going to carry her away.

He got himself off the bed, slowly, onto the floor beside her, and she caught his arm.

“Don’t. You’re hurt.”

“I’m all right.”

“You’re not.”

“I know,” he said, and leaned back against the side of the bed and drew her in.

And she shook. Not a little, not the trembling she’d hidden at Crestview. All of her, her breath coming apart in pieces, her face against his chest, and the harder she tried to stop it the worse it got.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“No.”

“I can’t—”

“You don’t have to.”

“I saw you fall.”

“I know.”

“I thought you were dead.”

His arms tightened. “I know.”

Then she cried, the way somebody cries who’s been holding her breath far too long, and he put his cheek on her hair and said I’m here, and when she said I know you’re here, he said it again anyway. He didn’t tell her to calm down. He didn’t tell her it was over. He stayed. One o’clock went, and two. His head ached. His back hurt from the floor. He didn’t move.

“Jun Hyuk?” she said at last, against his shirt. “In the yard. When I told you to stay behind me.”

“Yes.”

“I meant it.”

“I know.”

“I wasn’t trying to be brave. I couldn’t let them take you too.”

He kissed her forehead. “Nobody has ever stood in front of me like that.”

“You said that already.”

“I know.” He looked down at her. “I don’t know what to do with it.”

She shut her eyes. “Nothing. Just let me.”

His arms tightened round her. “All right.”

It was nearly three when the shaking stopped. She didn’t notice the moment. One minute her hands were going against his shirt, and the next they were only lying there, worn out.

“Can you breathe?”

“Yes.”

“Do you want to lie down?”

“With you.”

He got back onto the bed and she climbed in after him and lay with her head by his shoulder, away from the dressing.

“I don’t want to carry a gun again,” she said.

“You don’t have to decide tonight.”

“I don’t want to be afraid every time I go to Nam’s.”

“I know.” He found her hand. “I can’t promise nobody will ever try again. I can promise you won’t face it on your own. That I’ll tell you what I know. That I’ll stop deciding things for you because I’m frightened.” He was quiet. “I’ll try every day to make sure you never have to stand in front of a man with a gun again.”

“You can’t promise that either.”

“No.”

“But you can try.”

“Every day.”

“You don’t have to be brave for me,” he said, after a while. “Or protect me. Or prove you can.”

“I wasn’t proving anything,” she said. “I was choosing. I chose you.”

He couldn’t answer that. He turned his face and kissed her palm.

Before dawn he touched the red mark on her wrist where the man had held it, and she caught his hand.

“Don’t look at it like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re going to punish yourself for it.”

He was quiet. She kissed his knuckles.

“You came home,” she said.

“So did you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next Saturday she took the bus north with another cake, the way she used to. Nam was back in his own flat over the shop with his arm in a sling, and the shop below was shut with boards over the cabinet, and he was waiting for her at the top of his stairs.

“You’re late.”

“I came as soon as I could.”

“That’s what late people say.”

She put the box on his table and opened it. Smaller than the first. White icing, blue flowers, and across the top in letters that had come out crooked again: Still here. Happy birthday.

Nam looked at it. Then he turned his face to the window.

“Too much icing,” he said.

“I know.”

He wiped his cheek with the back of his good hand. “You’re a troublesome girl.”

She bent and kissed his forehead. He reached for her hand and held it, and cried, and didn’t pretend it was the icing.

chapters.title: The Paper Twin
chapters.desc: Her brother comes to mend the air conditioning and draw the man who can’t lift anything, and tells her about eleven ribbons. Then her husband asks about a farm with a red gate.
chapters.epigraph: “I knew. I didn’t mind. You were ten.”
chapters.content:
The air conditioning died at seventeen minutes past eleven on a Tuesday in July.

He was asleep on the sofa. She knew it had gone because the hum over the window stopped, and something clicked, and a thick warm quiet began to settle on the room. She looked at the remote, and at the ceiling, and at her husband, who had been told not to lift anything heavier than a glass of water for six weeks and had taken it as a personal insult from the whole of medicine.

“The air’s stopped.”

He opened one eye. “Ring someone.”

“I have. Raiden’s coming.”

He shut the eye. “Why Raiden?”

“Because he’s better at this than you.”

“I’m better at most things.”

“Not at air conditioning.”

He reached for his water and his hand stopped halfway, the way it still did sometimes, and she took the glass and put it into his palm.

“Thank you,” he said.

The doorbell went twenty minutes later. Raiden came in with a long paper bag and a toolbox, and Jinx behind him with a bottle of cold water and the face of a woman who’d already decided she would be the one fixing whatever Raiden had been asked to fix.

“Where’s the patient?”

“Here,” said Evangeline.

“You’re still alive,” said Raiden, looking down at him.

“Sorry to disappoint you.”

“Don’t worry. Give me time.”

“Raiden,” said Evangeline.

Jinx sighed. “Have they always been like this?”

“Since the New Year.”

Raiden looked at his head. The dressing was gone and his hair had grown back enough to cover most of the line where the staples had been, though you could see the mark at his hairline if you knew where to look. Then he pulled a chair up beside the sofa and took a pencil out of the paper bag.

“Sit still. I want to draw you.”

“No.”

“Good. Hold that face.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Jinx fixed the air conditioning. She didn’t ask anybody’s permission to get up on the step stool, and she didn’t wait for Raiden to finish explaining how the unit worked before she had the front off it.

“You’re describing the problem,” she told him. “I’m looking at it.”

“You’re very confident.”

“I’m usually right.”

“Usually?”

“Always, when it’s you.”

The filter had been seated crooked and a connector had worked loose. She had cold air coming out again inside a quarter of an hour, washed her hands at the kitchen sink, and started opening cupboards for the tea as if she’d lived there for years.

“Does he get any?” said Raiden.

“He gets water,” said Evangeline.

“Does his doctor know who he’s married to?”

“Unfortunately,” said Jun Hyuk.

Raiden drew. He’d always been good with his hands: he could mend a watch, draw a floor plan, take a lock apart without a sound. His drawings were exact without being cold. He noticed the things people did without knowing they did them. The way Jun Hyuk held a glass. The slight tilt of his head when he listened. The way his left hand lay on the sofa cushion with the fingers curled loosely towards his wife. Raiden drew all of it.

“What are you thinking?” Evangeline asked him.

“That he looks like a man who’s been told not to do something and is going to do it anyway.”

“Accurate,” said Evangeline.

Raiden smiled, and went on drawing, and then said, without looking up, “You used to follow me round. When I came home.”

She looked at him. “Did I?”

“All the time. You were very annoying.” His pencil stopped. “I hated you.”

He didn’t say it to be cruel. He didn’t look up to see what it did. He said it as if he’d finally found the right afternoon to put down something he’d been carrying.

“When I walked home from the farm I was ten. Mama had been dead five years. I’d seen her on New Years, at the farm, when Baba brought her, and that was all. And you’d had her. You’d had my cot and my room and my name next to yours on a piece of paper, and everybody in the house was so careful round you. If you cried, the house changed. I thought you were spoilt. I thought you knew exactly how to make people sorry for you.” He gave a short laugh with nothing in it. “I didn’t know why you weren’t allowed near the windows. I only knew you had things I hadn’t.”

Evangeline didn’t move. Jinx had stopped with the kettle in her hand.

“I took your ribbons,” said Raiden. “The ones in the wooden box. I took them out of your room and threw them in the canal off the back steps.”

She’d had eleven. One for every birthday on her papers, and one that had been Mama’s, blue, frayed at one end. She used to lay them out on her bed in a row though she hardly ever wore them. She’d thought she’d lost them.

“I watched you look,” said Raiden. “You asked Ah Sim. You opened every drawer you had. I didn’t say anything.”

“Why are you telling me now?”

“Because I should have told you then.” He turned the pencil over in his fingers. “Then when you were fifteen I found you in the bathroom, crying, and you wouldn’t say why. I thought you’d failed maths.” He looked at her at last. “I stopped hating you that day. I didn’t know what you were crying about. I only knew you were fifteen and you looked as if you’d found something that belonged to you and didn’t know if you were allowed to keep it. I didn’t know how to love you after that. I was still jealous. But I stopped thinking you deserved it.”

Evangeline looked at him.

“I knew,” she said.

He blinked. “What?”

“About the ribbons. You always came back with wet shoes.” A faint smile. “And once I saw you on the canal steps with something behind your back.”

He put a hand over his eyes. “God.”

“I didn’t know you’d thrown all of them. I thought you’d taken some.”

“Why didn’t you say anything?”

She tilted her head. “You were ten. I was sad about the ribbons. I didn’t mind you.” She counted on her fingers. “Eleven. I knew. I didn’t mind. You were ten.”

She got up and went round the table and put her arms round him. His arms stayed at his sides for one second. Then they came round her and held on.

“I’m sorry,” he said into her hair. “I really am.”

“I know. You can tell me things now.” She held him tighter. “And you can stop pretending you were always a very good brother.”

He laughed, wet. “You’re ruining it.”

“I’m being honest. You threw my ribbons in a canal.”

“You followed me everywhere.”

“I was ten.”

“Exactly.” He wiped his face. “Don’t tell anyone I cried.”

Jinx put three cups of tea down on the table. “I saw nothing,” she said. “I also heard everything.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Jun Hyuk hadn’t said a word. He’d listened from the sofa with his hands still in his lap.

“You’re very quiet,” Jinx told him.

“I’m listening.”

“He’s quiet with her,” said Raiden. “With everybody else he never stops.”

“That isn’t true.”

“Ask Nam. Ask Song. Ask your wife.”

“He talks quite a lot,” said Evangeline, “when he’s trying to persuade me of something.”

Jun Hyuk drank his water. Then he looked at Raiden.

“What farm were you at, the winter you were nine?”

The pencil stopped.

“River road,” said Jun Hyuk. “Past the old ferry town. A red gate. A white water tower behind the house.”

Raiden’s face had gone still. “How do you know that?”

“Old Ko and I came through there. December, two thousand seven.” He looked at his hands. “There’d been men through the valley that week. Old Ko’s unit was sent up after, to see what was left. There was a woman at the farm, and a boy. The boy didn’t speak to anybody.”

Raiden didn’t answer. Jinx’s hand went to his.

“Old Ko had a tin of peaches in the truck,” said Jun Hyuk. “He didn’t like peaches. He’d meant to buy pears. He told the woman we’d brought something for the kitchen and put it on the windowsill and didn’t make a fuss about it. He said a boy who’d been through what that boy had been through would want something sweet, and wouldn’t want to be told so.”

“That was you,” said Raiden.

“I was outside by the truck. I saw you take it.”

“I thought somebody had left it for me.”

“They had.”

Raiden looked down at the table. He remembered that farm as damp floors and old blankets and a kitchen that smelled of boiled cabbage, and the week nobody spoke above a whisper, and a cupboard door at the back of the scullery where he’d scratched the days. And a tin on a windowsill, cold from the winter, no note, no name, blue and yellow label. He’d got it open with a kitchen knife and eaten the peaches slowly and saved the syrup for last, and he’d thought about it for years and never asked anyone.

“You were on the back step when I came round,” said Jun Hyuk. “Scraping the bottom of the tin with your finger.”

Raiden laughed through his nose. “I was hungry. What did Old Ko say?”

“’Good. At least somebody appreciates a peach.’”

Raiden laughed properly then, small and real, and something loosened in the room.

“You never told me about the farm,” said Evangeline.

“I didn’t want anybody to know.”

She reached across and touched his hand. “I’m glad you got the peaches.”

“So am I,” said Raiden.

✦ ✦ ✦

He finished the drawing at twenty past four and turned it round. Jun Hyuk on the sofa with a glass in one hand and his head turned a little towards Evangeline, tired but not weak, his shoulders easy, his face softer than it ever was when anyone looked straight at him.

“That’s him,” said Evangeline.

“You made him look kind.”

“He is.” Raiden shrugged at Jun Hyuk. “Don’t let it go to your head.”

“Can I keep it?”

“I drew it for you.”

He packed his pencils. Jun Hyuk said, “I want to ask you something,” and Raiden looked up.

“Design a house.”

“What sort of house?”

“The safest house in the country.” He said it as if he were talking about the weather. “Not a fortress. Not something that looks like a bank vault. A proper house. Comfortable. Private. Somewhere she can open a window without thinking about who’s outside it.”

Raiden had stopped smiling. “Where?”

“Out of the city. North, in the hills. I don’t mind where.”

“How big?”

“Big enough for her family to come. Small enough she doesn’t feel she lives in a hotel.”

“Security?”

“Your problem.”

“Money?”

“Not a problem.”

“You’re asking me to design a house.”

“I’m asking you to design hers.” He was looking at Raiden, not at her. “I want her to have somewhere nobody tells her where she can go. Where the windows open. Where she can grow what she likes. Where she doesn’t have to keep a bag packed. And I want you to do it, because you know what she likes and what she doesn’t and how she walks through a room.”

“Jun Hyuk,” said Evangeline. “We’ve got a home.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

“Because I want you to have a choice. Not an escape house. Not a safe house. Not somewhere you go because somebody’s coming. A house you choose because you want to wake up in it.”

She looked down at the drawing in her hands.

“I’ll do it,” said Raiden. “On conditions. She gets the last word on everything. Not you. And I don’t start from nothing. I want old walls, a house with some years in it, and I’ll make it hold.”

“Done.”

“And the windows open. Every one. I’ll find the glass.”

“That’s the point,” said Jun Hyuk.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the door Raiden hugged her again. It was easier this time.

“Dinner next week. Both of you.” He looked at Jun Hyuk. “Unfortunately.”

“I’ll bring something.”

“Bring an appetite. Elowen’s cooking.” He touched the side of his sister’s head, the way he used to when they were small and she followed him everywhere. “Eleven ribbons.”

“I remember.”

When the door had shut she stood in the hall a long time with the drawing. Then she came and sat beside him on the sofa and put her head on his shoulder.

“Did Old Ko always leave food for people?”

“When he could.”

“Was he kind?”

He thought about it. “He was strict.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

A small smile. “Yes.”

“I wish I’d met him.”

“He’d have liked you. He liked people who fed other people.”

“Then he’d have loved Nam.”

“He’d have complained about Nam’s noodles.”

“Everybody complains about Nam’s noodles.”

“That’s because they’re terrible.”

“Don’t say that. He’ll find out.”

She lifted her face and kissed him, slowly, and when she drew back he followed her.

“You’re not supposed to be doing that.”

“The doctor said rest.”

“You’re kissing.”

“Quietly,” he said, and she laughed, and he drew her in carefully, mindful of his head, and she leaned over him and kissed him again with her hand on his chest.

“You really want to build me a house?”

“Yes.”

“With windows that open. And a garden. And a kitchen big enough to bake in.”

“How big?”

“Big enough.”

“All right.”

“And a room for Raiden’s drawings. And a chair for Nam.”

He kissed her before she could get to the end of the list.

That evening she framed the drawing and stood it on the shelf beside the one photograph from Old Ko’s box: a big soldier in a grey cap with a cigarette behind his ear and a boy of about eleven glaring at the camera. Two men from two parts of his life. One who’d raised him. One who’d been a hungry boy on a cold farm, joined to him by a tin of peaches neither of them had known about.

“Your brother’s a good man,” he said, from the sofa.

“He wasn’t always.”

“Neither was I.”

She came and sat down and put her hand over his. “Perhaps people are allowed to get better.”

He looked at her. “Perhaps,” he said.

chapters.title: He Takes a Job He Hates
chapters.desc: He wants a real name, a payslip, and a job nobody comes through the door for. So he applies to the harbour board, opening containers at the Iron Docks.
chapters.epigraph: “Then let it be the job.”
chapters.content:
On the morning of the first of August, Lee Jun Hyuk asked his wife to help him become boring.

She looked up from the basil. “Sorry?”

“Boring.” He was at the counter in a clean shirt with his hair still wet, and the line at his hairline had faded to a thin pale mark. The doctor had let him go back to ordinary life the week before, with the heavy lifting to come back slowly. He’d been restless for days. She’d noticed. “Very.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Probably.”

He put a folded sheet of paper in front of her. Not a list of names or addresses. Three headings in his small square hand.

Identity. A name that could be checked. A civil record with nothing missing. A bank account. Tax. A marriage that didn’t depend on a registry clerk remembering a big man in a torn jacket.

Work. A real employer. A salary. A job with a description. A record anyone could look up.

Home. An address he meant to keep. The electricity in his name. A life that didn’t need three exits and a car parked facing the road.

She read it twice. “Why now?”

He pulled out the chair opposite. “Because I don’t want the first thing anybody finds when they look for me to be a list of dead men.” He touched the edge of the paper. “I’ve spent my whole life making sure nobody could follow me. Names that weren’t mine. No address I meant to keep. I could leave a room in thirty seconds and never come back.” He looked at the window. “I don’t want to live like that any more.”

She folded it carefully. “All right. Where are you going to work?”

“At the Iron Docks. The harbour board’s putting in an inspection unit. They advertised. I applied.”

She stared at him. Then she laughed, and he looked mildly offended.

“You applied for a job. With a form.”

“Unfortunately.”

“What happened to a quiet life?”

“I said boring,” said Jun Hyuk. “I didn’t say pleasant.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Director Ou of the harbour board read his application in an office over the warehouses at the Iron Docks with the face of a man who’d been handed a complicated parcel and was thinking about sending it back unopened.

“You want a job. A real one. With a contract and a payslip and tax.”

“That’s the idea.”

“What can you do? Don’t be clever. On a form.”

Jun Hyuk looked at the form. “Logistics. Security assessment. Cargo inspection. Managing people. Routes.”

“Qualifications?”

“Not enough for the job you’re thinking of.”
