“Good. At least you’re honest.” Director Ou slid a photograph across the desk: a long row of containers under a grey sky. “Three terminals. No consistent inspection. Some boxes get opened properly. Some get checked on paper. Some get waved through because the man on the gate is tired or underpaid or looking at his phone.” Jun Hyuk’s face did something small at waved through, and Director Ou saw it and went on. “I want every box inspected on a schedule. Not torn apart by a man with a crowbar and a temper. A written procedure. Trained people. Seals recorded. Photographs. If something’s wrong, the authorities are rung.”

“I’ll need the power to hold a box if the seal doesn’t match.”

“Within the law.”

“Obviously.”

“And you don’t threaten the staff.”

“I don’t threaten people.”

Director Ou looked at him. Jun Hyuk looked back. The director had read the file Ms. Fong had put together.

“You don’t threaten them,” said Director Ou, “unless there’s a real reason. You don’t vanish for three days and expect the job kept open. You don’t use this port to settle your own business. You don’t kill anyone on harbour board property.”

Jun Hyuk considered this. “Define property.”

“Mr. Lee.”

“All right.”

Director Ou rubbed his forehead and reached for the phone. “Don’t thank me yet. You haven’t met Mrs. Koo.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Koo was fifty-eight, had worked the Iron Docks for twenty-three years, and had no intention of being impressed by a new supervisor. She was the first person to tell him his schedule was impossible.

“You’ve given eleven minutes to a standard dry box.”

“Yes.”

“It’s fifteen if the paperwork’s clean.”

“Then use fifteen.”

“And if it isn’t?”

“Stop and ring me.”

“You’re the new man. You don’t know this yard. Why are you telling us how to do our jobs?”

He looked at her and handed her the schedule back. “Show me.”

She showed him. Where the records had holes in them. Where the lights were bad. Where the inspection bay flooded after rain. Where the office didn’t write down a damaged seal because the form was a nuisance. She knew which driver always came twenty minutes early and which forklift man had a bad knee and which supervisor would sign anything put in front of him before lunch. He listened. He asked questions. He changed the schedule.

By the end of the morning she’d stopped calling him the new man. She called him Mr. Lee. Not affection yet. A start.

He hired the rest in a week. Two women from records who wanted to train for the yard. A retired customs officer who couldn’t bear being indoors. A young man who’d been passed over twice for being too careful and asking too many questions. Mrs. Koo as senior supervisor, though she said she hadn’t applied, and he said she hadn’t needed to. Every seal recorded before it was broken. Nobody in a box on their own. Nobody assuming an empty space was empty.

“If you’re tired, say so,” he told them at the first briefing. “If you’re not sure, stop. If something doesn’t look right, don’t talk yourself into it because a client’s waiting.”

A man at the back put his hand up. “What if the client complains?”

“Let him.”

“What if he takes the contract somewhere else?”

“Then he can tell the authorities why he wanted us not to look.”

Mrs. Koo made a small approving noise.

“I don’t need you to be brave,” he said. “I need you careful. There are people inside some of those boxes who can’t afford our mistakes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ms. Fong came on the sixth with a leather folder and a pen that looked as if it cost more than a car. She was the most expensive lawyer on Harbour Road, he was paying her himself, and she’d come to spend an afternoon explaining why a man couldn’t decide to be ordinary and expect the government to agree.

“Your record is unusual, Mr. Lee.”

“Yes.”

“Incomplete.”

“Yes.”

“Several names that don’t match.”

“Yes.”

She looked at him over her glasses. “Do you mean to answer everything in one syllable?”

“Only if it helps.”

“It doesn’t.”

Evangeline put her face in her tea.

It took weeks: old records to find, gaps to explain, affidavits, corrections made through the proper channels. Ms. Fong did all of it, and was thorough and had no sympathy at all for his impatience.

“Mr. Lee, the law isn’t a door you can kick in.”

“I know.”

“Then stop looking at me as if you’re considering it.”

At the end of it there was a civil record in the name of Lee Jun Hyuk with nothing missing from it, and the marriage registered again against the corrected record, with the original date kept: Saturday the eighth of April, 2023. When the new certificate came, Evangeline held it in both hands.

“You’re officially my husband.”

“Was there some doubt?”

“Legally, there were complications.”

“And otherwise?”

“Never.”

He took it from her and looked at it a long time and folded it back into its envelope. “Good. Now I can put my name on the electricity bill.”

“You’ve always wanted to do that?”

“No,” he said, and she laughed until she had to sit down.

✦ ✦ ✦

His first payslip came on Friday the sixteenth.

It was an ordinary sheet of paper. The company’s name at the top and his own under it. A pay period, a salary, tax taken off, a bank reference. No other name. No envelope of cash. No note from somebody who owed him. Just work, written down and paid for.

He read it twice and put it on the kitchen table.

“What’s that?”

“My payslip.”

She turned the stove off and came and read it. His name. The amount. The date. “Your first one. How does it feel?”

“Strange.”

“Good strange?”

“Paper strange.”

She took a magnet shaped like a white flower out of the drawer and pinned it to the fridge.

“What are you doing?”

“Keeping it.”

“It’s not a certificate.”

“It is to me.”

He stood in front of the fridge for a while, looking at his name held up by a flower. Then he reached out and straightened it.

“You’re proud,” she said.

“No.”

“You’re very proud.”

“Perhaps.”

She kissed his cheek. “Congratulations, Mr. Lee.”

He turned his head and caught her mouth. “Thank you, Mrs. Lee.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By the second week she’d started bringing him lunch in a steel tiffin with three tiers: rice, vegetables, fish or chicken, and sometimes fruit and a note under the lid.

“I can buy lunch,” he’d said the first time. “There’s a canteen.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

“Because I wanted to,” she’d said, and he’d eaten all of it.

On the Friday she sent noodles, packed so they wouldn’t go soft.

Jun Hyuk: The noodles are good.

Evangeline: I know.

Jun Hyuk: You knew?

Evangeline: I made them.

Jun Hyuk: That’s not what I meant.

Evangeline: Eat your lunch.

Mrs. Koo saw him smiling at his phone. “Your wife?”

“Yes.”

“She cooks.”

“Yes.”

“You’re lucky. Don’t forget to tell her.”

Under the lid of the tiffin was a note. Eat the vegetables. I know you. He ate the vegetables.

On Monday the nineteenth she came to the gate just before the afternoon shift changed. He was outside the inspection office in dark work trousers and a faded company coverall with the sleeves rolled up, a clipboard in one hand and a smear of grease on his wrist, listening to Mrs. Koo explain a seal that didn’t match. He looked different. Not less dangerous, not less able. Only placed, as if he belonged to the yard in a way she’d never seen him belong anywhere.

He saw her at the gate and his shoulders came down and his face went soft. He handed Mrs. Koo the clipboard and came over.

“You brought lunch yesterday.”

“You didn’t finish the fruit.”

“I finished it.”

“The tiffin came back with two pieces.”

“I was saving them.”

She smiled. He took the tiffin and put it down on the table by the gate.

“Wait there.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to kiss you.”

She looked round. There were at least a dozen people in sight. Mrs. Koo was watching from the office door. A forklift had stopped dead. Director Ou, crossing the yard with a clipboard, had already turned round.

“You’re in your coverall,” she said. “Your hair’s a mess. Your hands are filthy.”

He looked at his hands. “Not very.”

“All right,” said Evangeline.

He took her face in both hands and kissed her, not politely and not, in the middle of the Iron Docks with the sun coming down on the containers and a whole shift pretending badly not to look. She put her hands flat on his chest. He went on until she was smiling against his mouth.

Behind them somebody whistled.

“Mr. Lee!” called Mrs. Koo. “Your team’s waiting.” And then, louder: “Your wife can come again tomorrow.”

By the evening Director Ou had heard three versions. In one, Jun Hyuk had lifted her off the ground. In another, it had gone on for a full minute. In the third, Mrs. Koo had clapped. Mrs. Koo denied the third.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday the twenty-second they found the man in the squid reefer.

It started as a discrepancy. The temperature log didn’t match the voyage. The seal number was right, but the unit’s record showed a gap nobody could explain, and the papers said frozen squid for a processing plant outside the city. Mrs. Koo held it and rang him. He came with two inspectors and the yard medic, and they did it the way he’d taught them: papers, number, the unit’s record, the call to the police and the ambulance before anybody touched a door.

When they opened it, cold came rolling out across the bay. Cartons of squid stacked to the roof. And behind the last row, curled on his side under a torn foil sheet, a man.

For one terrible second nobody moved. Jun Hyuk was the first one forward.

“Medic. Now.”

The man was alive. Barely. His skin had gone grey and his lips blue, his clothes were wet, and when the light reached him his hands began to shake so hard they knocked against the floor.

“Can you hear me?” Jun Hyuk crouched in the door. “Don’t move. We’re getting you out. You’re nearly out.”

The ambulance crew took him. When he began to slip as they lifted him onto the stretcher, Jun Hyuk was under his shoulders before anyone could tell him not to, taking the weight for the moment it took them to get hold of him properly, and Mrs. Koo saw it, the old thing in him that moved before it thought.

When the ambulance had gone she found him standing by the open box. His hands were shaking, and not from the cold.

“You did well, Mr. Lee.”

“Not yet.” There’d be statements now. The log, the seal, who’d loaded him and who’d shut the doors and who’d known. “Nobody touches that box till the police are here. And get the ones who opened it checked over.”

He rang Director Ou.

“Is he alive?” said the director.

“Yes.”

“Good.” A pause. “I’m ringing Song.” Another. “You did that well. You found him. You held the cargo. You had the medic there. That’s the job.”

“I know.”

“Then let it be the job.”

He stood at the office window after the director had rung off. He’d been praised before, for things he didn’t want to remember, for things that had left blood on him. A man had gone into a box alive. A man had come out alive. And the people who found him had known what to do.

He picked up a pen and began the report.

✦ ✦ ✦

She heard about it at the sink that night, with her hands in the water and the tiffin coming apart in pieces on the draining board.

“Alive?”

“Yes. In hospital.”

She dried her hands. “Did you lift anything?”

He hesitated.

“Jun Hyuk.”

“Only for a second. He was slipping.” He caught her hand. “He’s alive.”

She looked at him a long time, and lifted his hand and kissed the knuckles. “I’m still going to scold you.”

“When?”

“After dinner.”

He lifted her onto the counter instead and stood between her knees.

“You’re supposed to be resting.”

“I’m standing very still,” he said, and kissed her, warm and slow, her fingers going into his hair and finding the mark at his hairline and staying careful of it. She was smiling too much to go on kissing him properly.

“What?”

“I like you.”

“Only like?”

She touched his face. “I love you.”

His face did what it always did. He put his forehead on hers. “I love you too.”

She looked past him at the fridge. “Your payslip’s crooked again.”

“Evangeline.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday the twenty-seventh Raiden rang him and said, “I’ve found it.”

It was in the northern hills, an hour and a half out, up the old road past the river and into the woods. A stone house on a lane of fig trees, with a tiled roof and a wall round it and a garden that went down to a stream. One woman had lived in it for thirty years and had just gone south to be near her daughter. Three bedrooms. A long room with windows on two sides. A wide front step for sitting on with tea.

“The walls are good,” said Raiden, standing in the empty kitchen. “The roof’s good. Everything else I’ll change. Eight weeks, if you let me get on with it and keep out of my way.”

Jun Hyuk walked every room. He checked the lane and the wall and the trees and the lines of sight. He stood in the garden and listened. No traffic. No television through a wall. Only the wind and the water.

He bought it that afternoon, through Ms. Fong, properly, with his own name on the deed. Not because he needed another safe house. Because he could see her waking up in it.

Evangeline: Are you home on time today?

Jun Hyuk: Yes.

Evangeline: I’ve made dinner. Guess.

Jun Hyuk: Noodles.

Evangeline: No.

Jun Hyuk: Fish.

Evangeline: No.

Jun Hyuk: You’re making me nervous.

Evangeline: Good. Come home and find out.

It was fish. He’d guessed fish second. “That was a strategic guess,” he said, and she laughed, and then narrowed her eyes at him over the pot.

“You’re in a good mood. You’re hiding something.”

“Perhaps.”

“Is it something I need to worry about?”

“No.”

She looked at him a moment more, and then put her arms round his waist. “Then tell me when you’re ready.”

He’d spent his whole life keeping things from people. He was learning, now, the difference between a secret that kept somebody safe and a surprise that gave her something to look forward to.

chapters.title: The Throne Lets Her Go
chapters.desc: The twenty-first floor of the Harbour Hotel, a notary, a pen, and a man of forty-four with her eyes. He signs her free, and tells her her mother’s name.
chapters.epigraph: “Goodbye, little sister.”
chapters.content:
On the twenty-first floor of the Harbour Hotel, behind a pair of pale wooden doors, a king was waiting to sign his sister free.

Evangeline stood outside them on Saturday the twenty-first of September in a plain ivory dress with the aquamarines at her ears, their mended gold showing. Jun Hyuk stood beside her in a dark suit. He’d checked the corridor twice.

“You’re doing it again,” she said. “Looking at the doors. Six times.”

“Seven.”

She smiled. He looked down at her. “Are you all right?”

She thought about it. “No. But I’m not frightened.”

He closed his fingers round hers. “Good.”

A man came down the corridor towards them, and it was Teo, the young guard from April, older round the eyes now. He bowed to her. “Your Highness.” And then, to her husband, “Mr. Lee.”

“Teo.”

“The King is ready.”

He opened the door. Jun Hyuk didn’t move. Evangeline turned round.

“Come with me.”

He looked past her at the room. “Of course.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The King was forty-four. That was the first thing she noticed. Not the insignia on his jacket, or the two officials by the windows, or the notary squaring papers at the long table. He was younger than she’d pictured him, with dark hair going silver at the temples and a face that had been trained since childhood to give nothing away. But round the eyes—

She stopped. She knew those eyes. Not because she’d ever seen them. Because she saw them every morning in the mirror. The same slight turn down at the outer corners. The same crease when he was trying not to smile.

He stood up. “Evangeline.”

He said it carefully, as if he’d been practising it. She bowed.

“Your Majesty.”

He looked at her, and then at the man beside her. “Mr. Lee.”

“Your Majesty.”

They sat. Jun Hyuk took the chair next to hers, close enough that their hands could meet under the table.

The notary went through the pages. A declaration of renunciation. A release of every title, privilege and claim. A statement that she made it freely, without pressure or payment. A promise that the crown would never use her name for a claim, an alliance, or a demand. The King would countersign. The notary would witness. It would go into the royal record.

She’d spent months with the language of papers like these. She understood every sentence. She understood what she was giving away, and what she wasn’t: her name, her marriage, the right to say where she lived, the right to be a woman who didn’t belong to a throne.

“Your Highness, if you would read it once more before you sign.”

She read it from beginning to end. Then she picked up the pen. Her hand was steady. Jun Hyuk watched her fingers. He didn’t tell her to take her time, or that she could change her mind. He sat beside her.

She signed. Evangeline Lee. The notary turned the page. She signed again, and again.

The King read it all through. He took the pen, and it stopped over the line.

“Once I sign, there’s no way back that anyone can find.”

“I understand.”

“No household, no title, no allowance, no place in the succession. And nobody will be permitted to use your name as an instrument.”

“That’s what I want.”

He signed. The notary witnessed. The King closed the folder himself.

“There,” he said, more. “You’re free.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The officials went into the next room, and the notary after them, and the King asked Teo to wait in the corridor. Teo looked at Evangeline, and she nodded, and the door shut, and there were three of them.

“My uncle has been disgraced,” said the King, at the window. The harbour lay under them in the September sun, its cranes and boats gone small and orderly. “His household has been investigated. Several of his men have been removed. The money that went to the Ferryman’s people has been found, and the companies it went through. He’s been stripped of his offices and sent to his estates in the north. He may not conduct royal business or receive anyone in the crown’s name.”

“Is he under arrest?”

“Not yet. I won’t tell you he’s been punished more than he has.” He turned. “He won’t be given the means to come after you again. I can’t promise nobody will ever try to use your name. But nobody will do it with my permission.”

“Thank you.”

He came back to the table and didn’t sit, and seemed to have lost the thread of what he’d meant to say.

“Your mother’s name was Seo Hwa,” he said.

The room went quiet.

Seo Hwa. She said it to herself. It was the first time she’d ever heard it. Not your mother. Not the woman who played the viola. A person. A name.

“She was twenty-three when I first saw her. I was seventeen. She played the viola in the household orchestra, and she wasn’t the best of them.” A faint smile. “She’d have been furious to hear me say so. She read better than any of them. But she had a habit of playing a passage exactly as written, and then changing one small thing, and making everybody else sound as if they’d been playing it wrong. She laughed easily. Not quietly. She used to laugh before she’d finished telling a joke, so nobody ever heard the end of it.” He looked at the window. “She liked the music and the lake and the kitchens, because the cooks didn’t care who she was. She disliked ceremonies and long dinners and anyone who said duty instead of answering a simple question.”

“That sounds familiar,” said Evangeline, and her voice wasn’t steady.

“Yes,” said the King.

He sat down across from her.

“She didn’t give you up. I want you to know that before anything else. They took you from her when you were two days old and told her you’d died. She didn’t believe them. She went on looking for you for two years. She asked everyone. She wrote letters nobody answered. Then she caught a fever that winter, and it was treated, and it got worse, and by the time the physicians understood, there was nothing to be done.” He looked at his hands. “I was away. I was told she was improving. When I came back she’d gone.”

Evangeline’s fingers had closed round Jun Hyuk’s under the table.

“My father asked one question every year after that,” the King said. “He’d call his secretary in and ask, Is the problem still moved? He never used your name. He never said daughter. He asked whether the problem had been moved, as if you were furniture somebody had left in the wrong room.” His face hardened. “When I was twenty-eight I went looking for you myself. I found a birth entry that had been made to disappear. A payment out of a private account. I followed it as far as I could, and every door had been shut, and everybody who’d ever known anything had been told to forget it. I was told you’d been taken abroad. I looked for two years. Then my father fell ill and there was a fight over the succession, and I was told that going on would bring the crown down.” He didn’t defend it. “I stopped.”

The silence afterwards wasn’t forgiveness. It was only the space where the truth had been put down.

“Did you ever think about me?”

He looked almost startled. “Every year. Whether you’d grown tall. Whether you liked music. Whether you were happy.” His eyes came to her face. “Whether you knew you had a brother.”

She hadn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took a small locked box out of the cabinet by the wall and opened it.

“Three things.”

The first was a photograph behind a sheet of thin paper. A young woman by a lake in bright sun, her head back, her eyes nearly shut, laughing with one hand up as if she’d just been caught at something, and a viola case on the grass beside her. Evangeline knew that face. Not from memory. From the mirror. The eyes. The line beside the left cheek when she smiled. It was like looking at herself before she’d been born.

“She’s laughing.”

“At me. I’d fallen in the lake. I was seventeen and I’d gone in after a hat.”

She looked up, and laughed out loud, and he watched her laugh.

“She laughed at me the whole afternoon,” he said.

The second was a wooden case, and in it a viola, its wood gone dark with years, the edges kept with great care. A small brass plate inside the lid. Seo Hwa.

“She played this at the lake festival. She liked playing out of doors. She said music sounded different near water.” He closed the lid and pushed it gently across the table. “It was hers. It should be yours.”

“I don’t know how to play.”

“Neither did she, once.”

The third was an envelope. “Something she wrote, the winter before. It was with her papers.” He didn’t open it. “Read it when you like.”

She put it in her bag. She looked at the photograph.

“Why did you keep them?”

“Because I couldn’t bear anybody else deciding what became of them.”

He didn’t ask her to thank him. He didn’t ask her to call him anything at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the corridor Teo was waiting. He looked at the case in Jun Hyuk’s hand and his face softened.

“Mr. Lee, may I have a word?”

Jun Hyuk looked at Evangeline. She nodded. They went a little way down the carpet together, and the King stood by the door and gave his sister a little room.

“Her mother played at the lake festival every summer,” said Teo, low. “I was on the outer grounds, a boy. She never stood on the main platform. She liked the little pavilion over the water, and people gathered round her without knowing they were listening to anybody in particular.” He paused. “One year she played after the orchestra had finished. On her own, nobody announcing her, no guards. She played until they lit the lamps. She was happy that night.”

“Thank you,” said Jun Hyuk.

“Take care of her. She’s spent a long time being told what she was supposed to be.”

“Not any more.”

Teo bowed. “Good.”

The King was waiting by the door. She’d rehearsed a goodbye in the car that morning: a bow, a sentence about honesty, thanks for the photograph and the viola. Standing in front of him, all of it was too formal.

“You don’t have to call me anything you don’t want to,” he said. “I won’t ask you to come to the palace. I won’t ask you to keep any of this private. If you ever want to come, the door’s open.”

“Will you come here? Not on business.”

A faint smile. “If I can.”

She stepped up to him and put her hand flat on his chest, over his heart. Not a royal greeting, not a farewell anybody had taught her.

“Goodbye,” she said. And then “Brother.”

His face changed. He looked as if he’d forgotten how to stand. He looked down at her hand and covered it with his own, and leaned forward and put his forehead against hers.

“Goodbye, little sister,” said the King, and let her go.

✦ ✦ ✦

The lift was empty. He stepped in with the viola case and she came after him with the photograph held against her chest, and the doors shut.

“She was happy,” she said, after a few floors.

“Yes.”

“She had my eyes.”

“Yes.”

“Jun Hyuk. Put the case down.”

He looked at her and set it carefully on the floor between them, and before he’d straightened up she had him by the lapels and was kissing him. He made a small surprised sound. Then his hand came to her waist, and he kissed her back, slowly at first and then with the quiet intensity she knew, while she held on to his jacket as if she needed something solid under her hands.

“What was that for?” he said, with his forehead on hers.

“For coming with me. For carrying it. For not saying anything when I needed you not to.”

“I know,” he said, and she kissed him again, and the doors opened at the ground floor on a hotel attendant studying the wall with great interest.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car she held the photograph on her knees. After a while she said, “I’ve got a brother.”

“Yes.”

“An older one. With my eyes.”

“Yes.”

“I don’t know what to do with that.”

“You don’t have to do anything.”

“What if I want to know him?”

“Then you learn.”

She looked out at the city going by in the sun. “I spent so long thinking there was something missing, and never knew what.”

He took his hand off the gearstick and put it over hers. “You’re not missing anything now.” And then, because that wasn’t right: “Not because of him. Not because of the crown. You were already whole.”

“I know,” she said, and leaned her head back against the seat.

At home she put the photograph on the kitchen table and the case beside it, and he put the kettle on, and she opened the envelope.

Half a page, in a slanting hand she’d never seen and knew at once. Not addressed to anyone. A few lines about the weather, and the musicians, and how the water by the pavilion caught the evening. And near the bottom, one sentence.

She will be two next month. I play a wrong note on purpose sometimes, and imagine her laughing, as if the viola were telling her a joke.

She read it twice and pressed it flat against her chest. He came and stood behind her and didn’t ask what it said. She reached back for his hand.

“She played for me,” she said. “She never stopped.”

“No.”

“I don’t remember any of it.”

He bent and kissed her hair. “You don’t have to remember it for it to have happened.”

The kettle came to the boil. They stood in the kitchen with her mother’s writing under her palm and the viola quiet in its case.

“Will you help me learn?”

“I can’t play.”

“Neither can I.”

“Then we’ll find someone.”

“And in the house, is there room for it?”

He looked at her. “There’ll be a room for it.”

She kissed him, and held him tight the way she had after the shop and after the hospital and after all the nights they’d both been afraid of losing something they’d only just learned to keep. There was no fear in it this time. Only the strange tender weight of having found one more piece.

That night she put the photograph on the fridge, under the flower magnet, next to his first payslip. One sheet of paper for the life she’d been kept from. One for the life she’d chosen. Both with names on them that were, finally and completely, her own.

chapters.title: A House With a Real Address
chapters.desc: A dark green door, windows that open, a glasshouse with nine pots in it, and a postbox with no name on it yet.
chapters.epigraph: “Hello, Mr. Lee.”
chapters.content:
He wouldn’t tell her where they were going.

He’d told her to wear something comfortable, bring a jacket and leave the viola at home, and that was all. At nine on Saturday morning, the twelfth of October, he took her hand in the hall of the flat, kissed her once, and walked her down to the car.

“Are we going somewhere?”

“Yes.”

“Where?”

“Somewhere.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the one you’re getting.”

When he started the engine she reached across and took his hand, and he turned it over and laced his fingers through hers, and for the first hour he drove without saying anything at all. The city thinned behind them. The buildings got lower and further apart. The road went up through the northern edges, past old stone walls and tiled roofs, and bent towards the hills. There were trees along it now, tall ones going gold. A man was selling persimmons under a striped awning. Two children rode bicycles down a lane.

“Are you going to tell me eventually?”

“When we get there.”

She brought his hand up and kissed the knuckles.

“What was that for?”

“For being mysterious.”

“Is it a reward?”

“Not especially.”

The road got narrower. They went through a village and over a stone bridge and down a lane lined with old fig trees, and there was nothing high anywhere, no lights, no cranes, only the hills and the trees and somewhere beyond the road the sound of water. He turned in between a pair of dark wooden gates. A gravel drive curved between two rows of trees, and at the end of it stood a house of pale stone with a dark tiled roof.

It wasn’t big. It didn’t look like a palace or a fortress, or like the houses of men who wanted the world to know how much money they had. It looked like a house. A real one. A wide front step. A small porch. Green climbing up one side. Behind it the garden went down towards a line of trees.

He stopped the car and turned the engine off. Neither of them moved.

“Welcome home,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The front door was dark green, with a brass handle and a little pane of glass and a bell that looked as if it had been rung for fifty years. He held out a set of keys.

“Is this yours?”

“It’s ours. If you want it.”

“Is it the house? The one you asked Raiden for?”

“Yes.”

“You bought it already?”

“In August.”

“August? You’ve had a house for two months and you didn’t tell me?”

“Raiden finished on Thursday. I wanted to show you.”

She took the keys. Her fingers weren’t quite steady getting the right one into the lock. The door opened onto a hall that smelled of wood and new paint, with the sun coming across the floor from a tall window at the end of it. She went in. She stopped.

The house was quiet. Not empty the way a place is when it’s been left. Empty the way a place is when it’s been waiting.

She went to the tall window. It was open. A light curtain moved in the air. She put her hand on the frame and turned round.

“The windows open.”

“All of them.”

She went into the long room. Windows on both sides looking out over the garden, clear glass, dark frames, catches simple enough for her to turn without trying. She turned one. It swung outwards and cool air came in over her hands. For years she’d lived behind windows that were sealed or armoured or watched or too dangerous to stand near. Even in the flat, with the little hatch, she’d never quite stopped thinking about what was on the other side.

“How?”

“Raiden. Every pane’s armoured. The frames and the hinges are part of the security, so they’re not ordinary windows. But they open, and they lock from inside, and he was very particular about it.”

“Of course he was.”

She opened the next one. And the next. The curtains lifted all down the room, and the house breathed, and she laughed, low, the way somebody laughs who’s found a thing she’d wanted so long she’d stopped asking for it. He stood in the doorway with his hands in his pockets. He’d imagined this. He hadn’t imagined how hard it would be to stand still while she did it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The kitchen was at the back: a long island, a deep sink, a proper oven, room for three people to cook without getting in each other’s way. She went round the island. She opened a cupboard, and another.

“How many cupboards?”

“Enough.”

“That isn’t a number.”

“I didn’t count.” She was in the pantry now, among the wooden racks. “There’s a kettle in the third one. And tea. And rice. Enough for breakfast.”

“How long have you been getting this ready?”

“Since August.”

She came out of the pantry and put her arms round his waist. “You’re impossible.”

“I’ve heard.”

“Thank you,” she said into his shirt.

Upstairs, the first bedroom looked over the garden, and a door from it went out onto a small balcony, and from the balcony she could hear the water properly: a stream, at the bottom of the slope, running over stones under ferns, with a little wooden footbridge over it under an old tree.

“That’s ours too?”

“Yes.”

Beside the wardrobe there was a small door she hadn’t noticed. His face changed a little.

“There’s something I have to show you.”

Behind it a short corridor ran into the thick of the house and ended at an armoured door. Beyond that was a small room: a bench, a cupboard, a lamp, water and supplies, its own air, a telephone that rang somewhere other than here, and a second door at the back.

“If there’s ever anything serious,” he said, “you come in here and lock it, and press that, and people come. That door at the back goes down under the garden and comes out past the wall by the lower road. Raiden has the drawings. Bao knows.”

She looked at it all. It didn’t look like a place meant to frighten anyone. It looked like a room got ready by somebody who knew that frightening things are easier to live through when there’s somewhere to go.

“Will we have to use it?”

“I hope not.”

“Will you tell me if something happens? Even if you think you’re protecting me by not?”

“Yes.”

He showed her the panel in the corridor once, what each part did, and then he stopped. “That’s enough for today. I don’t want you remembering this house as a lot of locks. I want you remembering the kitchen. The windows. The room where you’ll play your mother’s viola.” He touched her face. “The locks are here so you don’t have to think about them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The glasshouse was at the far end of the garden. She saw it from the back step and stopped.

“What’s that?”

“Yours.”

A dark green frame, clear glass, the roof angled to the light, a stone path up to the door, and the door standing open a little. Inside the sun came down across shelves and pots and a long worktable in the middle, a small sink, a bench under the side windows. It smelled of earth and leaves.

And on the shelves, set out by how much light each one wanted, were her plants. The basil. The mint. The rosemary and the thyme and the lemon balm and the little white flowers. All nine, out of the steel box and into proper pots, a little bigger than when she’d last watered them on Thursday.

“You moved them.”

“Raiden’s men brought them up yesterday, while you were at Elowen’s. I carried the basil myself.”

Beside each pot was a small wooden label in her own handwriting. He’d taken them out of the window box.

“You kept these?”

“They belong to the plants.”

She laughed, and her eyes had begun to shine. She went right in and opened the side windows, and they opened too, every one, and the air came through the glasshouse from the garden and the stream and the hills. Then she turned round. He was in the doorway, watching her. She went to him and put both hands flat on his chest.

“Did you do all this for me?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He brushed his thumb across her cheek. “Because you wanted a window box.”

“You measured the window at three in the morning.”

“I remember.”

“You built a balcony because I said basil.”

“I remember.”

She came up on her toes and kissed him in the glasshouse doorway, slowly, her hands on his chest and his at her waist, as if she wanted him to understand every part of what she couldn’t say. When she drew back he put his forehead on hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a bench by the stream under an old fig tree. She sat on it and took her shoes off and put her feet on the cold stone, and listened to the water.

“I can hear it from the bedroom.”

“I thought you’d like that.”

“Do you know what I want to do first? Have breakfast down here.”

“We’ll put a table there. Two chairs.”

“And an umbrella.”

“All right.”

“You’re agreeing to everything.”

“I’ve learned.”

She put her head on his shoulder. “We’ll ask everyone. Elowen and Zhendong. Raiden and Jinx. Baba. Nam.”

“Nam’ll complain about the road.”

“He complains about everything.”

“He’ll complain about the chairs.”

“Then we’ll give him a better one.” She looked at the water. “And I want to learn the viola here. With the windows open.”

“We’ll find Mrs. Yoon. What else?”

“What will you do here?”

He thought about it. “Sleep.”

“Only sleep?”

“Eat. Work, sometimes.”

“A desk? A chair that isn’t terrible?”

“You’re very worried about my chair.”

“You sit on horrible furniture.”

“I’ll get a good one.”

“And the garden. You don’t know anything about gardens. You’ll kill the basil.”

“I’ve kept you alive.”

She laughed. “That’s different.”

“Is it?”

“Completely,” she said. “So I’ll teach you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By the front gate, set into the stone pillar, there was a postbox painted the same dark green as the door. It had a small brass frame on the front for a name card. The card in it was blank.

“There’s no name,” she said.

“No.”

“Why?”

“I was waiting. I didn’t want to put mine there before you’d decided what the house was. Whose name you wanted on it. Yours, mine, both, whatever you like.” He took a folded paper out of his jacket. “And this. The deed. It’s in both names. Ms. Fong needs you to sign it before it’s done.”

She signed it on the top of the stone pillar with the pen he gave her, and handed it back. Then she slid the card out of its frame and held the pen over it a moment, and wrote.

LEE

No title. No crest. No explanation. Only the name she’d chosen when she married him. She slid the card back into the frame.

“Is that all right?”

He didn’t answer. He was looking at the postbox, still.

He’d spent years making sure nobody knew where he slept. False names. No forwarding address. Every door behind him ready to shut. He’d never imagined a postbox. Never imagined a letter. Never imagined somebody writing his name with hers and putting it outside a house where they were expected to stay.

His mouth went tight. He looked away.

“Jun Hyuk?”

He tried to say something and couldn’t. Then his eyes filled. He put his hand up over his mouth and bowed his head.

“Oh,” said Evangeline.

He laughed once, and it broke in the middle. She stepped in and put her arms round him, and he bent his head into her shoulder, and he didn’t move at all. Then his arms came round her, tight.

There was no blood this time. No fear. No one outside. Only a house, and a front door, and a stream, and a glasshouse with nine plants in it, and a name on a card.

“I’ve never had this,” he said.

“I know.”

“I can go out in the morning and come back.”

“Yes.”

“I can get a letter.”

She laughed through her own tears. “You can.”

“And you can open the door.”

She held his face. “Whenever I want.”

He put his forehead on hers. “Lee,” he whispered.

“Lee.”

He kissed her under the postbox, once, and again, holding her face in both hands as if the word on that card had given him something he’d never known how to ask for. When he let her go his eyes were still wet, and she wiped them with her thumbs.

“Hello, Mr. Lee.”

A small helpless smile. “Hello, Mrs. Lee.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate on the floor of the long room that night, on a blanket, from containers he’d brought up from the city, because there was no table yet and she wouldn’t let him have one sent in an hour. The windows were open. The curtains moved. They could hear the stream.

“Do you remember the first time I came to Nam’s?” she said, against his shoulder.

“Beef noodles.”

“I thought I’d never see you again.” She touched his hand. “And now there’s a house. With a glasshouse. And a stream. And a postbox.”

“Yes.”

“Will we get letters?”

“Nam, complaining about something. Elowen, inviting herself. Raiden, sending drawings. Jinx, something useful.”

“And the King?”

“If he wants to write, he knows where to send it now.”

She got up and went and opened the front window wider and stood in the air for a while. Then she came back and sat beside him.

“Thank you for giving me a home.”

He shook his head. “I didn’t.” He touched her cheek. “You made it one.”

She leaned in and kissed him. Out at the gate the little card sat in its brass frame. LEE. And that night, for the first time in his life, Lee Jun Hyuk went to sleep without working out how fast he could get out of the house. He thought about the windows he’d open in the morning, and the breakfast table they still had to buy, and the basil that needed watering, and the woman asleep next to him, whose name was on the same door as his.

chapters.title: The Neighbours Bring a Cake
chapters.desc: A neighbour brings a chestnut cake and he checks it. A ginger cat moves in. Then her father carries a cedar chest up four stone steps on his own.
chapters.epigraph: “Because you came back.”
chapters.content:
The first person to knock on the door of No. 9 Fig Tree Lane was carrying a cake.

He saw her through the front window on the Sunday morning before the bell went: an elderly woman on the step of the house next door, coming down her path with a round cake tin held in both hands, in a pale yellow cardigan and sensible shoes and an expression of cheerful determination. He watched her for three seconds. Then he checked the gate. Then the lane. Then her hands.

Evangeline, folding tea towels at the kitchen counter, looked up. “Someone’s coming.”

“I know.”

“Are you going to open the door?”

“Do you know her?”

“No.”

“Then why are you smiling?”

“Because she’s carrying a cake.”

He looked out of the window again. “That doesn’t establish anything.”

“Jun Hyuk.”

He checked the spyhole and the side pane and opened the door. The woman beamed up at him.

“Good morning! You’ll be the new neighbours. I’m Mrs. Bae, from next door. Bae Sun-ja. My husband’s inside trying to mend the television. He’s been saying he can do it himself since breakfast.” She held up the tin. “Chestnut sponge. A bit old-fashioned, but everybody likes it.”

“Lee Jun Hyuk,” he said. “Thank you.”

He didn’t take it. Mrs. Bae looked at him, and at the tin, and back at him.

“Is something the matter?”

“No.”

“You’re looking at it very hard.”

“He’s surprised,” said Evangeline, at his shoulder. “Thank you so much, Mrs. Bae. Won’t you come in?”

Mrs. Bae was delighted to come in for a minute. In the kitchen Jun Hyuk put the tin on the counter, took the lid off, and took a small knife out of the drawer.

“Are you going to cut it?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“To check it.”

It was round and golden and dusted with sugar, with chestnut cream between two soft layers and whole chestnuts on top, and it smelled wonderful. He looked at the tin. He looked at the cake. He looked at the paper it sat on. The kitchen went quiet.

“Young man,” said Mrs. Bae at last, “it’s a cake.”

“I know.”

“Did you think I’d put something in it?”

He looked at her. “No.”

“Then what are you checking?”

He considered this. “Habit.”

Mrs. Bae thought about it and nodded, as if she’d been given a perfectly sensible answer. “My husband has habits. He checks the front door three times before bed. I tell him it hasn’t moved.”

Evangeline pressed her lips together hard.

He cut a thin slice and put it on a plate and ate it in front of them both. He chewed. He swallowed. He looked at the cake. He looked at his wife. He said nothing.

Evangeline picked up the fork and took a bite of the same slice.

“Is it safe?” she said.

He looked at her.

“Good,” she said, with her mouth full, to Mrs. Bae. “Very good. Thank you for checking,” she said to him.

“You’re welcome,” said Jun Hyuk.

Mrs. Bae found all of this deeply entertaining. “Keep the rest. Bae and I can’t finish a whole one any more. If you need anything, knock. We’ve lived here thirty years and my husband knows everybody on this lane whether they want him to or not.” At the door she turned round. “Oh, and the cat may come and see you. Pudding. Ginger. Very friendly. Very greedy. If he likes you he’ll simply move in.”

“We’ll keep the door shut,” said Jun Hyuk.

“Good luck with that,” said Mrs. Bae, and went home.

Evangeline shut the door and leaned on it. “Well? Is Mrs. Bae a threat?”

“No.”

“Is the cake?”

“No.”

“Is Pudding?”

He looked at the window. “Possibly.”

She laughed until she had to sit down on the stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

Pudding came at four, through the garden gate, with the walk of a cat who had never once in his life been told no. He was large and ginger, with white feet and a pale bib and a tail held straight up like a question. Evangeline saw him from the glasshouse.

“Hello.”

Pudding looked at her and walked straight past into the house.

“Jun Hyuk! We have a visitor.”

He came out of the kitchen. Pudding sat on the hall floor and looked up at him. He looked down at Pudding. Neither of them moved.

“Whose cat is that?”

“Mrs. Bae’s.”

“Then why is he in our house?”

“Because he wants to be.”

Pudding got up on the sofa, turned round twice, settled in the corner, and when Evangeline sat down beside him climbed into her lap and began to purr.

“Don’t feed him,” said Jun Hyuk. “He might be on a diet.”

She looked at the cat. “Do you look like you’re on a diet?”

He went back into the kitchen. Five minutes later he came back with a small bowl of water and put it on the floor by the sofa without a word, and Pudding got down and drank.

“You brought him water.”

“He was thirsty. Don’t make it a thing.”

She reached for his hand and pulled him down onto the sofa beside her, and Pudding, apparently satisfied with the arrangements, climbed straight out of her lap and into his.

He went completely still.

“Well,” said Evangeline.

“Don’t.”

“He likes you.”

“He has poor judgement.”

Pudding kneaded his trousers and settled against his stomach and purred like an engine. Jun Hyuk put one hand on the cat’s back carefully, with the concentration of a man handling something more dangerous than anything he’d ever carried in a holster. She leaned over and kissed his cheek.

“Good afternoon, Mr. Lee.”

He sighed. He didn’t move the cat.

✦ ✦ ✦

They moved in on the Saturday after, the nineteenth. Not everything at once. The flat had years of them in it, and she wanted to go through it properly: some to come, some to give away, some to stay where it was until she’d decided. He’d arranged a van and three men to carry. She’d arranged for him to stop buying things without asking her. Neither arrangement was entirely successful.

The first thing they carried into the house was the menu from Nam’s.

It was soft at every fold now, the ink gone brown. His seven rules. Her eight. His nine crossed out and hers written under it. SHE NEVER PAYS. He is allowed to be spoiled too. And at the bottom of his first list, still there, 7. Don’t come back.

“Where?” she said.

He looked at the inside of the front door. “Here.”

They found a small frame in one of the boxes, and he fixed it to the inside of the door just above the lock. It looked ridiculous: a noodle-shop menu framed on the door of a stone house in the hills.

“Perfect,” said Evangeline.

“Some of it’s out of date,” he said. “Seven.”

“Why?”

“Because you came back.”

“Then we keep it,” she said. “You wrote it when you were afraid. Now it’s on our door. We’ll see it every time we go out, and every time we come home.” She touched the glass. “I like that.”

He bent and kissed her. They left it there.

✦ ✦ ✦

The furniture took six days. He’d assumed one. He’d underestimated his wife. She wanted to see the wood in daylight. She wanted to sit on every sofa before she chose one. She wanted a dining table that everyone would fit round, not one that looked important in a showroom, and curtains that moved, and a proper bookcase, and a rug that wouldn’t make the long room look like an office.

The bed took longest. She found a wide wooden frame with a headboard that curved at the corners, and he looked at the label.

“Too short.”

“It’s a king.”

“Still.”

“How long do you think you are?”

“Long enough.”

The salesman asked if they’d like to try it. She lay down in the middle and patted the space beside her, and he looked at the salesman, who found something fascinating on the far wall, and lay down. His feet went over the end.

“You’re right,” she said.

“Order the long one.”

She caught his sleeve. “Not the first thing we see. You said that about the sofa. And the table. And the curtains.”

“Do you want the bed or not?”

She laughed and leaned over and kissed him, there on the showroom mattress, and he caught her by the waist and kissed her back, and the salesman became interested in his catalogue.

The long one was ordered. So was the mattress. And while she was looking at lamps, he bought the matching bedside tables, which she found out about in the car.

“You bought them without asking.”

“You liked them.”

“I was looking at them.”

“For a long time.” He glanced at her. “Do you want them?”

She looked out of the window. “Yes.”

He took her hand. “Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By Wednesday it had begun to look like theirs. The sofa was in. The table had come. There were books on the shelves and tea in the cupboard and flowers by the stairs. Her mother’s photograph from the lake stood by the bed and her mother’s note was in the drawer. The viola had its own corner of the small room upstairs by the window. He had a desk. A proper chair. And a lamp she’d chosen because she said his old one made him look as if he were interrogating his paperwork.

That afternoon a car came up the lane, and Uncle Mok got out of it, and then her father.

Lin Jian was in his black coat, and he had something in his arms. A cedar chest, old and polished, dark with age, brass at the corners. Evangeline came down the path from the glasshouse.

“Baba.”

He looked at her and his face went soft. “I brought something. It was your mother’s. Mama’s. From before she married me. I kept it.”

There were four stone steps up to the front door.

“Let me help, sir,” said Uncle Mok.

“No. I’ll carry it.”

“Baba, it’s heavy.”

“I know.”

He lifted it. He went up the first step, and the second, and stopped on the third, and she came towards him and he shook his head. “Stay there.” He went up the last. Jun Hyuk was in the hall, and took one look at the chest and came forward, and didn’t take it from him. He opened the door wider and moved the shoes out of the way, and Lin Jian carried it into the long room and put it down under the window and stood with his hand on the lid, breathing hard.

“What’s in it?”

“Things she kept.”

He opened it. A silk scarf. A wooden hair comb. A cloth-bound notebook full of lists in Mama’s handwriting, things to plant and when, and on one page a pencil drawing of a small lemon tree in a pot. A photograph of a young woman under a tree, and beside her a young man in a black suit looking at something outside the picture: her father, at thirty, before any of it.

And at the bottom, tied with a thread, a bundle of ribbons.

Evangeline put her hand on them and counted without meaning to. Eleven. One of them was blue, frayed at the end.

She looked up. “These went in the canal.”

Her father didn’t look at her. He looked at the ribbons.

“I saw him from my office window,” he said. “Raiden. He was ten. He’d been home four months. He went down the back steps with his hands behind him, and came up without them.” He was quiet. “That night I went down with the pole off the barge, after dark, and found nine. The other two were on the mud at the bridge in the morning. Ah Sim washed them. I didn’t know what to say to either of you. So I put them in Mama’s chest and said nothing.” His mouth twisted. “As usual.”

She sat back on her heels with the ribbons in her lap and couldn’t speak.

Under them, folded small, there was a bundle of old pale silk. She knew it before she’d touched it. A grey heron standing in water, mountains behind, in thread so fine it shone.

“From behind the lights,” said her father. “I thought it should come with you.”

She held the blanket in both hands. “Why didn’t you give me these before?”

He was quiet. “I wasn’t ready. I thought if I gave you her things I’d have to admit she was gone. And if I kept them, some part of her would stay where I could find it.” He looked at her at last. “But you should have had them. So I’m asking you. Will you have them?”

“Yes,” said Evangeline, and took his hand.

He looked round the room then: the open windows, the garden, the flowers on the table, the menu framed on the inside of the door. Then at Jun Hyuk.

“Is she comfortable here?”

“Yes,” said Jun Hyuk.

Her father looked back at her. And then, for the second time in his life, he asked.

“Are you?”

“Very,” she said.

He nodded. “Good,” he said, and didn’t say anything else, and didn’t need to.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she came out of the bathroom in one of his shirts and found him sitting on the edge of the long bed, which had come that afternoon, looking at nothing.

“Are you working?”

“No.”

“Then what are you doing?”

“Looking at the house. Making sure we’re in it.”

She stood between his knees and put her hand on his face. “We’re in it.”

She went to the chest at the foot of the bed and took the silk out and shook it open. It wasn’t big enough for the bed. She spread it over the two of them anyway, and pulled the edge up over his shoulder.

“You’ll be cold.”

“Then come closer.”

He looked at the heron, and at her. “You’re keeping it here? Not in the chest?”

“I want it with us.”

He kissed her the kind of kiss that belongs to the end of a long day, in a room with the window open, in a bed that was finally long enough for him.

“Are you happy?” she asked.

There was no quick answer. He’d spent so many years measuring his life by what he could put up with and what he could carry and what he could leave, he’d never learned to answer a question like that without first checking it was safe. But she was waiting.

“Yes,” he said.

“Me too.”

Later, with her head on his chest and the silk over them both, she traced his collarbone with one finger.

“Do you remember the first time you saw me?”

“The box.”

“You looked very angry.”

“I was.”

“At me?”

“No.”

“I was standing in front of the others,” she said. “I thought if I was in front, the men would look at me first. And you said Stay behind me.” She smiled against him. “I think I liked you from then.”

“That’s unfortunate,” he said. “I was trying very hard not to like you.”

She lifted her head. “How did that go?”

He looked at her mouth. “Badly.”

She kissed him, and settled back down, and he pulled the silk higher over her shoulder. Outside the stream went on in the dark garden. Downstairs, on the inside of the front door, Nam’s menu hung in its frame, seven rules and all the rest, one of them still waiting to be rewritten. And for once, Lee Jun Hyuk didn’t need to keep watch. He had a home, and somebody asleep under the same blanket.

chapters.title: He Doesn’t Know How to Sleep Without a Weapon
chapters.desc: He doesn’t know how to sleep in a house with no gun under the bed. So she sleeps on his side, between him and the door.
chapters.epigraph: “Nowhere. That’s the point.”
chapters.content:
The first night they lived at No. 9 Fig Tree Lane, he woke at thirteen minutes past two. The second night, at a quarter to two. On the third, Evangeline woke because the mattress moved.

She didn’t open her eyes straight away. She knew the difference between him moving in his sleep and a man who’d stopped sleeping. His breathing had changed. His hand wasn’t at her waist. The warm place beside her had gone.

He was sitting on the edge of the bed with his back to her, his shoulders bare, one hand on his knee, looking at the bedroom door.

“Jun Hyuk?”

“Go back to sleep.”

She looked at the clock. Twenty past two. She put her hand on his arm. He let her, but his eyes stayed on the door.

“Did you hear something?”

“No.”

“Is something wrong?”

“No.”

She knew that answer. It was the one he gave when something was wrong and he didn’t want to bring it into the room.

“Come back to bed.”

“In a minute.”

He said it gently, and that was what made her sit up. “Are you going to watch the door all night?”

He nearly denied it. Then he looked away. “Just till I’m tired.”

She slid out and came round the bed and stood in front of him and held out her hand. He took it, and she put him back under the covers, and he lay down with his eyes on the door again. She lay against him with her palm on his chest. He shut his eyes for perhaps thirty seconds. Then they opened. She didn’t scold him. She moved closer until her forehead was on his shoulder. Some time after three, he slept. He woke before five.

✦ ✦ ✦

The guns weren’t under the bed any more. They hadn’t been since the move. Everything he’d once kept within reach was in a steel room behind the pantry that Raiden had built for it, with its own lock and a door nobody would ever open by accident. It was sensible. It was necessary. A house wasn’t a safe house. A bedroom wasn’t a place for the tools of his old life. He’d wanted her to walk barefoot down the hall without passing anything that reminded her of the men who’d taken her. He’d wanted to stop sleeping with one hand under the mattress.

He hadn’t thought about what it would be like to try to sleep without the things that had taught him how to stay alive.

He knew exactly where the room was. He knew what was in it. And every night some part of him lay listening for a danger he could no longer reach out and touch.

He didn’t tell her. He thought he was hiding it well. He wasn’t. On the fourth night she found him at the window. On the fifth, in the chair by the door. On the sixth, downstairs at the kitchen table, dressed, with a cup of tea he hadn’t drunk. On the seventh she went into the pantry and found him standing in front of the steel door.

“Couldn’t sleep?” he said.

“I woke up and you weren’t there.”

“I’m sorry. I don’t need to open it.”

“I didn’t ask you to.” She stood beside him. “Does having it close make you feel safer?”

He thought about it. “No. It makes me feel ready.”

There was a difference, and she understood it. He’d spent years making sure nothing could happen to him without an answer, sleeping light, waking fast, keeping the distance between himself and trouble as short as he could make it. Now he had a bedroom with curtains she’d chosen and a window that opened on the garden and a woman who slept with one foot tucked under his calf, and he couldn’t stop watching the door.

She took his hand. “Come to bed.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next night she got in on his side.

He’d finished checking the front door and came into the bedroom and found her there, and stopped.

“That’s my side.”

“I know.”

“You’re on the wrong side.”

“No.”

“Evangeline.”

“Jun Hyuk.” She patted the sheet beside her. “Come to bed.”

He got in, slowly, on her side, and she turned to him, and then, without asking, shifted herself until she lay between him and the door.

He looked down at her. “What are you doing?”

“Watching.” She tucked her hand under her cheek. “I’ll watch for you.”

He didn’t move. The curtain stirred.

“You don’t have to,” he said, low.

“I know.”

“You can’t watch everything.”

“I know that too.” She took his hand and put it round her waist. “Let me.”

He looked at her. His arm tightened. His eyes went past her shoulder to the dark doorway, and then down to her face, and she’d already shut her eyes. He listened to her breathe. After a while, he shut his own.

He slept until six.

She went on doing it. She never made it sound like a cure or a plan. She kept his side. If he woke, she woke. If he sat up, she sat up. If he turned towards the door, she moved closer until he had to look at her instead. Once, at half past two, he whispered, “You’re awake.”

“So are you.”

“Go back to sleep.”

“You’re in my way.”

“Your way? Where are you going?”

“Nowhere,” she said, and opened one eye. “That’s the point.”

He looked away, but she saw his mouth move.

Another night he woke all at once and reached across the bed, and his hand found her shoulder, and her neck, and the place under her jaw where her pulse was. She caught his wrist gently.

“I’m here.”

He stopped, with his fingers still on her skin. He was checking. Not on purpose. A pulse, a breath, proof. She brought his hand down and kissed the knuckles.

“Still here.”

“I’m sorry. I woke you.”

“I was awake already.”

“That isn’t better.”

“You’re very hard to comfort, you know.”

“I know.”

She tucked herself against his chest. “Then I’ll be hard too.”

He held her, and slept.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the second week Mrs. Yoon came up from the city to give the first lesson. Evangeline had been nervous since breakfast. She’d arranged the little room upstairs twice and moved the chair closer to the window and was wiping a table with no dust on it when he found her.

“What if I can’t?”

“Then you learn.”

“What if I sound terrible?”

“I’ll listen.”

“That isn’t reassuring.”

“I wasn’t trying to reassure you.” He took the cloth out of her hand and put the chair right and stood behind her with his hands on her shoulders. “You don’t have to be good at it today. You only have to start.”

Mrs. Yoon lifted Seo Hwa’s viola out of its case as if it were asleep. “Your mother had lovely hands,” she said. “Let’s see yours.”

She showed her how to hold it. The shoulder. The chin. The first sound was dreadful, a thin scrape that made Evangeline wince.

“Good,” said Mrs. Yoon.

“Good?”

“Now we know where we’re starting. Don’t apologise to the instrument. Again.”

He was watching from the doorway. She saw him and looked away quickly. Mrs. Yoon followed her eyes.

“Is that your husband? He’s very handsome. Does he know?”

Evangeline nearly dropped the bow. “He knows.”

“Then he can come in and sit there and not say a word.”

He sat, and lifted both hands to show he wouldn’t. The next note was still bad. But it lasted. And when she lowered the bow he was looking at her as if she’d done something extraordinary.

“Don’t,” she said.

“What?”

“That face. As if I’d won something.”

“You did,” said Jun Hyuk.

By the end of November she could make a handful of clean notes. She practised every morning in the little room with the window open. Some days he listened from the kitchen. Some days he sat in the doorway with his coffee. Some days he had to leave for the Iron Docks before she’d finished, and she’d find a note on the counter. The third one was better today. She always knew he meant the one that had sounded like a dying bird the week before.

✦ ✦ ✦

One afternoon after her lesson he found her at the desk in the little room with an exercise book open. On the first page, in her small careful hand, were three words.

THE OPEN DOOR

“What is it?”

“A foundation. For people who’ve been trafficked.” She turned the book towards him. “I’ve been talking to Nuo. And Eliana. And Song, about what happens after the police have finished. I keep thinking about the women from the box. The ones who were found and the ones who weren’t. And the ones who get out and find out being rescued doesn’t mean they’ve got anywhere to go.” She turned a page. “Some haven’t got papers. Some haven’t got money. Some can’t go home and some don’t want to be found by anybody. They need doctors, and lawyers, and somewhere to sleep where nobody knows their name. I want there to be somewhere they can go without having to explain everything first. Not somewhere that decides what they should do. Somewhere that gives them choices.” She looked at the three words. “Nobody should have to stand outside a locked door and wonder whether they’re allowed in.”

“Good name,” he said.

“I don’t want to run it on my own. I want it run properly. And I want the women who use it to have a say in how.”

“What do you need first?”

“A proper legal structure. A board. Rules that protect the people who come to us. I won’t have anyone’s story used without her permission.” She looked at him sideways. “And money. And I’m not asking you to buy me a foundation.”

“I know.”

“I want to build it properly.”

“Then we will. However you want.”

It came together slowly. A lawyer Eliana knew. A social worker who’d spent twenty years with survivors. A doctor who explained what care meant when someone had been hurt the way those women had been hurt. Nuo came to one of the first meetings with both hands round a cup of tea, and listened, and then said, “I don’t want anyone to think that because they helped me, they own what happened to me.”

“They won’t,” said Evangeline. “We’ll write it into the rules.”

“Then I’d like to help.”

One evening he came home with a thick folder and put it down by her elbow on the dining table. Inside was everything in the crates on the fifth floor, and in the places she knew less about: the gold, the stones, the notes in their bands, the buildings.

“I want to give it to the foundation.”

She stared at him. “All of it?”

“Everything that’s mine.” He sat down beside her. “I kept those things so I could leave in a hurry. Buy a way over a border. Pay someone to make a man disappear. Find a place nobody could follow. I thought that was what money was for.” He looked at the folder. “I don’t need to live like that.”

She closed the folder. “Some of it stays yours.”

“I’ve got enough.”

“You’ll keep enough to live on and keep this house and look after yourself and make your own choices. And enough that if the foundation ever disagrees with you, you won’t feel you have to run it because you paid for it.” She held his eyes. “I won’t let you give everything away because you think you don’t deserve to keep anything.”

His face changed. He looked down. She thought he’d argue.

“What do you think I should keep?” he said.

She told him. He listened. At the end he nodded.

“Independent trustees,” she said. “Proper accounts. An outside audit. No money without a paper trail.”

“You’re going to make me sign a great many things.”

“Yes.”

“Good.” He lifted her hand and kissed the fingers. “Use it well.”

“You trust me with it?”

“With everything.”

For once, giving something away didn’t feel like losing it. It felt like choosing what it would become.

✦ ✦ ✦

The month ended in rain. It began in the afternoon, soft and then steady enough to blur the garden past the bedroom window. He came home early from the docks, showered, made tea, and found her on the bed with a page of the foundation’s papers across her knees.

“Still working?”

“Two pages.”

He took them off her and put them on the bedside table. “Tomorrow.”

“Jun Hyuk.”

“Tomorrow.”

He sat down beside her and pushed her hair back behind her ear, and kissed her, slow, without any of the hurry that used to come with every hour they had alone. She reached for the silk at the foot of the bed and he lifted the edge so she could pull it over them, and she moved in close, and he kissed her shoulder, and her cheek, and her mouth.

“You’re quiet,” she said.

“I’m listening.”

“To what?”

“The rain.”

“Not the door?”

He went still for a second. Then he shook his head. “No.”

He undressed her under the silk, unhurried, as if he had nowhere at all to be, and she pulled his shirt off over his head and laughed when his hair fell in his eyes.

“What?”

“You’re handsome.”

“That isn’t funny.”

“It is when you’re trying to look serious.”

He kissed her until she forgot what she’d been laughing at. He kissed his way down her body in the grey rain-light, slow, and parted her with his mouth and stayed there until she was gripping the sheet and saying his name to the ceiling. When he came up over her she drew him in with her hands on his back, and he moved in her slowly, so slowly, his forehead on hers, the rain on the window and nothing else in the world, and she came apart under him with a long low sound, and he followed her down and lay with his face in her neck, breathing.

Afterwards she lay against him with the silk over them both, and noticed something.

He hadn’t checked. Not once. He hadn’t put his fingers under her jaw when she went quiet. He hadn’t counted her breaths or touched her wrist to be sure. He was only holding her.

“Jun Hyuk. You’re not checking.”

He didn’t understand for a second. Then he looked at where his hand lay on her waist.

“No,” he said.

“How does it feel?”

“Different.”

“Bad?”

“Not bad.” He was quiet. “I still wake up sometimes. But I don’t always get up.”

“That’s good.”

He kissed the middle of her palm. “You’re not watching the door tonight.”

“No. I think you can watch yourself now.”

He turned onto his side and drew her in. “Stay there anyway.”

“Always.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday was the twenty-third of November, the birthday that wasn’t on any paper. She didn’t make anything of it. At lunch she put an extra egg in his rice and said nothing at all, and he looked at the bowl and then at her, and ate it slowly, and didn’t get arrogant about it.

On the Sunday he slept for eight hours.

She woke first. The room was pale with morning. His arm lay across her waist and his breathing was deep and even, and there was no line between his eyebrows and nothing tight about his mouth. He was asleep. Properly. She looked at the clock and smiled, and touched his hair, and he stirred and opened his eyes and looked at her, and at the light, and back at her.

“What time is it?”

“Eight.”

He blinked. “Eight?” He looked at the clock and half sat up, and she laughed.

“You slept.”

“For eight hours.”

“I counted. Every minute.”

“That’s ridiculous.”

“Very.”

“Why didn’t you wake me?”

“Because you were asleep.”

He looked at her a long time, and then bent and kissed her. “Thank you,” he said, with his forehead on hers. “For staying there.”

“I wasn’t guarding the door. I was keeping you company.”

“All right,” he said.

Out in the garden everything was wet. The stream ran under the little wooden bridge. In the small room upstairs her mother’s viola was waiting for Tuesday. On the dining table the first papers of The Open Door lay in a neat pile for signing. And behind the pantry the steel room was still locked. It hadn’t gone. Nor had what was in it. But none of it had to be beside his bed.

He pulled the covers back up over them. “Five more minutes.”

“Eight hours wasn’t enough?”

“Apparently not,” he said, and shut his eyes, and didn’t have to make himself sleep. He did.

chapters.title: The Last Target
chapters.desc: Nam rings on a Thursday night. The Ferryman is back on the river after nine years, with thirty people and a date. Jun Hyuk takes the rifle out, and his wife sits down opposite him.
chapters.epigraph: “Let me show you you’re allowed forgiveness.”
chapters.content:
Nam rang at sixteen minutes past nine on Thursday night, the twenty-eighth of November.

Jun Hyuk was at the sink drying a cup. Evangeline was at the dining table with the planner’s drawings of the garden spread out in front of her, and she had circled the fig tree twice. The wedding would be on the twenty-first of December, the longest night of the year. She liked the idea of marrying him on the night the dark reached as far as it could go and then began, a minute a day, to give ground. He’d said it was romantic. Then he’d asked whether the garden would be too cold. She’d told him that wasn’t the point. He’d said he understood, and hadn’t looked as if he did.

His phone buzzed on the counter. “Nam,” he said, and answered it with the cup still in his other hand. “What’s wrong?”

She went back to her drawings. Then she noticed he’d stopped drying.

“Say that again.”

She watched it happen. It was slow enough that she nearly missed it: his shoulders settling, his face going still, the warmth that had been there a moment ago drawing back behind something she knew far too well.

“Where?” He listened. “When?” He looked at the black window over the sink. “Don’t go anywhere. I’ll ring you back.”

He put the phone down and stood holding it.

“Jun Hyuk?”

“Nam’s heard something.” He set the cup on the drainer carefully, as if it might go off. “The Ferryman.”

She’d heard the name in conversations that stopped when she came into a room. In the forty-one pages Judge Chau had signed. In the things he’d carried home from across the river in April and never quite put down. The man whose boats took women. The man who’d owned the route her box had travelled. The man nobody had ever made answer for anything.

She stood up. “He’s alive?”

“He’s on the river. He’s got a boat.”

“How many?”

“Thirty.”

The pencil rolled off the table. Neither of them reached for it.

His name was Gu Shanlin. Nine years ago he’d been the man behind the trucks that came through the east crossing in the rain, and Jun Hyuk had been the young soldier at the barrier who read the stamp and waved them on, and eleven women had died, and Gu Shanlin had gone on. Now, according to whoever Nam had been listening to in his back room, he meant to move thirty people across the river on Saturday the seventh of December. A new boat. A different landing. The same business.

Jun Hyuk made three calls that night. Song first. Then Nam again. Then someone whose name she didn’t catch. He didn’t tell her to go to bed. He didn’t tell her anything at all.

At eleven he went into the pantry, and she heard the lock.

She followed him. The steel room sat behind a plain door that looked like part of the shelving, and he’d never once opened it in front of her. He opened it now. He stood inside it, and when he came out he was carrying the rifle in its case, and he took it through to the kitchen and laid it on the cleared table.

“Go to bed,” he said, without looking up.

“You’re taking it out?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He did look up then. “Because Gu Shanlin is coming back.”

“Is this the only way?”

“I don’t know yet.”

It was an honest answer. She wished it had been a different one.

He went to work on it with a concentration she recognised from a hundred other nights: the kit laid out in order, each part cleaned and checked and set down in its place, nothing explained, nothing hurried. There was no excitement in it and no anger. It was a ritual. It was the same ritual that had kept him alive for years, and had also made him a man who couldn’t sleep without something like this under the bed.

She pulled out the chair opposite and sat down.

“What are you doing?”

“Keeping you company.”

“You should sleep.”

“So should you.”

He looked at her for a second longer, and went back to the table. She stayed.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday morning the planner rang, and she took the call in the garden in her coat.

“Yes, the twenty-first. Yes, we’ve decided. The longest night. That’s why.” She smiled at something the woman said. “No, no big canopy. Just enough to keep the flowers dry if it rains. White, and winter greenery. Nothing elaborate.” Through the kitchen window she could see him at the table, where he’d been since before it was light. “Six guests,” she said. “And my father.”

When she rang off he was standing in the back doorway.

“Wedding?”

“The twenty-first.”

He looked at the garden. “Three weeks.”

“Three weeks and one day.”

He came down the steps and she held out her hand and he took it. “Are you sure?” he said. “About having it here.”

She looked round her. The grass was still wet from the night. The old fig tree stood over the path with its branches half bare, and the stream went on under the little wooden bridge, and the house was behind them. Their house.

“I want to marry you here.”

“Then here.”

“There’s something else. I want to wear the aquamarines.” The mended ones, from Aurelia’s counter on Harbour Road, that she’d said she didn’t need to own and he’d gone back for anyway. “And I want Mama’s cedar chest open in the garden. Not all of it. The ribbons, and her notebook. I think she’d have liked the flowers.”

His face softened. He looked at the bare branches. “She probably would.”

She leaned up and kissed him. He kissed her back. Halfway through it his attention went, just once, to the kitchen window. She felt it go.

When she drew back she put her hand on his cheek. “Come inside and have breakfast with me.”

“I’ve got something to finish.”

“Later.”

He looked at her, and she held his eyes, and after a moment he said, “All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first night he cleaned the rifle once. The second night he did it again. By the third it had become a presence in the house, though it was never left anywhere and the steel room was locked behind it every time. Each evening the same thing: bring it out, sit down under the little chilli calendar she’d bought at a village market because every month had a red pepper with a different expression on its face, clean it, check it, put it away. November’s chilli looked alarmed. He sat under it every night. She sat opposite him every night, and didn’t ask him to stop.

Not yet. She knew the difference between a man preparing for something hard and a man using the preparing so he wouldn’t have to think about what it would cost him. He was doing both.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday morning she rang Song from the music room with the door shut. She hadn’t told him. She didn’t want to keep it secret. She needed to understand it first, before she could take it to him.

Song answered on the fourth ring. “Mrs. Lee.”

“Inspector. I need to ask you something. What would convict Gu Shanlin?”

He didn’t answer straight away.

“I know what he’s done,” she said. “The boats. The containers. The people who helped him. The judge.”

“Knowing isn’t proving.” His voice wasn’t unkind. “If you want him in front of a court and kept there, I need evidence a court will admit. What he did, when, who helped, who paid, and where the people he moved ended up. Records. Money. Communications. Physical evidence. Witnesses. The more of it that holds up on its own, the better.”

“Would the survivors’ word be enough?”

“It can matter a great deal. But I won’t ask thirty frightened people to carry a case on their backs if there’s another way to build it.”

She shut her eyes. That was what she’d wanted to hear.

“Does Jun Hyuk have records?” she said.

The line went quiet. “What kind?”

“Exercise books. He’s kept them since 2015.”

A long breath came down the phone. “Don’t touch them,” said Song. “If they’re what I think they might be, their condition matters. Don’t take pages out, don’t write on them, don’t put them in order, don’t ask him to tidy anything. And don’t promise me they’re evidence before I’ve seen them.”

“I won’t.”

“And Mrs. Lee. Don’t let him go after Gu on his own.”

“I won’t.”

“Make sure you mean that.”

“I do,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She knew where they were. A locked cabinet in his study, old mismatched books with soft corners and dates on the covers in his hand, some swollen from water, a few mended with tape. She’d watched him write in them on the nights he came home from the river road, and after calls with Song, and after a name or a place had turned up. She’d never asked him to explain a page. They were part of the life he’d had before her, a record of the things he couldn’t put down.

She stood in front of the cabinet a long time. Then she opened it.

The first book was dated 2015. The writing was smaller then, tighter, pushed hard into the paper. Dates. Vehicle descriptions. Places. Names. A list of men seen near a crossing. A short entry about rain. She stopped there, and thought of a dying judge in a chair telling Jun Hyuk about the papers in the car window.
