It wasn’t a confession, and it wasn’t proof of everything, but it was a record made at the time, of what he’d seen and what he’d been told and what he’d started to suspect. She turned on. A boat under another name. A warehouse. A payment. A man who’d changed who he was. Notes in the margins added months later, when something new came in.

Not one answer. Nine years of connections, and some of them might lead to Gu Shanlin.

She put the book back exactly where it had been, and went to find him.

He was in the pantry with one hand flat against the steel door. She waited until he turned. “Can we talk? Not here.”

At the dining table she told him. He listened to all of it with his face giving nothing away, and at the end he said, “Did you tell him about the books?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because they’re evidence.”

“They’re my notes.”

“They’re a record of what happened.”

“They’re not evidence until somebody establishes what they are.”

“That’s what Song said.”

He looked away. She reached across the table, and he looked at her hand for a while before he took it.

“I know you kept them because you couldn’t let the names disappear,” she said. “But you don’t have to carry them on your own.”

“Did he tell you to ask me?”

“No.”

“Then why are you doing this?”

“Because I don’t want the last thing you do for those women to be killing the man who hurt them.” She held on when he tried to draw back. “I don’t want him dead somewhere nobody can prove what he did. I want him alive in a courtroom. I want the people who worked for him named and the money followed and the people he moved found. I want the truth to outlive him.”

He didn’t speak. Then he said, “There are things in those books I shouldn’t have written. Some of it came from people who trusted me.”

“Then we protect them.”

“Some of it came from things I did.” His eyes came up. “Not all of it’s clean, Evangeline.”

She knew. There were men in those years who had stopped existing. There were things no court would turn harmless just because the Ferryman was guilty.

“I won’t ask you to pretend you didn’t do them,” she said. “And I won’t ask anybody else to pretend either. But I won’t let you decide that because you’ve done terrible things, you aren’t allowed to do a good one now. Let the books prove what they can. Let the law do what it can. And let what you did be judged by itself.”

He shut his eyes. When he opened them he said, “All right. I’ll ring him.”

“You don’t have to do it alone.”

“Neither do you,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night he brought the rifle out again, and she was already at the table when he came in. He didn’t ask why. He didn’t tell her to go to bed. After a while she moved her chair round to his side and sat with her arms on the table, watching his hands: the small scar by his thumb, the one along the base of his first finger. She knew the stories behind some of them. She’d kissed every one he’d let her.

“You’re looking at me.”

“Because you’re here.” She waited until his hands were still. “Can I ask you something? Do you want to kill him?”

His hands stopped altogether.

“Yes,” he said at last. “I want to find him. I want to know where he’s been and how many people he’s moved since the last time I saw his name. I want to know who helped him and who took the money. And I want to look at him and know he can’t do it again.” He didn’t look away from her. “And yes. I want to kill him. I don’t know how to stop wanting it.”

“Thank you for telling me.” She put her palm over the back of his hand, with the rifle between them on the cloth. “Then don’t pretend you don’t. But wanting something doesn’t mean you have to do it.” She turned his hand over, rough against hers. “You’re allowed to want justice. You’re allowed to be angry, and to hate him. But you’re not only allowed to be the man who hurts people who deserve it. You’re allowed to be the man who brings them home. The man who gives Song the books. The man who makes sure thirty people get off that boat alive.” His hand moved once under hers, and she held it. “Let me show you you’re allowed forgiveness.”

“From whom?”

“From yourself, eventually.”

“I don’t know if I can.”

“Then don’t decide tonight.” She kissed his forehead. “Just let me sit here.”

Some time later he lifted his hand from the table. He turned the rifle away from them, and stopped. He put it back behind the steel door and locked it, and came and stood behind her chair with his hands on her shoulders, and she leaned back against him.

“I don’t want you to be afraid of me.”

“I’m not.”

“You should be.”

“No. I’m afraid of what this will do to you. I’m afraid you’ll go somewhere I can’t follow, and decide the only way to finish it is to be the man you were before.” She reached up and found his cheek. “I’m not afraid of you.”

He bent and kissed her, and she turned in the chair and put her arms round his waist, and he held her there a long time.

At four minutes past midnight he went into the study and opened the cabinet. He took out the first book, and the second, and put them on the desk. He didn’t sort them. He didn’t take a page out. He looked at the dates on the covers. She came to the door.

“Are those for Song?”

“If he wants them.”

“He does.”

He touched the cover of the oldest one. “I wrote the names down because I was afraid I’d forget one.”

“You didn’t.”

“I thought if I kept them, I’d find him.”

“Perhaps now they can help other people find their way home.”

He looked at her, and something in his face gave a little. He shut the cabinet and took her hand, and they went up together.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning the planner sent the confirmation. 21 December. No. 9 Fig Tree Lane. Garden ceremony. She read it twice and took the phone to him at the kitchen table.

“Confirmed.”

“Good.”

“You don’t look excited.”

He reached for her and she came and stood between his knees, and he put his hands on her hips. “I’m trying to think about more than one thing.”

“I know.” She held his face. “Do you remember the night we were married? You said you couldn’t promise where you’d be. Only that you’d tell me when you could, and come back when you could. You came back. Then come back again. Not as a promise nothing bad will happen. Just come back to me when you’ve got a choice.”

“I will.”

He turned the phone face down on the table. Then, for the first time since Nam had rung, he reached for her without looking towards the pantry, and she climbed into his lap, and he kissed her under the little chilli calendar, slow, his hands spread on her back, and she held his face as if she had all the time in the world.

“Three weeks,” she said against his mouth. “Don’t be late.”

“I won’t.”

Behind the pantry the steel room was locked. In the study nine years of exercise books waited for Song. Somewhere on the river a man was getting a boat ready for thirty people. And for one quiet Sunday morning the rifle stayed where it was.

chapters.title: She Asks Him Not to Go
chapters.desc: She has asked him questions, and asked him to teach her, and asked him to come home. She has never once asked him to stay. Tonight she runs down the lane barefoot.
chapters.epigraph: “Then let me be the first.”
chapters.content:
At dawn on Friday the sixth of December, Jun Hyuk told her he was going to kill Gu Shanlin.

He said it standing in the kitchen with the first grey light coming across the counter and the kettle beginning to boil behind him, and there was no anger in his voice at all. That was what frightened her. He’d showered. His hair was still damp and he was in a clean dark shirt with the sleeves turned back, his phone beside his keys, as if he were going to work. The exercise books were out of the cabinet. There were ten of them, tied in a canvas bag by the study door.

“When?” she said.

“Tonight I go down to the river. Tomorrow night the boat comes in.”

“And you’ll be at the jetty.”

“Above it. Song’s people are on the road and on the far bank.”

“You’re going to bring the thirty out.”

“Yes.”

“And Gu?”

He looked at her. “I’m going to kill him.”

The kettle clicked off. Neither of them moved.

She’d known. Perhaps not the words, but she’d known since Nam’s call, from watching him carry the rifle out of the steel room every night and sit with it under the chilli calendar, a little further away each time.

He came round the counter to her. “This is the last one,” he said, almost gently. “The last target. I won’t keep doing this.”

She wanted to ask how he could know that. She wanted to ask whether a man who’d carried a list of names for nine years could put it down after one more night. Instead she turned her face into his hand.

“Come and eat something.”

“Evangeline—”

“Please.”

“All right,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The salted lemons were on the top shelf of the pantry, in the jar they’d packed in July of the year before last in the room over the Golden Nightingale: five lemons off Mama’s tree, cut and salted and pressed down, and left to wait. She’d opened it in the autumn and rationed it ever since. She brought it to the table. There was one left.

“Then keep it,” he said.

“I want to share it.”

She took it out and cut it. The rind had gone soft and dark with salt and time. She put half on his plate with his rice and egg, and he looked at it.

“With breakfast?”

“Yes.”

He tasted it, and his face changed a little.

“Good?”

“Very.”

She thought of her father on the four stone steps with the cedar chest in his arms. Of the notebook inside it, the lists of things to plant and when, the pencil lemon tree. Mama had never met this man. She’d never know who’d sat across a table from her daughter eating the last of her lemons.

“Baba says she put them in everything,” she said. “He says she was terrible at measuring.”

“That sounds familiar.”

“Are you saying I’m terrible at measuring?”

“I’m saying I’ve eaten some very salty things.”

She laughed. He reached across and wiped a grain of salt from the corner of her mouth with his thumb and kissed her and she kept hold of his hand when he drew back, their fingers knotted on the cloth over the plates. Then his phone went. He looked at it, and the softness left his face.

“I have to take this.”

He kissed her forehead and went out. She looked at his empty plate. The last of Mama’s lemons was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

After lunch she went to the glasshouse. The garden was cold but the glass had kept a little of the thin December sun. The basil needed cutting back. The rosemary leaned over the edge of its pot. She sat down on the wooden bench and did nothing at all.

Then she began to shake.

It started in her hands, a small tremor that made her fingers feel as if they belonged to someone else. She pressed them together and it went into her wrists, and then her shoulders, and she wrapped her arms round herself. She’d been frightened before. In the box. In the hospital. In the flat when men broke the locks. On the floor of Nam’s with blood running down his face into the broth. But she’d never known in advance. This time she knew exactly where he was going and what he meant to do there. She knew he’d be ready. She knew that ready had never once meant he came home whole.

She thought of the chairs that would stand under the fig tree, and the winter greenery, and the cedar chest open in the cold. She’d chosen the longest night because she liked the idea of beginning on the night the dark went furthest and then started to give way. She hadn’t imagined the man she was marrying again might leave before it came.

A sound came out of her. She put her hand over her mouth. There was nobody to hear it, which made it worse.

She stayed until it passed. Then she washed her face at the little sink and went back into the house.

At four she took the viola out. Mrs. Yoon had set her an exercise, a few bars that had to be held steady instead of hurried. The first note came out thin. She stopped, moved her hand, tried again, and it wavered and broke. From the kitchen came his voice on the phone, too low for words. She tried again, and this time the note held, and she played the next one, and the next. It wasn’t beautiful. But it was music, and she kept on until her left hand ached.

He was in the doorway when she put it away.

“You played.”

“Not very well.”

“Did you enjoy it?”

She thought about it. “Yes.”

“Then it was good.” He came in and looked at the music on the stand.

“Will you listen tomorrow?” she said. “When you’re back.”

He paused. “Of course.”

His phone rang again.

✦ ✦ ✦

By evening the house was too quiet. He checked what he’d take and packed it, and made calls, and listened, and answered in short sentences. She moved through the rooms as if there were ordinary things to do: a towel folded, a cup put away, the flowers on the hall table straightened, the kitchen window checked. She was trying not to look at the clock.

At eight he came into the bedroom in dark plain clothes with his watch on.

“Have you eaten?”

She shook her head.

“Evangeline.”

“I’m not hungry.”

He touched her cheek. “Come downstairs.”

He made her a small bowl of soup and put it in front of her, and she ate because he was watching, and he ate because she was. Afterwards he washed and she dried, shoulder to shoulder at the sink, and the ordinariness of it nearly undid her. When he turned round she was still holding the towel. He took it out of her hands.

“Come here.”

She stepped into his arms and let herself rest there. Then she heard him say, “I should go,” and her fingers tightened in his shirt. Not enough to stop him. Just enough that he’d notice.

“Evangeline?”

“All right,” she said, and let go, and turned away to hang up the towel.

✦ ✦ ✦

Around half past ten he took the truck keys off the hook. Jun Hyuk checked the front door and the garden gate, and went out, and came back in once more and found her at the foot of the stairs.

“Keep your phone with you. If Song rings, answer. If you need anything, ring Elowen or Raiden. Don’t go anywhere on your own.”

“I won’t.”

He took her hand and kissed the knuckles. “I’ll ring you when I can.”

He let go. He opened the front door and the cold came into the hall, and she stood just inside the threshold while he went down the steps. He turned once at the bottom, and gave her a small nod, and crossed the garden. He opened the truck door and stopped beside it and looked back at the house for one second. Then he got in, and the door shut, and the engine started, and only when the lights began to move did she.

“Don’t go.”

It came out before she’d decided to say it. The truck was already at the end of the lane. She ran down the steps barefoot.

“Jun Hyuk!”

The brake lights came on. The door opened and he was out of the cab and coming back up the lane fast. “What’s happened? Are you hurt?”

She shook her head. She was standing on the frozen stones with her arms round herself and she couldn’t find a single word.

He put his hands on her face. “Evangeline.”

“Don’t go,” she said, and her eyes filled.

He went still.

She’d asked him questions. She’d asked him to teach her things. She’d asked him to come to the flower market, and to the house, and to let her look after him, and to come home. She had never once asked him to stay for her sake. Not like this, not when it was something he believed he had to do.

“Please don’t go.”

The engine ran on behind them in the dark, the driver’s door hanging open.

“Talk to me,” said Jun Hyuk.

“I don’t know how.”

“Take your time.”

Then the tears came and wouldn’t stop. “I know there are thirty people. I know you have to stop the boat and get them out, and I know he’s done terrible things and you’ve spent nine years trying to find him.” She caught his wrists. “But I don’t want you to go there to kill him. I don’t want you to die on that jetty. I don’t want you to leave me with another promise that you might come back. I don’t want to wake up tomorrow and find out the last thing I said to you was about soup.” She put her forehead against his chest. “I don’t want to be brave tonight. I don’t want to be the woman who understands why you have to go. I don’t want to understand it. I want you to stay.” Her voice went. “Just for me.”

He shut his eyes. She had his shirt in both fists.

He didn’t say anything. Then he said, “I know.”

“No, you don’t.”

“You’re right.” His arms tightened. “I didn’t know you were carrying this much.”

She laughed once, a broken sound. “I’ve been carrying it all day.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because you had so much to do.”

“Evangeline.” He made her look at him. “You’re not another thing I have to finish before I leave. You’re the person I’m leaving.”

She saw it land on him as he said it. Then he pulled her into his arms again, and lifted her off the cold stones, and carried her back up to the house.

✦ ✦ ✦

The truck sat at the end of the lane with its lights on.

She didn’t sit down. She went to the study door and came back with the canvas bag and put it on the dining table in front of him.

“Song will be at the jetty tomorrow night. I rang him again this afternoon. He’ll take them from you there and sign for them properly. All ten. As they are. Nothing taken out, nothing changed.”

He looked at the bag, and at her. “You’ve thought about this.”

“I have.”

“You didn’t tell me.”

“I was afraid you’d think I was trying to stop you going.”

“Are you?”

“Yes,” she said. “But not at the cost of thirty people.”

“I can’t leave them on that boat. If we wait, he’ll change the route.”

“I know. So go for the thirty.” She took his hand. “Don’t go for Gu. Let Song have the books. Let the people who’ve spent years building this finish it. You don’t have to be the last punishment.”

“I don’t know how to leave him alive.”

“Then let somebody else decide what happens to him.” Her voice dropped. “I’m asking you to bring thirty people home. I’m asking you to come home too.”

He looked down at their hands, and he seemed much younger. Not the man who walked into containers. Just someone who’d been taught early that the only safe way to keep a thing was to make sure nobody could take it, and was now being asked to put down something he’d held for nine years.

He stood and drew her up into his arms. “I don’t know what happens tonight,” he said into her hair. “I can’t promise you nothing will happen. I can’t promise I’ll be home at a certain time. But I can promise I’ll ring.”

“When?”

“As soon as I can do it safely. Not when everything’s finished. As soon as I can.” He drew back to look at her. “I’ll give Song the books. I’ll go to the jetty for the thirty.”

“And Gu?”

His mouth tightened. “If I get the chance to bring him in alive, I’ll take it. I’ll try.”

Not the promise she wanted, but one he was making honestly. She took his face in both hands and kissed him, and it wasn’t gentle: her tears still wet on his cheeks, his arms round her as if he meant to remember the exact shape of her. He tasted of salt, of her crying, and of the lemon from that morning still on his tongue. He kissed her until her hands stopped shaking.

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked her to the front door, and this time she held his hand all the way. Under the porch light he stopped.

“You’ve never asked me for anything like that before,” he said. “Why tonight?”

She thought about it. “Because I finally understood I was allowed to. I’ve spent so long being grateful you came back. I thought asking you to stay would be unfair. But I’m your wife, and I want things too. I want breakfast with you. I want to hear you complain about the garden. I want you to sit through my terrible viola, and help me choose the flowers.” She smiled through it. “I want you to come home and tell me what you ate. I want all of it.”

His eyes were wet. She’d never seen him quite like this, not in the shower with the coat on, not at the postbox with the card in his hand. He looked almost frightened by how simple it was.

He put his forehead to hers. “Nobody ever asked me to stay. Not like that.”

“Then let me be the first.”

He kissed her under the porch light, long and salt-wet, and when he let her go he held her face in his palms. “I’ll ring.”

“I’ll answer.”

He went down the steps. This time she didn’t call him back. At the truck he turned once and she lifted her hand, and he lifted his, and the door shut, and she stood under the porch light until the red tail lamps had gone round the bend.

✦ ✦ ✦

After midnight she went up to bed and lay on his side under the heron silk, and couldn’t stay there. She went to the music room and opened the case. Seo Hwa’s viola lay in its lining. The first note shook. She tried again and it held, and she played Mrs. Yoon’s little exercise through, one bar and then another, imperfect, filling the room.

Her phone lay dark on the desk beside the music. She looked at the open doorway.

Asking someone to stay didn’t always mean they could. Sometimes it meant asking them to remember that they were wanted somewhere. On a road going down to the river, he was carrying that with him. He’d spent nine years looking for the last man on his list. Tonight, for the first time, he was going somewhere because thirty people needed him, and because someone was waiting for him to come back.

chapters.title: He Goes Anyway — Then Turns Back
chapters.desc: The bank above the old jetty, eleven at night, a rifle, and a bag of exercise books. At 12:41 he rings his wife.
chapters.epigraph: “I can’t hear anything but you.”
chapters.content:
At 10:53 on Saturday night Jun Hyuk lay in the dead bracken above the old jetty with the rifle beside him and a canvas bag of exercise books by his left foot.

The river was black. On the far bank the lights of the villages shook in the water, and a cold wind came up through the reeds with the smell of wet earth. He’d been there nearly an hour. He hadn’t written in them since Thursday.

The plan was as simple as plans involving the Ferryman ever were. Song’s people were on the road behind the landing. More of them were on the far bank, watching where the boat had come from. When it touched, the thirty would be brought off and taken somewhere warm, the boat would be held, and Gu Shanlin would be arrested if he could be reached. Jun Hyuk’s job was to tell them which man he was.

He hadn’t promised what he’d do once he’d found him.

A single lamp burned on a post by the landing. He looked at his watch. 11:04. He thought of Evangeline. Not on purpose. She was there at the back of his mind, the way the house was there when he was away from it: the kitchen, the chilli calendar, the music room, the heron silk folded at the foot of their bed. Her voice under the porch light. Then let me be the first.

He looked at the river, and waited.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 11:38 Nam was still on his feet. Elara had told him twice to sit down and let somebody else carry the blankets, and he’d said that his back room was his back room. There were thirty clean blankets on the shelves. A big pot of broth on the stove. Rice. Hot water in the kettle and tea in the tin beside it. He’d pushed the tables against the walls to make space, moved the photographs off the damp wall, put clean cloths over the cats’ baskets, and set a plate of biscuits by the door.

“For the children,” he said.

“There may not be any children,” said Elara.

“There might be.” He looked at her as if that settled it.

Evangeline came in just before midnight with Raiden behind her carrying two bags of clean clothes from the house. She was in her thick coat with her hair tied back, and under Nam’s fluorescent tube her face was pale.

“You’re late,” said Nam.

“I’m not.”

“Then I’m early.” He took a bag from Raiden. “Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Soup.”

“Whose?”

“Yours. From the pot you sent home on Wednesday.”

He nodded, satisfied, and looked at her properly. “Has he rung?”

She shook her head. Nam didn’t ask again. He knew Jun Hyuk. He knew her too. He went back to the stove and stirred.

She stood in the back-room doorway and counted the blankets without meaning to. Thirty. Then she took out her phone and looked at it, and put it away.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six minutes past midnight the boat came.

He saw its lights first, low on the water, and then the shape of it, riding deeper than it should, the engine dropping in pitch as it came in towards the landing. He couldn’t see faces from the bank. He could see how close they stood, how little room there was between them, the way some held their arms tight to their bodies against the cold.

It touched the jetty. A man in a grey suit stepped down onto the boards.

Gu Shanlin.

Jun Hyuk knew him from photographs, from other men’s descriptions, from nine years of names in the margins. He’d got older and thinner. He wore a clean grey suit and leather shoes entirely wrong for a river at night, and looked like a man on his way to a business dinner. He stood under the lamp with a small ledger in one hand and began to count.

One. Two. Three.

They came off in a line. Some stumbled. A woman held a small boy by the wrist. An old man had to be lifted down. A girl kept looking back over her shoulder as if she expected someone to come out of the dark behind her. Gu Shanlin counted without touching any of them. He didn’t hurry. He didn’t look afraid.

Nine years. Nine years for him, and nine years for the eleven, who’d been dead all that time while he went on counting.

Just after twelve Jun Hyuk had him in the sights.

The rifle was steady. The distance was clear. Gu stood by the lamp with the ledger, half turned away, talking to another man, and Jun Hyuk could see the line of his jaw and the grey at his temple, and watched him turn back to count again.

His finger lay against the trigger. He didn’t feel angry. That surprised him. No heat, no rush. Only a huge familiar stillness. He’d imagined this a great many times, and always believed he’d feel something when it came. Relief. An ending. Instead he felt the cold on his face and the weight of nine years in his hands.

Gu turned and looked almost straight at the bank. The man who sold women. The man who’d built a route out of locked doors. The man who counted people like parcels.

Jun Hyuk’s finger tightened. He thought of the tower at West Basin. The truck in the rain. Judge Chau’s hands shaking on forty-one pages. Eleven women who never reached the other side. The box.

Then he heard her. Not from the river. From the porch, last night. I want breakfast with you.

His finger stayed where it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 12:41 he took his phone out with his left hand and kept Gu in view while it rang. Once. Twice.

“Jun Hyuk?”

He shut his eyes. “Yes.”

“Are you all right?”

“Above the landing. The boat’s in.”

“Are they there?”

“Thirty.”

He heard her breathe. “Are they safe?”

“Not yet.”

She didn’t ask about Gu. He looked down at them clustered under the lamp. “Not yet,” he said again.

“I’m at Nam’s,” she said. Behind her he could hear a pot being moved, a door, Nam shouting for somebody to bring more cups.

“I know.”

“There’s broth. And thirty blankets.”

His throat closed. “Good.”

She was quiet. Then, very low: “Are you still holding the rifle?”

He looked at his hand. “Yes.”

“Jun Hyuk. Look at me.”

“I can’t.”

“Then listen.” She spoke carefully, as if she were sitting in the bracken beside him. “You’ve done what you promised. You’ve brought the books. You’ve come for the people. You’ve told Song where they’d be.”

“Gu’s there. I can see him. I could end it.”

Her voice shook. “But you don’t have to.”

Gu was talking to the man beside him. The passengers stood pressed together in the light. Jun Hyuk’s finger didn’t move.

“Evangeline.”

“I’m here.”

“I can’t hear anything but you.”

It came out before he could stop it. He’d spent nine years listening for the Ferryman. Tonight there was the river and the engine and the people on the landing, and over all of it, louder than any of it, his wife breathing into the phone.

He lifted his finger off the trigger. He lowered the rifle.

For several seconds he did nothing. Then he said, “I’m coming home.”

Her breath caught. “You’re coming home?”

“I’m choosing to come home.”

He couldn’t tell whether she was crying. “Come home,” she said.

“I will.”

He didn’t leave the thirty. He didn’t leave the river. He left the place he’d been watching Gu Shanlin from. He made the rifle safe and cased it, and stood. “I’m going down,” he said.

“To the boat?”

“To the people. Song’s coming in.”

“Then help them.”

“Keep the broth warm.”

A small wet laugh. “I will.”

He rang off, slung the bag of books over his shoulder, and went down the bank.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first one to see him was the old man, at the end of the jetty, holding a woman’s arm. His coat was far too thin, and when Jun Hyuk came out of the dark he stepped back. Jun Hyuk stopped several paces off with his hands open where they could be seen.

“You’re safe,” he said. The man didn’t understand. He said it again, slower, in the words he had of their language. “Safe. Police are coming. Nobody’s sending you back.”

The girl with the child pressed to her chest stared at him. “Are you taking us somewhere?”

“Somewhere warm.”

“Is he cold?” He nodded at the boy, and she nodded, and he took off his coat and held it out instead of stepping closer. She hesitated, and took it, and wrapped the boy in it. Someone near the boat was talking fast. A woman had started crying. Another asked whether they’d be arrested. “No,” said Jun Hyuk. “You’ll be taken somewhere safe. You can tell the police what happened when you’re ready. One at a time. Slowly.”

He didn’t promise what he couldn’t control. He didn’t ask them to trust him. He stayed.

One of the crew began edging away. A shout went up from the far side of the landing and everyone moved at once. For the first time that night Gu Shanlin looked unsure. He looked at the dark bank, and at the river. He dropped the ledger, and ran.

Jun Hyuk watched him go past the edge of the lamplight. He didn’t follow. He stood by the passengers.

The road lit up. Engines, doors, and over it all Song’s voice: “Keep everyone where they are. Medical first.” Officers went down to the boat. Others went after the men who’d tried to slip off. Gu was gone into the dark before they reached the jetty.

The old thing came back into Jun Hyuk’s body. Move. Follow. Finish it. He’d half turned.

Then the girl touched his sleeve. “Sir? Where are we going?”

He turned back. “Somewhere warm.”

“Will you come too?”

“For a little while.”

Song came across the boards, looked first at the passengers, and then at him. “Where’s Gu?”

“Gone.”

“You saw him?”

“Yes.”

“Clear view?”

Jun Hyuk looked at him. Song looked at his face, and then at the bag on his shoulder.

“The books.”

“Ten. As they were. I haven’t touched a page.”

Song didn’t take it. “Not here. Not in the mud at one in the morning with half his lawyers already awake. I want every page listed and signed for with an officer watching, so no court can ever say they went through anybody’s hands but mine. Tomorrow night. I’ll send you the time.” He was quiet a moment. “Did you have a chance to take him?”

“Yes.”

“And?”

“I didn’t.”

Song’s face didn’t change. “Good,” he said. “Don’t make me say it twice.” And he went to the medics.

By 1:26 the last of the thirty had been brought up off the landing. One woman wouldn’t let go of the man who’d helped her down off the boat. The little boy had fallen asleep in his mother’s arms in Jun Hyuk’s coat.

“Two crew in custody,” said Song. “We’re looking for the rest.” He followed Jun Hyuk’s eyes to the black water. “We’ll find him.”

Jun Hyuk said nothing.

“Those books won’t make you clean, Lee,” said Song. “Evidence isn’t a certificate of anything. It helps us prove what happened.” He paused. “But tonight you brought thirty people off that boat.”

“That’s what I came for.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after two he rang her. She answered before the first ring had finished.

“I’m safe,” he said. “All thirty are off. They’re with the police and the medics.”

“All thirty?”

“Yes.”

She started to cry. He stood by the vehicle looking at the wet road and waited. Then in the background Nam’s voice said, “Ask him if he’s eaten,” and a tired smile came onto Jun Hyuk’s face.

“Nam says—”

“I heard. Have you?”

“No.”

“There’s broth. Are you coming?”

He looked at the river. The place where Gu had stood was empty. For nine years he’d believed that when he got to this night he’d have to finish it himself. He’d been wrong. He hadn’t finished the Ferryman. He hadn’t undone eleven deaths, or made the past go away. But thirty people were alive, and he was still here.

“I’m coming,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 3:17 he came through the back door of Nam’s Noodles. The shop was warm and every light was on and the corridor smelled of broth. Nam stood behind the counter with his arms folded and looked him up and down: face, shoulders, hands.

“You’re late.”

“Sorry.”

“You’re not bleeding.”

“No.”

“Good. Sit down.”

The back room was full. Elara knelt talking to a woman with a little girl beside her. Somebody had found more cups. A man was asleep against the wall. Twelve of the thirty had been brought here to sleep before the morning, because Song had no better room within an hour of the river and Nam had told him so.

Evangeline stood by the kitchen door. When she saw him she stopped. Neither of them moved. Then she came across the room and he opened his arms and she walked straight into them, and he held her hard with his face in her hair.

“I’m home.”

She drew back and looked him over for blood, and he let her. Then she touched his cheek. “You came back.”

“I said I would.”

“You chose.”

“I did.”

She kissed him and it held everything she hadn’t been able to say since Friday morning. He put his forehead to hers. “I heard you. On the bank. I couldn’t hear anything else.”

“Then remember my voice.”

Nam appeared beside them with a bowl. “Romantic later. Broth now.”

She laughed through her tears. He sat at the little table and she sat next to him and he ate slowly with his hands warming round the bowl. After a while Nam said, to nobody in particular, “Thirty.”

“Thirty,” said Jun Hyuk.

Nam looked at the back room. “Good,” he said, and went back to his stove.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four they stood outside under the shop sign while Raiden brought the car round. A thin line of grey had come up over the roofs. She was in his coat now, which a nurse had given back to him, and he had his arm round her.

“Gu got away,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Does that hurt?”

He thought about it. “Yes.”

“Do you wish you’d stayed on the bank?”

“No.” He considered it properly, because she’d want him to. “I wish he hadn’t got away. I wish the eleven had lived. I wish the thirty had never been put on that boat. But I don’t wish I’d pulled the trigger.”

“Then let Song find him. You promised me.”

He breathed out. “I did.”

At home the porch light was still on. She unlocked the door and stood aside for him, and he stopped in the hall. Nam’s menu hung in its frame on the inside of the door, soft at every fold, brown at the edges. His seven rules and her eight, nine crossed through and hers under it. And at the foot of the first list, still there, 7. Don’t come back.

“You never kept that one,” she said.

“No.”

“Good.”

He touched the glass over the seventh line with one finger. Then he turned to her. “Come upstairs.”

“Are you going to sleep?”

He looked at her. “Yes.”

He washed his face and lay down, and she pulled the heron silk over them both, and for a while he lay on his back looking at the ceiling. “I keep thinking about the river,” he said. “I had him. I could have ended it. But I heard you.” He turned his head towards her. “I thought I was going there to finish something. I think I was going because I didn’t know what else to do with nine years.”

She kissed his shoulder. “You don’t have to know tonight.”

He turned into her and held her against his chest with one hand between her shoulder blades. “You asked me to stay,” he said, a while later. “I didn’t know what to do with that.”

“What did you do?”

“I came back.”

“That’s a good start.”

He kissed her slowly, and again, and put his forehead against hers. “I want to be here.”

“Then be here.”

He shut his eyes. And for the first time in nine years, the last name on his list wasn’t the last thing he thought of before he slept.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke at twenty to ten. He was still asleep. Not lying still with half his mind on the stairs. Asleep, his face turned towards her, his mouth a little open, one arm over her waist. She didn’t move. On the bedside table her phone had a message from Song.

All thirty accounted for. Initial medical checks done. The old bridge, 11:45 tonight, with the books. I’ll drive you in. We’ll speak then.

She read it twice and put the phone down. He shifted and his arm tightened round her, and he didn’t wake. For once there was nothing he had to watch, and nothing he had to hold, and nothing he had to finish before morning. Out in the garden the stream ran under the little bridge, and the house at No. 9 Fig Tree Lane was full of pale winter light, and Lee Jun Hyuk slept on.

chapters.title: Staying
chapters.desc: Ten exercise books through a car window at midnight, a rifle handed over a desk, and a lamp on three extension leads at the gate.
chapters.epigraph: “I want to learn how to stay.”
chapters.content:
At eight minutes to midnight on Sunday, Lee Jun Hyuk stood beside his truck at the old bridge with ten exercise books in a canvas bag.

The river was quiet. The boat had been towed downstream and sealed. The thirty had been taken somewhere with beds and doctors and people who’d ask their questions slowly. The men who’d been caught were in cells. Gu Shanlin was still missing.

He’d slept most of the day. When he woke in the afternoon she’d been beside him, reading, with one foot tucked under his calf, and they’d eaten in the kitchen at four with the light already going, and at nine she’d fallen asleep on the sofa mid-sentence, having not slept at all the night before. He hadn’t woken her. He’d put the heron silk over her and written a note and left it on the counter by the kettle. Gone to give Song the books. Back before it’s light. He hadn’t written about the rifle. It was locked in the steel box behind the cab, and the key was on his ring, and he hadn’t decided anything yet.

A pair of headlights came across the bridge. Song’s car stopped beside him and the window came down.

“You’re late.”

“Seven minutes.”

“That’s late.” Song leaned across and unlocked the passenger door. “In there. On the seat. Don’t put them on the floor.”

Jun Hyuk set the bag on the seat. Song switched on the light and looked inside without touching anything. The books were stacked the way they’d come out of the cabinet: covers soft, spines mended, a brown ring on the corner of the first, the seventh with a page folded back at a date. He drew on a pair of gloves and lifted the first one out and opened it.

Dates going back nine years. Names. Places. Vehicles. Payments. Meetings, routes, people who’d turned up in the same places and then stopped turning up anywhere. Some entries were whole pages. Some were three lines, pressed so hard into the paper that the words stood up on the page beneath.

“All ten?”

“All ten.”

“Originals? Nothing taken out?”

“I kept everything.”

Song turned a few pages under the little light. “Some of this will hold up on its own. Some of it’s hearsay. Some of it will put names to people we haven’t found yet.” He looked up. “And some of it will put a name to you.”

“Especially those,” said Jun Hyuk.

Song closed the book and laid it back in the bag. “Why now?”

Jun Hyuk looked at the water moving under the bridge. “Somebody asked me.”

“Who?”

“My wife.”

Song looked at him a long time. Then he let out a short breath through his nose. “Of course she did. She asked you to hand these over?”

“She asked me to stop trying to be the person who decides what happens to Gu.”

“And you agreed because she asked.”

“Because she was right.”

“That’s a new development.” Song rested his wrist on the wheel. “You understand what comes next. I don’t think you do. If these are admitted you’ll be called. Not as the man who pointed Gu out on a jetty. As a witness who answers for nine years. Under your own name. Lee Jun Hyuk, sworn, in a room with a prosecutor and a defence and a judge, and you won’t get to choose the questions. They’ll ask about the men you killed. They’ll ask about the eleven. They’ll ask about the truck you waved on in 2015 and every man whose death you never reported. They’ll ask whether it was justice or revenge, and whether you had any right to decide who lived.”

“I know.”

“They won’t be kind.”

“I don’t expect them to be.”

Song looked almost dissatisfied. “You’re not going to tell me you did what you had to?”

“No.”

“Or that the books make it different?”

Jun Hyuk looked at his hands. “No.”

“Good.” Song took a form from the glove box and a pen, and held them out through the window. “Custody. Every item, every page count. An officer will log them when I’m in, and you’ll get a copy of the list. Nothing comes out of the originals without a judge saying so.”

Jun Hyuk read it through under the courtesy light, and signed. Lee Jun Hyuk. He’d written those letters on a great many forms that were never meant to survive, to get through a door or rent a room under a name that would lead nowhere. Now he wrote them under a statement that could put him in a witness box.

Song took it. “Gu’s still out there. If you see him again, you ring us.”

“Yes.”

“You don’t follow him. You don’t decide the law’s taking too long.”

“I understand.”

Song looked at him a moment longer. “Go home, Lee. Your wife asked you to stay. Don’t make her ask twice.” The window went up, and the car turned on the bridge and went back the way it had come.

✦ ✦ ✦

He opened the box behind the cab and looked at the rifle case.

It had been part of his life so long he couldn’t remember the first night he’d slept with it in reach. There had always been a reason. A room that wasn’t safe. A road that wasn’t clear. A man who might come through a door. A name in an exercise book. He’d once believed that if he kept it close enough nothing could happen to the people he loved. He knew better now. He also knew that knowing better didn’t make his hands forget.

He shut the box, and drove to the station.

At 12:46 Song was still at his desk with the books beside him under an officer’s lamp. He looked up when Jun Hyuk came in carrying the case. “Forgotten something?”

Jun Hyuk put it on the desk. “My rifle. Lock it up.”

Song didn’t touch it. “For how long?”

“Indefinitely.”

“You’re sure?”

“No.” Jun Hyuk looked at the case. “But I don’t want it anywhere I can reach.”

“Because you had him in your sights last night.”

“Yes.”

“And you think if you keep it you’ll go looking for him again.”

He thought about the question. “I think there are parts of me that still know how to do that without asking anyone. I don’t want to find out whether they’d win.”

Song looked at him, then stood and called an officer. The rifle was received, logged, photographed, labelled and carried away. Nobody made him any promises about what would happen to it. Nobody told him that giving it up made him a different man. It didn’t. He signed where they showed him, answered what they asked, and watched the case go through a door at the end of the room.

He didn’t feel lighter. He only felt the absence of something his body had been expecting.

“How does it feel?” said Song.

“Strange.”

“Good strange?”

“I don’t know yet.”

“Then go home and find out.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The drive took two and a half hours. The roads were almost empty. He kept both hands on the wheel and didn’t put the radio on. The river road. The industrial district. The last petrol station before the northern hills, where he stopped and got out to stand in the cold and look at his hands. There was a faint line across his right palm where the handle of the case had pressed. He rubbed it with his thumb, and got back in. He didn’t check the box behind the cab. There was nothing in it.

At 3:58 a.m. Evangeline was standing at the green gate in her coat and nightdress, holding a lamp.

It was the reading lamp from her side of the bed, and it was on the end of three extension leads plugged one into the next, running from the hall socket under the front door and down the path between the rosemary pots. She’d tried the porch light first. It didn’t reach. The bend in the lane meant you couldn’t see the gate from the house. So she’d brought the lamp. Hardly sensible, but it was the only thing she’d been able to think of at four in the morning.

She’d woken at midnight to his note and an empty house. Around half past twelve her phone had said The books are with Song. At 1:20, The rifle’s with him too. She’d read the second one a great many times. She hadn’t asked when he’d be back. She knew how long the road was and that he’d been awake most of two days, and she wanted him to drive carefully. So she’d written, I’ll leave the light on.

I know, he’d written.

The lane was empty. Her bare feet were cold on the stones. Then she heard the engine, and lifted the lamp, and headlights came round the bend through the trees. The truck stopped at the gate, and the lights were full on her, and then the engine died and the door opened.

He looked at her. At the lamp. At the three extension leads snaking off across the garden in the dark. Back at her.

“What are you doing?”

She held it a little higher. “Helping.”

“With what?”

“Finding the gate.”

He looked at the green gate, three feet away and perfectly visible in his headlights. Something moved at the corner of his mouth, tired. “Come here.”

She put the lamp on the wall and ran to him and he met her halfway. She took his face in her hands. “You’re home.”

“I’m home.”

She looked at his eyes and his shoulders and his hands, and he let her. “Are you hurt? Did you eat?”

“At the station. Nothing worth remembering.”

“I’ll make you something.”

“Later.” He touched her cheek. “You’re freezing.”

“I was waiting.” She looked past him at the truck, and then she took both his hands and turned them over, empty, in hers.

“I gave it away,” he said. “I don’t know what I’m supposed to feel.”

“You don’t have to feel anything yet. Just come inside.”

He bent and kissed her in the cold, his hands careful on her face, his thumbs under her cheekbones, the lamp shining beside them on the wall. When they parted she put her forehead to his.

“Welcome home.”

“Thank you,” he said, and shut his eyes.

He didn’t let her walk up the stairs. Halfway along the hall he stooped and lifted her, and she gave a startled laugh.

“I can walk.”

“I know.”

“Then why—”

“Because I want to.”

At the bedroom door he set her down. The room was dark except for the lamp on his side. He looked at the heron silk at the foot of the bed, and then at her, and she saw him gathering words. He’d said it once before, on her birthday at the Glass Pavilion, trying to repeat the line she’d found at sixteen in the back of a grammar, and he’d mangled it so badly she’d laughed until she cried. She’d said it for him properly. He’d kept it all these months, and never found the right moment.

He said it now, slowly, in the old court language. His pronunciation wasn’t perfect, but it was clear. You are my home.

She stopped breathing.

He said it again, without looking away.

She’d taught him those words. But hearing them in his voice, in the language she’d learned alone in a library because nobody had ever told her it was hers, made them something else entirely.

“Say it again.”

He did. Her eyes filled.

“Did I get it right?”

“All of it.”

“I don’t mean the building,” he said, in their own language. “Or the address. I mean you.”

She reached for him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first light came slowly, grey and then pale at the curtains, and they didn’t hurry. So much of their marriage had been lived round danger that they sometimes forgot there could be nothing urgent at all. No door to watch. No road. No call. Nobody waiting for him to leave.

He undressed her slowly, stopping each time she touched his face. She drew his shirt off over his head and put her palms flat on his chest, and found he was shaking.

“Jun Hyuk?”

He bowed his head. Then the first tear fell, and she caught it with her thumb.

“I’m sorry.”

“For what?”

He didn’t answer. She drew him down onto the bed and into her arms, and he folded against her with his forehead on her shoulder and cried at first and then not quietly. It wasn’t the breaking she’d seen in the shower after Kiln Street. There was nothing to survive this time. No wound, no one coming. Only a man who’d spent years teaching himself to need nothing, finding out he was allowed to want an ordinary morning.

When he lifted his head his eyes were red. “I thought I’d feel relieved.”

“Maybe you will.”

“I wanted to come home.”

“You’re here.”

He kissed her, slowly, and she kissed him back and pulled him over her. He kept touching her: her face, her hair, her shoulders, the hollow of her throat, as if he were learning that the person he loved could stay under his hands without being in any danger. She guided him into her and he went still there, holding himself on his forearms, looking at her, and she watched his eyes fill again. She wound her legs round him and he began to move, so slowly, long and deep and unhurried, his breath unsteady against her cheek. When she kissed his eyelids he let out a breath that trembled all the way through him. When she said his name he cried again, and she didn’t ask him to stop. She held him with her heels at the backs of his thighs and her hands spread on his back and met every stroke, and the light came across the bed, and the pleasure built in her slow as the morning, until she came under him with her mouth against his shoulder and his name broken in it. He followed her with his face in her neck and a sound that was half a sob, and stayed there, his whole weight on her because she pulled him down when he tried to lift it.

She kissed the wet off his cheek. “I’m here.”

“I know.”

“You’re safe.”

He shut his eyes. And for once he didn’t answer I know. He just let her hold him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later she lay with her cheek on his chest under the silk, tracing his collarbone. His breathing had slowed at last.

“Are you all right?”

“I think so.” He was quiet. Then: “I want you to stay.” He looked almost embarrassed. “I know you live here. I know we’re married. I know—”

She put her mouth to his chest to stop him. “I want you to stay.”

“I’m staying.”

“Not just today.”

“Not just today.”

“Not only when you’re sure the house is safe. Not only when there’s something useful for you to do.”

His mouth moved. “That’s going to be difficult.”

“I know.”

“But I’ll try.” He looked at her. “I want to learn how to stay.”

“Then we’ll learn.”

At seven he left a message at the yard office for Mrs. Koo that he’d be in on Tuesday, and put the phone face down on the table. He was asleep a few minutes later.

She lay beside him and didn’t feel tired enough to close her eyes. His face was turned to her, one hand under her head and the other across her waist. The house was quiet. No engine. No footsteps. No phone. The light moved slowly over the wall.

At some point he shifted in his sleep and turned towards the door, the old habit finding its way through without waking him. She watched it happen. Then she slid out from under his arm, climbed across him, and lay down on the side of the bed nearest the hall, between him and the door. His hand searched the empty sheet. She reached back and caught it, and his fingers closed round hers, and he didn’t wake.

She brought his hand to her chest and turned her face to the door. It was shut. The house was safe. The rifle was somewhere he couldn’t reach, and the books were with Song, and the steel room behind the pantry had a new code that afternoon, one he’d asked her to choose and not tell him. The man he’d wanted to kill was still out there. None of it was finished.

But Jun Hyuk was asleep, and she was watching. Not because she had to. Because she wanted to. And for the first time since she’d known him, Lee Jun Hyuk slept without reaching for anything but her.

chapters.title: Someone Else Finishes It
chapters.desc: Friday the thirteenth of December, before dawn, a farmhouse on the far side of the river. He hears about it on the inspection-shed television.
chapters.epigraph: “Tell the truth when they ask you. And remember them.”
chapters.content:
On Tuesday morning Lee Jun Hyuk went back to work.

He was at the Iron Docks gate at a quarter past seven in his dark work jacket with the thermos she’d filled, and his first box of the day was off the southern route. Household appliances, said the manifest. The seal was intact and the number matched. He cut it and opened the doors. Washing machines. Fridges. Six cartons of kitchenware where the paperwork said eight. He counted, wrote up the difference in the report, and signed it. Lee Jun Hyuk. His own name, on a page that would sit in a file in an office with a kettle in it.

He’d been doing it four months: opening containers, checking seals and papers, teaching other people to notice what wasn’t there as carefully as what was. It was ordinary work. He was beginning to understand why he liked it.

At eight Mrs. Koo put a cup of coffee by his elbow.

“You’re early.”

“I’m on time.”

“You’re always early.”

“Then why are you surprised?”

She gave him a look and went away. He nearly smiled. His phone buzzed.

Evangeline: Did you eat breakfast?

He sent her a photograph of the empty thermos.

Evangeline: That’s not proof.

Jun Hyuk: There was an egg.

Evangeline: One egg is not breakfast.

Jun Hyuk: And rice.

Evangeline: Better.

He looked at the screen a moment longer than he needed to, and put it away. The next box was waiting.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Wednesday the ten exercise books had become a thing he deliberately didn’t follow. Song had rung once to say the list of contents was done and the books were with the investigating team. There were questions. There’d be more. He answered whatever he was asked, but he didn’t ring to find out what they’d found, or whose names had come up, or how many officials were sitting in rooms that week being asked about payments. He went to work. He opened containers. He corrected a junior inspector who’d noted a discrepancy without the original manifest number. He ate the lunch she packed. He came home.

Sometimes he slept. Sometimes he woke in the middle of the night and reached across to make sure she was there, and she was, on his side, between him and the door. She never made him explain.

On Thursday evening she found him in the glasshouse, looking at the rosemary.

“You’re thinking,” she said.

“Am I?”

“Your face is doing the thing where somebody’s given you a hard problem and you mean to solve it by staring at a wall.”

“I’m not looking at a wall.”

“You’re looking at the rosemary.”

“That’s different.”

She stood beside him and he took her hand. “Song hasn’t rung,” he said. “I don’t want to know until there’s something definite.”

She leaned her head against his arm. “Then don’t ask.”

He kissed her hair. For once, he didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

Friday the thirteenth of December began with rain.

At seven the Iron Docks were nearly empty. The first shift was in but the yard was still waking, and water ran across the concrete in thin bright streams and pooled under the loading platforms. He was on the bench in the inspection shed under the television with a manifest on his knee and his lunch tin beside him, still shut. She’d packed rice and greens and a little chicken, and put a folded note under the lid.

She was sitting beside him. She had a meeting in the city at ten with the foundation’s lawyer, and she’d brought his lunch herself on the way because she wanted to see the docks in the morning. She was in the pale blue coat with her hair tucked behind her ears and a paper bag between her feet with two cups of tea in it.

The television was always on for the morning news. Neither of them was watching it. A presenter was talking over pictures of a river crossing. He went on reading.

Then the name came.

“...Gu Shanlin, known as the Ferryman, was arrested before dawn this morning at a farmhouse on the northern bank of the river.”

His hand stopped on the page.

On the screen a low farmhouse with a tiled roof, a yard of mud, police cars along a narrow road. Then a man brought out through a gate with his hands cuffed behind him, grey-haired, in a dark coat over a pale shirt. Gu Shanlin, without the grey suit, looking like what he was.

“The arrest follows a long investigation into a trafficking network operating across the eastern river routes. Police have confirmed that fourteen further suspects have been detained since dawn, among them people believed to have arranged the movement of victims, falsified shipping records, and provided the network with protection.”

Fourteen. The names began to come up on the screen.

He knew the first. Then the second. Then the third. A man who’d signed false shipping declarations in 2017. A man he’d watched in a warehouse doorway in the winter of 2019. A name in the margin of the fifth book, next to a payment nobody had ever explained. Fourteen people who’d existed for years in small black handwriting in a locked cabinet, being read aloud on the morning news.

The arrests, said the presenter, had followed the examination of documents, financial records, communications, and information from witnesses.

He looked down at his hands. She moved closer.

The picture changed. An old photograph, grainy, from a roadside camera. A white truck going through a checkpoint in heavy rain. A date under it.

17 NOVEMBER 2015.

He stopped breathing.

The road was wet. The plate was readable. He knew the truck. He knew the barrier. He knew the rain.

“Investigators have also confirmed that newly obtained records refer to a consignment that passed through an eastern checkpoint in November 2015. Authorities are reviewing the circumstances of that crossing, which is believed to have involved eleven women who later died in transit.”

The photograph stayed on the screen, and he could see all of it again. The papers through the window. The stamp. His own hand coming up to wave the truck on. The driver looking at him. The rain running down the windscreen. Thinking that he’d finish his shift and go home.

The manifest slid off his knee onto the floor. She took his hand. He didn’t look at her. He was looking at the white truck.

“I remember the rain,” he said, so quietly she could hardly hear. “The driver had his window down. He asked me if the road ahead was clear.” His jaw moved. “I told him it was.”

The picture went away. He didn’t see what replaced it.

“I told him it was clear.”

She moved until her shoulder was against his. She didn’t tell him it wasn’t his fault. She didn’t tell him he’d been young, or following orders, or that the arrests made it right. She held his hand, and when his fingers began to shake he turned his palm up and she laid hers flat against it, and neither of them said anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

Around half past seven Mrs. Koo came in with the morning’s sheets, looked at the screen and then at his face, and switched the television off at the wall. She put the sheets down on the far end of the bench and went out again without a word. The quiet seemed bigger than the shed. Out in the yard a reach stacker went past with a box in its arms, and a man shouted something about a seal number, and the ordinary morning went on without them.

She opened his lunch tin. The rice was still warm. She put the chicken beside him and a spoon into his hand. “Eat something.”

“I’m not hungry.”

“I know.”

He looked at the spoon, and then took a mouthful. She sat with him while he ate. After a few minutes she unfolded the note from under the lid and put it on his knee. Don’t forget to eat. I love you.

His face changed. Not much. Just enough for her to see what it was costing him to keep it still.

She put her hand on his cheek and he turned into her palm.

“Eleven,” he said.

“Eleven.”

“I remember every part of that day. I remember the stamp. I remember thinking I could go home.” His voice broke. “I went home. They didn’t.”

She put her forehead against his. “No.”

He shut his eyes. She kissed him there on the bench under the dead television, not to stop the tears and not to make him forget, but because he was there, and she loved him, and she wanted him to feel that home could hold this too. His hand came up to her face.

“I’m sorry,” he whispered.

“Don’t apologise to me.”

“Then who?”

“Tell the truth when they ask you. And remember them.”

He looked down at their hands. “I will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She rang her lawyer from the car park and moved the meeting. She drove. He sat with one hand on his knee, and the other held hers whenever the road allowed. They stopped at a petrol station and she bought him tea and he drank it. They went up into the northern hills without speaking.

At the gate he didn’t go in. He stood looking down the garden path. The rain had stopped and the sky had cleared, and the stream ran fast and cold under the little wooden bridge.

“Would you like to walk?”

He nodded. They went down the stone path to the water and he crouched on the bank, and she sat beside him. For a while they listened to the stream.

Then he took out of his coat a clean notebook he’d bought weeks ago and never used, and from inside it a folded sheet of paper. Song had sent it that morning before six. Not a statement, not an account of anything. A list of the eleven women whose deaths had now been documented in connection with the crossing in November 2015. Their names.

He unfolded it. He didn’t ask her to read it. He began with the first name, slowly. Then the second. The third. He stopped before the fourth and swallowed and went on. Some of them were hard to say, and he tried each one with care. By the last his voice was rough.

Then he read them again. Not as entries, not as a number, not as a consignment in a report. As women.

When he’d finished he closed the notebook.

“They had names,” he said. “I knew that. But I never said them.”

She rested her head on his shoulder. “Now you have.”

“I don’t know if that’s enough.”

“It isn’t.” She held his eyes when he turned. “But it matters.”

He put the list inside the notebook, and didn’t write anything else in it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday morning she went to the nursery in the village and came back with a tray of rosemary cuttings. He was in the glasshouse with a screwdriver, fighting a loose shelf bracket.

“What are those?”

“Rosemary.”

“I can see that.”

“Eleven,” she said.

He put the screwdriver down.

“I thought we could plant them along the stream. For remembrance.” She didn’t say they’d make anything right. She didn’t say growing something could balance anything. She stood beside him and waited.

He picked up the tray. “Where do you want them?”

“Along the water. Where they’ll get the morning.”

They planted them that afternoon in the soft ground by the stream. She knelt with the trowel and made the holes. He loosened each root ball and set the cutting in and firmed it down. The first went by the stone at the foot of the bridge. The second by the flat rock. The third where the sun reached the bank first in the morning. They spaced them with care. Eleven small plants. Eleven places. When the last was in she pressed the soil round it with her fingers, and he poured water from the jug, and they sat back on their heels.

“Do you think they’ll grow?”

“Yes.”

“All eleven?”

“We’ll look after them.”

He took her hand. “I don’t know what the trial will be like. They’ll ask me about the truck. They’ll ask what I saw. They’ll ask why I let it through.”

“Then tell them.”

“I don’t know what they’ll think of me.”

“You don’t get to choose what they think,” she said. “You only get to tell them the truth.”

He leaned over and kissed her, small and quiet, and put his forehead against hers. “Thank you. For sitting beside me.”

She brushed soil off his sleeve. “Where else would I be?”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening he took the clean notebook with the list inside it upstairs and stood it on the shelf beside the photograph of Old Ko and the boy, and Raiden’s drawing of a house with windows that opened.

She came up behind him and put her arms round his waist. “Is that where you want it?”

“Yes.” He covered her hands with his. “I think he’d have liked you.”

“Old Ko?”

“He liked people who asked too many questions.”

She laughed against his back. “Then he’d have liked me.”

“He would.”

He turned round in her arms. The news hadn’t undone him. It hadn’t made anything smaller. He still remembered the rain and the stamp and the truck and eleven names, and he’d have to say all of it again in a room with bright lights, to people who wouldn’t know what it cost him, without asking any of them to forgive him. But Gu Shanlin was in a cell. Fourteen others were with him. The books weren’t hidden in a cabinet any more. And down by the water, eleven small plants were waiting for spring.

“I’m here,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I’m here.”

She drew him closer. “Then stay.”

chapters.title: A Wedding With Six Guests
chapters.desc: The longest night of the year, a garden in December, herbs from the glasshouse, and a groom who can only say one word.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll keep choosing her.”
chapters.content:
The longest night of the year came in, without snow. Winter here was damp, not white. The air smelled of wet earth and woodsmoke, and on the morning of Saturday the twenty-first of December a thin mist lay over the garden at No. 9 Fig Tree Lane.

She woke before it was light. He was still asleep, one arm under her pillow, his other hand loose at her waist. He’d slept the whole night. She’d learned not to take that for granted. She kissed his shoulder and slid out.

“Where are you going?”

“Downstairs. The wedding’s today.”

His eyes opened and went to the clock. “You were up at five.”

“I was excited.”

“You were straightening the herb labels in the glasshouse.”

“They were crooked.”

He drew her hand to his mouth and kissed the knuckles one by one before he let go. “Don’t carry anything heavy. Don’t climb anything. And—”

“Jun Hyuk.” She bent and kissed his forehead. “Today you’re allowed to worry about getting married.”

A faint helplessness came into the corners of his mouth. “That’s what I’m doing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By nine the garden looked like somewhere a wedding might happen. Not a large one. Wooden chairs under the bare fig tree, facing the stone path from the house. A long table by the stream in white linen, and candles in glass holders, though the afternoon wouldn’t need much help getting dark. The eleven rosemary cuttings had taken in the bank, and she’d tied a narrow ribbon round each little stake. She hadn’t wanted flowers cut somewhere else. She wanted the garden to be part of it.

He’d wound warm lights through the fig tree and tested every bulb three times.

In the glasshouse she chose what she’d carry: rosemary, mint, lemon balm, a little thyme, tied with a length of pale ribbon. When she turned round he was in the doorway in a dark suit, plain and perfectly cut and so unlike anything he usually wore that she forgot what she’d been going to say.

He came and fiddled with the ribbon round the stems, his big fingers careful on the small job. “Too tight?”

“You’re pulling it.”

He loosened it at once, and she laughed, and he brushed a strand of hair behind her ear. “You’re beautiful.”

“You’re handsome too.”

“I know. You keep telling me.”

She was still laughing when he went. He’d been disappearing into the music room all morning, and every time she asked what he was doing he said nothing. He was bad at nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia came first, at half past ten, with a small velvet case, and stood in the hall refusing to take her coat off.

“I’m not one of the six,” she said. “I’m the jeweller. I’m going home to my husband, and you can show me the rings in daylight next week.” She put the case in Jun Hyuk’s hand. “Before you ask, nobody else touched them.”

“I wasn’t going to ask.”

“Your face was.”

He opened it. Two rings on white silk. Evangeline’s was a narrow silver band with one small aquamarine set into it. It wasn’t instead of the first ring. She’d wear the plain one with the river house cut inside it as well, as she had every day since April of last year. This was for the life they’d made after.

His own was plainer and a little heavier, the same silver. He tilted it to the light. Inside, small, were two lines of numbers.

“The gate,” said Aurelia. “No. 9.”

He read them twice. They didn’t lead to a house across a river that he’d made ready in case everything went wrong. They led to a green gate and a fig tree and a kitchen where someone left the light on when he was late.

“Thank you.”

“She said you’d like it,” said Aurelia, and kissed his cheek, and went.

The six came before noon. Nam first, in his best coat, carrying a paper bag that he insisted had nothing important in it and that smelled of new bread. His wrist had mended well enough to carry it. He looked at the chairs, and the fig tree, and Jun Hyuk.

“Well,” he said, and nodded once. “Good.” It was as near as he came to a speech.

Then Elowen and Zhao, Elowen with a small wrapped parcel and Zhao holding her coat; Eliana with her camera and her round glasses; Raiden, and Jinx, who began straightening the place settings at once with the calm of a woman who’d long since accepted that the men in her life couldn’t be trusted with a table.

Mrs. Bae had refused her invitation, explaining that she and Mr. Bae were perfectly happy supervising from their own side of the wall, and had sent over a chestnut sponge instead. Her head appeared above the coping. “Lee Jun Hyuk! Your collar’s crooked.” It wasn’t. “She’s nervous,” said Mr. Bae, beside her. “I’m not nervous,” said Mrs. Bae, and then, the teasing going out of her face: “Enjoy it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty to one he went up to the music room. Mrs. Yoon was by the open window with Seo Hwa’s viola on her knee. The curtains moved in the cold.

“She doesn’t know?” said Mrs. Yoon.

“No.”

“Good.” She put the instrument to her shoulder. “She’s practised for months. I think I owe her this.”

He stood in the door while she tried a phrase, something slow and unhurried that seemed to belong to the winter air, and then he went down into the garden.

✦ ✦ ✦

Evangeline came downstairs at one in an ivory dress with long sleeves and a narrow waist, the skirt soft round her ankles. No veil. Her hair pinned loosely, a few strands left free. The aquamarines caught the light when she turned her head. She held the herbs in both hands.

Her father was waiting at the foot of the stairs. He’d adjusted his cuff so many times that morning that Elowen had finally taken his watch away from him. Now he stood in front of her and neither of them moved.

“Your mother would have liked this dress,” said Lin Jian. He looked at the herbs. “And she’d have asked why you were carrying the garden.”

“I thought they belonged here.”

“Then you’re right.” He offered his arm, and at the door he stopped. “I used to think if I kept you somewhere safe enough, nothing could happen to you. I was wrong about a great many things. I was wrong to make your life small because I was afraid of losing you.” He swallowed. “I know you’ve chosen your life. I only want you to know you never needed my permission to be happy.”

“Baba.”

He smiled, and it shook. “Come on. He’s waiting.”

Jun Hyuk stood under the fig tree. He’d never in his life been so aware of his hands. He clasped them in front of him, let them go, clasped them again.

“You’re fidgeting,” said Raiden.

“Don’t.”

“Your hands are shaking.”

Jinx put an elbow into Raiden’s ribs and he shut his mouth.

Then the music began.

It came from the open window upstairs and drifted down over the garden, and Evangeline knew the instrument before she knew the tune. She looked up at the house, and then at him under the tree, and her eyes filled. He hadn’t told her. Of course he hadn’t. He’d wanted to give her something of her mother’s, in the place that was theirs.

She came down the stone path on her father’s arm with the music following her, and Jun Hyuk forgot his hands, and the people watching, and every word he’d thought he might say. He could only see her.

At the tree Lin Jian stopped and didn’t let go of her straight away. He looked at Jun Hyuk. “Make her happy.”

“I will.”

“Don’t promise what you can’t control.”

Jun Hyuk was quiet a moment. “I’ll keep choosing her.”

It wasn’t the answer Lin Jian had expected. Perhaps that was why he accepted it. He kissed his daughter’s forehead. “My girl.” And he put her hand in Jun Hyuk’s and stepped back.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were no speeches. They’d been married a year and eight months already. This was a promise made in front of the people who’d seen pieces of the road. Nam with both hands folded on his stick. Elowen already crying with Zhao’s arm round her. Eliana with the camera forgotten in her lap. Raiden trying hard to look composed. Jinx. And over the wall, Mrs. Bae leaning so far forward that Mr. Bae had a fist in the back of her cardigan.

The officiant was a quiet friend of her father’s who’d agreed not to make an occasion of it. He said a little about promises, and about the ordinary work of staying, and asked them for their vows.

She’d written hers the night before, and rewritten them that morning, and in the end she’d written what she meant. She held both his hands.

“When I first met you, you told me to stay behind you. I thought you meant be quiet, and small, and let you decide where I could go and what I could face. I didn’t understand you yet. You were trying to get me out of that place alive. I’ll always be grateful.” Her thumb moved over his knuckles. “But I don’t want to spend my life behind you. I want to stand beside you. I want to be the person you come home to, and the one who tells you when you’re being impossible. I want to grow old with you and argue with you about the garden and make you eat when you forget, and keep putting plants in every room until you stop pretending you don’t like them.” Nam laughed, once. “And when the world’s frightening, I want you to remember you don’t have to face it alone. I don’t choose you because you saved me, or because you’re strong, or because you promised to protect me. I choose you because you’re the man I love, and I want the life that comes after today. All of it. Even the hard parts. Especially the ordinary ones.” She lifted their hands and kissed his fingers. “I choose you, Lee Jun Hyuk. Today, and every day after.”

There was silence: six people, a winter garden, and a man who seemed to have lost every word he’d ever learned.

“Mr. Lee?” said the officiant.

He opened his mouth. Nothing came. He swallowed. She didn’t rescue him. She held his hands and let him take as long as he needed. He looked at her face, and the aquamarines, and the herbs from their glasshouse, and past her at the house, the open window, the green gate, the postbox where she’d written their name.

“Evangeline,” he said.

That was all. He said it as if it held every promise he couldn’t make himself say out loud.

“Yes,” she said.

They exchanged rings under the fig tree. She slid the silver band onto his finger and turned his hand to see the numbers inside.

“You had this made?”

“Before we moved in.”

“You kept it a secret for two months?”

“Don’t tell anyone.”

He took her hand, his thumb on the small scar by her knuckle, and slid the aquamarine onto her finger beside the old ring, and then lifted her hand and pressed his mouth to the new band.

“By the promises you have made—” the officiant began.

Jun Hyuk was already looking at her. “May I?”

“Yes.”

He kissed her. Not carefully, not like a man afraid that wanting something too much would make it vanish. He kissed her under the bare tree with the music coming down from the window and the cold on her cheeks, one hand at the back of her neck and his other arm drawing her in until there was no space left, and kissed her again, and then, apparently forgetting there was anyone in the garden at all, rested his forehead on hers with his eyes shut.

Raiden cheered. It was loud enough to launch Pudding, who’d been asleep on a chair under the table, straight up off the cushion and into the rosemary.

Pudding reappeared at the edge of the garden, looked at all of them with deep disapproval, and stalked off home over the wall. Evangeline was laughing. Not politely, not into her hand. Out loud, her head back, eyes squeezed shut. Jun Hyuk stared at her. The sound seemed to reach somewhere in him that had been waiting a long time. He smiled. And when Raiden cheered again, he didn’t tell him to stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate outside under the lights, Nam’s bread beside Mrs. Bae’s sponge. Jun Hyuk barely ate. “You’ve moved the same piece of bread three times,” she said. “Today I’m allowed to be distracted,” he said, and looked at her until her face went warm.

Elara came through the gate at 3:47 in navy scrubs under an open coat, her hospital pass still clipped on. “I know,” she said. “I’m late.” She looked at the chairs and the lights and Evangeline’s dress, and her face crumpled. She’d sat by Jun Hyuk’s bed in June watching Evangeline be afraid. Now she looked from one of them to the other and cried before she’d even sat down. “I was going to come in and be normal.”

“You’ve never been very good at normal,” said Evangeline, and held her.

By dusk the longest night had begun to gather. The lights in the fig tree glowed warmer, and the little lamps along the bank lay on the water, and the rosemary stood in the dark ground with its ribbons. Mrs. Bae came round at last with a blanket. “Good. You look married. Keep her warm,” she told Jun Hyuk, and put it round Evangeline’s shoulders herself.

Then the evening grew small, and one by one they went. Lin Jian went last, and held his daughter at the gate without saying anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

When the gate was shut she went into the house and came back with Old Ko’s tin box.

He knew it at once. Letters. His mother’s photograph. His father’s watch. A folded square of target paper in a clear sleeve, from a range in the hills last spring, that she hadn’t known he’d kept until this week. He’d shown her the box once and not gone through it since.

“I found something in the lining,” she said. “Where the cloth had come away at the bottom.”

She took out a small card, yellow with age, torn at one corner, with a faint blue stamp from an aid station on the river road and a printed heading, and a few lines in a hand she’d matched against the letters in the box. A date. A time. Boy, well. And under it, in darker ink:

Lee Jun Hyuk. 23 November 1990.

He didn’t touch it.

He’d always had the date. Old Ko had known it, and told him, and kept it with an extra egg in the rice and a warning not to get arrogant. But Old Ko was in the ground with his spoon, and every paper Jun Hyuk had ever owned said the eleventh of March, because a clerk had needed a date for a form when he was nine. Some part of him had always wondered whether Old Ko had picked a day.

“Your mother wrote it,” said Evangeline. “On the night you were born.”

He reached out, and stopped with his fingers just above the paper. “She wrote this?”

“It’s her hand. It’s the same as the letters.”

“She knew the date.”

“Of course she did.”

“She wrote my name.” His voice wasn’t steady. “I thought nobody ever wrote it down.”
