She came round the table and stood in front of him and took his face in her hands. “She knew you before anyone did. There was a day. There was a name. There was a mother who wrote it down.” She put her forehead against his. “And now there’s a house where we can keep it.”

He’d been eight when she died at another aid station on the same river road. He’d waited a long time after that for someone to remember. He was thirty-four now, in his own garden, with a ring on his finger, holding proof that someone had once written his name because he’d been born.

He began to cry for the first time that day with his head bowed against her shoulder and the card still held safe in one hand, and she wrapped both arms round him under the wedding lights.

“Happy birthday, my husband,” she whispered. “Late.”

He let out a broken breath that was nearly a laugh. “Can we keep it somewhere I can see it?”

“We’ll find a frame tomorrow. And next year we’ll have the twenty-third properly.”

“Nam should come,” he said. “And the others.” He looked at their hands. “And you.”

“Especially me.”

They stayed out until the candles had burned down. The numbers inside his ring had brought him here. Not to a place where he could hide. To a place where he could be found.

“Are you happy?” she said.

He kissed the ring on her finger. “I have a birthday,” he said. “I have a wife. I have somewhere to come back to.”

“You always did. Even before the house.” She put her hand flat on his chest. “Here.”

He covered it with his own, and kissed her under the bare fig tree, and the longest night settled round them. Inside, the lights stayed on.

chapters.title: Forgiven
chapters.desc: Epilogue. Three years later, the longest night again. Eleven rosemary bushes taller than the wall, and a letter with no name on it.
chapters.epigraph: “You do not owe anybody anything any more.”
chapters.content:
Three years later the rosemary had grown taller than the garden wall.

Eleven bushes stood along the stream at No. 9 Fig Tree Lane, thick and dark and fragrant, silver-green in the low winter light. In summer they grew so wild that Evangeline cut them back twice a month. In winter they turned sturdier and held their shape against the cold. Jun Hyuk still watered them himself. He said the irrigation was perfectly capable of doing it. She said she knew. He watered them anyway.

On the morning of Tuesday the twenty-first of December 2027, the longest night of the year, she found him out there with the can in one hand and the secateurs in the other.

“You’re talking to them again.”

“I’m counting.”

“Eleven?”

He nodded. She came down the stone path in her dressing gown with two cups of tea and the cold making the tip of her nose pink, and he put down the secateurs and took one.

“They’re taller than me now,” she said.

“Not all of them. The one at the end’s shorter.”

“Because you keep trimming it.”

He considered this. “Somebody has to.”

She laughed and leaned into his side, and they stood by the water.

The garden had changed. The fig tree was broader. The little bridge had been mended twice. The glasshouse had far more pots than its shelves could reasonably hold, and in a big glazed planter by the door stood a lemon tree grown from a cutting of Mama’s, which her father had brought up in a bucket the first spring and pretended was nothing. The house had changed too. There were photographs up the stairs now. Elowen and Zhao on the day of the flower shop. Raiden and Jinx laughing at Nam’s birthday table. Evangeline with her mother’s viola, looking frightened of it. And one of Jun Hyuk asleep on the sofa with Sergeant on his chest, which Mrs. Bae had taken through the window and had framed, and which he had never managed to get rid of.

“Are you coming to the music room?” she said.

“Are you playing?”

“I am.”

“Then yes.”

Three years ago her viola had sounded like a question. Now it sounded like music.

✦ ✦ ✦

He no longer went looking for people. He ran inspections. The difference mattered to him.

After the Ferryman’s network came apart, the government had widened the inspection programme to every major port in the country, and Jun Hyuk had been asked to help write it: how suspect cargo was opened and recorded, how a worker could report something without losing his job for it. He’d insisted on outside oversight. He’d insisted on proper training. He’d insisted that no team anywhere be built round one man’s instincts, including his. It had taken months of meetings and arguments and paperwork, and he’d hated nearly all of it, and he’d stayed.

In three years, two hundred and nine people had been found alive in containers, holds and lorries through the work and the systems round it. He kept the number in a small notebook. Not because he thought it balanced anything. Because he refused to let them become a figure he could forget. Every name that could be found was written down, and everyone who wanted help was offered it.

The Open Door had grown alongside: independent trustees, advisers who’d come through it themselves, partner shelters, doctors, lawyers, people who found jobs for women who’d never been allowed one. Evangeline had refused to let it become a monument to anyone who’d done any saving. It belonged to the people who’d survived. She’d learned to say no to donors who wanted photographs, to end a meeting the moment someone asked a woman to tell her story for the third time, to see when help came with too many conditions. Jun Hyuk had learned to sit through budget meetings without looking as if he’d rather be shot. Mostly.

Before he left for the port that morning he kissed her in the kitchen.

“Don’t forget your lesson. And eat lunch.”

“You’re not allowed to tell me to eat lunch after three years of forgetting yours.”

“I’ve improved.”

“You have.” She caught his sleeve as he turned. “Happy longest night.”

His face softened. “Happy longest night, Wife.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In March of the year before, he’d stood in court for eleven days.

He’d expected the questions. The photographs. The dates. The names. He’d expected to be asked about the white truck on the seventeenth of November 2015, and the eleven, and the men who’d died by his hands in the years after. What he hadn’t expected was how hard it would be to hear his own voice say those things in a room where everyone was writing them down.

He answered every question. He didn’t say he’d been forced to wave the truck on. He didn’t claim to have known what was in it. He didn’t use the women he’d brought out later as an excuse for the ones he’d failed. When the prosecutor asked whether he understood that what he’d done had contributed to their deaths, he said yes. When the defence asked whether he’d spent the years since trying to make amends, he said that wasn’t for him to decide.

Evangeline was there every day. Sometimes behind him. Sometimes beside the lawyers. She never reached for his hand while he was giving evidence, because he needed to answer in his own voice. But every morning on the courthouse steps she kissed his cheek. On the eleventh day he came out of the witness room looking emptied out, and walked straight to her.

“Done?”

“For today.”

“Did you tell the truth?”

“Yes.”

“Then come home.”

The case against Gu Shanlin had rested on a great deal more than ten exercise books: money followed through a dozen accounts, messages, the testimony of survivors and of crew, things brought up out of the river, months of work by people Jun Hyuk never met. The books had helped them see the shape of it. They hadn’t been the whole of it. Gu Shanlin was convicted and sent to prison for life. Jun Hyuk read the news once, and closed the page, and went home and helped her repot the lemon tree.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were still galas. Evangeline hadn’t expected that part of her life to come back, but the foundation sometimes accepted invitations where its work could be helped, and the King sent for them to an official dinner once a year, and she wore something elegant and stood under chandeliers. Jun Hyuk went with her, and was surprisingly good at it. He remembered names. He could talk to ministers and donors and diplomats and people who’d built whole lives out of small talk, and give away nothing he didn’t want to. He never asked her to stop watching the exits. He knew some habits stayed after the danger had gone. He knew she liked to stand where she could see the doors, and that when a room got too full her hand would look for his without her turning her head. And he knew that, in those rooms, he could talk for both of them.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the summer of 2025 they’d spent a week at the lake.

The house on the shore belonged to the royal household and had stood quiet for years. The King had arranged it so there was nobody in it but the people who kept it. Evangeline spent the first morning opening every window, and the second she found the old jetty, and Jun Hyuk sitting on the end of it with his shoes off and his trousers rolled.

“You’re not supposed to sit there. It’s older than you are.”

“So’s the house.”

She sat beside him with her feet over the water, and then shifted. “Move.” He moved his legs, and she settled sideways into his lap with her arms round his neck and kissed him, slowly, in the warm light, his hand at her waist and the other behind her head.

“Teo says she used to come down here after rehearsals,” he said, against her hair.

“I wish I could have seen her.”

That evening a letter came, in a plain envelope with no crest. To my sister. The King wrote that the house had been quiet without her mother. That he’d first seen Seo Hwa at the summer festival here when he was seventeen, the year he’d gone into the lake after his hat, and that the wind had taken her music off the stand that same afternoon and she’d laughed and played the rest from memory. That their father had pretended to be annoyed and then asked her to play it again. That he was glad Evangeline had come. You don’t have to come back to the palace to be my sister. I hope you know that.

She read it twice and kept it in the viola case, in the pocket in the lid where her mother’s handwritten music had been folded all those years, the slow lake piece with small corrections pencilled in the margins and three words beside the last movement that she still couldn’t read without her throat closing.

“I think I want to visit him next year,” she said.

“Then we will. We get in the car.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By late afternoon on the twenty-first the house smelled of rosemary and warm bread. She’d spent the morning practising. She’d played the slow air from the lake piece in public two autumns ago, by the water where her mother had played it. But the last movement had beaten her for two years. There was one passage Mrs. Yoon said wanted more patience than she had, and every time she reached it she stopped.

At four she sat in the music room with the window open and put the viola under her chin and began. The opening came warm and steady. The music went out through the room and down the stairs and out into the winter garden. The middle rose and fell. She didn’t stop when one phrase wavered. She went on. The last movement came, and she breathed, and played it through.

When the last note had gone she sat still with the bow above the strings.

He was in the doorway, home early, still in his work coat, his hair damp from the cold.

“How long have you been there?”

“Long enough. All of it.”

“I didn’t stop,” she said.

“I know.”

“I used to stop.”

“I remember.” He came in while she laid the viola in its case. “She’d have liked that.”

She thought of a woman by a lake with her head back, laughing. Music written in a hand she’d never known and now could read. “Do you think so?”

“Yes,” he said, without a pause.

She took his hand and kissed the silver band on it. “Come outside with me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d just reached the gate when she saw someone standing in the lane. A young woman in a navy nurse’s uniform under a long grey coat, her hair tied back, a cream envelope in both hands.

“Evangeline.”

“Nuo?”

They’d seen each other at foundation meetings, at the bakery by the bridge, at Nuo’s graduation. But never like this, in a hospital pass at the green gate, an emergency nurse in her second year. Evangeline opened the gate and they held each other.

“You don’t look any different,” said Nuo.

“You do.”

“Good or bad?”

“Good.”

Nuo looked past her. “Lee Jun Hyuk.”

He inclined his head. “Nuo.”

“I can’t stay. I’m on at six. I wanted to bring you this myself.” She held out the envelope. “It came through the foundation. The woman who brought it asked whether I was the nurse who used to work at the bakery. She said you’d understand.”

The writing on the front was careful and a little uneven. No name. No address. On the back, at the bottom: For Evangeline and the man who brought us out.

“Take care of each other,” said Nuo, and went away down the lane in the wind.

✦ ✦ ✦

They opened it in the kitchen. He made tea. Inside was one sheet, no greeting, no signature.

To the two people who stood at the door when we had nowhere to go.

Some of us have found homes. Some of us are still looking. Some of us are learning how to sleep without being afraid.

We remember the man who told us we were safe.

We remember the woman who held our hands.

We remember that nobody asked us to be grateful. We were allowed to be frightened. We were allowed to be angry. We were allowed to begin again.

You gave us a way forward. We made our own lives from it.

You do not owe anybody anything any more.

Please live.

He’d read it over her shoulder. He stood at the counter with the two cups and didn’t move.

“Did you hear what it said?” she asked.

“You don’t owe anybody anything any more.” He set the cups down. “I don’t know how to believe that.”

“I know.”

He sat beside her with the letter between them and looked out at the rosemary. “Two hundred and nine. Some of them will never want to see us. Some of them might hate me.”

“That’s all right too. Their lives belong to them. Their forgiveness belongs to them.” She moved closer. “And yours?”

“I don’t know.”

“You don’t have to decide tonight what you deserve. But you can decide whether you’re allowed to live. You can come home. You can eat dinner. You can sleep. You can have a birthday. You can be happy when something makes you happy. You don’t have to suffer every day to prove you remember them.”

His eyes filled. “I remember them.”

“I know. And you told the truth. You can’t go back and change what happened. But you can live differently now.”

He leaned into her hand. “I think I’m tired,” he said. “Not from work. I thought if I stopped being angry, I’d forget. I thought if I let myself be happy it would mean I didn’t care.”

“You can remember them and still love your life.”

His face gave way, and she went into his arms, and he held her with his cheek on her hair. And for the first time he let himself think that forgiveness might not come as a verdict. That it might come as a letter with no name. A garden with eleven bushes in it. A wife who knew when to speak and when to let a silence do its work. Permission to wake up tomorrow and want something. Not because the past had gone. Because it hadn’t taken everything.

✦ ✦ ✦

The garden lights were on in the fig tree when they went out again, and the longest night had come down over everything, and the lamps lay in the stream. She stood by the postbox with her fingers on the cold white wall behind it, and he came up behind her and put his arms round her and his chin on her shoulder.

“We’ll keep the letter somewhere safe,” she said.

“We will.”

She turned in his arms. He was older than the man who’d crouched in a doorway at West Basin. There were more lines round his eyes now, and silver at his temples. But he no longer looked like someone waiting for the next reason to leave. She touched the ring on his hand.

“Do you remember what you said at our wedding?”

“Evangeline.”

She laughed. “Yes. That.”

“I had more to say,” he said. “I couldn’t. Would you like to hear it now?”

“Yes.”

He took her hands. “I choose you. I choose the house and the garden and the terrible number of plants.”

“They’re not terrible.”

“They’re everywhere.”

“Because you keep buying them.”

He nearly smiled. “I choose the mornings. The arguments. The music. I choose coming home. I choose being here when you’re tired, and listening when you don’t want to talk, and telling you when I’m frightened instead of pretending I’m not.” His thumb moved over her rings. “And I choose to live. With you.”

She pulled him down by the lapels of his work coat and kissed him against the white wall by the postbox, slow at first, and then she smiled into his mouth and he kissed her again, harder, his hand flat on the wall beside her head.

“Come inside with me,” he said against her lips.

“Because it’s cold?”

“Because I want to spend the longest night with my wife.”

“Then take me in.”

He opened the gate for her and followed her through and shut it behind them. The letter lay on the kitchen table. The eleven bushes stood along the stream. Upstairs her mother’s viola rested in its case with the lake piece folded in the lid. For once he didn’t count the exits, or check the locks twice, or look down the lane to see whether anyone was coming. He took his wife’s hand and went in. And this time he believed he was allowed to stay.

chapters.title: A Princess at the Supermarket
chapters.desc: November 2022. She is twenty-four and has never once bought her own groceries. He follows her round the supermarket at six metres.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to know everything the first time.”
chapters.content:
Evangeline Lin had never bought groceries.

She’d been to markets, of course. The flower market under the viaduct, where she could spend a whole morning over a tray of white orchids. The little shop near the house on the hill where the owner kept sweets in jars behind the counter. Once, years ago, she’d gone with Elowen to a bakery and watched her sister argue the price of a cake down by a third. But she had never stood in front of a shelf and decided which rice to buy. She’d never compared the price of eggs. She’d never pushed a trolley. At twenty-four she was finding out, on Sunday the twentieth of November, that ordinary life had an astonishing number of decisions in it.

The supermarket by the bus station was the biggest in the border town: one long bright floor of strip lighting and wide aisles and more kinds of cooking oil than she’d known existed. She stopped in front of them and stared.

He was six metres behind her.

He hadn’t meant to be. He’d walked her from Nam’s because the road by the bus station was busy on a Sunday, and he’d meant to stand outside by the trolleys while she went in. Then she’d picked up a bag of rice at the door, read the whole label, turned it over, and examined the back as if it were a contract she was being asked to sign, and he’d come in after her.

She moved on to the next shelf. He stayed six metres behind. She compared two bottles of soy sauce for nearly four minutes. He stayed. At one point she turned round, and he was immediately interested in a tin of tomatoes.

She looked at him. She nearly said his name. He’d told her it at Nam’s the week before, across the window table, and she’d been carrying it about with her ever since like something she’d been lent. She hadn’t said it yet. She found she didn’t want the first time to be in front of the tinned tomatoes.

“You’re following me,” she said instead.

“I’m shopping.”

“You don’t eat tinned tomatoes.”

“I might.”

She looked at his basket. One packet of instant noodles, one bottle of water, and the tomatoes. She smiled. “All right.”

He put the tin back. She went on shopping. He went on following.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first problem was rice. There was a whole wall of it, and she stood holding two bags.

“Which one do you buy?”

He looked at the bags. “Rice.”

“I know it’s rice.”

“Then either.”

“That isn’t helpful.”

He took the smaller one out of her hand. “This one. It’s easier to carry.”

She looked at the price. “It’s more expensive.”

“By a little.”

“Then why would I buy it?”

“Because it’s easier to carry.”

She stared at him, put it back, and took the cheaper one, and looked pleased with herself. He said nothing. He put the cheaper bag in her trolley. “Good choice.”

She narrowed her eyes. “Don’t be patronising.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

His mouth moved at one corner. He pushed the trolley on, and she followed, still slightly offended.

The rest went into the trolley one serious decision at a time. Eggs, after she’d opened four boxes to check none was cracked. Soy sauce. A jar of dark honey, because there was no honey in the flat over the Golden Nightingale and she’d noticed. Two bottles of cooking oil. Carrots, potatoes, onions and tomatoes, chosen one by one from the bins with the gravity of somebody assembling a delegation.

Then she reached the till.

The cashier scanned the honey and the eggs and the rice and picked up the carrots, and stopped. “Miss, these need weighing.”

“Weighing?”

“At the scales. Over there.” The woman pointed. Behind Evangeline the queue had grown to five. The belt stopped.

“Oh.”

She gathered the bags of vegetables and walked across to the scales with the feeling of everyone in the queue watching her back. There were pictures on the machine. A carrot. A potato. An onion. She put the carrots on and the screen changed and showed her a number and three buttons and a little slot. She pressed the carrot. Nothing happened. She pressed it again and a different number came up. Somebody behind her sighed. Her ears began to go red. She took the carrots off and tried the potatoes, and the machine beeped at her, and a label came out of the slot, and she looked at the label and the potatoes and the machine and had no idea at all what she was supposed to do next.

“Excuse me,” she said to the woman next in line for the scales. “I’m sorry. Could you—”

A hand came past her shoulder. “Put them down.”

He’d left his basket somewhere. He took the carrots out of her hands, set them on the plate, pressed the picture, took the label and stuck it on the bag. Then the onions. Then the tomatoes. His movements were quick without being hurried, and he didn’t look at the people waiting, and he didn’t tell her it was easy. He just finished.

“There.”

She looked at the four labels. “That’s all?”

“That’s all.”

“I didn’t know. I’ve never used one.”

“I know.”

“They were waiting.”

“They’ll survive.” He took the trolley handle and turned it back towards the till. “Come on.”

At the till he showed her where to put the bags. The cashier told her the total, and she took her card out of her purse, and he stepped back.

“What?”

“You’re paying.”

“I know I’m paying.”

She put the card in. The screen gave her several instructions. She read every one. Then she looked round at him. “Which one?”

“Follow the screen.”

“I am.”

“Then press yes.”

She pressed yes. It asked for her number. She shielded the keypad with her hand, quite fiercely, as if he’d been about to read it over her shoulder, and he looked at the ceiling. The machine thought about it and beeped and a receipt came out.

She held it. She looked at it, and then she smiled, properly, all the way to her eyes. “I bought groceries.”

“Yes.”

“With my own money. And I paid.”

She looked so pleased that he nearly smiled back. “Well done.”

She lifted her chin. “I know.”

He took the heavy bag. She took the light one. They went out together into the cold.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the flat over the Golden Nightingale he undid the three locks, and she carried the shopping up and put it all on the counter by the camp stove and began to sort. Rice in the cupboard. Eggs in the little fridge. Vegetables in the basket she’d brought up the Sunday before. Soy sauce beside the stove. Honey next to the tea.

He leaned in the doorway and watched her. There was a cushion on the floor by the wall now. There was a plant on the sill. None of them had been there in October.

“What?” she said.

“Nothing.”

“You keep looking at me.”

“You bought groceries.”

She smiled at the shelf. He came over and picked up one of the bottles of oil, and then the other, and turned them both round so the labels faced her.

“You bought two.”

“I thought one might be different.”

They were identical. She looked at them.

“Oh,” she said.

He waited. She pressed her lips together. And then he smiled. Not the polite one he gave strangers, or the small careful one he sometimes let out when she teased him. This one came slowly and started in his eyes.

She looked away. “Don’t.”

“I’m not saying anything.”

“Your face is.”

He put the oil down. She busied herself with the carrots. He reached for the kettle. “Tea?”

“Yes, please.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When she’d drunk it she put her coat on, and he went down with her to the steel door at the bottom of the stair as he always did. The lane was already dark. She wound her scarf round, and got the end of it wrong.

“Thank you for helping me,” she said.

“You did most of it.”

“I couldn’t work the scales.”

“Now you can.”

“I was nervous at the card machine.”

He looked at her. “Why?”

She hesitated. “Everyone was waiting. I didn’t want to be in anyone’s way.”

“You weren’t doing anything wrong.” He reached out and put the end of her scarf right. “You don’t have to know everything the first time.”

She looked up. They were close. His hand was still at her collar, on the wool. Her eyes went to his mouth, and he saw them go there. Of course he did. His thumb moved once against the scarf. He could have kissed her. He wanted to badly. He didn’t move. He’d learned that when something mattered she sometimes needed a moment to decide what she wanted, and he wasn’t going to make her uncertainty into an answer for her. So he stood there in the cold doorway and let her decide.

She looked at his face. At his mouth again. She took a small step closer, and his breathing changed.

She reached up and picked a thread of lint off his shoulder. “Your coat’s dirty.”

He looked down at it. “Is it?”

“Yes.” She smiled. Then she said, “I forgot something. Wait here.”

She went back across the road to the supermarket, and he stood under the shop sign of the closed bar with his hands in his pockets and watched the automatic doors for eleven minutes. When she came out she had a large soft bag held against her chest in both arms, and when he went to take it from her she turned so he couldn’t reach.

“No.”

“It looks heavy.”

“It isn’t.”

“What is it?”

“It’s for next week,” she said. “You can’t have it yet.”

He looked at the bag, and at her face over the top of it, determined and slightly pink. “All right,” he said.

He walked her to the bus stand by the bridge. She got on, with the bag on her knee, and found a window seat, and looked out at him as the doors closed. He was still standing there. She lifted her hand. He lifted his. He stayed until the bus had gone over the bridge and round the bend, and then he went back to a flat with honey on the shelf and two identical bottles of oil and a cushion on the floor, and stood in the doorway of it for some time.

On the bus she held the bag on her lap and didn’t open it. She knew what was in it. Three thick white bath towels. Three white hand towels. A bottle of mild washing liquid. A packet of wooden pegs. She’d seen him come out of his shower on the first Sunday with his hair dripping onto a kitchen cloth, and she hadn’t said a word.

Next Sunday she’d climb his stair with the bag, and he’d open it, and he’d say You bought towels, as if she’d done something impossible.

And perhaps, she thought, watching the river go by in the dark, by then she’d be ready to say his name.

chapters.title: He Tries to Cook Breakfast
chapters.desc: November 2024, Fig Tree Lane. He wants to bring her breakfast in bed, once, like a man in a video. Mrs. Bae brings an extinguisher from 1987.
chapters.epigraph: “Love has made you both strange.”
chapters.content:
At 6:12 on the third Sunday in November, Lee Jun Hyuk watched a cooking video for the fourth time.

The man on the screen was smiling. He had a clean kitchen and a white apron and a wife who looked delighted when he brought her breakfast in bed. He cracked two eggs into a bowl, whisked them, cooked them in butter with a little garlic, and laid them beside neat toast and a handful of dressed greens. It looked easy.

Jun Hyuk looked at the kitchen at No. 9 Fig Tree Lane. He could open a container faster than that man could make an omelette. He could find a false floor in a shipment, spot a forged seal at four metres, and remember the plates of lorries he’d seen nine years ago. He could make breakfast.

He put on the apron. It was pale yellow with small lemons embroidered across the pocket. She’d bought it because she said the lemons were sweet. He’d considered it unnecessary until she kissed him for wearing it. He tied it round his waist and checked the stairs. The bedroom door was still shut. Good. Today his wife was going to wake up to breakfast made by her husband, like a film.

He hadn’t considered the smoke alarm.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first mistake was the garlic. He’d peeled three cloves instead of two. The second was the heat. The third was believing a man in a video.

He stood over the pan and watched the garlic go from pale gold to a colour he didn’t like. He turned the gas down. It went on darkening. He took the pan off the flame altogether, and a thin grey thread rose out of it, and he looked at it.

“Don’t,” he told it.

It didn’t listen. He scraped it into the bin and started again. Smaller this time. The video had said finely chopped, and he chopped it finely, perhaps too finely, and put the butter in, and waited for it to melt, and tipped the garlic in. The smell was promising. He turned to get the eggs.

Behind him there was a small sharp crack.

One egg had rolled off the counter. The yolk spread slowly across the tiles towards the cupboard. He shut his eyes. He’d killed men without making this much mess. He picked up the other egg, and it broke in his hand.

He looked at his palm. He looked at the floor. He said nothing at all.

The toast, which he’d forgotten, was black.

Around half past six the smoke alarm in the kitchen went off. A second joined it in the hall. A third, at the top of the stairs. The whole house began to scream.

He opened the window, turned off everything that could be turned off, and flapped the tea towel under the nearest alarm. The tea towel caught the smoke and the alarm got louder. He looked at the stairs. No movement. Good. He took the pan out of the back door.

The garden gate banged. Mrs. Bae came through it in a knitted cardigan over her nightdress, carrying a fire extinguisher in both arms.

“LEE JUN HYUK!”

He turned round with the pan in his hand. She looked at the smoke drifting out of the kitchen window, and at the pan, and at the yellow apron with the lemons on it. Her face became complicated.

“What’s happened?”

“Breakfast.”

“Breakfast?”

“Yes.”

She hoisted the extinguisher. It was red and battered and old. A faded label on its side said 1987. “Where’s the fire?”

“There isn’t one.”

“Then why is your house shouting?”

“The alarms.”

“I can hear that!” She marched past him into the kitchen.

He looked at the extinguisher. “Is that still usable?”

Mrs. Bae stopped and turned round slowly. “Would you like me to find out on you?”

He stepped aside. She inspected the stove, the bin with the ruined garlic in it, the eggshells, the yolk on the tiles, the scorched tea towel, and the toast. “Good heavens,” she said. “Is that supposed to be food?”

“Yes.”

“Then you’ve got a problem.” She looked at the ceiling. “Where’s Evangeline?”

“Asleep.”

“You’re trying to surprise her.”

He didn’t answer. Her face softened, slightly. “Oh,” she said, and put the extinguisher down. “Well. Don’t burn the house down before she gets to eat it. Less heat. And butter before garlic, not after.”

“I know.”

“Clearly,” said Mrs. Bae. At the door she looked at the apron again. “And take that off. You look ridiculous.”

He looked down at the lemons. “No.”

Mrs. Bae gave him a long look and went home.

✦ ✦ ✦

Evangeline woke to the sound of someone arguing with the kitchen. At first she thought it was Mrs. Bae. Then she heard her husband.

“That isn’t what I did. No. I followed the instructions. I did.”

She sat up. The bedroom smelled of smoke. “Jun Hyuk?”

The arguing stopped. She pulled on her cardigan and ran downstairs, and found him standing at the counter holding a glass of cold water, his hair on end, his sleeves rolled up, a streak of flour on his jaw, and the yellow apron still tied round his waist. The windows were all open. There was a fire extinguisher by the back door. There was a pan soaking in the sink.

“What happened?”

“Nothing.”

She looked at the extinguisher, and the pan, and the apron. “Did you try to cook?”

He looked at her. “Yes.”

“For me?”

A pause. “Yes.”

Her face changed. The amusement went out of it and something so warm came in instead that he nearly wished she’d laughed. “Oh,” she said.

He looked away. “I was going to bring you breakfast.”

She came closer. “What’s wrong with your hand?”

There was a red mark across two of his fingers. “Nothing.”

She took his wrist. “Jun Hyuk.”

“Hot pan.”

She led him to the sink and turned the cold tap on and held his fingers under it. He watched her do it.

“It’s fine,” he said.

“I know.”

“Then why are you doing that?”

“Because I want to.” She moved his hand a little under the water. “Does it hurt?”

“A little.”

“Why didn’t you wake me?”

“You were asleep.” He looked at the pan. “It was very bad.”

She pressed her lips together.

“Don’t laugh,” he said.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

She turned her face away. Her shoulders went. He stared at the back of her head.

“Evangeline.”

That was enough. She laughed. Not a small polite laugh. She put her hand over her mouth and her eyes went to crescents and she had to lean on the counter. He watched her. After a moment he sighed, and the corner of his mouth went.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“You’re not.”

“No, I’m not.” She came back and dried his fingers gently. “Did you burn the garlic?”

“Twice.”

“And the eggs?”

“One fell.” She looked at the mark on the tiles by the cupboard. “The other one broke,” he admitted.

“And the toast?”

“It was supposed to be brown.”

“Not black.”

“I know that now.” He put his hands on her waist. “You’re enjoying this.”

“Very much.”

“I was trying to do something nice.”

Her laughter went soft. She put her palms flat on his chest. “I know. You did. You got up early. You watched videos. You wore the apron.” She touched one of the lemons. “And you set off every alarm in the house.”

“Not every alarm.”

She raised her eyebrows.

“Most,” he said.

“That’s very romantic.”

He gave her a flat look, and she reached up and kissed him. He kissed her back with one hand at her waist and the other held carefully away from her because of his fingers, and then he forgot about his fingers and pulled her in properly, and the kiss went deep and slow there at the sink in the smoke, and the smoke alarm at the top of the stairs gave one last, offended beep.

From the garden came Mrs. Bae’s voice. “I CAN STILL HEAR YOU!”

Evangeline buried her face in his shirt. He shut his eyes. “She should go home.”

Mrs. Bae’s footsteps retreated. The gate clicked.

“She brought a fire extinguisher,” said Evangeline into his chest.

“Yes.”

“From 1987.”

“Apparently.”

She laughed into his shirt, and he kissed the top of her head.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty past seven she took over the kitchen. He sat on a stool at the island with his sleeves still rolled and watched. Soft scrambled eggs. Mushrooms. Toast that stayed brown. A plate of greens with oil and a squeeze of lemon. Tea in two cups. She moved round the kitchen without looking, reaching for things where she knew they’d be. She tasted before she salted. She tucked her hair behind her ear. She washed the knife the moment she’d finished with it. She hummed. He liked watching her cook more than he could have explained to anyone.

She turned with the tray. “All right.”

“You’re taking it up?”

“That’s what you wanted, isn’t it?”

He stood and took the tray out of her hands.

“Careful. Don’t spill it.”

“I won’t.”

“You’re carrying it as if it’s evidence.”

He looked at the tray. “What’s wrong with that?”

“Nothing, Husband.”

They ate in bed, her against the pillows with her knees under the quilt, him beside her with his tea. It was good. He looked at his plate, and at her.

“You made that fast.”

“I’ve done it before.”

“Next time I’ll do it properly.”

“Next time?”

“Yes.”

“I’ll supervise.”

“I don’t need supervising.”

She looked at him. He drank his tea. “All right.”

She fed him a forkful of egg off her plate, and then took his hand and turned it over and looked at the red fingers and kissed them, one and then the other.

“Your greens are better than mine,” he said.

“You didn’t make any greens.”

“I was going to.”

“Then you’ll have to try next time.” She smiled against his mouth when he leaned over to kiss her. “Although perhaps we should start with something simpler.”

“Like what?”

“Toast.”

He stared at her. She laughed. “Jun Hyuk, you burned the toast.”

“It was a difficult morning.”

“Poor husband,” she said, and he caught her hand and kissed the palm.

✦ ✦ ✦

At noon Mrs. Bae knocked on the front door with a small covered pot. “Soup,” she said, and peered past him. “Is she alive?”

“Yes.”

“Did you feed her?”

“Yes.”

“Something edible?”

“Yes.”

She looked satisfied, and then her eyes dropped. “You’re still wearing that.”

Evangeline appeared behind him. “I like it.”

Mrs. Bae looked at her, and at him, and at the lemons. She shook her head. “Love has made you both strange,” she said, and went home.

Evangeline put her arms round his waist from behind. “Thank you for trying.”

“Next Sunday,” he said.

“You’re trying again?”

“Yes.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Probably.”

She laughed. He turned round and kissed her forehead and looked over her head at the kitchen. “I’ll make the greens.”

“Together,” she said.

“Together.”

In the kitchen, for now, the smoke alarm stayed quiet.

chapters.title: The Neighbour’s Cat Chose Him
chapters.desc: Winter 2024. A ginger cat with half an ear, a terrible thief, decides the big man next door belongs to him.
chapters.epigraph: “Move, Sergeant.”
chapters.content:
By December, Pudding had stopped visiting No. 9 Fig Tree Lane and started inspecting it.

In October he’d come through the garden gate once or twice a week, sat on the sofa as if he’d been invited, and gone home to the Baes for his dinner. By the second week of December he came every morning. On Monday he stole a piece of chicken off a cooling plate. On Tuesday he stole Jun Hyuk’s chair. By Wednesday he’d decided the house was his.

Jun Hyuk disagreed.

“He has a home,” he told Evangeline.

Pudding was sitting on the kitchen counter washing a paw.

“He does,” she said.

“Next door.”

“Yes.”

“Then why is he here?”

Pudding looked at Jun Hyuk. Jun Hyuk looked back. The cat yawned.

“I think he likes you,” said Evangeline, behind her tea.

“He likes the chicken.”

“He came yesterday when we weren’t cooking.”

“He smelled something.”

“We were eating oranges.”

Jun Hyuk glanced at the cat. Pudding blinked at him, slowly.

“I don’t like cats,” said Jun Hyuk.

She kissed his cheek. “Of course you don’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Bae said Pudding had always been difficult. He was ginger and broad round the middle, with white feet and a pale bib and the top half of his left ear missing. Nobody knew how he’d lost it. He’d turned up in the Baes’ garden one hard winter years ago, starving and rude, and had gradually decided they could be tolerated. He was a dreadful thief. Fish off plates, bread out of bags, once a whole dumpling off the end of Mrs. Bae’s chopsticks on its way to her mouth. And he hated being picked up.

Except by Jun Hyuk. This was the part that offended Jun Hyuk most.

Pudding had no interest at all in being held by Evangeline, who adored him. He’d permit a scratch from Mrs. Bae, provided she didn’t try to kiss his head. But the moment Jun Hyuk sat down on the sofa the cat would appear from nowhere, climb onto his lap, turn round twice and settle as though there had been a long-standing arrangement.

“Get him off,” said Jun Hyuk, the first evening it happened that month.

“He’s comfortable.”

“He’s on me.”

“I can see that.”

“Move him.”

She leaned over and scratched under the cat’s chin, and Pudding began to purr like a small engine.

“Traitor,” said Jun Hyuk.

Pudding shut his eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

The trouble was three in the morning. Not every night. Some nights Jun Hyuk slept through with his hand on her waist. Others he woke all at once, his body already moving before his mind had caught up, and his hand went to the space under the bed. There was nothing there. There hadn’t been for weeks. He’d given his rifle to Song himself, and what was left in the steel room behind the pantry was locked behind a code Evangeline had chosen and wouldn’t tell him. He’d asked her to do that. He didn’t regret it. His body hadn’t caught up yet.

Just after three on a Thursday he sat on the edge of the bed, breathing slowly, looking at the door.

She stirred. “Jun Hyuk?”

“Go back to sleep.”

She sat up and reached for his hand, and folded back the quilt. “Come back.”

“I’m fine.”

“I know.”

Something landed on the mattress with a soft thud. A ginger shape. Pudding had come in through the gap in the bedroom door, crossed the room in the dark and jumped straight onto Jun Hyuk’s thighs. He turned round once, stepped over one leg, climbed higher, and settled against Jun Hyuk’s chest as if that were the obvious place to be.

“What’s he doing?”

“Coming to bed,” said Evangeline, awake enough now to be enjoying herself.

“He has his own bed.”

“Apparently not.”

The cat was warm and heavy. His purr went through Jun Hyuk’s shirt. He put one front paw against Jun Hyuk’s collarbone and went completely limp.

“Take him.”

She stroked the cat’s back instead. Jun Hyuk breathed out. He was still sitting up. But his shoulders had begun to come down.

“Lie down,” she said.

“He’ll fall.”

“I’ll hold him.”

She kept a hand on the cat while Jun Hyuk lowered himself back onto the pillows, slowly, and Pudding didn’t stir. His head ended up under Jun Hyuk’s chin. She switched off the lamp. A few minutes later she heard her husband’s breathing deepen. She looked across in the dark. He was asleep. So was the cat. She lay perfectly still, afraid to move in case she woke either of them, and smiled at the ceiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

By January Pudding had a routine. He arrived in the morning. He inspected the kitchen. He stole something if he was given the chance. Then he found Jun Hyuk. If Jun Hyuk was in the study, Pudding sat on the papers. If he was in the glasshouse, Pudding sat outside the door and complained until it opened. If he was in the garden, Pudding followed him between the young rosemary by the stream and now and then attacked a leaf.

Jun Hyuk went on saying he didn’t like cats. He also put a small bowl of water by the back door, because, he said, Pudding drank out of the stream and might get ill. Evangeline found a packet of cat treats in the kitchen drawer behind the string. She didn’t mention it. She noticed he’d started leaving the warmest cushion on the sofa empty. She didn’t mention that either.

One afternoon she came downstairs and found him sitting on the floor by the sofa mending a split seam on that cushion with a needle and thread, with Pudding asleep across his knees and one of his big hands resting on the cat’s back to keep him there.

He looked up. “Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You’re thinking it.”

“I am.” She sat down beside him on the rug. Pudding opened one eye, saw her, and shut it again. “Do you want a cat?” she said.

“No.”

“All right.”

He pulled the thread through. Pudding stretched, showing his round stomach, and Jun Hyuk moved his hand so as not to disturb him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Bae came over on a Saturday afternoon and found him kneeling by the rosemary with Pudding sitting on his back. She stopped at the gate. “Ah.”

He looked round. “Mrs. Bae.”

“He’s been here all morning.”

“Yes.”

“Did you feed him?”

“No.”

Pudding gave a single loud miaow. Mrs. Bae raised an eyebrow. Jun Hyuk sighed. “Yes.”

“The chicken?”

“Some.”

“How much?”

He didn’t answer. She folded her arms. “He doesn’t come home any more. He sleeps here. He eats here. He follows you about. I told you in October. If he likes you, he moves in.” She looked at the cat on his back and then at him. “Would you like to keep him?”

Jun Hyuk looked over his shoulder. Pudding had settled against the back of his neck with his eyes half shut.

“He’ll need to see a vet,” said Jun Hyuk.

Mrs. Bae smiled. “Yes.”

“And proper food. And he’s not to eat off the table.”

“Good luck with that. I’ll bring his things over tomorrow.”

“Mrs. Bae. His name’s Pudding.”

Mrs. Bae tilted her head. “Then why do you keep calling him Sergeant?”

He went still.

Evangeline, who’d just come out of the back door with two cups of tea, stopped on the step. “Sergeant?”

Jun Hyuk stood up. Pudding slid off his back and landed neatly on the grass. “It’s a practical name.”

She pressed her lips together. “Why?”

“He supervises.”

She laughed. He looked at her. “He’s very strict,” he said, and the cat came and rubbed against his ankle.

“Then Sergeant it is,” said Mrs. Bae solemnly.

✦ ✦ ✦

The adoption was concluded with little ceremony. Mrs. Bae brought over his food, his blanket, a scratching post and a basket he had never once used, and a small envelope containing his vaccination record. Jun Hyuk read every line of it at the kitchen table. He checked the dates. He rang the vet in the village and made an appointment for Tuesday.

“Most people just say they’ve got a cat,” said Evangeline.

“He has medical records.”

“Yes.”

“And a diet. He shouldn’t have too much fish. And he should be kept in at night.”

“Yes, Husband.”

On the counter, Sergeant was trying to get his head into a bag of bread. Jun Hyuk reached over and moved it away without looking up. “Sergeant. Don’t.”

The cat looked at him and miaowed.

“He’s listening,” said Evangeline.

“He isn’t.”

Sergeant jumped down and followed him into the sitting room.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night the cat slept on his chest again. It had become a habit. At first Jun Hyuk had complained about the weight. Then about the claws. Then that the cat took up too much of the bed. Evangeline had pointed out that he was the one who’d started sleeping with an arm curled round him. He’d denied it.

He woke at 3:14. He didn’t sit up. He lay still and listened. The house was quiet. The stream went on outside. The cat was warm on his chest, and her hand lay on the sheet beside his. He looked at the bedroom door. Then at her, asleep, her hair across her cheek. He reached out and moved it off her face.

“Jun Hyuk?” she murmured.

“Sleep.”

She opened one eye. “Are you all right?”

He looked down at the cat, who was purring. “Yes.”

She smiled and shut her eye. He lay awake another minute, listening to her breathe. Sergeant shifted and pushed his face into the side of Jun Hyuk’s throat and settled again. Jun Hyuk’s hand rested on his back. He slept.

At six she woke and found him sitting on the edge of the bed with the cat still asleep against his chest, one hand holding Sergeant in place and the other stretched towards the bedside table, trying to reach his phone without waking him.

“Good morning,” she said.

“Morning.”

“Did you sleep?”

“Yes.”

“All night?”

He nodded.

“Sergeant helped,” she said.

“He was in the way.”

“Of course.”

Sergeant stretched, yawned, climbed off him, walked across the quilt, stepped over her legs and lay down exactly between them. She laughed and scratched his head, and he began to purr.

Jun Hyuk watched the two of them. Then he leaned over the cat and kissed her. She smiled into it. Sergeant pushed his head up between their faces. Jun Hyuk stopped. He looked at the cat. The cat looked at him. There was a long silence.

“Move, Sergeant,” he said.

She burst out laughing. He kissed her again anyway, and let the cat stay exactly where he was. For a man who didn’t like cats, he was becoming remarkably accommodating.

chapters.title: She Learns to Shoot
chapters.desc: February 2024, a range in an orchard in the hills. She misses fourteen times and hits the compost heap once.
chapters.epigraph: “Three is a room.”
chapters.content:
The first time Evangeline asked him to teach her to shoot, Jun Hyuk thought she was joking.

It was a Sunday afternoon in February, in the kitchen on the sixth floor, and she was slicing pears while he stood behind her reading something on his phone.

“Teach me,” she said.

He looked up. “What?”

“How to shoot.”

The knife went on moving in her hand, slice after neat slice. He put the phone down. “Why?”

She laid the knife on the board and turned round. “Because I don’t want to be helpless in a room with someone dangerous.”

“You’re not helpless.”

“I know. But when something happens, there are two people in the room. You and me. I don’t want you to be the only one who knows what to do.” She said it. “If there are two people in that room, I want it to be two.”

He looked at her. Then he reached past her and moved the knife back from the edge of the counter.

“All right.”

She blinked. “Really?”

“Next Sunday.” He looked at her. “You won’t enjoy it.”

“I might.”

“You won’t.” He kissed her forehead. “I’ll be honest with you.”

“That’s very encouraging.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Ngan’s orchard lay in the hills off the northern road, old apple trees on terraces going down to a stream, and the range sat behind a tin storage shed against a high earth bank. Mr. Ngan had known Jun Hyuk for years and owed him a favour he’d never been asked to repay. When Jun Hyuk explained, Mr. Ngan looked at Evangeline, and then at him.

“Your wife?”

“Yes.”

“She wants to learn?”

“Yes.”

Mr. Ngan nodded slowly. “Then teach her properly.”

Jun Hyuk had already arranged that. A qualified instructor, a quiet woman in her fifties called Mrs. Ho, would run every session and keep every piece of equipment. He’d stand beside his wife, but he wasn’t going to pretend that being good with a weapon made him a substitute for being taught right.

Evangeline listened to the safety rules without interrupting, asked whenever something wasn’t clear, and repeated each one back. She wore ear defenders and glasses and a jacket of his that came down to her knees because the hills were colder than she’d expected. She looked serious. Almost solemn. He found it unbearable.

Then she tried.

She missed.

She missed again. By the fourth she was frowning. By the seventh she looked personally offended by the target.

“You’re rushing,” he said.

“I’m not. I’m being careful.”

“You’re being careful and rushing.”

“How can I be both?”

“Apparently,” he said, and she gave him a wounded look and turned back.

The eighth missed. The ninth. The tenth caught the very edge of the paper.

“That doesn’t count,” she said.

“It’s on the target,” said Mrs. Ho.

“It barely counts.”

“It counts,” said Jun Hyuk.

She seemed dissatisfied with his generosity. The next three went nowhere near. The fourteenth went into the earth bank. The fifteenth hit paper. The sixteenth didn’t. On the seventeenth Mrs. Ho looked off towards the end of the range, and Jun Hyuk followed her eyes to a small fresh hole in the side of Mr. Ngan’s compost heap.

He looked back at his wife. She was staring at the target.

“Was that mine?”

He considered lying. “Yes.”

She shut her eyes.

“Don’t,” he said.

“Don’t what?”

“Look like that. As if the target’s insulted your family.”

She turned away. He looked at the compost heap, and back at her. He’d stood in front of men who could put a round through a moving car. He’d never in his life been so worried about anyone’s dignity.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the third Sunday she’d developed a particular face for missing. It was quiet. Her mouth went into a thin line and her eyebrows drew together and she looked at the paper, then at the ground, then at the paper again, as if the result might change if she gave it long enough. He’d begun to recognise it before she’d even lowered her hands.

She missed twice in a row and let out a sharp breath.

“You’re shutting your eyes,” he said.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“I am not.”

“Evangeline.”

She looked away, and he understood. It wasn’t the noise. She’d heard worse than this in a noodle shop. It wasn’t the equipment. She was trying so hard not to make a mistake that she flinched before the moment came, and her eyes closed before she could stop them.

“Look at me,” he said. She turned her head. “You’re trying to do it perfectly.”

“I want to do it properly. I’m not asking you to make me good in one afternoon.”

“I know.”

“Then why do you keep looking at me like that?”

“Like what?”

“As if you’re worried.”

He was quiet. Then: “Because I am. Not because you’re missing. Because you’re being hard on yourself.” He glanced at Mrs. Ho, who’d stepped back to give them a moment. “May I?”

She nodded. He came and stood behind her, careful not to crowd her, and spoke low by her ear, the same things Mrs. Ho had said, and let her settle her own stance without taking it over.

“Don’t rush. You’ve got time. Keep your eyes open.”

“I know.”

“Then do it.”

She made a small sound of irritation. He smiled. “That’s my girl.”

The next one hit the paper. Not the centre. Nowhere near the centre. But the paper.

She stared at it and looked over her shoulder. “Did you see?”

“I saw.”

She smiled so brightly that he forgot where they were standing. He wanted to kiss her badly. He waited until Mrs. Ho had finished the session and every piece of equipment was cleared and locked away. Then he lifted the ear defenders off her head.

“One,” he said.

“One.”

“You’re proud of me?”

He pushed a strand of hair off her forehead. “Very.”

She went up on her toes and kissed him, and he caught her waist and kissed her back, there behind Mr. Ngan’s shed in the cold with the apple trees going down the hill, a kiss entirely inappropriate for a man who’d spent the last hour telling her to concentrate.

“That’s not part of the lesson,” he said, when she let him go.

“It is now.”

He kissed her again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Six weeks after the first Sunday she put three shots into the paper at three metres.

They weren’t close together. One sat high. One was near the edge. But all three were where they were meant to be. She lowered her hands and looked, and then she took the ear defenders off and turned to him.

“Three.”

“Three.”

“Three is a room,” she said.

He went still. He knew what she meant. Not a guarantee, not a promise that a weapon could make danger go away, or that she could stand against everyone who’d ever want to hurt her. Only this: that if there were two people in a room, she wouldn’t have to be the one who waited for him to save her. She’d asked to learn. She’d stayed through the hard parts. Now she could do something she couldn’t do six weeks ago.

“Yes,” he said. “It is.”

“I want to keep practising. I want to get better.”

“You will.”

She looked at him sideways. “You’re not going to tell me I’m good enough already?”

“No.” He touched her cheek. “You’re allowed to want to get better.”

Her face softened, and then she smiled. “Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He kept that target. She didn’t know. He’d folded it while she was talking to Mrs. Ho and put it in his inside pocket, and at home that night he slid it into a clear sleeve and dated it in his own hand and put it in Old Ko’s tin box, under his mother’s photograph and his father’s watch and the bundle of letters he still didn’t read often. He didn’t write anything beside it. He didn’t need to. It belonged there. Not as a victory. Just as a small record of something she’d chosen to learn and worked at until her hands were surer than they’d been.

She found him that evening in the little study off the sitting room as he was shutting the box.

“What’s that?”

“Nothing.”

“That’s not nothing.” She came and put her hands on his shoulders. “Did I do well today?”

He turned in the chair. “Yes.”

“Even though they weren’t together? Even though I missed so many times?”

He reached for her waist and drew her in. “Especially because you kept trying.”

She bent and kissed him, and he spread his hands on her back. When she drew away she looked at the shelf.

“What’s in the box?”

“Old things.”

“Yours?”

“Some.”

She thought about asking. Then she decided not to, and kissed his forehead instead. “Goodnight, Husband.”

He caught her hand before she could go. “Next Sunday we go again.”

Her face lit up. She bent and kissed him once more, and went.

When she’d gone he opened the box and looked at the paper in its sleeve, under his mother’s face. Three small holes in a target. A small achievement. A life going on.

He shut the lid and put it back on the shelf.

chapters.title: He Learns Her Favourite Colour
chapters.desc: October 2023, a year to the day after West Basin. He has bought her blue things for a year. Nobody ever asked.
chapters.epigraph: “It isn’t really the colour. It’s that it reminds me doors can open.”
chapters.content:
Elowen asked her to lunch on Saturday the fourteenth of October because it was a year to the day, and nobody was supposed to say so.

It wasn’t an important lunch. Three sisters at the kitchen table in the house on the hill, three dishes of vegetables, a pot of soup, and a cake Evangeline had brought up on the bus because she’d been trying a new recipe. Zhao was away until Monday. Eliana had come over from the Walled City with her laptop and a bag of oranges, and was watching Evangeline cut the cake as if she were working something out.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“Who keeps buying you blue things?”

Evangeline put the knife down carefully.

“That coat,” said Eliana, pointing at the hall, where a coat of the palest blue there is hung on its peg. “It’s new. Those earrings are new. That scarf. Half your flowers used to be white, and now every time I see you there’s something blue in them.”

“I bought the coat,” said Evangeline.

“You’ve never bought a coat in your life.”

Elowen, beside her, became busy with the soup.

“Fine,” said Eliana, who could smell a closed door the way other people smelled rain, and filed it away. “Then what’s your favourite colour?”

“Pale blue.”

Eliana frowned. “Is it?”

“Why?”

“Because I don’t think I’ve ever heard you say so.”

Elowen looked up from her bowl. “That’s because it isn’t.”

Evangeline blinked. Eliana leaned back, delighted. “I knew it.”

“Then what is it?” said Evangeline.

“I don’t know,” said Elowen. “Nobody ever asked you. Mama dressed you in pale blue when you were tiny. She said it made you look like the sky after rain. You wore it so often everyone decided it was your colour.” She reached over and touched her sister’s sleeve, which was also pale blue. “Even you.”

Evangeline looked down at it. She’d seen photographs of herself in pale blue: a little girl with neat hair beside a woman she remembered mostly from pictures now. She’d never once thought to question it.

“Well,” said Eliana. “Somebody should ask her.”

On the bus back into the city Evangeline sat by the window with the cake tin empty on her knee and tried to answer the question herself, and found she couldn’t do it straight away. She knew what she liked. She liked white orchids and the smell of basil and the sound of the river behind Nam’s yard. She liked a bowl of broth that had been going since 1991. She liked the colour of his eyes when he was trying not to laugh. But a favourite colour seemed to belong to a girl who’d been allowed to choose things, and she’d only recently become one. By the time the bus came over the river, she thought she knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him that evening, on the sixth floor, with the city going dark outside the sealed windows and her shoes off on the sofa.

“Eliana asked me my favourite colour.”

He was at the counter making tea. “What did you say?”

“Pale blue. Elowen said that’s only because nobody ever asked.”

He brought the two cups over and sat beside her, and looked at her with his perfectly serious face.

“What’s your favourite colour?”

She put her book down. He’d bought her aquamarines, and a pale blue coat, and a scarf the colour of a winter sky, and blue flowers every week since September. He’d never asked. She thought about it properly, because he’d want her to.

“Orange,” she said.

He blinked. “Orange?”

“Yes.”

He looked round the room as if he expected to find evidence. “Since when?”

“Since West Basin.”

His face changed.

“Do you remember when you opened the door?” she said. “The floodlights outside were orange. I’d been in the dark so long I couldn’t remember what anything looked like. Then the door opened and this enormous orange light came in, and you were in the middle of it, crouching down, talking.” She looked at her hands. “It was the first colour I saw properly after. I think I liked it because it meant the door was open.”

He didn’t say anything. Then he put his tea down.

“Evangeline. Why didn’t you tell me?”

She smiled a little. “You never asked.”

He laughed once as if he couldn’t believe it, and stood up and held out his hand. “Come here.”

“I’m already here.”

“Come here.”

She took his hand and he pulled her up off the sofa into his arms and kissed her. It wasn’t a careful kiss. One hand at the back of her neck, the other arm round her waist, and he kissed her so hard and so long that her fingers curled into his shirt and her feet left the floor.

She was laughing when he let her breathe. “What was that for?”

“A year of buying the wrong colour.”

“Only a year?”

“Don’t,” he said, and put his forehead against hers. “Orange.”

“Yes.”

He nodded, as if he were writing it down somewhere permanent. “Orange.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Then he picked up his jacket and his keys.

“Where are you going?”

“Out. Twenty minutes.”

He was back in nineteen, with the cold on his coat and one flower in his hand: a single orange tulip from the woman with the stall by the station steps, who’d been packing up and had sold him the last one in her bucket. He found the narrow glass from the back of the cupboard and filled it and put the tulip in it on the kitchen table, and she stood by the counter watching him.

“Why one?”

He took his jacket off. “Because you only need one.”

She smiled. He came and stood in front of her.

“Today,” he said.

She nodded. She hadn’t wanted anyone to say it. She hadn’t wanted dinner, or flowers, or anybody asking how she felt about the date. He’d understood that. He’d said nothing all day. He’d made her breakfast and kissed her before her bus and told her he’d be home early, and he had been, and he hadn’t said a word. He took her hand now.

“I remember,” he said.

“I know.”

He looked at the tulip. “I remember the light.”

She was back there. The cold floor. The dark. The sound of a bolt going back. A big man in the orange floodlight looking into a box he’d expected to be full of guns.

She held his hand tighter. “I remember you.”

He lifted her hand and kissed the knuckles. “Good.”

She put her forehead against his chest and he held her there. After a while she looked up. “Do you know what I like most about orange? It isn’t really the colour. It’s that it reminds me doors can open.” She touched his face. “And you were standing on the other side.”

He shut his eyes, and pulled her in again.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first orange thing after that came on Monday: a small silk scarf, burnt orange with fine gold thread at the edges, folded on her pillow when she went up to bed. He was in the doorway.

“Do you like it?”

“I love it.”

He nodded, as if a report had been filed.

On Tuesday there were orange tulips on the kitchen table, a whole bunch this time. On Wednesday a ceramic bowl in a warm amber glaze. On Thursday a little orange notebook, which he said was for her recipes. On Friday an orange cushion appeared on the sofa, and she began to suspect he was taking the matter seriously indeed.

On Saturday she found him on Harbour Road standing in front of a florist’s window full of orange ranunculus, and slipped her hand into his.

“Jun Hyuk. You don’t have to buy me every orange thing you see.”

“I know.”

She waited. He went on looking at the window. “That one’s nice,” he said.

She laughed. He bought it anyway.

That night she sat on the sofa with the orange cushion behind her back and the orange notebook on her knee, writing down the cake from Saturday, and he sat at the other end with his feet on the floor and his tea in his hand and watched her the way he watched her when he thought she wasn’t looking.

“What?” she said, without looking up.

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me.”

“I was buying you the wrong colour,” he said slowly, as if he’d only just understood it. “I thought I’d chosen badly. I hadn’t. I was buying you the colour everybody else had chosen for you.”

She lowered the pen.

“Now I know the one you chose,” he said.

She put the notebook down and came along the sofa and climbed into his lap, and took the cup out of his hand and put it on the floor, and kissed him until he forgot what he’d been saying. On the kitchen table the first tulip, the single one, was still standing in its narrow glass, wide open now in the lamplight, the colour of a door with the light coming through it.

chapters.title: The Borderland Boy
chapters.desc: Spring 1999. A boy of eight with a name written inside his collar, an aid station on the river road, and a sergeant with one spoon.
chapters.epigraph: “That’s a big name for a small boy.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Lee Jun Hyuk remembered about the aid station on the river road was the smell. Wet earth. Disinfectant. Smoke from a cooking fire that never seemed to go out.

The second thing was his mother’s hand. It had been warm when she held his. By the time the Grey Lanterns brought them in off the road, her fingers had gone cold.

He was eight. It was the spring of 1999, and the river was loud that year, swollen with rain. The road beside it had gone to mud. The aid station was a few canvas shelters and trestle tables and one low building whose roof let the rain in wherever it liked.

She’d been ill for days. He remembered her coughing into a cloth. He remembered her telling him to stay close. He remembered a woman with tired eyes giving him a cup of water and saying his mother needed to rest. He remembered waiting.

He didn’t remember the moment she died. He remembered the tired woman coming out of the building and kneeling in the mud in front of him, and him looking past her at the doorway.

“Is my mother sleeping?”

The woman didn’t answer straight away. She put both hands on his shoulders. And somehow, at eight, he understood.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Grey Lanterns didn’t keep children. They had rules about everything: where to sleep, how much food a man could carry, which roads were safe and how long a unit could stay in one place. Children weren’t part of the arrangement. Nor was anyone’s family. The boy had nowhere else to go, so for the first weeks he stayed where he was.

Somebody gave him a blanket. Somebody else found him a shirt far too big for him. The tired woman, who was the nurse, made sure he ate twice a day. Nobody knew what to do with him. He didn’t cry much. He didn’t ask questions. When people spoke to him he answered politely. When they told him to sit he sat, and when they told him to wait he waited. He was good at waiting.

One morning the nurse found him standing by a table of clean bandages.

“Would you like to help?”

He nodded. She showed him how to fold them. Not in half, not in little squares. In thirds, so they’d open in one movement when somebody needed them in a hurry. He learned it in an afternoon. The next morning he came back, and the morning after. Soon she didn’t need to explain anything. He sat at the end of the table and folded bandages in thirds and stacked them in neat piles, and when the folding was done he rolled them, and he became particular about the edges. If one was uneven he undid it and began again.

“It doesn’t have to be perfect,” the nurse told him once.

He looked at the crooked roll in his hands. “I can do it again.”

She didn’t tell him to stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sergeant Ko first noticed him because of the shoes. It was late afternoon, the rain had stopped but the road was still too soft for the trucks, and Ko Baek-san was hunting for a missing inventory sheet when he saw two small shoes under the supply table. He crouched.

“What’s your name?”

The boy looked at him. “Lee.”

“Lee what?”

The boy didn’t answer. Ko looked at the stacked bandages. “Did you do these?”

A nod.

“All of them?”

Another nod. Ko picked one up. It was rolled tight, the end tucked under the last turn. “Do you like doing it?”

The boy thought about the question seriously. “It needs doing.”

Ko looked at him for a while. Then he put the bandage back. “That’s true,” he said, and asked nothing else that day.

But the next day he caught himself looking for the small shoes under the table. It became a habit. Ko would finish his duties and wash his hands and sit down on the wooden bench outside the building, and the boy would sit at the other end of it. At first they didn’t speak much. Ko talked anyway. He talked about the river and the weather and the food, and told the boy the unit’s cook had once burned rice in a pot full of water. The boy listened. Sometimes he answered. Sometimes he only watched the river. Ko didn’t mind.

One evening he sat beside the boy nearly an hour without saying anything that mattered. The sun was going down. The boy had his hands folded in his lap. Ko saw a loose thread at the back of his collar.

“Come here.”

He turned the collar to straighten it, and there was something written inside, faded but still clear. He tipped the cloth to the last of the light.

Lee Jun Hyuk.

Ko read it twice. “Lee Jun Hyuk,” he said. “That’s a big name for a small boy.”

The boy looked down at his hands. “Mother wrote it. Inside. So people know.”

Ko’s smile went. He ran his thumb over the stitching, careful not to pull it. “She wanted people to know who you were.”

The boy said nothing. They watched the river. Then the boy asked “Do you know where she is?”

Ko didn’t pretend not to understand. “No,” he said. “But I know she gave you a name. And I know you’re still here.”

The boy stared at the water. After a moment he leaned sideways until his shoulder was against Ko’s arm. Ko didn’t move. He stayed there until it was dark.

✦ ✦ ✦

The boy stayed at the aid station a year. Spring went to summer and summer to autumn, and the river fell and rose again. He folded bandages in thirds and rolled them. He learned the sound of every vehicle on the road. He learned not to stand in doorways. He learned to make himself useful. And he learned that Sergeant Ko always ate last.

Ko had a tin bowl and one spoon, silver once, gone dark, with a dent in the handle. He kept it in his top pocket. He ate whatever the cook had made, usually rice, sometimes soup, now and then something that might once have been a vegetable. One evening he saw the boy watching him.

“Do you want some?”

The boy shook his head.

“You’re hungry.”

“No.”

“That’s not what I asked.” Ko moved the bowl along the bench. “Come here.”

The boy came and sat beside him. Ko took a mouthful and then held out the spoon.

“Eat.”

He did. Rice with a little salt and something green through it. Ko took another mouthful and held the spoon out again. They ate the whole bowl like that, the same spoon going back and forth. Afterwards Ko washed it, wiped it, and put it back in his top pocket. The next evening he did the same. Nobody discussed it.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the next spring the unit was moving on. The station was being handed over to another group. The supplies had been counted, the trucks checked, the last patients sent on. Ko came out of the building with a folded list and found the boy on the bench with a small cloth bag beside him.

“What’s that?”

“My things.”

The boy opened it. A shirt. A spare pair of socks. A strip of cloth his mother had used to tie his hair back when he was smaller. And a brown envelope the nurse had given him the day before, with his mother’s papers in it, that he’d never opened.

Ko looked at the bag. “Where do you think you’re going?”

“I don’t know.”

The unit had already been told the boy would stay with the relief workers. A place might be found for him somewhere inland. Might. Ko had heard that word too many times to believe it. He also knew every rule. The Grey Lanterns didn’t take children. They didn’t make private arrangements that might put a unit at risk. And he knew this boy had spent a year learning to make himself small enough to fit whatever space people left for him.

“Would you like to come with me?”

“With your unit?”

“With me.”

The boy looked up. “Am I allowed?”

Ko’s jaw set. “I’ll deal with it.”

He didn’t ask permission. He told the commander he was taking responsibility for the boy. The commander repeated the rule. Ko said he knew it. The commander asked whether Ko understood what he was doing. Ko said yes. There was a long argument behind the canvas that the boy mostly didn’t hear, sitting outside with his bag between his feet, and at the end of it somebody needed a form filled in for him, and a clerk with no date to hand wrote 11 March in the box because it was that day.

Ko came out carrying two bowls, one with rice in it and one empty. “Come on.” He gave the boy the empty one. “Carry that.”

At the back of the truck he stopped and looked down. “One thing. You’re not going to be useful every day. Some days you’ll be tired. Some days you’ll be angry. Some days you’ll do nothing at all.”

The boy frowned. “That’s allowed?”

Ko stared at him. “Yes.”

The boy thought about it, and nodded. Ko bent and straightened his collar so the name was tucked in safe. “Lee Jun Hyuk,” he said. “Big name.” He held out his hand. “Come along, then.”

The boy took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

“That’s how I met him,” said Jun Hyuk.

It was a Sunday afternoon in January, in the sitting room at No. 9 Fig Tree Lane, with winter sun lying across the floor. He was sitting on the rug with his back against the sofa. She was beside him with her legs tucked under a blanket. On the low table between them was the silver spoon she’d given him for a birthday that wasn’t his, two years ago. She’d asked him, this morning, why he’d kept it by his cup all this time, and somehow it had led to the river road.

“He shared his,” she said. “The one they buried with him.”

“Every night, for years. When I was sixteen he gave me my own bowl and told me I still ate too slowly.” He was quiet. “He talked to me for a year before I said more than ten words back. That’s where I learned it. If somebody’s frightened, you keep talking, so they hear a voice that isn’t. He did it to me first.” A faint smile. “Then I didn’t stop. He said he’d made a monster.”

She picked up the spoon and turned it over. “Did he ever tell you why he took you?”

“He said the unit needed another pair of hands.”

“Did you believe him?”

“At eight. Now I know he was a terrible liar.” He looked at the spoon in her fingers. “I used to think he took me because I was useful. I could fold bandages. I could carry things. I didn’t complain. But he took me before I’d done anything for him.”

“Because you were a little boy who’d lost his mother,” she said. “Not because you were useful.”

Something went across his face. He looked away, and back. “Yes.”

She put the spoon down and climbed carefully into his lap, and he caught her round the waist.

“Sergeant Ko,” she said.

“Yes.”

She looked at him, and then over his shoulder at the cushion on the sofa, where a large ginger cat with half an ear lay asleep in the sun. “Jun Hyuk. You named the cat after him.”

He didn’t deny it. “He supervises,” he said.

She laughed with her forehead against his, and then stopped laughing. “Your mother wrote your name in your collar so people would know who you were. And Sergeant Ko read it.” She touched his cheek. “Then he made sure somebody did.”

His arms tightened round her. He didn’t seem to have any answer. Then he kissed her, slowly, his hand at the back of her head, and when he drew back he put his forehead to hers.

“Big name for a small boy,” he murmured.

“Still a big name.”

She traced the line between his eyebrows. “Did you know you were going to be loved, when you got into that truck?”

“No.”

“Neither did I, when you opened that door.” She smiled. “But somebody took our hands.”

He drew her down against his chest. Outside the stream went on under the little bridge. On the table the spoon caught the light. And Jun Hyuk held his wife and thought about a wooden bench by a muddy road, a tired sergeant beside a silent boy, and one hour in which nobody had asked the boy to be useful. He’d spent the rest of his life trying to understand what it meant to be allowed to stay. He thought perhaps he was finally learning.

chapters.title: Paper Twins
chapters.desc: April 2025. For seventeen years Raiden has said he’s the older twin. Then the King sends her birth entry.
chapters.epigraph: “You made me a day.”
chapters.content:
The argument began with a piece of paper bearing the King’s signature.

It had come in a stiff envelope on the Thursday before: a certified copy of her birth entry from the royal record, the one that had been made to disappear twenty-seven years ago and that her brother had spent two years of his life looking for. It had been restored, and sealed, and sent to her with a short note in his own hand. So that it is written down somewhere that you were born. She’d cried a little over the note. She hadn’t expected the entry itself to cause a diplomatic incident at her own dining table.

Raiden held it at arm’s length, as if distance might make it less offensive. “No.”

“Raiden.”

“No.”

Eliana, who’d come up with him for lunch, leaned over and read it again. “It says the seventh of April.”

“Forgery.”

“It’s got the King’s signature at the bottom.”

“An exceptionally good forgery.”

Jun Hyuk was at the counter cutting a pear into slices. “Why would the King forge his sister’s birthday?”

Raiden turned on him. “Stay out of this.”

“I’m only asking.”

“You’re enjoying it.”

“A little,” said Jun Hyuk, and put another slice on the plate.

Evangeline covered her mouth.

“Don’t laugh,” said Raiden. “I have been the older twin for seventeen years.”

“We’re not actually twins.”

“Exactly. Which makes this even more suspicious.” He put the paper down and pointed at it. “Our papers both say the ninth. I was born on the ninth. You were put on the ninth. I have always maintained that I was born at dawn and you were registered at lunchtime, and therefore I’m older.”

“Baba took her out on her own every seventh of April,” said Eliana. “You used to complain she got noodles and you didn’t. You’ve known for years.”

“I was never shown a document,” said Raiden with dignity.

“Well, now you have been,” said Eliana. “She’s two days older than you.”

Raiden looked at the paper. “Two days.”

“Yes.”

He turned to Evangeline. “You’re telling me I’ve spent seventeen years being older than someone who’s older than me?”

She tilted her head. “Apparently.”

“That’s unacceptable.”

“Would you like me to apologise?”

“Yes.”

“I’m sorry you were born later.”

Eliana shrieked with laughter. Raiden looked betrayed. Jun Hyuk turned away to the sink, and his shoulders moved once.

“Even you?” said Raiden.

Jun Hyuk set down the knife. “Sorry.” He didn’t look sorry at all.

✦ ✦ ✦
