He’d been planning her a birthday party for nearly a month, and he hadn’t told her.

Not because he wanted to surprise her with something large. He knew she hated being the centre of a room full of people, and he had no intention of filling the house with decorations she’d feel obliged to smile at. He wanted something else. A day that was hers. He’d known her real birthday since the first spring, when he’d left a plain silver ring beside her teacup on the morning of it. But two Aprils had gone by since, and both of them had been about other things: a husband leaving for the river, and a country being turned down in its own language. She’d spent years hidden, and then years protected, and then a year learning to choose things for herself. He wanted her to have one day when nobody decided anything for her.

So he asked Elowen what she liked. He asked Mrs. Bae which cake. He asked Eliana if she’d come. And he asked Raiden.

Raiden objected to the date at once. “The seventh’s a Monday.”

“We’re doing it on Tuesday.”

“Why Tuesday?”

“Because it’s the eighth. It’s between yours and hers.”

Raiden narrowed his eyes. “That isn’t a birthday.”

“It’s between.”

“That’s worse.” Then he said, “Will Baba come?”

“Yes.”

Raiden hesitated. “Obviously I’ll come,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday afternoon No. 9 Fig Tree Lane looked different. There were flowers along the verandah, and a long table under the fig tree, and a jar of orange tulips beside the cakes. She hadn’t been allowed in the kitchen all day. This was partly because he wanted to surprise her and partly because he’d become extremely particular about the kitchen since an incident with the smoke alarms in November.

Elowen brought her down. At the garden door she stopped.

Her father was by the fig tree, being talked at by Mrs. Bae. Jinx and Eliana were laying out plates. Nam sat in a chair under the tree complaining that nobody had brought him enough tea. Raiden stood at the end of the table holding a cake box as if it contained evidence for the prosecution. And Jun Hyuk stood at the foot of the steps with his hands in his pockets.

“Happy birthday,” he said.

She looked round at all of it again, and then at him. “You did all this?”

He nodded. She said his name, and he came up the steps and took her hand.

“I wanted you to have one,” he said.

“A birthday?”

“A proper one.”

Her fingers closed round his. He bent and kissed her forehead. “Happy birthday, Wife.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden’s cake was orange.

Not orange-flavoured. Orange. The icing was an aggressive shade, and across the top, in dark chocolate, were two words: OLDER ONE.

She stared at it. Eliana had her phone up and filming before anybody could stop her.

“Raiden. What’s this?”

“My cake.”

“It isn’t your birthday.”

“It’s a statement.”

“An interesting statement,” said Jun Hyuk.

Raiden ignored him and set it down beside the one Jun Hyuk had ordered: smaller, white, with orange flowers piped round the edge and a little silver fig leaf on top. Raiden looked at it with deep suspicion.

“That’s not fair. His is prettier.”

“Yes,” said Jun Hyuk.

“You’re not even denying it.”

“No.”

She laughed. Raiden pushed the orange one towards her. “Anyway. This one’s for the older one.”

She looked at the words, and at him. “Thank you.” She leaned in. “You needed it more.”

Eliana made a strangled noise behind her phone. “What does that mean?” said Raiden.

“It means I don’t mind sharing,” said Evangeline sweetly.

He looked at her. Then he picked up a fork. “I’m eating the orange one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They lit both cakes. Nobody could agree which should go first. Raiden said his deserved priority. Eliana said the birthday girl went first, obviously. Nam said both cakes were wasting perfectly good icing and he was getting old. Jun Hyuk listened to it for almost a minute, and then looked at his wife.

“Together?”

“Together,” she said.

Raiden came and stood beside her. “I want it recorded that I’m older.”

“You’re two days younger,” said Eliana, filming.

“Forgery.”

“One, two, three,” said Elowen, and the paper twins bent and blew out both cakes at once.

Eliana lowered her phone. “Draw.”

“That’s not a draw,” said Raiden.

“It is if we share,” said Evangeline.

He looked at her. Then, reluctantly, he smiled. “Fine.” And he cut the orange cake himself and gave her the first slice.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when the garden had gone quieter and the guests were still round the table, she slipped away to the verandah. He found her sitting on the wooden step with her shoes off beside her, looking at the stream.

“Tired?”

“A little.”

“Too many people?”

“No.” She smiled. “It was lovely.”

He sat down beside her.

“I’ve never had a birthday party,” she said. “I had birthdays. Baba always remembered. Elowen sometimes brought me something. But never a party, where I could ask people and choose a cake and have somebody sing. I used to wonder what it would feel like. Not anything grand. Just a day that belonged to me.”

“And now?”

“Now I’ve got one.”

He took her hand. “Every year.”

“You don’t have to promise me that.”

“I want to.” He kissed her hand. “Every year, if you want it.”

She leaned over and kissed his cheek. Then the other cheek. Then the corner of his mouth.

“What?” he said.

She touched his face. “You made me a day.”

He looked at her a long time. Then he put his arm round her waist and pulled her into his lap, and she laughed and put a hand on his shoulder, and he kissed her, slow at first and then with the quiet certainty that always made her forget what she’d meant to say. She kissed him back with both hands in his hair, there on the step in the evening light, until she’d forgotten there was a garden full of family behind them.

“WE CAN ALL SEE YOU,” shouted Raiden from the table.

She hid her face in his shoulder. Jun Hyuk shut his eyes. “He’s very loud.”

“He’s always been loud.”

“Apparently that’s how he became the older twin.”

She laughed into his collar. He kissed her temple and looked past her at the table, where Raiden was now arguing with Eliana about who’d had the bigger slice. “Happy birthday, Evangeline.”

“Thank you, Husband.”

And for the rest of the evening the two cakes stood side by side under the fig tree, one white and one orange, both without their candles, both shared.

chapters.title: He Talks for Both of Them
chapters.desc: The Chen Foundation’s spring gala, May 2025, as Aurelia sees it. Her husband talks to everyone so she never has to.
chapters.epigraph: “She turned down a husband. The crown came with him.”
chapters.content:
Aurelia Chen had always found Evangeline Lee hard to read.

Not unfriendly. Never that. Evangeline had a gentle way of smiling, and a quiet attentiveness that made people feel listened to even when she said almost nothing. She noticed when a glass was empty, or a conversation had made somebody uncomfortable, or a guest had been standing on their own too long. But she rarely offered anything about herself. In all the years Aurelia had known the Lin sisters she could have counted the words Evangeline had spoken to her on two hands. Eleven, perhaps, in the first year. A few more if you counted good evening.

Aurelia had never minded. Some people didn’t like crowded rooms, and Evangeline, for all that she’d been born to a palace and raised in the Walled City, seemed happiest in her garden with her husband and as far as possible from anyone who wanted something from her.

Which was what made her arrival at the Chen Foundation’s spring gala on Saturday the seventeenth of May so interesting. Because Lee Jun Hyuk was talking enough for both of them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ballroom was already full when the Lees came in. Aurelia was by the doors with Chen Si, greeting donors, and she saw him first: a black suit, perfectly cut, no tie, a relaxed and composed face, and his hand wrapped round his wife’s. He was talking to the event director before he’d reached the desk.

“Mr. Chen. Good evening.”

Chen Si gave him his hand. “I was beginning to think you wouldn’t come.”

“I was told there’d be food.”

“There is.”

“Then I made the right decision.”

Chen Si laughed. Jun Hyuk turned to Aurelia. “Mrs. Chen. Congratulations on the evening. Have you met my wife?” He knew perfectly well she had. She’d sold him the aquamarines.

“Hello, Mrs. Chen,” said Evangeline, and for a second her eyes warmed with recognition, and then Jun Hyuk was already answering the director’s question about the foundation’s new shelter programme, and Evangeline stood beside him and listened.

Aurelia watched him. He was good at this. Not merely polite. He remembered names. He asked people about their work and listened to the answers with an attention that made even the most self-important guest feel important. And he was doing something else as well, which Aurelia noticed within ten minutes. He never let go of his wife’s hand. Not when he shook other hands, not when he greeted the board, not when a waiter brought him water. His fingers stayed loosely laced through hers all evening, as if letting go were a pointless inconvenience.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first hour went easily. He talked to the chairman of a shipping line, to a woman who ran a children’s reading scheme, to a senior official who was delighted to have someone prepared to hear his views on port regulation in full. Evangeline stayed beside him. She smiled when she was introduced and nodded where it was called for and sometimes said a few words. And Jun Hyuk seemed to know, every time, the moment before a conversation became too much.

A donor’s wife leaned in, glittering. “Is it true you turned down a crown?”

“She turned down a husband,” said Jun Hyuk pleasantly. “The crown came with him.”

The woman laughed, delighted, and decided that was the whole story.

Another guest asked whether she missed palace life.

“My wife has a garden, a stream, and a husband who makes very good tea,” said Jun Hyuk. “I think she’s managing.”

Evangeline lowered her eyes. Aurelia caught the small private smile. The guest laughed, satisfied, and Jun Hyuk moved them on.

Aurelia began to understand. He wasn’t talking because his wife had nothing to say. He was talking because he knew she didn’t always want to say it. There was a difference. He never cut across her when she chose to answer. He never corrected her, never put words in her mouth when she was clearly about to speak. He only kept the conversation going when she didn’t want to be in it. It was almost seamless, and lovely.

✦ ✦ ✦

During the second course Aurelia found herself next to Evangeline. Jun Hyuk had been drawn down the table by a man from the port authority, and without a dozen people looking at her Evangeline seemed easier.

“Are you enjoying it?”

“It’s beautiful.”

“We spent months on it.”

“I like the flowers.” Evangeline looked at the white orchids and pale green leaves running down the middle of the table. “They look as if they belong here.”

It was a small conversation. Fourteen words, perhaps. But Evangeline looked comfortable, and Aurelia caught herself wishing they had more chances to talk.

Then Jun Hyuk came back and put a glass of water by his wife’s plate before he sat down. “Have you eaten enough?”

“Yes.”

“You haven’t touched the fish. Two bites.”

“You’re counting?”

“Of course.”

Aurelia laughed. He looked at her. “Something funny?”

“Nothing at all.”

Evangeline leaned across and said something in his ear. He listened, and his face softened. “All right,” he said, and moved the fish closer to her. Aurelia watched them look at each other, and realised a whole conversation had just taken place without a word of it said aloud.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened after dinner. Evangeline was standing by the tall windows. Jun Hyuk had gone across the room to answer a trustee, still in sight, but not beside her.

A young man went up to her, and Aurelia recognised him at once. Yeom Ji-ho, the minister’s son, attached to his country’s mission that spring. Well dressed, rich, and far too used to people being impressed by his surname. He bowed slightly.

“Miss Lee. I’ve wanted to meet you for a year.”

Evangeline turned. “Good evening.”

“You may know who I am. They chose me for you, last April.” He smiled as if it were a charming story. “I didn’t realise you’d be so beautiful in person.”

Her smile went still. “Thank you.”

“Are you here alone?”

“No. My husband is here.”

He glanced round. “Ah. Your husband.” He said the word as though it were an administrative error. “Perhaps you’d spare me one dance before he comes back. For what might have been.”

“I don’t think so.”

“Just one.”

She shook her head. He leaned in. “Come now. Surely your husband doesn’t mind you enjoying yourself.”

Her face stayed polite. But her right hand had gone to the rings on her left, and closed over them.

Then a hand came down on the young man’s shoulder. Not roughly, not yet. Firmly enough to stop him coming any closer.

“She said no,” said Jun Hyuk. “She said it last April as well.”

His voice was perfectly calm. Yeom Ji-ho turned round. “Mr. Lee. I was only—”

“I heard.”

The hand stayed where it was. The young man’s smile slipped. “I didn’t realise she was uncomfortable.”

“Now you do.” A beat. Jun Hyuk took his hand away. “Enjoy your evening.”

He didn’t wait for an answer. He turned to his wife. “Come on, love.”

She slipped her hand into his. “Are you all right?” he said, low.

“Yes.”

“Do you want to leave?”

“Not yet.”

“All right.” He kissed her temple and led her back into the room. Aurelia watched the minister’s son stand alone by the windows, looking as if he’d just discovered his surname didn’t make him especially important here, and took a sip of champagne. Interesting, she thought.

✦ ✦ ✦

The band went into a slow waltz. Jun Hyuk turned from a director to his wife. “Would you like to dance?”

She looked at the crowded floor. “Here?”

“Unless you’d rather the kitchen.”

She smiled, and gave him her hand. He took her into the middle of the floor and put his hand at her waist, and they began to move. He said something. She smiled. He said something else, and she laughed: not loudly, the small unguarded laugh Aurelia had heard perhaps three times in her life. He looked down at her as if he’d been waiting all evening for that sound.

Then he stopped dancing. “What?” she said.

He didn’t answer. He took her face in his hands and kissed her, right there in the middle of the ballroom. Not a polite kiss for an audience. A proper one, warm and unhurried and entirely unconcerned with the room, and her hand closed on his lapel. A few guests turned. Somebody laughed. He didn’t seem to notice. When he lifted his head she was pink to the ears.

“Beautiful,” he said.

“You’ve said that all evening.”

“Because you keep being beautiful.” And he went on dancing.

Later Aurelia saw him across the room with a glass of water in one hand, being lectured by a shipping chairman and listening as if it mattered. Then his eyes went past the man. Evangeline was by the flowers with Elowen, and she’d looked across the room at him with a smile that was warm and entirely private. His face changed at once. He excused himself mid-sentence and crossed the room and took her hand, and bent his head to hear whatever she was saying, and smiled.

Aurelia had thought Evangeline was hard to read. Now she wondered whether she’d been looking in the wrong place. Evangeline wasn’t expressive with strangers. She didn’t fill silences because they made her uncomfortable, or smile to make people feel important. But when her husband looked at her she seemed to have a whole language, and he understood every word of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Lees left a little before midnight. Jun Hyuk thanked the organisers and said goodbye to the board and apologised to Chen Si for missing the last speeches, and then he fetched his wife’s coat and helped her into it and turned the collar right and checked her scarf.

“Thank you for having us,” he said to Aurelia.

“Thank you, Mrs. Chen,” said Evangeline. She hesitated. “The flowers were beautiful.”

“I’ll remember you said so.”

He held the door. As they went down the steps Aurelia heard him ask if she was tired, and heard the answer. “A little.”

“Home?”

“Yes.”

“All right, love.”

The door swung shut. She’d once thought Evangeline didn’t need to say much. Now she thought her husband would talk for twenty people if it meant his wife never had to say a word she didn’t want to.

Aurelia looked at the place where they’d stood. Perhaps next time she’d hear a few more words. If she didn’t, that was all right too. Some people spoke with words. And some, she’d learned that evening, spoke with the way they held someone’s hand.

chapters.title: The Silver Ring Engraving
chapters.desc: Spring 2026. Two lines of numbers inside a silver ring, worn for three years. A house across the river that she has never seen.
chapters.epigraph: “So you’re her. I’ve had the sheets aired every Thursday for three years.”
chapters.content:
On Saturday the twenty-fifth of April, at Serafina Song’s wedding, Evangeline beat Aurelia Chen at a game nobody understood.

The banquet was in the garage under the railway bridge, the one Serafina and her new husband had bought from the railway at auction in the autumn. Strings of warm bulbs ran along every girder. Two hundred borrowed chairs stood at trestle tables in white cloth, with flowers in old glass bottles and nine dishes from Mr. Kwok, and every eleven minutes a train went over and the bottles hummed. Jun Hyuk had spent the first twenty minutes by the shutter with Big Wu, discussing a leak in the arch. Aurelia had spent the same twenty minutes on the champagne. Evangeline was enjoying herself enormously.

Then Mr. Kwok’s nephew brought out a row of small glasses and a wooden spoon, and announced a game his village played at weddings, with rules that changed each time somebody asked about them. Aurelia volunteered first, confident that years of formal dinners had prepared her for any social challenge in the world.

She lost. Evangeline won.

Aurelia stared at the glasses. “I don’t understand.”

“Neither do I.”

“You beat me.”

“Apparently.”

“You’re much more competitive than you look.”

Evangeline laughed out loud. Across the garage Jun Hyuk stopped in the middle of a sentence about guttering and turned towards the sound. Big Wu followed his eyes, sighed, and said, “Go on, then,” and went back to looking at the roof.

Jun Hyuk crossed the garage and put his hand on the back of her chair. “Having fun?”

“Yes.”

“Winning?”

“Yes.”

He looked at Aurelia. “She cheats.”

“I do not!”

Evangeline caught his hand, laughing, and he bent and kissed her temple. “Good. Keep winning.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was in the car on the way home that she asked him. They were on the river road with the dark coming down and the lights of the far bank over the water. She turned her left hand so the passing streetlamps caught the rings on it. The new one, with its small aquamarine. And the old one, plain silver, the one he’d left by her teacup on her birthday three years ago with two lines of numbers cut inside it, small enough that you’d only see them if you tilted it to the light. A house across the river, past the old customs road. A back door, a telephone, a water tank, a lane down to a village. A woman there, paid by him, who’d know to expect someone and wouldn’t ask why. She’d read the note at four in the morning and worn the ring every day since. She’d never seen the place.

“Can we go and see it?” she said. “The house in the ring.”

His hands stayed steady on the wheel. For a while he said nothing. “Are you sure?”

“I’ve wondered for three years.”

“All right,” he said.

“Really? When?”

“Whenever you want.”

She put her hand on his thigh. “Next Saturday?”

He covered it with his. “Next Saturday.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They went north on Saturday the second of May, and had lunch at Nam’s on the way, where Nam looked at the two of them and the overnight bag and said, “You’re going over,” and didn’t ask anything else. They crossed at the River Bridge in the afternoon, at the proper gate, with their own passports in their own names, which still felt to Jun Hyuk like a kind of magic. On the far side the old customs road ran out along the bank between fields, past a shut-up checkpoint with grass in the barrier slot, and he turned off it onto a lane she’d never have noticed, and drove slowly.

“You’re nervous,” she said.

“A little.”

“Why?”

“I haven’t been here since that spring.”

She understood. More than a house: it was what he’d made when he still believed he might not come back. The place he’d got ready for her in case the world took him first.

“We’re going together this time,” she said. “Not because we have to.”

He looked at her. “Because we want to.”

“Exactly.”

The lane went down between two walls into a village of perhaps forty houses, and out the other side, and stopped at a gate. Behind it stood a low house of grey brick with a tiled roof and green shutters, and a fig tree in the yard leaning over the wall, and beyond it the ground fell away to the river.

A woman of about sixty was sweeping the step. She straightened when the car stopped, and looked at Jun Hyuk getting out, and then at Evangeline.

“So you’re her,” she said. “I’ve had the sheets aired every Thursday for three years.”

Her name was Auntie Wai. She’d lived in the village all her life. He’d paid her since April of the year they married to keep the house ready for a woman who might come up the lane one night on her own and need a bed and a telephone and no questions. Nobody ever had. She’d swept the step anyway, every morning.

Evangeline took both of Auntie Wai’s hands, and couldn’t say anything.

“Well,” said Auntie Wai, gruffly. “Come in. The kettle’s on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a plain house. A main room with a stove. A kitchen. Two small bedrooms. A back door onto the yard, and the water tank on its stand, and the old telephone on the wall in the passage, which still worked because Auntie Wai paid the bill. Evangeline went through it slowly. She opened every shutter. She touched the walls. She stood in the back bedroom and looked out at the fig tree.

“Did you ever sleep here?”

“Once. The night I bought it. Alone.”

“Who else would have been here?” she said, teasing, and then saw his face and stopped.

“The Ferryman’s people kept women here,” he said. “Before they moved them inland. It was empty by the time I found it. I thought if it had to be anything, it could be the one place on this side of the river where somebody could get out instead of in.”

She stood still in the little room. Then she came and put her hand flat on his chest. “Show me the rest.”

Behind the stove a section of the brick was newer than the rest. He moved the table and opened it. Inside, wrapped and sealed, were bundles of notes, a few small bars of gold, and a flat packet. He laid them out on the table. The last thing was a passport. Never used. A different name. A different place of birth. A different life.

She looked at it, and at the money, and at him. “All this was for me?”

“Before I gave you the ring.”

“Did you think I’d need to be someone else?”

“I thought there might be a day when being Evangeline would put you in danger.” He didn’t look away. “This would have let you go.”

“Without you?”

He was quiet. “If that was what you needed.”

She understood what he’d built here. Not a holiday house. An exit. Enough to start again and buy time and vanish from every record that had ever made her worth selling. He’d made it because he loved her, at a time when he didn’t know how to love anybody without getting ready to lose them.

She put the passport down. “Do you still think we need it?”

“No.”

“Do you still want me to have it?”

“I want you to have choices.”

“I have choices.” She took his hand and kissed the knuckles. “And I choose to stay with you. I don’t need another name to do it.”

He looked at the passport. “Would you like to burn it?”

“Together?”

“Together.”

They used the stove. The money and the gold they’d take home and account for and hand to the foundation’s auditors. The papers were different. She held the passport and looked at the name in it that wasn’t hers. She’d been called so many things that weren’t. Princess. Royal blood, documented. A valuable girl. Something to be moved. Something to be protected. She’d fought a long time to be Evangeline. She didn’t want another name.

He opened the stove door and they fed it in, page by page, and she watched them curl and go dark and fall into ash. He didn’t look away until it was done.

“That’s one door,” she said.

“Yes.”

“We don’t need it any more.” She turned in his arms. “But somebody might.”

He looked at her.

“Women still come over that river at night,” she said. “Not all of them in boats Song knows about. They need somewhere on this side with a back door and a telephone and a woman who doesn’t ask why. You’ve already made it. Auntie Wai’s already here.” She put her palm on his cheek. “Give it to The Open Door. Let it be the first house on the far side.”

He didn’t say anything. Then he bent and put his forehead against hers. “Yes,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They stayed a week. Evangeline and Auntie Wai sat at the kitchen table with tea and the foundation’s papers and argued, cheerfully, about where the second bed should go. Jun Hyuk mended the hinge on the gate and the tap on the water tank and a loose shutter that had been banging for two years. In the afternoons they walked down the lane through the fields to the river, where there was a stony ford below a willow and the water ran clear and cold over the stones.

On the third day she stood at the edge with her shoes in her hand and looked down at her feet.

“Cold?” he said. He’d already rolled his trousers to the knee.

“Very.”

“Do you want to go back?”

“I want to try.”

She stepped in, and gasped, and laughed, and took his hand. The water came to her ankles, then her shins. She splashed him. He looked down at his wet shirt, and then at her. “Sorry,” she said.

“Are you?”

“Not really.”

He caught her round the waist and lifted her clean off the stones, and she shrieked and grabbed his shoulders. “Jun Hyuk!”

“You wanted to go in.”

“I didn’t say you could carry me!”

He stopped where the water reached his knees and looked at her, held up against him with her feet dripping. “Can I?”

She was laughing too hard to answer. She nodded. He let her down slowly until her feet found the stones, and she held onto his shoulders and stood in the cold river with him, and then she leaned up and kissed him, and he smiled against her mouth, and she kissed him again with the sun on their faces and the water running round their legs.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last evening they sat on the step with the fig tree over them and watched the light go off the river. She turned the old ring on her finger.

“Do you remember why you chose this place?”

“It was off every road anybody watched. The village didn’t care. The lane didn’t go anywhere.”

“Very practical.”

“I was being practical.” He looked down at her. “Now I like the fig tree.”

She laughed. He took her hand and lifted it, and kissed the ring, and the numbers lay against his mouth. Once they’d been the numbers of a place where she could disappear. Now they were the numbers of a door, on the far side of the river, that would open.

When Auntie Wai waved them off in the morning, they left together. Not running, not hiding. Already planning to come back.

chapters.title: Clean Towels
chapters.desc: October 2025. She goes to the lake country for four days to play her mother’s air. He folds twenty-two towels.
chapters.epigraph: “One for you to fix.”
chapters.content:
Evangeline packed for four days. Jun Hyuk watched from the bedroom doorway.

There was a suitcase open on the bed, a smaller bag on the chair, and folded clothes laid out in rows beside them. Her mother’s viola case leaned against the wardrobe.

“You’re taking too much.”

“I’m taking what I need.”

“It’s four days.”

“Four days is a long time.”

He looked at the bed. “That’s six dresses.”

“Five.”

He counted.

“One’s for the concert,” she said.

“That’s still six.”

“Then stop counting.”

He leaned on the frame and smiled. She folded a pale cardigan and laid it on top.

Mrs. Yoon was taking her to the lake country for the autumn concert at the old pavilion where the household orchestra used to play in summer. It was a small thing, musicians and village people and a few visitors, and Evangeline had been asked to play the slow air from her mother’s lake piece. She’d practised it for months. He’d heard every version: the first frightened notes, the places she stopped and started again, the slow climb until she could play it without looking at the page. He knew where she breathed. He knew which passage still tightened her fingers. He knew that whenever she reached the last phrase she lifted her chin slightly.

He wasn’t going. The invitation was for her and Mrs. Yoon, and she’d wanted to make the journey herself. She’d said she’d be fine. He’d said he knew. He still didn’t like it.

“Four nights,” he said. “Ring when you get there.”

“I will.”

“And when you leave the hotel.”

“Jun Hyuk.”

“And after the concert.”

She put the cardigan down and crossed the room and stood in front of him. “Are you going to miss me?”

“Obviously.”

“Then say that instead of giving me a timetable.”

His face went soft. “I’ll miss you.”

She went up on her toes and kissed him. “Good. I’ll miss you too.”

He held her a little longer than he needed to. Then he picked up the viola case and carried it down to the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house was too quiet on the first night. He’d known it would be. He’d spent years in places where silence was useful: it meant nobody had followed him, nobody was outside, nobody had found the door. This was different. No music from the room upstairs. No footsteps on the landing. Nobody asking whether he’d eaten when she already knew the answer. Sergeant slept on the sofa, entirely unconcerned.

He made dinner and ate half of it. He washed up and checked the doors and went to bed. At 2:13 he woke, and his hand went across to her side, and stopped. Her pillow still smelled of her hair. He lay looking at the ceiling for a while. Then he got up.

By the second night he’d washed every towel in the house.

It hadn’t been a decision. He’d taken one down from the bathroom and noticed a corner was out, and refolded it. Then he’d found another in the basket, and another, and at some point Sergeant had come down and sat by the laundry door watching him with the calm judgement of a cat who’d never done a useful thing in his life.

He folded the big bath towels first. Then the hand towels. Then the kitchen ones. She folded them her own way, the way she’d taught him by the sink over the Golden Nightingale on a Sunday in December three years ago. In half, long ways. Then again. Then in thirds, so it sat on the shelf with the edges inside. He’d watched her do it hundreds of times since.

At 3:08 he finished the last bath towel. At 3:19 he unfolded it, because one edge was wrong, and did it again. At 3:47 he went up and looked at the empty bed. Just after four he came back down and refolded all twenty-two.

Sergeant yawned.

“Don’t start,” Jun Hyuk told him.

The cat shut his eyes. Jun Hyuk looked at the stacks. Every one exactly her way. He still couldn’t sleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

Under the old pavilion roof by the lake, Evangeline stood with the viola under her arm and looked at the water. The autumn air was cool. Mrs. Yoon set the music stand beside her, though she wouldn’t need it.

“Ready?”

She nodded.

She’d played this before. In the music room at No. 9 with the window open. In the garden, with him under the fig tree listening. At the lake house in July, where she’d first got through it without stopping once. But this was the piece her mother had played, by this water, and for most of Evangeline’s life Seo Hwa had been a name without a voice. Then a photograph. A note. An old viola with a nameplate. Mrs. Yoon’s patient hands over hers. Now Evangeline could play the music herself.

The audience was small. People from the villages. A few musicians. Elderly people who’d come every year for longer than she’d been alive.

She began. The first notes were quiet. Beyond the pavilion the lake lay still under a pale sky. She played the opening phrase and the next, and didn’t hurry, and let the music settle.

Halfway through she saw an old woman in the front row, small, in a dark shawl, with her hands folded in her lap. She was crying.

Evangeline nearly lost the next note. But Mrs. Yoon was watching from the side, and she remembered what she’d been told a hundred times. Don’t reach for the next note before you’ve finished this one. So she finished it, and played on, and played the last phrase with her chin lifted a little, and when it faded the pavilion was silent before anyone clapped.

The old woman waited until people had begun to drift away. Then she came up slowly on a wooden stick. “May I speak to you?”

Evangeline put the viola down. “Of course.”

The woman looked at her. “Your mother played that,” she said. “Here. At the summer festival, in 1997. I was sixty-three. The rain had stopped and the lake was all mist and everyone had gone in under the roof, and she stayed out and played that, on her own.” Her eyes were wet again. “In rehearsal that morning she’d missed a note and laughed and said the lake had distracted her. I always remembered.”

Evangeline couldn’t speak. “Did you know her?”

“Not to talk to. I was the woman who brought the tea.” She took Evangeline’s hand in both of hers. “She played beautifully. You played it beautifully too.”

“Thank you.”

“No, child. Thank you. I thought I’d never hear it again.”

Evangeline held her hand until she was ready to go.

Afterwards Mrs. Yoon asked if she was all right, and Evangeline could only nod, and look at the lake. For the first time her mother’s music had reached somebody who’d heard it before. It hadn’t gone. It had only been waiting.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in the kitchen when the car came up the lane around half past four on the fourth afternoon. He heard the gate, and the engine, and dried his hands and went out.

She was by the car with her suitcase and the viola case. She saw him and her face changed. “Jun Hyuk.”

He crossed the drive and she barely had time to put the case down before he had her in his arms. She laughed into his shoulder.

“I’ve only been gone four days.”

“Four days.”

“That’s not very long.”

He drew back far enough to look at her. “It was.”

“Did you miss me?”

“Terribly.”

He kissed her by the car, and she put her arms round his neck, and he held her as if he’d been waiting the whole four days to do exactly that. Then he picked up her suitcase. She reached for the viola. He took that too.

“I can carry it.”

“I know.”

“Then give it to me.”

“No.”

She laughed. “You’re impossible.”

He kissed her forehead. “Welcome home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She noticed the towels, of course. The bathroom shelves were full of neat stacks. The hand towels sat in their basket. Even the kitchen towels were folded by the sink. She picked up the top bath towel. Exactly her way. The next. The same. She went through them. Twenty-two.

“Did you do these?”

He was leaning in the doorway. “Yes.”

“All of them?”

“They needed folding.”

Then she found one at the bottom of the hand-towel pile folded in half and no more, the edges uneven. She held it up. “What’s this?”

“That one.”

“You folded twenty-two towels properly and left this one?”

“Thought you might want to fix it,” he said.

She didn’t understand. Then she did. She put the towel down. “Jun Hyuk.”

He reached for her waist. “I missed you.”

She stepped into his arms. “I missed you too.” She touched the shadows under his eyes. “You did these at four in the morning.”

He didn’t ask how she knew. “I kept thinking I’d hear you playing.”

“Next time I’ll ring you and play down the phone.”

“That isn’t the same.”

“No,” she said. “It isn’t.”

“Did it go well?”

“Tell you at dinner,” she said, and did: the pavilion and the mist on the water, and the old woman with the tea who’d heard her mother play the same air in 1997, and how they’d held hands afterwards. He listened without interrupting. When she’d finished he kissed her forehead.

“Your mother would have been proud.”

“I wish she could have heard it.”

“Someone who heard her did,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night he carried her up the stairs. She said she could walk. He said he knew. She asked why he was carrying her, then. He said because he wanted to. At the top, under the landing light, he stopped and kissed her, slowly, and she smiled into it with her arms round his neck.

“Your cat’s watching,” she said. Sergeant was sitting on the bottom step.

“Our cat.”

“He thinks you’re ridiculous.”

“He has no opinion.”

Sergeant miaowed.

“See,” said Jun Hyuk, and carried her the rest of the way.

Later she went along the landing for a glass of water and passed the bathroom. The loose towel was still on top of the stack. She picked it up, and folded it in half, long ways, and again, and then in thirds, and tucked the edges in and put it back on the pile.

He was in the doorway when she turned round. He looked at the towel, and at her.

“Now it’s done,” she said.

He came and took her hand. “Good.”

“Next time I go away, you should come.”

“Will Mrs. Yoon allow it?”

“She might.”

“And if she doesn’t?”

“Then you can fold the towels.”

He laughed. “Twenty-two.”

“And one for me to fix?”

He bent and kissed her. “One for you to fix.”

He held her there in the bathroom doorway under the small light, and for the first time in four nights he knew exactly where he wanted to be. Not because the towels were folded, or the house was in order. Because she was home.

extras.title: Paper Birthday
extras.line: The date on his papers is wrong. She writes it down anyway, and goes looking for a spoon.

extras.title: Every Word
extras.line: Thirteen days over the river. She hardly speaks. He finds out where she keeps the rest.
